# Private Dependencies

Vercel Agent installs private npm packages using your repository's existing package manager. Add `NPM_TOKEN` or `NPM_RC` as a shared team environment variable to authenticate with your registry.

## How it works

Your package manager runs its usual install command while Vercel Agent authenticates package downloads as registry requests leave the sandbox.

Credential values stay outside the sandbox, so the agent and sandbox processes cannot read them.

Registry authentication only covers package downloads. Publishing and registry administration aren't supported. Keep credentials out of prompts and commands.

## Configure a credential

Add your credentials in your Vercel team's settings:

1. Open **Settings**, then select **Environment Variables**.
2. Add a [Shared Environment Variable](/docs/environment-variables/shared-environment-variables) using the name and value described below.
3. Select **Development** or **Preview**, then save the variable.

You don't need to link these variables to individual projects. Vercel Agent checks Development before Preview and ignores Production and project-level variables.

### NPM\_TOKEN

Use `NPM_TOKEN` for packages hosted on `registry.npmjs.org`. Set its value to an npm access token with read access to the private packages your repository needs.

### NPM\_RC

Use `NPM_RC` for a custom registry or multiple registries. Set its value to the registry configuration from your `.npmrc` file.

For GitHub Packages:

```ini filename="NPM_RC"
@acme:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com/
//npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=${GITHUB_PACKAGES_TOKEN}
```

For JFrog Artifactory:

```ini filename="NPM_RC"
@acme:registry=https://acme.jfrog.io/artifactory/api/npm/npm-local/
//acme.jfrog.io/artifactory/api/npm/npm-local/:_authToken=${ARTIFACTORY_TOKEN}
```

Replace `@acme` and the registry URL with your own. Add each referenced token, such as `GITHUB_PACKAGES_TOKEN`, as a Shared Environment Variable in the same environment as `NPM_RC`. Each token needs read access to the packages in its registry.

To use multiple registries, add an entry for each package scope and its registry credentials. You can also set `registry` to choose the default registry.

When both `NPM_RC` and `NPM_TOKEN` are set in the same environment, `NPM_RC` takes precedence.

## Override credentials for Vercel Agent

To give Vercel Agent different credentials from your builds, use `VERCEL_AGENT_NPM_RC` or `VERCEL_AGENT_NPM_TOKEN`. Within each environment, Vercel Agent selects the first defined variable in this order:

1. `VERCEL_AGENT_NPM_RC`
2. `VERCEL_AGENT_NPM_TOKEN`
3. `NPM_RC`
4. `NPM_TOKEN`

To disable registry authentication, set `VERCEL_AGENT_NPM_RC` to an empty string in Development. This also stops fallback to Preview.

## Requirements

- Registry URLs must use HTTPS with a DNS hostname and no custom port.
- `NPM_RC` supports token and basic authentication. Client certificates are unsupported.

## Troubleshooting

If a private package fails to install:

- Check that the token has read access to the package.
- Check that registry URLs and package scopes match your dependencies.
- Add any variables referenced by `NPM_RC` to the same environment as `NPM_RC`.

If a Development `NPM_RC` or `VERCEL_AGENT_NPM_RC` references a missing variable, Vercel Agent retries the same configuration key in Preview. To use that fallback, define the configuration and its referenced variables in Preview.

Empty or malformed configuration stops lookup instead of falling back to a lower-priority variable.

# Security Review

> Vercel Security Review is available in Public Beta on Enterprise and Pro plans

Security Review is part of [Vercel Agent](/docs/agent). It scans your code for security vulnerabilities and reports what it finds in the [Vulnerabilities](/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%7E%2Fsecurity%2Fvulnerabilities\&title=Open+Vulnerabilities) dashboard.

It helps you find issues such as code injection, authorization bypass, and credential exposure before they reach your users.

## How to set up Security Review

To enable Security Review, navigate to the [**Agent**](/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%7E%2Fsettings%2Fagent\&title=Go+to+Agent+settings) settings page.

1. In the **Security Reviews** section, turn on **Review Deployments Automatically**.
2. Under **Projects to Review**, choose which projects to review:
   - All projects (default)
   - Specific projects, up to 100
3. Click **Save** to confirm your settings.

Once you've enabled Security Review, it automatically reviews new code changes in the projects you selected, whether or not they come from a pull request.

> **💡 Note:** To fix findings with Vercel Agent, you also need **Enable Chat** turned on in
> the same settings page.

## How it works

Security Review runs automatically when code is pushed to a connected GitHub repository.

Reviews start when code is pushed, and every project from a single push event is reviewed together. Because reviews start from push events rather than pull requests, Security Review also covers direct pushes and force pushes to your production branch.

Each review compares the source against a base, so it covers what changed rather than your whole code repository:

- **Deployment reviews**: The base is the previous deployment of the branch, falling back to the GitHub API when no previous deployment exists.
- **Pull request reviews without a deployment**: The finding is tracked against the branch and pull request rather than a deployment.
- **Monorepos**: Reviews are scoped to each project's root directory.

When no base exists, such as a project's first review, the review reads the full source.

Security Review reports its findings to the [Vulnerabilities](/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%7E%2Fsecurity%2Fvulnerabilities\&title=Open+Vulnerabilities) dashboard and adds its own GitHub check to each commit it reviews. On a private or internal repository, when the commit is on a branch with an open pull request, Security Review also posts its findings as comments on that pull request, each linking to the finding.

## Managing reviews

Check out [Managing Security Reviews](/docs/agent/security-review/usage) for details on triaging findings, fixing them with Vercel Agent, writing security policies, and the roles and permissions required.

To triage findings from your terminal or an agent, use [`vercel security vulnerabilities`](/docs/cli/security#vulnerabilities) to list, inspect, dismiss, and reopen them.

## Pricing

Security Review uses provider inference at the underlying token rate with no markup, plus the Vercel Token Rate of $0.25 per million tokens. Reviews run per Git push event rather than per pull request, so cost scales with how often you push and how much code changed.

See [Vercel Agent pricing](/docs/agent/pricing) for complete rates and cost-tracking information.

## Privacy

Findings show snippets of your source code, including any confidential, personal, or sensitive data those snippets contain.

In the [Vulnerabilities](/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%7E%2Fsecurity%2Fvulnerabilities\&title=Open+Vulnerabilities) dashboard, the Owner, Member, Developer, and Security roles see findings for every project, a Contributor sees only the projects assigned to them, and the Billing and Viewer roles see none. When Security Review posts a finding to a private or internal repository's pull request, anyone with access to that repository can read it, which can be a wider audience than the dashboard. On a public repository, Security Review posts only its check, which names what it reviewed and links to the Vulnerabilities dashboard, so an unpatched vulnerability isn't disclosed publicly, and the findings stay in the dashboard.

## Limitations

Security Review analyzes your code, not your running application. It isn't a security audit, and it doesn't perform runtime or penetration testing. It helps you find vulnerabilities but doesn't guarantee your application is free of them.

title: "Managing Security Reviews"
description: "Triage findings, fix them with Vercel Agent, and give reviews the context of your team"
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.090Z"

# Managing Security Reviews

> Vercel Security Review is available in Public Beta on Enterprise and Pro plans

Once you've [set up Security Review](/docs/agent/security-review#how-to-set-up-security-review), every finding it reports appears in the [**Vulnerabilities**](/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%7E%2Fsecurity%2Fvulnerabilities\&title=Open+Vulnerabilities) dashboard. This is your central hub for triaging findings across your team and fixing them with Vercel Agent.

To shape what future reviews look for, write a [security policy](#set-a-security-policy) in your team's **Agent** settings or a project's **Security** settings.

## Triage findings

The list shows open findings by default. You can search it, and filter by status, severity, environment, and branch. Each project also has its own Vulnerabilities page. You can also list, inspect, dismiss, and reopen findings from the terminal with [`vercel security vulnerabilities`](/docs/cli/security#vulnerabilities).

Click a finding to open its detail page, which shows the project, environment, branch, commit, and the deployments where the finding was first seen and closed. **Summary**, **Details**, and **Suggested Fix** explain the issue, and you can copy the whole finding as Markdown or JSON.

Severity is one of **Critical**, **High**, **Medium**, or **Low**. Severity ratings are AI-generated estimates rather than scores against a fixed rubric, so review each finding against your own application.

A finding stays open until you fix or dismiss it:

- **Open**: Security Review reported the finding, and nobody has fixed or dismissed it.
- **Dismissed**: You decided the finding doesn't need a fix.
- **Closed**: A later review no longer detects the issue. Vercel sets this itself, and it doesn't confirm that the issue is fixed.

## Fix a finding with Vercel Agent

**Fix with Vercel Agent** opens [Vercel Agent](/docs/agent) in the sidebar with the finding already described, so you can ask about it before Vercel Agent proposes anything. The button appears only when **Enable Chat** is on in your team's **Agent** settings.

1. In the Vulnerabilities dashboard, click the finding.
2. Click **Fix with Vercel Agent**.
3. Work with Vercel Agent in the sidebar. It confirms the vulnerability is still present, applies the smallest fix it can, and runs your type checks, lint, and tests.
4. Review the pull request it opens, then merge it when you're satisfied with the fix.

Vercel Agent opens the pull request against the branch the finding is on, and nothing merges on its own. For a project with no connected Git repository, it creates a preview deployment instead and replies with a downloadable patch, so your project's source doesn't change until you apply it.

When the merged change deploys, the next review checks whether the issue still appears and closes the finding if it doesn't.

## Dismiss or reopen a finding

Dismiss a finding when it isn't exploitable in your application, when it's an accepted risk, or when it's a false positive.

1. In the Vulnerabilities dashboard, click the finding.
2. Click **Dismiss Vulnerability**.
3. Confirm in the dialog.

Dismissed findings stay in the dashboard so you can review them later. To reopen one, filter by **Dismissed**, click the finding, and click **Reopen Vulnerability**. It returns to open, and the next review treats it like any other open finding.

## Track findings in your audit log

When Security Review reports a new vulnerability, Vercel records a `vercel-agent-security-finding-created` event in your team's [audit log](/docs/audit-log), naming the severity, the vulnerability class, and the project. Enterprise teams can read it in the audit log CSV export, or send it to a SIEM with an [Audit Log Drain](/docs/drains/reference/audit-logs). The event doesn't appear in your team's [Activity log](/docs/activity-log).

## Review findings in GitHub

Security Review adds its own GitHub check to each commit it reviews. On a private or internal repository, when that commit's branch has an open pull request, it also posts findings as comments on the pull request, each linking to the finding in the Vulnerabilities dashboard.

When you open or reopen a pull request, Security Review posts the findings already recorded for that branch.

Those comments can include the finding details, and anyone with access to the repository can read them. On a public repository, Security Review posts only its check, which names what it reviewed and links to the Vulnerabilities dashboard, so an unpatched vulnerability isn't disclosed publicly. Review those findings in the dashboard instead.

## Set a security policy

Policies are instructions that tell Security Review how to review your code. Write a policy to describe your threat model, point reviews at sensitive areas, or skip issues that don't apply to your application.

A policy is written in plain language, up to 32,000 characters. The more specific it is, the better Security Review understands what matters in your codebase:

- **Context about your application**: "This is an internal admin tool behind SSO. All routes under `/api/admin` require an authenticated employee."
- **Areas to focus on**: "Pay close attention to authorization checks in `app/api/billing`."
- **Issues to ignore**: "Don't report missing rate limiting on `/api/health`. Vercel Firewall rate limits this route."

Policies are treated as context, not as commands. Security Review's core behavior, identifying security vulnerabilities in your code, takes precedence over any conflicting policy content.

### Add a team policy

1. From your team, go to **Settings**, then open **Agent**.
2. In the **Security Reviews** section, find the **Policy** field. It appears once **Review Deployments Automatically** is on.
3. Enter your policy and click **Save**.

### Add a project policy

1. From your [dashboard](/dashboard), select the project you'd like to configure, then open **Settings**.
2. Open **Security**.
3. Under **Security Review Policy**, enter your policy and click **Save**.

Security Review applies both policies, with the project policy adding context on top of what the team policy already says. Policy changes apply to reviews that start after you save them.

### Security is a shared responsibility

Security is a shared responsibility between Vercel and you. Security Review is a tool to help you find vulnerabilities, and it can miss issues. Policies change what reviews look for, so changing a policy can cause Security Review to miss vulnerabilities it would otherwise report, and you're responsible for that effect.

For more on how these responsibilities are divided, see the [shared responsibility model](/docs/security/shared-responsibility).

## Roles and permissions

What you can do with Security Review depends on your [team role](/docs/rbac/access-roles).

| Action                                         | Roles                                                                        |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| View findings                                  | Owner, Member, Developer, Security; Contributors for their assigned projects |
| Dismiss or reopen a finding                    | Owner, Member, Developer, Security                                           |
| Fix a finding with Vercel Agent                | Any role that can use [Vercel Agent](/docs/agent) chat                       |
| Add or edit a team or project policy           | Owner, Member                                                                |
| Turn reviews on and set **Projects to Review** | Owner                                                                        |

Findings include source code and how to exploit it, so the Billing and Viewer roles can't see them, and a Contributor sees findings only for the projects assigned to them.

# Running Claude Code Durably on Vercel

> **⚠️ Warning:** Claude Code support is experimental. Claude Code isn't built to be safe for
> multiple tenants: it's a command-line tool for one user, it keeps its state on
> disk, and its built-in tools run commands and change files on the machine it
> runs on. So `durable-harness` currently runs it only in a Vercel Sandbox. See
> [Security](/docs/agent-harnesses/security#why-claude-code-and-codex-run-only-in-a-sandbox).

Each session of [Claude Code](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/overview) gets its own [Vercel Sandbox](/docs/sandbox), and Claude Code runs only there:

- **In the Sandbox:** Claude Code itself: the `claude` CLI, its agent loop, any built-in tools you turn on, and the session's files in `/workspace`.
- **In your function:** none of Claude Code. Your function only drives it: the Claude Agent SDK sends the CLI its messages and reads what it streams back. Your function also sends the CLI's model calls to AI Gateway, runs your own tools, and writes the session's durable log.

The Sandbox holds no secrets. A crashed turn resumes on a new function, and if the Sandbox is gone, on a new one with the same files. To learn how durability works, see [Running Agent Harnesses Durably](/docs/agent-harnesses).

## Get started

- ### Install the packages
  ```bash package-manager
  npm i durable-harness @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk@0.3.296 @vercel/sandbox zod
  ```
  `durable-harness` supports one Agent SDK version at a time, so install the one it pins, and keep it exact in `package.json`, with no `^`. With another version, a turn fails with the version to install, and the session is kept.

- ### Create the agent
  ```ts {3} filename="lib/agent.ts"
  import { claudeCode } from 'durable-harness/claude-code';

  export const agent = claudeCode({ model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5' });
  ```
  `claudeCode()` runs Claude Code in a Vercel Sandbox by default, so you don't pass anything to get one. A session's Sandbox starts with its first turn. Model calls go through AI Gateway with the deployment's OIDC token, so you don't need an Anthropic API key.

- ### Add the chat route
  `POST` sends a message and streams its turn as server-sent events, and `GET` reconnects to a turn that's still running:
  ```ts filename="app/api/chat/route.ts" framework=nextjs-app
  import { agent } from '@/lib/agent';
  import { withSessionOwnership } from '@/lib/session-ownership';

  export const { GET, POST } = withSessionOwnership({
    createRoute: (authorize) => agent.chatRoute({ authorize }),
    start: () => agent.sessions.start({ config: { traceAudience: 'unknown' } }),
  });
  ```
  ```ts filename="api/chat.ts" framework=other
  import { agent } from '../lib/agent.js';
  import { withSessionOwnership } from '../lib/session-ownership.js';

  export const { GET, POST } = withSessionOwnership({
    createRoute: (authorize) => agent.chatRoute({ authorize }),
    start: () => agent.sessions.start({ config: { traceAudience: 'unknown' } }),
  });
  ```
  Add the [`withSessionOwnership` helper](/docs/agent-harnesses/security#check-session-ownership) to `lib/session-ownership.ts` and implement its authentication and persistent ownership store. It records the owner before submitting a session's first message, and checks ownership on later messages and reconnects.
  > **⚠️ Warning:** In production (`NODE_ENV=production`, which includes every Vercel deployment),
  > a chat route without `authorize` refuses every request with a 401. Every
  > session starts a Sandbox, so to serve anyone, pass `authorize: 'public'` with
  > `allowPublicSandbox: true`, and cap each session's model spend with
  > `sandbox({ budget: { sessionUsd } })`. Whoever can use the route runs the
  > agent on your AI Gateway credits. See
  > [Security](/docs/agent-harnesses/security#chat-routes).
  POST `{ "text": "..." }` to start a session, and read its ID from the `x-session-id` header. Send `{ "sessionId": "...", "text": "..." }` for the next message. To redirect a running turn or reconnect to one, see [Steer a running turn](#steer-a-running-turn) and [Reconnect to a running turn](#reconnect-to-a-running-turn).

- ### Add the queue route
  [Vercel Queues](/docs/queues) delivers each turn to a queue route: a function that drives the turn, with your plan's [maximum duration](/docs/functions/limitations#max-duration), while Claude Code runs in the session's Sandbox. Set it up in `vercel.json`, or let `durable-harness` write the same settings with `harnessFunctions()` in `vercel.ts` or with `withDurableHarness` on Next.js:
  #### vercel.json
  ```ts {3,6} filename="api/flow.ts"
  // A Vercel Function in your api directory. It imports the module that
  // makes your agent, so it can drive the agent's turns.
  import '../lib/agent.js';
  import { flowHandler } from 'durable-harness';

  export const POST = flowHandler();
  ```
  ```json filename="vercel.json"
  {
    "functions": {
      "api/flow.ts": {
        "maxDuration": "max",
        "experimentalTriggers": [
          {
            "type": "queue/v2beta",
            "topic": "__harness_wkf_workflow_*",
            "retryAfterSeconds": 5,
            "initialDelaySeconds": 0
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  }
  ```
  The trigger subscribes `api/flow.ts` to the queue. `npx durable-harness vercel-json --write` writes this entry into your `vercel.json`.
  #### vercel.ts
  ```ts {3,6} filename="api/flow.ts"
  // A Vercel Function in your api directory. It imports the module that
  // makes your agent, so it can drive the agent's turns.
  import '../lib/agent.js';
  import { flowHandler } from 'durable-harness';

  export const POST = flowHandler();
  ```
  ```ts {8} filename="vercel.ts"
  // The same settings as in vercel.json, worked out from the packages you
  // installed when the project builds. Install @vercel/config as a dev
  // dependency.
  import type { VercelConfig } from '@vercel/config/v1';
  import { harnessFunctions } from 'durable-harness/vercel';

  export const config: VercelConfig = {
    functions: harnessFunctions(),
  };
  ```
  #### Next.js
  ```ts {10} filename="next.config.ts"
  // Writes the queue route and its trigger, and keeps the harness packages
  // out of the server bundle. You don't add a queue route or a vercel.json.
  import type { NextConfig } from 'next';
  import { withDurableHarness } from 'durable-harness/next';

  const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
    // your existing config
  };

  export default withDurableHarness(nextConfig);
  ```
  If the app also uses the Workflow SDK, wrap both, as in `withWorkflow(withDurableHarness(nextConfig))`. The queue route then moves to `/.well-known/durable-harness/v1/flow` and needs one `vercel.json` entry, which `npx durable-harness vercel-json --write` adds, or `harnessFunctions()` in `vercel.ts`. Without it, the build on Vercel fails and prints the entry.

- ### Deploy
  ```bash
  vercel deploy
  ```
  The Sandbox image is built once per project, when the first session starts. To build it ahead of time, run `npx durable-harness sandbox prepare`.

  On your machine, run `vercel link` first. `next dev` (or `vercel dev` for other frameworks) then starts each session's Sandbox on Vercel, since there's no local Sandbox. It keeps sessions in `.workflow-data`, so add that to `.gitignore`. On its first request, it resumes the sessions a stopped server left mid-turn.

## Steer a running turn

Send a message with `"kind": "steer"` while a turn runs to redirect it. Claude Code takes it at its next step, after the tool or model call that is running. From the browser, post it to the chat route:

```ts {4}
await fetch('/api/chat', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ sessionId, text: 'Use TypeScript instead', kind: 'steer' }),
});
```

The response streams the turn, like any other message. From server code, such as a webhook, call `agent.sessions.send(sessionId, text, 'steer')`.

## Reconnect to a running turn

If the stream drops, the turn keeps running. Reconnect with `GET /api/chat?sessionId=...&cursor=...`, where the cursor is the last event `id` you read. The stream continues with the next event, with nothing lost or repeated. An `EventSource` on that URL reconnects by itself if its connection drops, and the stream ends with an `end` event when the turn is done:

```ts {1,7}
const source = new EventSource(`/api/chat?sessionId=${sessionId}&cursor=${lastEventId}`);

source.onmessage = (event) => {
  lastEventId = event.lastEventId;
  render(JSON.parse(event.data)); // your own UI
};
source.addEventListener('end', () => source.close());
```

If a crash cut off the turn, the turn resumes and the model starts its reply over. Before the new reply, the stream sends a `{ type: 'restart', text }` event: show its `text` in place of the turn's text so far, then append what streams after it.

## Run more than one agent

An app can make several agents, each with its own chat route. The queue route serves them all. Two agents of the same harness need a `name` each:

```ts {3-4} filename="lib/agents.ts"
import { claudeCode } from 'durable-harness/claude-code';

export const reviewer = claudeCode({ name: 'reviewer', model: 'anthropic/claude-opus-5.5' });
export const fixer = claudeCode({ name: 'fixer', model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5' });
```

Keep each name stable, because sessions that already started carry it. Two agents with the same name throw when their module loads, so the build fails.

## Tools

Claude Code starts with no tools: the model can call only the tools you pass in `tools`, and those run in your function, not in the Sandbox. To write them, see [Tools, files, and documents](/docs/agent-harnesses/tools).

To turn on Claude Code's own tools, pass `builtins: true`. They run in the Sandbox, on the session's files in `/workspace`:

```ts {5} filename="lib/agent.ts"
import { claudeCode } from 'durable-harness/claude-code';

export const agent = claudeCode({
  model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5',
  builtins: true,
});
```

`true` turns on Bash, Read, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit, and WebFetch. To turn on fewer, list them, as in `builtins: ['Read', 'Edit']`. Each call is in the session's log before it runs, and none runs again after a crash: the model is told which calls finished and which a crash interrupted. See [Security](/docs/agent-harnesses/security).

## The Sandbox

Each session's `/workspace` is on a [Drive](/docs/sandbox/concepts/drives) that outlives the session's Sandbox, so a session that moves to a new Sandbox keeps its files.

A session's Drive lasts until you delete it: close the session with `agent.sessions.close(sessionId)`, then call `deleteSessionSandbox(sessionId)` from `durable-harness/sandbox`, for example when your user deletes the session. To also delete the Drives of sessions that have been idle for a number of days, call `sandboxCleanup({ idleDays })` from a [cron job](/docs/cron-jobs).

To configure the Sandbox, pass `workspace: sandbox({ ... })`:

```ts {2,6-9} filename="lib/agent.ts"
import { claudeCode } from 'durable-harness/claude-code';
import { sandbox } from 'durable-harness/sandbox';

export const agent = claudeCode({
  model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5',
  workspace: sandbox({
    region: 'iad1',
    network: 'deny-all',
  }),
});
```

With `network: 'deny-all'`, the Sandbox can't reach the internet. Claude Code still works, since your function makes its model calls.

| Option | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `region` | Your function's region if Sandbox runs there, else `iad1` | Where the Sandbox and its Drive run. An existing Drive keeps its region |
| `vcpus` | `2` | `1`, `2`, `4`, or `8` vCPUs |
| `network` | `'allow-all'` | `'deny-all'`, or `{ allow: [...] }` with the hosts commands can reach |
| `env` | None | Environment variables for commands. The model can read them, so pass none that's secret |
| `idleMs` | 5 minutes | How long the Sandbox stays up after a turn |
| `commandTimeoutMs` | 10 minutes | The longest a command can run |
| `driveSize` | 10 GiB | The Drive's size in bytes, from 1 GiB to 16 TiB. Storage is billed by the bytes used, so this caps a session's storage. An existing Drive keeps its size |
| `budget` | 4 hours of Sandbox time, no spend cap | `{ turnUsd, sessionUsd, vmSeconds }`, per turn and per session |

A turn starts in the chat route's own request, which drives it for up to 60 seconds before the queue route takes over. A command still running at that handover is stopped, not run again, so a long command early in a turn, such as an install or a build, can be cut off. A slow first start of the session's Sandbox can run into the same handover. This is a current limitation of Vercel Queues, and a fix is on the way. Until then, pass `drive: 'queue'` to `agent.chatRoute()` for an agent that runs long commands: the queue route then drives the whole turn, with your plan's [maximum duration](/docs/functions/limitations#max-duration).

## What happens when a function crashes

If the function running a turn fails with an error, another function resumes the turn right away. If it disappears without a trace, for example when it runs out of memory, the queue redelivers the turn once its message lease runs out, and the turn resumes from the log. When the function driving the turn goes away, the Sandbox stops the CLI, and the next function resumes the turn on the same Sandbox or on a new one with the same Drive.

## Self-host on another World

On Vercel, sessions live in Vercel's World, and on your machine in `.workflow-data`. To keep them in another [World](https://workflow-sdk.dev/worlds), such as Postgres on your own servers, install it and set `WORKFLOW_TARGET_WORLD`:

```bash filename=".env"
WORKFLOW_TARGET_WORLD="@workflow/world-postgres"
WORKFLOW_POSTGRES_URL="postgres://user:password@host:5432/database"
```

To use a World you create, pass it as `claudeCode({ model, world })`, and start it yourself, as [Pass a World yourself](/docs/agent-harnesses/self-hosting#pass-a-world-yourself) shows.

For the tables, the server, and recovery at startup, see [Self-hosting durable agent harnesses](/docs/agent-harnesses/self-hosting).

On your own server, `vercel.json` and `vercel.ts` don't apply, and your server mounts the queue route itself. Your server drives each turn, and Claude Code still runs in a Vercel Sandbox. Give `sandbox()` a [Vercel access token](/docs/rest-api#creating-an-access-token) and the team and project its Sandboxes belong to. The token stays on your server and never reaches the Sandbox:

```ts {7-11} filename="lib/agent.ts"
import { claudeCode } from 'durable-harness/claude-code';
import { sandbox } from 'durable-harness/sandbox';

export const agent = claudeCode({
  model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5',
  workspace: sandbox({
    credentials: {
      token: process.env.VERCEL_TOKEN!,
      teamId: process.env.VERCEL_TEAM_ID!,
      projectId: process.env.VERCEL_PROJECT_ID!,
    },
  }),
});
```

## Limitations

- `durable-harness` supports only the Agent SDK version it pins, and fails a turn if you installed another. Claude Code's transcript format is internal to the CLI, so the version moves only with a `durable-harness` release.
- Provider-hosted tools, such as the model provider's web search, are off unless you list them in `providerTools`. They reach the internet from the provider, whatever the Sandbox's network allows.
- A Sandbox session can't run past your plan's [maximum session duration](/docs/sandbox/pricing#runtime-limits). Before it would, `durable-harness` replaces the Sandbox between turns, keeping the Drive.
- Every session starts a Sandbox, even with no tools. Sandbox time and Drive storage are billed, as [Sandbox pricing](/docs/sandbox/pricing) shows.
- The Sandbox allows all outbound traffic by default. To restrict it, pass `network: 'deny-all'` or `{ allow: [...] }` to `sandbox()`. See [Security](/docs/agent-harnesses/security#what-these-controls-dont-cover).
- The Agent SDK runs in your function, so it needs the Node.js runtime. It can't run in the Edge runtime or a browser.

## More resources

- [`durable-harness` on GitHub](https://github.com/vercel-labs/durable-harness)
- [Claude Agent SDK](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/agent-sdk/overview)
- [Vercel Sandbox](/docs/sandbox)

# Running Codex Durably on Vercel

> **⚠️ Warning:** Codex support is experimental. Codex isn't built to be safe for multiple
> tenants: it's a command-line tool for one user, it keeps its state on disk,
> and its built-in tools run commands and change files on the machine it runs
> on. So `durable-harness` currently runs it only in a Vercel Sandbox. See
> [Security](/docs/agent-harnesses/security#why-claude-code-and-codex-run-only-in-a-sandbox).

Each session of [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) gets its own [Vercel Sandbox](/docs/sandbox), and Codex runs only there:

- **In the Sandbox:** Codex itself: `codex app-server`, its agent loop, any built-in tools you turn on, and the session's files in `/workspace`.
- **In your function:** none of Codex. Your function only drives it: it sends `codex app-server` its messages and reads what it streams back. Your function also sends Codex's model calls to AI Gateway, runs your own tools, and writes the session's durable log, which keeps Codex's rollout file.

The Sandbox holds no secrets. A crashed turn resumes on a new function, and if the Sandbox is gone, on a new one with the same files. To learn how durability works, see [Running Agent Harnesses Durably](/docs/agent-harnesses).

- ### Add the queue route

  #### vercel.ts

  #### Next.js
  ```ts {10} filename="next.config.ts"

  // out of the server bundle. You don't add a queue route or a vercel.json.

  };

  export default withDurableHarness(nextConfig);
  ```
  If the app also uses the Workflow SDK, wrap both, as in `withWorkflow(withDurableHarness(nextConfig))`. The queue route then moves to `/.well-known/durable-harness/v1/flow` and needs one `vercel.json` entry, which `npx durable-harness vercel-json --write` adds, or `harnessFunctions()` in `vercel.ts`. Without it, the build on Vercel fails and prints the entry.

- ### Deploy
  ```bash
  vercel deploy
  ```
  The Sandbox image is built once per project, when the first session starts. To build it ahead of time, run `npx durable-harness sandbox prepare`.

  On your machine, run `vercel link` first. `next dev` (or `vercel dev` for other frameworks) then starts each session's Sandbox on Vercel, since there's no local Sandbox. It keeps sessions in `.workflow-data`, so add that to `.gitignore`. On its first request, it resumes the sessions a stopped server left mid-turn.

## Steer a running turn

Send a message with `"kind": "steer"` while a turn runs to redirect it. Codex adds it to the running turn at its next model request. From the browser, post it to the chat route:

```ts {4}
await fetch('/api/chat', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ sessionId, text: 'Use TypeScript instead', kind: 'steer' }),
});
```

The response streams the turn, like any other message. From server code, such as a webhook, call `agent.sessions.send(sessionId, text, 'steer')`.

## Reconnect to a running turn

If the stream drops, the turn keeps running. Reconnect with `GET /api/chat?sessionId=...&cursor=...`, where the cursor is the last event `id` you read. The stream continues with the next event, with nothing lost or repeated. An `EventSource` on that URL reconnects by itself if its connection drops, and the stream ends with an `end` event when the turn is done:

```ts {1,7}
const source = new EventSource(`/api/chat?sessionId=${sessionId}&cursor=${lastEventId}`);

source.onmessage = (event) => {
  lastEventId = event.lastEventId;
  render(JSON.parse(event.data)); // your own UI
};
source.addEventListener('end', () => source.close());
```

If a crash cut off the turn, the turn resumes and the model starts its reply over. Before the new reply, the stream sends a `{ type: 'restart', text }` event: show its `text` in place of the turn's text so far, then append what streams after it.

## Run more than one agent

An app can make several agents, each with its own chat route. The queue route serves them all. Two agents of the same harness need a `name` each:

```ts {3-4} filename="lib/agents.ts"
import { codex } from 'durable-harness/codex';

export const reviewer = codex({ name: 'reviewer', model: 'openai/gpt-5.5' });
export const fixer = codex({ name: 'fixer', model: 'openai/gpt-5.5' });
```

Keep each name stable, because sessions that already started carry it. Two agents with the same name throw when their module loads, so the build fails.

## Tools

Codex starts with no tools: the model can call only the tools you pass in `tools`, and those run in your function, not in the Sandbox. To write them, see [Tools, files, and documents](/docs/agent-harnesses/tools).

To turn on Codex's own shell and `apply_patch`, pass `builtins: true`. They run in the Sandbox, on the session's files in `/workspace`:

```ts {5} filename="lib/agent.ts"
import { codex } from 'durable-harness/codex';

export const agent = codex({
  model: 'openai/gpt-5.5',
  builtins: true,
});
```

Codex runs each command under its own sandbox inside the Sandbox, when it can start one. Each command is in the session's log before it runs, and none runs again after a crash: the model is told which commands finished and which a crash interrupted. See [Security](/docs/agent-harnesses/security#what-these-controls-dont-cover).

## The Sandbox

Each session's `/workspace` is on a [Drive](/docs/sandbox/concepts/drives) that outlives the session's Sandbox, so a session that moves to a new Sandbox keeps its files.

A session's Drive lasts until you delete it: close the session with `agent.sessions.close(sessionId)`, then call `deleteSessionSandbox(sessionId)` from `durable-harness/sandbox`, for example when your user deletes the session. To also delete the Drives of sessions that have been idle for a number of days, call `sandboxCleanup({ idleDays })` from a [cron job](/docs/cron-jobs).

To configure the Sandbox, pass `workspace: sandbox({ ... })`:

```ts {2,6-9} filename="lib/agent.ts"
import { codex } from 'durable-harness/codex';
import { sandbox } from 'durable-harness/sandbox';

export const agent = codex({
  model: 'openai/gpt-5.5',
  workspace: sandbox({
    region: 'iad1',
    network: 'deny-all',
  }),
});
```

With `network: 'deny-all'`, the Sandbox can't reach the internet. Codex still works, since your function makes its model calls.

| Option | Default | What it sets |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `region` | Your function's region if Sandbox runs there, else `iad1` | Where the Sandbox and its Drive run. An existing Drive keeps its region |
| `vcpus` | `2` | `1`, `2`, `4`, or `8` vCPUs |
| `network` | `'allow-all'` | `'deny-all'`, or `{ allow: [...] }` with the hosts commands can reach |
| `env` | None | Environment variables for commands. The model can read them, so pass none that's secret |
| `idleMs` | 5 minutes | How long the Sandbox stays up after a turn |
| `commandTimeoutMs` | 10 minutes | The longest a command can run |
| `driveSize` | 10 GiB | The Drive's size in bytes, from 1 GiB to 16 TiB. Storage is billed by the bytes used, so this caps a session's storage. An existing Drive keeps its size |
| `budget` | 4 hours of Sandbox time, no spend cap | `{ turnUsd, sessionUsd, vmSeconds }`, per turn and per session |

A turn starts in the chat route's own request, which drives it for up to 60 seconds before the queue route takes over. A command still running at that handover is stopped, not run again, so a long command early in a turn, such as an install or a build, can be cut off. A slow first start of the session's Sandbox can run into the same handover. This is a current limitation of Vercel Queues, and a fix is on the way. Until then, pass `drive: 'queue'` to `agent.chatRoute()` for an agent that runs long commands: the queue route then drives the whole turn, with your plan's [maximum duration](/docs/functions/limitations#max-duration).

## What happens when a function crashes

If the function running a turn fails with an error, another function resumes the turn right away. If it disappears without a trace, for example when it runs out of memory, the queue redelivers the turn once its message lease runs out, and the turn resumes from the log. When the function driving the turn goes away, the Sandbox stops Codex, and the next function resumes the turn on the same Sandbox or on a new one with the same Drive.

## Self-host on another World

On Vercel, sessions live in Vercel's World, and on your machine in `.workflow-data`. To keep them in another [World](https://workflow-sdk.dev/worlds), such as Postgres on your own servers, install it and set `WORKFLOW_TARGET_WORLD`:

```bash filename=".env"
WORKFLOW_TARGET_WORLD="@workflow/world-postgres"
WORKFLOW_POSTGRES_URL="postgres://user:password@host:5432/database"
```

To use a World you create, pass it as `codex({ model, world })`, and start it yourself, as [Pass a World yourself](/docs/agent-harnesses/self-hosting#pass-a-world-yourself) shows.

For the tables, the server, and recovery at startup, see [Self-hosting durable agent harnesses](/docs/agent-harnesses/self-hosting).

On your own server, `vercel.json` and `vercel.ts` don't apply, and your server mounts the queue route itself. Your server drives each turn, and Codex still runs in a Vercel Sandbox. Give `sandbox()` a [Vercel access token](/docs/rest-api#creating-an-access-token) and the team and project its Sandboxes belong to. The token stays on your server and never reaches the Sandbox:

```ts {7-11} filename="lib/agent.ts"
import { codex } from 'durable-harness/codex';
import { sandbox } from 'durable-harness/sandbox';

export const agent = codex({
  model: 'openai/gpt-5.5',
  workspace: sandbox({
    credentials: {
      token: process.env.VERCEL_TOKEN!,
      teamId: process.env.VERCEL_TEAM_ID!,
      projectId: process.env.VERCEL_PROJECT_ID!,
    },
  }),
});
```

## Limitations

- `durable-harness` runs Codex 0.160.0 in the Sandbox. Codex's rollout format is internal to the CLI, so the version moves only with a `durable-harness` release.
- Provider-hosted tools, such as the model provider's web search, are off.
- A Sandbox session can't run past your plan's [maximum session duration](/docs/sandbox/pricing#runtime-limits). Before it would, `durable-harness` replaces the Sandbox between turns, keeping the Drive.
- Every session starts a Sandbox, even with no tools. Sandbox time and Drive storage are billed, as [Sandbox pricing](/docs/sandbox/pricing) shows.
- The Sandbox allows all outbound traffic by default. To restrict it, pass `network: 'deny-all'` or `{ allow: [...] }` to `sandbox()`. See [Security](/docs/agent-harnesses/security#what-these-controls-dont-cover).
- `durable-harness` drives Codex from your function, so it needs the Node.js runtime. It can't run in the Edge runtime or a browser.

## More resources

- [`durable-harness` on GitHub](https://github.com/vercel-labs/durable-harness)
- [Codex](https://github.com/openai/codex)
- [Vercel Sandbox](/docs/sandbox)

# Running eve Agents Durably on Vercel

[eve](/docs/frameworks/agents/eve) is Vercel's framework for durable AI agents. Every eve session already runs as a durable workflow on the [Workflow SDK](https://workflow-sdk.dev) and its Worlds, the same foundation as the other harnesses in these guides. A crash, a function timeout, or a redeploy resumes the session from its last completed step.

There's nothing to add: you don't install `durable-harness`, write a flow route, or configure a queue. To learn how durability works, see [Running Agent Harnesses Durably](/docs/agent-harnesses).

## Get started

- ### Create an agent
  The eve CLI scaffolds a new agent project, installs its dependencies, and opens the terminal UI:
  ```bash
  npx eve@latest init my-agent
  ```
  To add eve to an existing app, follow the [eve framework guide](/docs/frameworks/agents/eve#create-an-agent).

- ### Deploy
  Configure [authentication](/docs/frameworks/agents/eve#configure-who-can-call-the-agent) for your callers, then deploy to Production from the new project:
  ```bash
  cd my-agent
  npx eve deploy
  ```
  See [Deploying eve to Vercel](/docs/frameworks/agents/eve#deploy-to-vercel) for project linking, credentials, and deployment checks.

## Offload work to a daemon

For tools that need system binaries or CPU-heavy processing, publish a job to [Vercel Queues](/docs/queues) and let a [Vercel Daemon](/docs/daemons) process it. The eve session can wait without holding compute until the worker returns the result through the session API. eve manages session durability; make the worker's jobs safe to retry.

Follow [Use Vercel Daemons with eve agents](/kb/guide/vercel-daemons-eve-agents) for the implementation.

For agents, tools, channels, and everything else, see the [eve documentation](https://eve.dev/docs) and [eve on Vercel](/docs/frameworks/agents/eve).

title: "Running fx Durably on Vercel"
description: "Deploy an fx agent with libfx so its sessions survive crashes, function timeouts, and redeploys on Vercel."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.036Z"

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Running fx Durably on Vercel

[fx](https://github.com/vercel-labs/fx) is an agent harness with its kernel written in Zig. Its JavaScript package, `libfx`, is durable by default: it saves each step of a turn as it runs, and the same code runs on your machine and on Vercel. To learn how durability works, see [Running Agent Harnesses Durably](/docs/agent-harnesses).

## Get started

- ### Install libfx
  `libfx` includes its native addon and Vercel's World, so you don't install anything else:
  ```bash package-manager
  npm i libfx
  ```

- ### Create the agent
  Create the agent, and set `idempotent` on every tool:
  ```ts {8,15,18-19,23} filename="lib/agent.ts"
  import { createFxAgent } from 'libfx';
  import { getOrder, refundOrder } from './orders'; // your own code

  const tools = [
    {
      name: 'get_order',
      description: 'Looks up an order',
      idempotent: true, // safe to run again after a crash
      inputSchema: { type: 'object', properties: { id: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['id'] },
      execute: (input: { id: string }) => getOrder(input.id),
    },
    {
      name: 'refund_order',
      description: 'Refunds an order',
      idempotent: false, // never runs twice
      inputSchema: { type: 'object', properties: { id: { type: 'string' } }, required: ['id'] },
      // executionId is the same each time this call runs: use it as an idempotency key
      execute: (input: { id: string }, { executionId }: { executionId: string }) =>
        refundOrder(input.id, { idempotencyKey: executionId }),
    },
  ];

  export const agent = createFxAgent({ model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5', tools });
  ```

- ### Add the chat route
  `POST` stores the prompt and streams the turn. When no other function holds the session, the same function runs the turn, and [Vercel Queues](/docs/queues) keeps the prompt in case that function stops. `GET` reconnects from a `cursor`:
  ```ts {5-14,21-22} filename="app/api/chat/route.ts" framework=nextjs-app
  import { agent } from '@/lib/agent';
  import { getUser, ownsSession, saveSession } from '@/lib/auth'; // your own auth and session store

  export async function POST(request: Request) {
    const user = await getUser(request);
    if (!user) return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 });
    let sessionId = new URL(request.url).searchParams.get('sessionId');
    if (sessionId) {
      if (!(await ownsSession(user, sessionId))) return new Response('Not found', { status: 404 });
    } else {
      sessionId = await agent.newSessionId();
      await saveSession(user, sessionId); // so this user can use it later
    }
    const turn = agent.session(sessionId).prompt(await request.text());
    return new Response(turn.readable);
  }

  export async function GET(request: Request) {
    const params = new URL(request.url).searchParams;
    const sessionId = params.get('sessionId');
    const user = await getUser(request);
    if (!user || !sessionId || !(await ownsSession(user, sessionId))) return new Response('Not found', { status: 404 });
    const stream = agent.session(sessionId).stream(Number(params.get('cursor') ?? 0));
    return new Response(stream);
  }
  ```
  ```ts {5-14,21-22} filename="api/chat.ts" framework=other
  import { agent } from '../lib/agent.js';
  import { getUser, ownsSession, saveSession } from '../lib/auth.js'; // your own auth and session store

  export async function POST(request: Request) {
    const user = await getUser(request);
    if (!user) return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 });
    let sessionId = new URL(request.url).searchParams.get('sessionId');
    if (sessionId) {
      if (!(await ownsSession(user, sessionId))) return new Response('Not found', { status: 404 });
    } else {
      sessionId = await agent.newSessionId();
      await saveSession(user, sessionId); // so this user can use it later
    }
    const turn = agent.session(sessionId).prompt(await request.text());
    return new Response(turn.readable);
  }

  export async function GET(request: Request) {
    const params = new URL(request.url).searchParams;
    const sessionId = params.get('sessionId');
    const user = await getUser(request);
    if (!user || !sessionId || !(await ownsSession(user, sessionId))) return new Response('Not found', { status: 404 });
    const stream = agent.session(sessionId).stream(Number(params.get('cursor') ?? 0));
    return new Response(stream);
  }
  ```
  Every route checks who's calling, and that the session is theirs: a route that serves anyone runs turns on your AI Gateway credits, and lets anyone with a session ID read or steer it. See [Security](/docs/agent-harnesses/security).

  The response streams the turn as JSON lines. The first line, `turn_start`, carries the session's ID, and every line has a `cursor`. To redirect a running turn or reconnect to one, see [Steer a running turn](#steer-a-running-turn) and [Reconnect to a running turn](#reconnect-to-a-running-turn).

- ### Add the queue route
  Vercel Queues delivers every turn the chat route doesn't run, and the rest of any turn it couldn't finish, to a queue route that runs it, with your plan's [maximum duration](/docs/functions/limitations#max-duration). Set it up in `vercel.json` or `vercel.ts`, or let `withDurableHarness` write it on Next.js:
  #### vercel.json
  ```ts {3} filename="api/libfx.ts"
  import { agent } from '../lib/agent.js';

  export const POST = agent.wakeHandler();
  ```
  ```json filename="vercel.json"
  {
    "functions": {
      "api/libfx.ts": {
        "maxDuration": "max",
        "experimentalTriggers": [{ "type": "queue/v2beta", "topic": "__libfx_wkf_workflow_session" }]
      }
    }
  }
  ```
  The trigger subscribes `api/libfx.ts` to the queue. On Next.js, you can put the route in `app/api/libfx/route.ts` instead, and use that path as the key.
  #### vercel.ts
  ```ts {3} filename="api/libfx.ts"
  import { agent } from '../lib/agent.js';

  export const POST = agent.wakeHandler();
  ```
  ```ts {5-8} filename="vercel.ts"
  // Install @vercel/config as a dev dependency.
  import type { VercelConfig } from '@vercel/config/v1';

  export const config: VercelConfig = {
    functions: {
      'api/libfx.ts': {
        maxDuration: 'max',
        experimentalTriggers: [{ type: 'queue/v2beta', topic: '__libfx_wkf_workflow_session' }],
      },
    },
  };
  ```
  The trigger subscribes `api/libfx.ts` to the queue. On Next.js, you can put the route in `app/api/libfx/route.ts` instead, and use that path as the key.
  #### Next.js
  If your app uses Next.js, `durable-harness` can write the queue route for you. Install it next to `libfx`:
  ```bash package-manager
  npm i durable-harness
  ```
  ```ts {10} filename="next.config.ts"
  // Writes the queue route and its trigger, and keeps libfx's native addon
  // out of the server bundle. You don't add a queue route or a vercel.json.
  import type { NextConfig } from 'next';
  import { withDurableHarness } from 'durable-harness/next';

  const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
    // your existing config
  };

  export default withDurableHarness(nextConfig);
  ```
  The route reaches each agent through its module's exports, so export every agent at the top level of its module, as `lib/agent.ts` does. If your `vercel.json` or `vercel.ts` already subscribes a route to libfx's topic, `withDurableHarness` leaves that route in place. In an app that also uses the Workflow SDK's `withWorkflow`, wrap both, and add the `vercel.json` entries that `npx durable-harness vercel-json --write` prints.

- ### Deploy
  ```bash
  vercel deploy
  ```

On your machine, run `vercel link` and `vercel env pull`, or set `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY`, so model calls can authenticate. The same code keeps sessions in files under `$TMPDIR/libfx/sessions`. To keep them in another World, such as Postgres, see [Self-host on another World](#self-host-on-another-world).

> **💡 Note:** Make tools `idempotent: true` wherever you can. A harness runs them without waiting for
> the log, and reruns them after a crash. Before an `idempotent: false` tool, it waits until
> the log has recorded the call, so the tool never runs twice.

## Steer a running turn

`session.steer(text)` steers the running turn: it cuts a streaming reply short, or waits for a running tool, and the turn continues with it. With no turn running, the steer starts one. Any server can steer a session:

```ts {6-7} filename="app/api/chat/steer/route.ts" framework=nextjs-app
import { agent } from '@/lib/agent';
import { getUser, ownsSession } from '@/lib/auth'; // your own auth and session store

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  const { sessionId, text } = await request.json();
  const user = await getUser(request);
  if (!user || !(await ownsSession(user, sessionId))) return new Response('Not found', { status: 404 });
  await agent.session(sessionId).steer(text);
  return new Response(null, { status: 204 });
}
```

```ts {6-7} filename="api/chat/steer.ts" framework=other
import { agent } from '../../lib/agent.js';
import { getUser, ownsSession } from '../../lib/auth.js'; // your own auth and session store

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  const { sessionId, text } = await request.json();
  const user = await getUser(request);
  if (!user || !(await ownsSession(user, sessionId))) return new Response('Not found', { status: 404 });
  await agent.session(sessionId).steer(text);
  return new Response(null, { status: 204 });
}
```

## Reconnect to a running turn

If the response ends before the turn does, the turn keeps running. Reconnect with `GET /api/chat?sessionId=...&cursor=...`, with the last `cursor` you read. The `GET` handler in the chat route streams the session from just after that cursor and stays open for its next turns, so stop reading at the turn's `turn_end`.

## Run more than one agent

An app can make several agents, each with its own chat route. Give each one a `name`:

```ts {4-5} filename="lib/agents.ts"
import { createFxAgent } from 'libfx';
import { tools } from './tools'; // your tools, each with idempotent set

export const support = createFxAgent({ name: 'support', model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5', tools });
export const coding = createFxAgent({ name: 'coding', model: 'anthropic/claude-opus-5.5', tools });
```

A session's turns run only on an agent with the name of the agent that created it. Keep each name stable, because sessions that already started carry it. An agent without a `name` is named `default`.

One queue route serves every agent. Import every module that creates one, and mount libfx's `wakeHandler()`:

```ts {1-2,4} filename="api/libfx.ts"
import { wakeHandler } from 'libfx';
import '../lib/agents.js'; // every module that creates an agent

export const POST = wakeHandler();
```

On Next.js, `withDurableHarness` imports every module that exports an agent, so you don't write this route.

## Tools

An fx agent has only the tools you give it. To give it fx's own `read_file`, `glob_files`, `grep_files`, `edit_file`, `write_file`, and `shell`, add `fxTools()` from `durable-harness/fx` to its tools, with a workspace for them. They never run on your function's disk, in its processes, or with its environment, which other sessions on the instance share:

#### Virtual workspace

```bash package-manager
npm i durable-harness just-bash
```

```ts {2-3,6} filename="lib/agent.ts"
import { createFxAgent } from 'libfx';
import { virtual } from 'durable-harness';
import { fxTools } from 'durable-harness/fx';
import { tools } from './tools'; // your tools, each with idempotent set

export const agent = createFxAgent({ model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5', tools: [...fxTools(virtual()), ...tools] });
```

The tools run on a virtual workspace at `/workspace` in your function, where `shell` is [just-bash](https://www.npmjs.com/package/just-bash), whose commands can't reach the function's files, processes, or environment. Each call that changes files records the change in the session's log, so the files follow the session to any function, and a call that a crash interrupts runs again without changing anything twice.

#### Vercel Sandbox

```bash package-manager
npm i durable-harness @vercel/sandbox
```

```ts {2-3,6} filename="lib/agent.ts"
import { createFxAgent } from 'libfx';
import { sandbox } from 'durable-harness';
import { fxTools } from 'durable-harness/fx';
import { tools } from './tools'; // your tools, each with idempotent set

export const agent = createFxAgent({ model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5', tools: [...fxTools(sandbox()), ...tools] });
```

The tools run in the session's own [Vercel Sandbox](/docs/sandbox), with its files on a [Drive](/docs/sandbox/concepts/drives) at `/workspace` that lasts across turns. The agent stays in your function, and the Sandbox starts at the first tool call. What a call wrote stays on the Drive even if a crash interrupts it, so libfx never runs an interrupted call again, and tells the model it may have partly run. On your machine, run `vercel link` and `vercel env pull` first: the Sandbox starts on Vercel, under the linked project.

Every session can start a Sandbox, and the chat route is your own, so check who's calling, as the chat route above does, and cap each session's Sandbox time with `sandbox({ budget: { vmSeconds } })`. A Sandbox runs for at most 4 hours a session by default. See [Security](/docs/agent-harnesses/security#chat-routes).

If you pass the agent a World of your own, as [Self-host on another World](#self-host-on-another-world) shows, pass it to `fxTools()` too, as in `fxTools(virtual(), { world: sessions })`. For tools you write, see [Tools, files, and documents](/docs/agent-harnesses/tools) and [Security](/docs/agent-harnesses/security).

## What happens when a function crashes

After a crash, Vercel Queues redelivers the turn, and a new function continues it from its last saved step. An `idempotent: true` tool that was running runs again. An `idempotent: false` tool returns an error that tells the model it may have partly run, so the model can check before it calls it again.

Turns aren't limited to one function. Shortly before the function's deadline, libfx saves the turn and continues it in a new invocation.

## Self-host on another World

libfx chooses where sessions live by itself: Vercel's World on Vercel, and files in `FX_SESSIONS_DIR`, by default `$TMPDIR/libfx/sessions`, in Node.js elsewhere. It doesn't read `WORKFLOW_TARGET_WORLD`. To keep sessions in another [World](https://workflow-sdk.dev/worlds), such as Postgres on your own servers, install it and pass it to `world()` from `libfx/durable-world`:

```ts {7,12} filename="lib/agent.ts"
import { createFxAgent } from 'libfx';
import { world } from 'libfx/durable-world';
import { createWorld } from '@workflow/world-postgres';
import { tools } from './tools'; // your tools, each with idempotent set

// libfx's own queue topics and jobs, apart from the rest of the app.
const sessions = createWorld({ connectionString: process.env.WORKFLOW_POSTGRES_URL!, namespace: 'libfx', jobPrefix: 'libfx_' });
await sessions.start();

export const agent = createFxAgent({
  model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5',
  tools,
  durability: world(sessions, { queueDurable: true }),
});
```

libfx never starts or closes a World you pass in, so start it before the agent's first prompt, and close it after `agent.close()`. The Postgres World delivers to the agent in its process. For a World that delivers over HTTP, mount `agent.wakeHandler()` where it delivers. For the Postgres tables and connection string, see [Self-hosting durable agent harnesses](/docs/agent-harnesses/self-hosting).

## See sessions in Agent Runs

To see each session in Agent Runs, pass `hooks: agentRunsHooks()` from `durable-harness/fx` to `createFxAgent`, and set up Agent Runs as [Observability](/docs/agent-harnesses/observability#set-up-agent-runs) shows.

## Limitations

- While a turn can run for much longer, a single model request or tool call can't run longer than the [maximum duration](/docs/functions/limitations#max-duration) of the function running it, the chat route or the queue route.
- Renaming an agent, or naming one that had no `name`, leaves its sessions with no agent to run them. A function that gets a turn for an agent it doesn't create refuses it, and the queue delivers it again.
- On your machine or on the Postgres World, a server that's killed or restarted mid-turn leaves the turn open until the session's next message, or until you call `session.resume()`. The next message's response streams only its own turn: read the resumed one with `GET` from your last cursor.

## More resources

- [`libfx` README](https://www.npmjs.com/package/libfx)
- [fx](https://github.com/vercel-labs/fx)

# Agent Harnesses You Can Run Durably on Vercel

Each guide gets one harness running durably on Vercel: the agent, a chat route, and the route that resumes a turn after a crash. Pick the harness your agent uses:

| Harness                                                         | Package                               | Runs in                                                       |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Pi](/docs/agent-harnesses/pi)                                  | `durable-harness/pi-durable` or `/pi` | Your function, with files in a virtual workspace or a Sandbox |
| [fx](/docs/agent-harnesses/fx)                                  | `libfx`                               | Your function, with files in a virtual workspace or a Sandbox |
| [OpenCode](/docs/agent-harnesses/opencode)                      | `durable-harness/opencode`            | Your function, with files in a virtual workspace or a Sandbox |
| [eve](/docs/agent-harnesses/eve)                                | `eve`                                 | An eve app, durable by default                                |
| [Claude Code](/docs/agent-harnesses/claude-code) (experimental) | `durable-harness/claude-code`         | A Vercel Sandbox                                              |
| [Codex](/docs/agent-harnesses/codex) (experimental)             | `durable-harness/codex`               | A Vercel Sandbox                                              |

The `durable-harness` guides share one setup, and each shows it for Next.js and for other frameworks. fx and eve are durable on their own, so their guides use `libfx` and `eve` directly. To learn how durability works, see [Running Agent Harnesses Durably](/docs/agent-harnesses).

These pages apply to every `durable-harness` guide:

- [Tools, files, and documents](/docs/agent-harnesses/tools): what tools do after a crash, where an agent's files live, and typed state with a session.
- [Observability](/docs/agent-harnesses/observability): each session in Vercel Agent Runs.
- [Security](/docs/agent-harnesses/security): what may run in your function, and where commands and files the model picks run instead.
- [Self-hosting](/docs/agent-harnesses/self-hosting): sessions in another World, such as Postgres, on your own servers.

# Observability for Durable Agent Harnesses

> Agent Runs are available in Beta on all plans

Agent Runs shows each session of a durable agent in the Vercel dashboard, with its turns, every model and tool call, timing, and token usage. `durable-harness` sends it a trace with `agentRuns()`, the same integration [eve uses](/docs/agent-runs). This page applies to the guides for [Pi](/docs/agent-harnesses/pi), with either variant, [fx](/docs/agent-harnesses/fx), [OpenCode](/docs/agent-harnesses/opencode), [Claude Code](/docs/agent-harnesses/claude-code), and [Codex](/docs/agent-harnesses/codex).

Here's a Pi session in Agent Runs. Select a span to see its timing, tokens, input, and output, and open the Conversation and Metadata tabs:

*A Pi session in Agent Runs, with made-up values. Its second model call was
interrupted when its function died, and ran again on a new function.*

Vercel bills Agent Runs usage at [Tracing rates](/docs/tracing/configure-tracing#usage-and-pricing) during beta.

## Set up Agent Runs

- ### Install the tracing packages
  `durable-harness` records traces with `@vercel/agent-runs` and sends them with OpenTelemetry's SDK. It loads them only for Agent Runs. Install the versions it's tested with:
  ```bash package-manager
  npm i @vercel/agent-runs@0.0.1 @opentelemetry/sdk-trace-base@2.2.0 @opentelemetry/resources@2.2.0 @opentelemetry/otlp-transformer@0.208.0
  ```
  Without them, `agentRuns()` throws with this list. Agent Runs needs Node.js 24. The rest of `durable-harness` runs on Node.js 22 or later.

- ### Declare the integration
  Declare the integration in `agent-runs.ts`:
  ```ts {3} filename="agent-runs.ts"
  import { agentRuns } from 'durable-harness/instrumentation/otel';

  export default agentRuns();
  ```
  A public session's trace records its model and tool inputs and outputs, and any other session's records only metadata, such as its models, tools, timing, and token usage. To change that, see [Control what Agent Runs receives](#control-what-agent-runs-receives).

  Importing the module makes no network requests, and it doesn't replace your app's global OpenTelemetry provider.

- ### Register it
  Call `register()` once per process, before the agent runs a turn. On Next.js, call it from `instrumentation.ts`. With Vercel Functions in `api/`, call it in the module that makes your agent, so every function that runs turns registers it:
  ```ts {4} filename="instrumentation.ts" framework=nextjs-app
  export async function register() {
    if (process.env.NEXT_RUNTIME !== 'nodejs') return;
    const { default: runs } = await import('./agent-runs');
    runs.register();
  }
  ```
  ```ts {4} filename="lib/agent.ts" framework=other
  import { pi } from 'durable-harness/pi';
  import runs from '../agent-runs.js';

  runs.register(); // once per process, before the agent runs a turn

  export const agent = pi({ model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5' });
  ```
  For an fx agent, also pass `agentRunsHooks()` from `durable-harness/fx` to `createFxAgent`, and make sure `register()` runs before you create the agent. libfx checks for Agent Runs once, when you create the agent, so an agent created before `register()` records only metadata, even for public sessions.

  On Next.js, `instrumentation.ts` already runs before your modules. With Vercel Functions in `api/`, call `register()` above `createFxAgent`:
  ```ts {2,5} filename="lib/agent.ts" framework=nextjs-app
  import { createFxAgent } from 'libfx';
  import { agentRunsHooks } from 'durable-harness/fx';
  import { tools } from './tools'; // your tools, each with idempotent set

  export const agent = createFxAgent({ model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5', tools, hooks: agentRunsHooks() });
  ```
  ```ts {2-3,6,8} filename="lib/agent.ts" framework=other
  import { createFxAgent } from 'libfx';
  import { agentRunsHooks } from 'durable-harness/fx';
  import runs from '../agent-runs.js';
  import { tools } from './tools.js'; // your tools, each with idempotent set

  runs.register(); // before the agent is created

  export const agent = createFxAgent({ model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5', tools, hooks: agentRunsHooks() });
  ```
  For an fx agent with its own World, as in `durability: world(sessions)`, pass that World to `agentRunsHooks({ world: sessions })` too.

- ### Turn on tracing
  Vercel collects traces only for an environment with a sampling rule. Open [**Settings → Tracing**](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%5Bproject%5D%2Fsettings%2Ftracing\&title=Go+to+Tracing+settings) for your project:
  1. Select **Add Sampling Rule**.
  2. Choose **All Environments**, **Production**, or **Preview**.
  3. Set **Rate** to `100%`, so a trace holds every span of its session.
  4. Select **Save**.
  You can also manage sampling rules with [`vercel traces config`](/docs/cli/traces#manage-trace-sampling-rules), in Vercel CLI 62.5 or later. Without a sampling rule, Agent Runs still lists each session, but without its trace, model, or token usage.

- ### Deploy and open a session
  ```bash
  vercel deploy
  ```
  Send a message to the chat route, then open [**Observability → Agent Runs**](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%5Bproject%5D%2Fobservability%2Fagent-runs\&title=Agent+Runs) and select the session.

  The list shows each session's status and token usage. A session whose turn has finished shows as **Waiting**, ready for its next message. The session's page shows the model, timing, model and tool call spans, and token usage. By default, authenticated sessions have an unknown audience, so their traces don't record titles, messages, replies, or tool inputs and outputs. To capture content intentionally, see [Control what Agent Runs receives](#control-what-agent-runs-receives).

## What a trace shows

Each session is one trace, across every function that drives it:

- Each turn is an `invoke_agent` span, with an `agent.step` span for each step and the model and tool calls nested in it. A turn that continues in a later function, after a crash or when its function runs out of time, stays one turn.
- Model calls carry token usage, including cached input when the provider reports it, and cost when the provider supplies it.
- A turn that resumes after a crash reads its finished calls back from the log, so they don't appear twice. A function that finds nothing to do adds no spans.

## Inspect runs with Vercel CLI

Use [`vercel agent-runs`](/docs/cli/agent-runs) to investigate your durable agent's sessions from a terminal or coding agent with shell access. Find projects with activity, then list runs and inspect a session:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel agent-runs projects --scope my-team
vercel agent-runs list --scope my-team --project my-app
vercel agent-runs inspect run_1234567890 --scope my-team --project my-app
vercel agent-runs trace run_1234567890 --scope my-team --project my-app --json --max-field-length 0
```

Replace the example team and project with your own, and use a run ID from the list response. Commands query production by default; add `--environment preview` to inspect preview sessions.

`inspect` shows metadata, lifecycle events, usage, and subagents. `trace` retrieves the recorded conversation. The example uses `--json --max-field-length 0` to preserve returned field values without CLI truncation. The default Markdown view shortens long content. See the [CLI reference](/docs/cli/agent-runs) for time filters and pagination.

The CLI can only return content Agent Runs collected. [Tracing must be enabled](#turn-on-tracing), and your [capture settings](#control-what-agent-runs-receives) determine whether messages and tool inputs and outputs are available. The [Agent Runs limitations](#limitations) below also apply when investigating sessions through the CLI.

## Control what Agent Runs receives

A session's audience decides what its trace records. A public session's trace records its title and its model and tool inputs and outputs. A private or unknown session's trace records only metadata, and the content it leaves out is never recorded, saved, or exported. A session's audience comes from:

- **The chat route.** A route with `authorize: 'public'` makes its sessions public. Any other route leaves them unknown.

- **The agent.** Set `traceAudience` to `'public'` or `'private'` to decide for every session of the agent:

  ```ts {1} filename="lib/agent.ts"
  export const agent = pi({ model: 'anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5', traceAudience: 'private' });
  ```

- **The storage, with `durable-harness/pi-durable`.** Pass `traceAudience` to `openWorldStorage` when it starts a session. The session keeps it, including in the turns the queue route resumes. On a session that exists, it applies to that storage only. `resumeWith(open, { traceAudience })` sets it for the turns the queue route drives in a session that has none.

- **The fx agent.** `agentRunsHooks({ audience })` sets it for every session of that agent.

- **The integration.** `agentRuns({ audience })` sets the audience of sessions that have none.

To change what an audience records, pass `capture` to `agentRuns()`. It gets a session's audience and returns `{ emit, recordInputs, recordOutputs }`. This one keeps the default for public and private sessions, and sends no trace for a session whose audience is unknown:

```ts {4-8} filename="agent-runs.ts"
import { agentRuns } from 'durable-harness/instrumentation/otel';

export default agentRuns({
  capture: (audience) => ({
    emit: audience !== 'unknown', // no trace at all
    recordInputs: audience === 'public',
    recordOutputs: audience === 'public',
  }),
});
```

> **⚠️ Warning:** A public audience shows the session's model and tool content to every project
> member who can read traces. If your agent processes personal, sensitive, or
> regulated data, you may need to disclose this capture under applicable laws
> and in your privacy materials.

To send the same traces to another OpenTelemetry destination, pass its span processors as `spanProcessors`. They get the same spans, with the same content. A tracing failure never fails a turn. It's logged as a warning, or passed to `onError`. In a script or a test, call `forceFlush()` before the process exits.

## Limitations

- Claude Code and Codex run in separate processes in a Sandbox. OpenCode runs an embedded server in your function. Model request and response capture for these harnesses has size limits; larger content is left out or truncated.
- A subagent's calls don't show as a run of their own.
- Agent Runs is shared with eve, and some of its views may not list `durable-harness` sessions yet, even when their traces are recorded. Open the session from the table of runs.

## More resources

- [Agent Runs for eve](/docs/agent-runs)
- [Tracing](/docs/tracing)
- [Vercel Observability](/docs/observability)
- [`durable-harness` on GitHub](https://github.com/vercel-labs/durable-harness)
