# Vercel CDN overview

Vercel's CDN is a globally distributed network that caches content near your visitors, routes requests, and runs compute close to your data. Every deployment includes it automatically.

Unlike traditional CDNs that only cache static assets, Vercel's CDN is framework-aware. It reads your routing, caching, and rendering configuration at build time, with the following benefits:

- **Git-driven and previewable**: Every CDN change is scoped to a branch and deployed to a unique [preview URL](/docs/deployments/environments#preview-environment-pre-production), so you can test routing, caching, and security rules before they reach production.
- **Global network**: [126+ PoPs across 51 countries and 20+ Vercel regions](/docs/regions), with built-in request acceleration and high-availability architecture.
- **Framework-aware, zero config**: CDN configuration and [caching policies](/docs/caching) are an output of the build and deployment process if you are using a supported framework, eliminating the need to define manual cache-control headers.
- **Standard CDN directives**: When needed, you can override [routing and caching rules](/docs/routing). You can also proxy and cache responses from external backends with [external rewrites](/docs/routing/rewrites#rewrites-to-external-origins), and [invalidate content by tag](/docs/caching/cdn-cache/purge) across all frameworks and backends.
- **Default protections**: Unmetered, always-on [DDoS mitigation and network-level security](/docs/vercel-firewall) on every deployment at no extra cost.

## What you can build

You can use Vercel's CDN across a range of architectures:

- **Static sites and marketing pages**: Pre-render pages at build time and serve them from the CDN without invoking your origin.
- **E-commerce storefronts**: Cache product catalogs with [ISR](/docs/incremental-static-regeneration) and revalidate in the background when inventory or pricing changes.
- **Content-driven platforms**: Let editors publish CMS changes that propagate globally within seconds, without a redeployment.
- **SaaS dashboards**: Serve authenticated pages with [Vercel Functions](/docs/functions) while the CDN caches shared assets and API responses.
- **AI-powered applications**: Stream responses from AI models through [streaming functions](/docs/functions/streaming-functions) and cache deterministic results with [runtime cache](/docs/caching/runtime-cache).
- **Multi-region APIs**: Set [Cache-Control headers](/docs/caching/cache-control-headers) for per-region caching and use [rewrites](/docs/routing/rewrites) to proxy requests to external backends.
- **Hybrid architectures**: Mix static, ISR, and dynamic routes in the same project. The CDN applies the right strategy per route from your framework configuration.

### Get started with templates

Deploy a CDN-ready template to see routing, caching, and revalidation in action:

[View all CDN templates](https://vercel.com/templates/cdn)

## How Vercel CDN works

Every request flows through the CDN's routing, caching, and compute layers before reaching your application code. Each layer can resolve the request or pass it to the next.

- [How a request flows through the CDN](/docs/how-vercel-cdn-works)
- [Compression](/docs/how-vercel-cdn-works/compression)

### Global network and regions

Vercel operates 126 Points of Presence (PoPs) across 51 countries. Behind them, compute-capable regions run your code close to your data. Traffic flows between PoPs and regions over a private, low-latency network.

- [Region list and infrastructure details](/docs/regions)

## Routing

The CDN evaluates routing rules before checking any cache. Redirects return a new URL to the client. Rewrites map a public URL to a different backend path. Header rules modify request and response metadata.

- [Redirects](/docs/routing/redirects)
- [Rewrites](/docs/routing/rewrites)
- [Reverse proxy with external rewrites](/docs/routing/rewrites#rewrites-to-external-origins)

## Security

The CDN enforces security before requests reach your application. Every deployment uses HTTPS with automatically provisioned SSL certificates and TLS 1.2/1.3 support. A platform-wide firewall with DDoS mitigation inspects every request at the CDN level. You can also configure a Web Application Firewall (WAF) with custom rules at the project level.

- [CDN security overview](/docs/cdn-security)
- [Encryption & TLS](/docs/cdn-security/encryption)
- [Security headers](/docs/cdn-security/security-headers)
- [Vercel WAF](/docs/vercel-firewall/vercel-waf)

## Caching

Vercel maintains multiple caching tiers to reduce how often your functions run.

### Incremental Static Regeneration

Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) serves cached pages to visitors while regenerating content in the background. When the cache expires, Vercel re-renders the page and updates all regions so visitors always get a fast response. Vercel manages caching, request collapsing, and purging automatically when you use ISR with Next.js, SvelteKit, Nuxt, or Astro.

- [How ISR works](/docs/incremental-static-regeneration)
- [Getting started with ISR](/docs/incremental-static-regeneration/quickstart)
- [ISR usage and pricing](/docs/incremental-static-regeneration/limits-and-pricing)
- [Request collapsing](/docs/incremental-static-regeneration/request-collapsing)

### CDN cache and runtime cache

The CDN cache stores responses across Vercel regions, closest to your visitors. The runtime cache stores fetch results, database queries, and computed values inside your functions.

- [CDN cache](/docs/caching/cdn-cache)
- [Cache-Control headers](/docs/caching/cache-control-headers)
- [Runtime cache](/docs/caching/runtime-cache)

## System headers

Every deployment includes system-level headers on requests and responses. You can use these headers to inspect routing decisions, caching status, and request identity for debugging and observability.

- [Response headers](/docs/headers/response-headers)
- [Request headers](/docs/headers/request-headers)

## Image optimization

You can resize, crop, and convert images to modern formats like WebP and AVIF. Vercel transforms and caches the results on the CDN, so you don't need a separate image pipeline.

- [Image optimization](/docs/image-optimization)

## Custom error pages

You can configure branded error pages for 5xx server errors so visitors see a consistent experience when something goes wrong.

- [Custom error pages](/docs/custom-error-pages)

## Pricing and usage

CDN pricing covers [CDN requests](/docs/manage-cdn-usage#cdn-requests), data transfer to visitors, and [Fast Origin Transfer](/docs/manage-cdn-usage#fast-origin-transfer). Pricing can vary by the region where requests originate.

For resource definitions, rates, usage dashboards, and ways to manage or stop charges, see [CDN pricing and usage](/docs/manage-cdn-usage).

### CDN service tiers

Vercel offers three CDN service tiers for different reliability, cost, and usage patterns: [On-demand CDN](#on-demand-cdn), [Flat Rate CDN](#flat-rate-cdn), and [Flex CDN](#flex-cdn).

#### On-demand CDN

On-demand CDN is the usage-based model for teams that want CDN usage to scale automatically with demand. You pay for the CDN resources your team uses, without choosing a predefined capacity level.

Use On-demand CDN when you need the highest level of reliability, have mission-critical or highly variable traffic, or prefer to pay directly for usage.

#### Flat Rate CDN

[Flat Rate CDN](/docs/pricing/flat-rate-cdn) is a Pro feature that gives your team a fixed monthly price for CDN capacity that matches your typical usage.

Use Flat Rate CDN when you want reliable delivery and predictable monthly CDN costs. Short-term spikes in usage **do not** change your bill, but remain subject to the [fair use guidelines](/docs/pricing/flat-rate-cdn#fair-use-guidelines).

#### Flex CDN

Flex CDN is a best-effort service tier for projects that can tolerate reduced reliability.
Traffic on Flex CDN has no latency or availability guarantees, regardless of level.

Flex CDN is available only to teams using Flat Rate CDN. To move a project onto Flex, see [Excluding projects from Flat Rate CDN](/docs/pricing/flat-rate-cdn#excluding-projects-from-flat-rate-cdn).

title: "Encryption and TLS"
description: "Learn how Vercel encrypts data in transit and at rest."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.134Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/cdn-security/encryption"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Encryption and TLS

Every **deployment** on Vercel is served over an HTTPS connection. Vercel automatically generates [SSL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_Layer_Security) certificates for these unique URLs at no cost.

The CDN automatically forwards any HTTP requests to your **deployment** to HTTPS using the `308` status code:

```bash
HTTP/1.1 308 Moved Permanently
Content-Type: text/plain
Location: https://<your-deployment-host>
```

*An example showing how all \`HTTP\` requests are forwarded to \`HTTPS\`.*

HTTPS redirection is an industry standard and can't be disabled. This ensures that all web content is served over a secure connection, protecting your users' data and privacy.

> **💡 Note:** If your client needs to establish a WebSocket connection, connect using HTTPS
> directly. The WSS protocol doesn't support redirects.

## Supported TLS versions

​Vercel supports TLS version [1.2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_Layer_Security#TLS_1.2) and TLS version [1.3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_Layer_Security#TLS_1.3).

## TLS resumption

​Vercel supports both Session Identifiers and Session Tickets for [TLS session resumption](https://hpbn.co/transport-layer-security-tls/#tls-session-resumption). This improves Time to First Byte (TTFB) for returning visitors.

## OCSP stapling

Vercel [staples an OCSP response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OCSP_stapling) to each TLS handshake. This lets clients skip the network request to check certificate revocation, improving TTFB for first-time visitors.

## Supported ciphers

To protect data integrity, Vercel only supports strong ciphers with [forward secrecy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward_secrecy).

Supported cipher algorithms:

- `TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256` (TLS 1.3)
- `TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384` (TLS 1.3)
- `TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256` (TLS 1.3)
- `ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256` (TLS 1.2)
- `ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256` (TLS 1.2)
- `ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384` (TLS 1.2)
- `ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384` (TLS 1.2)
- `ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305` (TLS 1.2)
- `ECDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305` (TLS 1.2)

This is the [recommended configuration from TLSRef](https://docs.tlsref.org/server-side-tls.html#intermediate-compatibility).

## Post-quantum cryptography

Vercel offers the `X25519MLKEM768` key exchange mechanism during TLS handshakes to protect your deployments against future quantum computing attacks. Your browser negotiates this mechanism automatically if you use:

- Chrome 131 and above
- Firefox 132 and above
- Safari 26 and above

## Encrypted Client Hello (ECH)

Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) encrypts the Server Name Indication (SNI) during the TLS handshake. The SNI is the one part of an otherwise-encrypted HTTPS connection that still exposes which hostname a visitor is connecting to. With ECH, network observers see a connection to Vercel's shared public name, `vercel-ech.com`, rather than your domain.

Vercel manages ECH at the platform level and enables it automatically where it's available.

Browsers use ECH when they can read the ECH configuration from your domain's [HTTPS DNS record](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/HTTPS_RR). ECH works in recent versions of Chrome, Edge, and Firefox. When a browser or its DNS resolver doesn't support ECH, the connection falls back to a standard TLS handshake with no loss of security.

## Support for HSTS

The `.vercel.app` domain (and therefore all of its sub domains, which are the unique URLs set when creating a deployment) support [HSTS](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Strict-Transport-Security) automatically and are preloaded.

```bash
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload;
```

*The default \`Strict-Transport-Security\` header for \*.vercel.app*

Custom domains use HSTS, but only for the particular subdomain.

```bash
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000;
```

*The default \`Strict-Transport-Security\` header for custom domains*

You can modify the `Strict-Transport-Security` header by configuring [custom response headers](/docs/caching/cache-control-headers#custom-response-headers) in your project.

You can set the `max-age` parameter to a different value. It controls how long the client remembers that your site is HTTPS-only. Since Vercel doesn't allow HTTP connections, there's no reason to shorten it.

> **💡 Note:** You can test whether your site qualifies for HSTS Preloading
> [here](https://hstspreload.org/). It also allows submitting the domain to
> Google Chrome's hardcoded HSTS list. Making it onto that list means your site
> will become even faster, as it is always accessed over HTTPS right away,
> instead of the browser following the redirection issued by the CDN.

## How Vercel handles certificates

Vercel uses a wildcard certificate issued for `.vercel.app` to handle all deployment URLs. Vercel generates these certificates through [Let's Encrypt](https://letsencrypt.org/) and keeps them updated automatically.

When you generate custom certificates with `vercel certs issue`, Vercel stores the keys in the database and [encrypts them at rest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_at_rest#Encryption) within the CDN.

When a hostname is requested, the CDN reads the certificate and key from the database to establish the secure connection. Both are cached in memory for optimal SSL termination performance.

## Full specification

For a complete breakdown, see the [SSL Labs report for vercel.com](https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest/analyze.html?d=vercel.com). You can select any IP address. The results are the same for all.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CDN security

Vercel's CDN applies multiple layers of security to every incoming request before it reaches your application. Encryption, firewall protection, and DDoS mitigation all happen at the CDN level, so your deployments are protected by default.

## Encryption and TLS

Vercel serves every deployment over HTTPS and automatically provisions SSL certificates for all deployment URLs and custom domains. The CDN forwards HTTP requests to HTTPS with a `308` status code.

The CDN supports TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 with strong cipher suites that provide [forward secrecy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward_secrecy). TLS session resumption reduces Time to First Byte (TTFB) for returning visitors, and [OCSP stapling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OCSP_stapling) speeds up certificate validation for first-time visitors.

Vercel also supports post-quantum cryptography through the `X25519MLKEM768` key exchange mechanism. This protects your deployments against future quantum computing attacks in Chrome 131+, Firefox 132+, and Safari 26+.

The CDN also supports [Encrypted Client Hello (ECH)](/docs/cdn-security/encryption#encrypted-client-hello-ech), which encrypts the hostname in the TLS handshake so network observers can't see which site a visitor connects to. Vercel manages ECH automatically, with nothing to configure.

- [Encryption & TLS details](/docs/cdn-security/encryption)

## Supported protocols

The CDN negotiates the following protocols through [ALPN](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7301):

- [HTTPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTPS)
- [HTTP/1.1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertext_Transfer_Protocol)
- [HTTP/2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP/2)

## Firewall protection

The Vercel Firewall inspects every request as it arrives at the CDN, before it reaches your application. It operates in three layers: [platform-wide firewall](#platform-wide-firewall), [Web Application Firewall (WAF)](#web-application-firewall-waf), and [bot management](#bot-management).

### Platform-wide firewall

All Vercel customers get an enterprise-grade firewall at no cost. It runs automatically and includes DDoS mitigation and protection against low-quality traffic. You don't need to configure anything.

- [DDoS mitigation](/docs/vercel-firewall/ddos-mitigation)

### Web Application Firewall (WAF)

You can configure custom rules, managed rulesets, and traffic challenges at the project level. The WAF lets you block, challenge, or log requests based on IP, path, headers, geographic location, and other attributes.

- [WAF overview](/docs/vercel-firewall/vercel-waf)
- [Custom rules](/docs/vercel-firewall/vercel-waf/custom-rules)
- [Managed rulesets](/docs/vercel-firewall/vercel-waf/managed-rulesets)

### Bot management

Vercel classifies incoming traffic to separate legitimate bots from automated threats. You can challenge non-browser traffic, control AI crawlers, and allow verified bots like search engines to pass through unchallenged.

- [Bot management](/docs/bot-management)
- [Firewall observability](/docs/vercel-firewall/firewall-observability)

## Security headers

You can configure HTTP security headers to protect visitors from common web vulnerabilities. Vercel applies HSTS automatically on `.vercel.app` domains and custom domains.

Headers you can configure:

- **Content-Security-Policy (CSP)**: Restrict which sources can load scripts, images, and other resources to prevent cross-site scripting (XSS).

- **Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS)**: Tell browsers to always connect over HTTPS.

- **X-Frame-Options**: Prevent your pages from being embedded in iframes to block clickjacking.

- **X-Content-Type-Options**: Stop browsers from MIME-type sniffing responses.

- [Security headers](/docs/cdn-security/security-headers)

## HSTS

The `.vercel.app` domain and all subdomains support HSTS by default and are preloaded in browser HSTS lists. Custom domains also use HSTS. You can modify the `Strict-Transport-Security` header in your project's [response headers configuration](/docs/headers/response-headers).

- [HSTS details](/docs/cdn-security/encryption#support-for-hsts)

title: "Content Security Policy"
description: "Learn how the Content Security Policy (CSP) offers defense against web vulnerabilities, its key features, and best practices."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.134Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/cdn-security/security-headers"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Content Security Policy

Content Security Policy is a browser feature designed to prevent cross-site scripting (XSS) and related code-injection attacks. CSP provides developers with the ability to define an allowlist of sources of trusted content, effectively restricting the browser from loading any resources from non-allowlisted sources.

When a browser receives the `Content-Security-Policy` HTTP header from a web server it adheres to the defined policy, blocking or allowing content loads based on the provided rules.

[XSS](/kb/guide/understanding-xss-attacks) remains one of the most prevalent web application vulnerabilities. In an XSS attack, malicious scripts are injected into websites, which run on the end user's browser, potentially leading to stolen data, session hijacking, and other malicious actions.

CSP can reduce the likelihood of XSS by:

- **Allowlisting content sources** – CSP works by specifying which sources of content are legitimate for a web application. You can define a list of valid sources for scripts, images, stylesheets, and other web resources. Any content not loaded from these approved sources will be blocked. Thus, if an attacker tries to inject a script from an unauthorized source, CSP will prevent it from loading and executing.
- **Inline script blocking** – A common vector for XSS is through inline scripts, which are scripts written directly within the HTML content. CSP can be configured to block all inline scripts, rendering script tags injected by attackers (like `<script>alert('XSS Attack!')</script>`) ineffective.
- **Disallowing `eval()`** – The `eval()` function in JavaScript can be misused to execute arbitrary code, which can be a potential XSS vector. CSP can be set up to disallow the use of `eval()` and its related functions.
- **Nonce and hashes** – If there's a need to allow certain inline scripts (while still blocking others), CSP supports a nonce (number used once) that can be added to a script tag. Only scripts with the correct nonce value will be executed. Similarly, CSP can use hashes to allow the execution of specific inline scripts by matching their hash value.
- **Reporting violations** – CSP can be set in `report-only` mode where policy violations don't result in content being blocked but instead send a report to a specified URI. This helps website administrators detect and respond to potential XSS attempts, allowing them to patch vulnerabilities and refine their CSP rules.
- **Plugin restrictions** – Some XSS attacks might exploit browser plugins. With CSP, you can limit the types of plugins that can be invoked, further reducing potential attack vectors.

While input sanitization and secure coding practices are essential, **CSP acts as a second line of defense**, reducing the risk of [XSS exploits](/kb/guide/understanding-xss-attacks).

Beyond XSS, CSP can prevent the unauthorized loading of content, protecting users from other threats like clickjacking and data injection.

## Content Security Policy headers

```bash
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' cdn.example.com; img-src 'self' img.example.com; style-src 'self';
```

This policy permits:

- Content to be loaded only from the site's own origin by default (`default-src`), unless a more specific directive below allows other sources.
- Scripts to be loaded from the site's own origin and cdn.example.com.
- Images from the site's own origin and img.example.com
- Styles only from the site's origin.

## Best Practices

- Before enforcing a CSP, start with the `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` header. You can do this to keep an eye on possible violations without actually blocking any content. Change to enforcing mode once you know your policy won't break any features.
- Avoid using `unsafe-inline` and `unsafe-eval` . The use of `eval()` and inline scripts/styles can pose security risks. Avoid enabling these unless absolutely necessary as a best practice. Use nonces or hashes to allowlist particular scripts or styles if you need to allow inline scripts or styles.
- Use nonces for inline scripts and styles. To allow that particular inline content, a nonce (number used once) can be added to a script or style tag, the CSP header, or both. This ensures that only the inline scripts and styles you have explicitly permitted will be used.
- Be as detailed as you can, and avoid using too general sources like `*`. List the specific subdomains you want to allow rather than allowing all subdomains (`*.domain.com`).
- Keep directives updated. As your project evolves, the sources from which you load content might change. Ensure you update your CSP directives accordingly.

Keep in mind that while CSP is a robust security measure, it's part of a multi-layered security strategy. Input validation, output encoding, and other security practices remain crucial.

Additionally, while CSP is supported by modern browsers, nuances exist in their implementations. Ensure you **test your policy across diverse browsers**, accounting for variations and ensuring the same security postures.

title: "Chat SDK Adapters"
description: "Choose platform and state adapters for a Chat SDK bot on Vercel."

# Chat SDK Adapters

Chat SDK uses **platform adapters** to receive events and deliver messages, and a **state adapter** to share subscriptions, locks, and cached data across requests. Choose a platform adapter for each place your bot runs and a state adapter for its deployment environment.

## Platform adapters

These adapters cover common destinations for bots deployed on Vercel. Follow each adapter's documentation for its credentials, webhook setup, and supported features.

| Platform | Package | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Discord](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/discord) | `@chat-adapter/discord` | Community bots, slash commands, and threads. |
| [GitHub](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/github) | `@chat-adapter/github` | Bots that participate in issues and pull requests. |
| [Gmail](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/gmail) | `@chat-adapter/gmail` | Receive labeled emails and send replies in email threads. |
| [Linear](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/linear) | `@chat-adapter/linear` | Bots that respond in issue comment threads and agent sessions. |
| [Linq](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/vendor-official/linq) | `@linqapp/chat-sdk-adapter` | Send and receive iMessage and SMS messages. |
| [Liveblocks](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/vendor-official/liveblocks) | `@liveblocks/chat-sdk-adapter` | Bots that read and reply in Liveblocks comment threads. |
| [Microsoft Teams](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/teams) | `@chat-adapter/teams` | Conversations and cards in Teams. |
| [Resend](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/vendor-official/resend) | `@resend/chat-sdk-adapter` | Inbound email and replies in email threads. |
| [Slack](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/slack) | `@chat-adapter/slack` | Workspace messages, threads, and interactive responses. |
| [Telegram](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/telegram) | `@chat-adapter/telegram` | Chat messages and bot interactions. |
| [Twitch](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/twitch) | `@chat-adapter/twitch` | Read and reply in channel chat through EventSub webhooks. |
| [Web](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/web) | `@chat-adapter/web` | A browser chat interface connected to the same bot. |

The [adapter directory](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters) includes more platforms and identifies who maintains each adapter:

- **Official** adapters are maintained by Vercel.
- **Vendor-official** adapters are maintained by the platform vendor.
- **Community** adapters are maintained by third-party developers.

### Check capabilities and delivery requirements

A shared API doesn't give every platform the same capabilities. Check the [platform feature matrix](https://chat-sdk.dev/docs/platform-adapters) before depending on streaming, attachments, buttons, or message editing.

Also check how the platform delivers events. For example, Discord interactions arrive through HTTP webhooks, while regular messages and reactions require its [Gateway connection](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/discord#http-interactions-vs-gateway). The Web adapter requires your application's authentication through `getUser`.

To process background jobs from a conversation, keep the webhook in Vercel Functions and use [Vercel Daemons with Chat SDK](/docs/chat-sdk/integrations/daemons). The worker consumes queued jobs and replies with credentials from Vercel Connect.

## State adapters

On Vercel, use a shared database so subscriptions and processing state remain available when requests reach different function instances.

| State adapter | Package | When to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Redis](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/redis) | `@chat-adapter/state-redis` | Store shared state in Redis. Reads `REDIS_URL` by default. |
| [ioredis](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/ioredis) | `@chat-adapter/state-ioredis` | Use an existing ioredis-based Redis setup. |
| [PostgreSQL](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/postgres) | `@chat-adapter/state-pg` | Use PostgreSQL for bot state. Reads `POSTGRES_URL`, falling back to `DATABASE_URL`. |
| [Memory](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/memory) | `@chat-adapter/state-memory` | Run local tests with state held in one process. |

Provision a database through the [Vercel Marketplace](/marketplace/category/storage), or connect an existing database through your project's [environment variables](/docs/environment-variables). The [quickstart](/docs/chat-sdk/quickstart#link-your-project-and-connect-redis) shows Redis setup.

State adapters coordinate message processing. For work that needs durable execution across interruptions, combine your bot with [Workflows](/docs/workflows) or [eve](/docs/chat-sdk/eve).

## Configure adapters with the CLI

Pass the platform and state adapter names to [`create-chat-sdk`](https://chat-sdk.dev/docs/create-chat-sdk). For example, scaffold one bot with Slack, Microsoft Teams, Redis, and Vercel Connect:

```bash filename="Terminal"
pnpm create chat-sdk@latest my-bot --adapter slack teams redis --connect --pm pnpm -y
```

The CLI generates the adapter configuration and webhook routes. Complete each platform's connector setup and supply the environment variables listed in `.env.example`. Follow the [quickstart](/docs/chat-sdk/quickstart) for a complete Slack example.

## Use Vercel Connect

For supported adapters, [Vercel Connect](/docs/connect/frameworks/chat-sdk) supplies provider credentials at runtime. Trigger-capable connectors also verify provider events and forward them to a deployed webhook route.

Connect support varies by adapter. In particular, Notion and Telegram use Connect for outbound credentials while retaining their native inbound verification. See the [Connect capability table](/docs/connect/frameworks/chat-sdk#check-platform-capabilities) before configuring a new platform.

## Next steps

- [Create and deploy a Slack bot](/docs/chat-sdk/quickstart)
- [Route Chat SDK messages to an eve agent](/docs/chat-sdk/eve)
- [Browse all adapters](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters)
- [Build your own adapter](https://chat-sdk.dev/docs/contributing/building)

title: "Using eve with Chat SDK"
description: "Send Chat SDK messages to an eve agent with a channel, persistent state, and Vercel Connect."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.138Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/chat-sdk/eve"

# Using eve with Chat SDK

Use [eve's Chat SDK channel](https://eve.dev/docs/channels/chat-sdk) to send platform messages into an [eve agent](/docs/frameworks/agents/eve). Your Chat SDK handlers choose which events start a turn; eve runs the agent and delivers its response back to the conversation.

This is useful when you already have Chat SDK handlers or need an adapter from the [adapter directory](/docs/chat-sdk/adapters). For a new Slack-only eve agent, the built-in Slack channel provides a guided setup with `eve add channel/slack` and Vercel Connect.

## Prerequisites

- An [eve project](/docs/frameworks/agents/eve#create-an-agent) with instructions and model credentials configured for deployment
- Node.js 24 or later and the [Vercel CLI](/docs/cli)
- Permission to install an app in a Slack workspace

The example adds a Chat SDK channel to your eve project. Use it as the project's Slack entry point; an existing Slack channel must not mount the same webhook path.

## Install the dependencies

From your eve project, install the current eve release, Chat SDK, the Slack and Redis adapters, and Vercel Connect:

**pnpm**

```bash
pnpm i eve@latest chat @chat-adapter/slack @chat-adapter/state-redis @vercel/connect
```

**yarn**

```bash
yarn add eve@latest chat @chat-adapter/slack @chat-adapter/state-redis @vercel/connect
```

**npm**

```bash
npm i eve@latest chat @chat-adapter/slack @chat-adapter/state-redis @vercel/connect
```

**bun**

```bash
bun add eve@latest chat @chat-adapter/slack @chat-adapter/state-redis @vercel/connect
```

## Connect Slack and Redis

Link the eve project to Vercel and create a Slack connector:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel link
vercel connect create slack --name my-agent --triggers
```

Complete Connect's guided setup and Slack workspace installation, then attach the connector to your project:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel connect attach slack/my-agent --environment production --triggers --trigger-path /eve/v1/slack
```

Use the connector UID returned during setup if it differs from `slack/my-agent`, both here and in the code below. Connect forwards Slack events to `/eve/v1/slack` on your Production deployment.

Add a Redis database through the [Marketplace](/marketplace/category/storage):

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel integration add upstash/upstash-kv
```

Ensure `REDIS_URL` is available in the project's Production environment. You can also use an existing Redis database by adding its connection URL to your [environment variables](/docs/environment-variables).

## Add the channel

Create `agent/channels/chat.ts`, or `agent/channels/chat.js` for JavaScript:

**agent/channels/chat.ts**

```typescript filename="agent/channels/chat.ts"
import { createSlackAdapter } from '@chat-adapter/slack';
import { createRedisState } from '@chat-adapter/state-redis';
import { connectSlackAdapter } from '@vercel/connect/chat';
import { chatSdkChannel } from 'eve/channels/chat-sdk';

export const { bot, channel, send } = chatSdkChannel({
  userName: 'my-agent',
  adapters: {
    slack: createSlackAdapter({
      ...connectSlackAdapter('slack/my-agent'),
    }),
  },
  state: createRedisState(),
});

bot.onNewMention(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.subscribe();
  await send(message.text, {
    thread,
    idempotencyKey: message.id,
  });
});

bot.onSubscribedMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await send(message.text, {
    thread,
    idempotencyKey: message.id,
  });
});

export default channel;
```

**agent/channels/chat.js**

```javascript filename="agent/channels/chat.js"
import { createSlackAdapter } from '@chat-adapter/slack';
import { createRedisState } from '@chat-adapter/state-redis';
import { connectSlackAdapter } from '@vercel/connect/chat';
import { chatSdkChannel } from 'eve/channels/chat-sdk';

export const { bot, channel, send } = chatSdkChannel({
  userName: 'my-agent',
  adapters: {
    slack: createSlackAdapter({
      ...connectSlackAdapter('slack/my-agent'),
    }),
  },
  state: createRedisState(),
});

bot.onNewMention(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.subscribe();
  await send(message.text, {
    thread,
    idempotencyKey: message.id,
  });
});

bot.onSubscribedMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await send(message.text, {
    thread,
    idempotencyKey: message.id,
  });
});

export default channel;
```

`chatSdkChannel` returns a Chat SDK `bot`, an eve `channel`, and a `send` function. Export the channel as the module default so eve discovers it. Call `send` inside a Chat SDK event handler, passing the thread to start or continue that conversation's session.

The example subscribes to mentioned threads and passes the platform message ID as an `idempotencyKey`. This lets eve reject repeated input within its recent-key window; Chat SDK's separate event deduplication doesn't guarantee delivery to eve.

Redis stores Chat SDK subscriptions and coordination data. eve manages the agent session separately.

## Deploy and test

Deploy the agent:

```bash filename="Terminal"
pnpm exec eve deploy
```

The channel mounts `GET` and `POST` handlers at `/eve/v1/slack`, matching the Connect trigger destination. eve owns the webhook lifecycle, so you don't need the Next.js Route Handler from a standalone Chat SDK app.

Invite the installed app to a Slack channel and mention it with a question. The agent should answer in the thread. Reply in the thread to continue the session. Check [runtime logs](/docs/logs/runtime) and [eve observability](https://eve.dev/docs/observability/otel) if events arrive but the agent doesn't respond.

## Adapt delivery to another platform

Swap the Slack adapter for another [platform adapter](/docs/chat-sdk/adapters#platform-adapters) and complete its authentication setup. By default, each adapter key becomes a route under `/eve/v1`: an adapter registered as `resend`, for example, receives webhooks at `/eve/v1/resend`. Connect is available only for supported adapters.

The channel streams replies by default. For email and other destinations that can't edit sent messages, set `streaming: false` in `chatSdkChannel` so the reply is posted when the turn completes. See the [eve channel reference](https://eve.dev/docs/channels/chat-sdk) for route overrides, attachments, and human input handling.

## Next steps

- [Choose platform and state adapters](/docs/chat-sdk/adapters)
- [Configure Connect credentials and triggers](/docs/connect/frameworks/chat-sdk)
- [Explore eve channels](https://eve.dev/docs/channels/overview)

title: "Chat SDK with Hono"
description: "Add a Chat SDK bot to Hono, receive Slack events through Vercel Connect, and deploy on Vercel."

# Chat SDK with Hono

Use a Hono POST handler to receive Slack events and Vercel Functions to keep your bot running after the webhook responds.

## Prerequisites

Start with an existing Hono project configured for [deployment on Vercel](/docs/frameworks/backend/hono), the latest [Vercel CLI](/docs/cli), and permission to install an app in your Slack workspace.

## Install Chat SDK

From your project directory, install the packages with pnpm:

```bash filename="Terminal"
pnpm add chat @chat-adapter/slack @chat-adapter/state-redis @vercel/connect @vercel/functions
```

## Create your bot

Create `lib/bot.ts` at the project root. This bot uses Vercel Connect for Slack authentication, stores subscriptions in Redis, and responds to mentions and thread replies. Keep this module on the server.

**lib/bot.ts**

```typescript filename="lib/bot.ts"
import { Chat } from 'chat';
import { createSlackAdapter } from '@chat-adapter/slack';
import { createRedisState } from '@chat-adapter/state-redis';
import { connectSlackAdapter } from '@vercel/connect/chat';

export const bot = new Chat({
  userName: 'my-bot',
  adapters: {
    slack: createSlackAdapter({
      ...connectSlackAdapter('slack/my-bot'),
    }),
  },
  state: createRedisState(),
});

bot.onNewMention(async (thread) => {
  await thread.subscribe();
  await thread.post('Hello! Reply here to chat.');
});

bot.onSubscribedMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(message.text);
});
```

**lib/bot.js**

```javascript filename="lib/bot.js"
import { Chat } from 'chat';
import { createSlackAdapter } from '@chat-adapter/slack';
import { createRedisState } from '@chat-adapter/state-redis';
import { connectSlackAdapter } from '@vercel/connect/chat';

export const bot = new Chat({
  userName: 'my-bot',
  adapters: {
    slack: createSlackAdapter({
      ...connectSlackAdapter('slack/my-bot'),
    }),
  },
  state: createRedisState(),
});

bot.onNewMention(async (thread) => {
  await thread.subscribe();
  await thread.post('Hello! Reply here to chat.');
});

bot.onSubscribedMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(message.text);
});
```

## Add the webhook route

Add the route to `src/index.ts`. For a new entry point, use the following example. If you already export a Hono app, register the route on that instance.

**src/index.ts**

```typescript filename="src/index.ts"
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { waitUntil } from '@vercel/functions';
import { bot } from '../lib/bot';

const app = new Hono();

app.post('/api/webhooks/slack', (c) => {
  return bot.webhooks.slack(c.req.raw, { waitUntil });
});

export default app;
```

**src/index.js**

```javascript filename="src/index.js"
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { waitUntil } from '@vercel/functions';
import { bot } from '../lib/bot';

const app = new Hono();

app.post('/api/webhooks/slack', (c) => {
  return bot.webhooks.slack(c.req.raw, { waitUntil });
});

export default app;
```

`c.req.raw` provides the original Web `Request`. Pass it to the adapter before middleware or handlers consume its body. The default export lets Vercel detect and deploy your Hono app. `waitUntil` from `@vercel/functions` keeps the invocation alive while the bot finishes processing.

## Connect Slack and deploy

From the project directory, link your app to Vercel and connect a Redis database:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel link
vercel integration add upstash/upstash-kv
```

Ensure the integration supplies `REDIS_URL` in the project's **Production** environment. If you already have Redis, add its connection URL as `REDIS_URL` in your project's [environment variables](/docs/environment-variables). Use separate databases for development and production.

Create a Slack connector and allow token requests from the project's Production and Development environments. Attach its trigger to your production webhook route:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel connect create slack --name my-bot --triggers
vercel connect attach slack/my-bot --environment production --environment development --triggers --trigger-path /api/webhooks/slack
```

Follow the prompts to authorize and install the Slack app. If you choose a different connector name, update `slack/my-bot` in your bot configuration and attach command. Connect manages the Slack credentials and verifies provider events before forwarding them. The adapter verifies the forwarded request with Vercel OIDC.

Deploy your app:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel --prod
```

Invite the bot to a Slack channel and mention it. It should reply with a greeting and echo subsequent replies in that thread. Check [runtime logs](/docs/observability/runtime-logs) if it does not respond.

Vercel deployments receive `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN` automatically. For local outbound API calls, configure a development `REDIS_URL` and run `vercel env pull .env.local`. This supplies a Development OIDC token, which can access the connector because the attachment above enables Development.

Connect forwards inbound events to deployed URLs, not `localhost`. To test inbound events before production, [attach the trigger to a Preview branch](/docs/cli/connect#vercel-connect-attach).

## Next steps

- [Hono on Vercel](/docs/frameworks/backend/hono)
- [Hono request API](https://hono.dev/docs/api/request#raw)
- [Add more platform adapters](/docs/chat-sdk/adapters)

title: "Chat SDK with Next.js"
description: "Add a Chat SDK bot to Next.js, receive Slack events through Vercel Connect, and deploy on Vercel."

# Chat SDK with Next.js

Use an App Router Route Handler to receive Slack events and `after` to process them after responding. For a new bot, use the [Chat SDK quickstart](/docs/chat-sdk/quickstart), which scaffolds a Next.js app with `create-chat-sdk`. Follow this guide to add the bot to an existing app.

## Prerequisites

Start with an existing Next.js 15.1 or later project configured for [deployment on Vercel](/docs/frameworks/full-stack/nextjs), the latest [Vercel CLI](/docs/cli), and permission to install an app in your Slack workspace.

## Install Chat SDK

From your project directory, install the packages with pnpm:

```bash filename="Terminal"
pnpm add chat @chat-adapter/slack @chat-adapter/state-redis @vercel/connect
```

## Create your bot

Create `lib/bot.ts` at the project root. This bot uses Vercel Connect for Slack authentication, stores subscriptions in Redis, and responds to mentions and thread replies. Keep this module on the server.

**lib/bot.ts**

```typescript filename="lib/bot.ts"
import { Chat } from 'chat';
import { createSlackAdapter } from '@chat-adapter/slack';
import { createRedisState } from '@chat-adapter/state-redis';
import { connectSlackAdapter } from '@vercel/connect/chat';

export const bot = new Chat({
  userName: 'my-bot',
  adapters: {
    slack: createSlackAdapter({
      ...connectSlackAdapter('slack/my-bot'),
    }),
  },
  state: createRedisState(),

  await thread.subscribe();
  await thread.post('Hello! Reply here to chat.');
});

bot.onSubscribedMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(message.text);
});
```

**lib/bot.js**

## Add the webhook route

Create `app/api/webhooks/slack/route.ts`. If your app uses a `src` directory, put both `app` and `lib` inside `src` so the relative import stays the same.

**app/api/webhooks/slack/route.ts**

```typescript filename="app/api/webhooks/slack/route.ts"
import { after } from 'next/server';
import { bot } from '../../../../lib/bot';

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  return bot.webhooks.slack(request, {
    waitUntil: (task) => after(() => task),
  });
}
```

**app/api/webhooks/slack/route.js**

```javascript filename="app/api/webhooks/slack/route.js"
import { after } from 'next/server';
import { bot } from '../../../../lib/bot';

export async function POST(request) {
  return bot.webhooks.slack(request, {
    waitUntil: (task) => after(() => task),
  });
}
```

Return the adapter's response directly. Passing each background task to `after` keeps it running after the webhook response. Use the Node.js runtime, which is the App Router default, for the Redis connection.

## Connect Slack and deploy

From the project directory, link your app to Vercel and connect a Redis database:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel link
vercel integration add upstash/upstash-kv
```

Ensure the integration supplies `REDIS_URL` in the project's **Production** environment. If you already have Redis, add its connection URL as `REDIS_URL` in your project's [environment variables](/docs/environment-variables). Use separate databases for development and production.

Create a Slack connector and allow token requests from the project's Production and Development environments. Attach its trigger to your production webhook route:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel connect create slack --name my-bot --triggers
vercel connect attach slack/my-bot --environment production --environment development --triggers --trigger-path /api/webhooks/slack
```

Follow the prompts to authorize and install the Slack app. If you choose a different connector name, update `slack/my-bot` in your bot configuration and attach command. Connect manages the Slack credentials and verifies provider events before forwarding them. The adapter verifies the forwarded request with Vercel OIDC.

Deploy your app:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel --prod
```

Invite the bot to a Slack channel and mention it. It should reply with a greeting and echo subsequent replies in that thread. Check [runtime logs](/docs/observability/runtime-logs) if it does not respond.

Vercel deployments receive `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN` automatically. For local outbound API calls, configure a development `REDIS_URL` and run `vercel env pull .env.local`. This supplies a Development OIDC token, which can access the connector because the attachment above enables Development.

Connect forwards inbound events to deployed URLs, not `localhost`. To test inbound events before production, [attach the trigger to a Preview branch](/docs/cli/connect#vercel-connect-attach).

## Add browser chat with the Web Adapter

The [Web Adapter](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/web) lets a browser chat UI use the same bot as Slack. Browser messages go to `onDirectMessage`, and the adapter streams the bot's replies back to the client. Your app authenticates these requests; Vercel Connect continues to handle the Slack integration.

### Configure the adapter

Install the Web Adapter and its client dependencies:

```bash filename="Terminal"
pnpm add @chat-adapter/web ai @ai-sdk/react
```

Implement `getUserFromSession(request)` in `lib/auth.ts` using your application's authentication provider. This is an application-defined helper, not a Chat SDK export. It must validate the session and return a stable `{ id: string, name?: string }` for a signed-in user, or `null` to reject the request with HTTP 401. User IDs must not contain `:`. See [Web Adapter authentication](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/web#authentication). For a Passport-protected app, follow [Chat SDK with Vercel Passport](/docs/chat-sdk/integrations/passport) to resolve a verified identity and use per-user history.

Update `lib/bot.ts` with the Web Adapter and a direct-message handler, keeping the Slack adapter, Redis state, and existing handlers:

**lib/bot.ts**

```typescript filename="lib/bot.ts"
import { Chat } from 'chat';
import { createWebAdapter } from '@chat-adapter/web';
import { getUserFromSession } from './auth';
import { createSlackAdapter } from '@chat-adapter/slack';
import { createRedisState } from '@chat-adapter/state-redis';
import { connectSlackAdapter } from '@vercel/connect/chat';

export const bot = new Chat({
  userName: 'my-bot',
  adapters: {
    web: createWebAdapter({
      userName: 'my-bot',
      protocol: 'ai-sdk',
      getUser: getUserFromSession,
    }),
    slack: createSlackAdapter({
      ...connectSlackAdapter('slack/my-bot'),
    }),
  },
  state: createRedisState(),
});

bot.onDirectMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(`You said: ${message.text}`);
});

bot.onNewMention(async (thread) => {
  await thread.subscribe();
  await thread.post('Hello! Reply here to chat.');
});

bot.onSubscribedMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(message.text);
});
```

**lib/bot.js**

```javascript filename="lib/bot.js"
import { Chat } from 'chat';
import { createWebAdapter } from '@chat-adapter/web';
import { getUserFromSession } from './auth';
import { createSlackAdapter } from '@chat-adapter/slack';
import { createRedisState } from '@chat-adapter/state-redis';
import { connectSlackAdapter } from '@vercel/connect/chat';

export const bot = new Chat({
  userName: 'my-bot',
  adapters: {
    web: createWebAdapter({
      userName: 'my-bot',
      protocol: 'ai-sdk',
      getUser: getUserFromSession,
    }),
    slack: createSlackAdapter({
      ...connectSlackAdapter('slack/my-bot'),
    }),
  },
  state: createRedisState(),
});

bot.onDirectMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(`You said: ${message.text}`);
});

bot.onNewMention(async (thread) => {
  await thread.subscribe();
  await thread.post('Hello! Reply here to chat.');
});

bot.onSubscribedMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(message.text);
});
```

The `ai-sdk` protocol matches the React client below. Redis stores the server-side message history; the adapter does not trust the browser as a source of prior conversation turns.

### Add the browser endpoint

Create `app/api/chat/route.ts`. If you use a `src` directory, keep `lib` inside it as described above. This endpoint receives browser requests directly, without a Connect trigger.

**app/api/chat/route.ts**

```typescript filename="app/api/chat/route.ts"
import { after } from 'next/server';
import { bot } from '../../../lib/bot';

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  return bot.webhooks.web(request, {
    waitUntil: (task) => after(() => task),
  });
}
```

**app/api/chat/route.js**

```javascript filename="app/api/chat/route.js"
import { after } from 'next/server';
import { bot } from '../../../lib/bot';

export async function POST(request) {
  return bot.webhooks.web(request, {
    waitUntil: (task) => after(() => task),
  });
}
```

### Connect the browser client

Create `app/chat/page.tsx` as a Client Component. The Web Adapter helper configures the AI SDK transport for `/api/chat`:

**app/chat/page.tsx**

```tsx filename="app/chat/page.tsx"
'use client';

import { useChat } from '@chat-adapter/web/react';

export default function ChatPage() {
  const { messages, sendMessage, status, error } = useChat({
    api: '/api/chat',
    threadId: 'support',
  });
  const busy = status === 'submitted' || status === 'streaming';

  return (
    <section aria-label="Chat">
      {messages.map((message) => (
        <p key={message.id}>
          {message.parts
            .map((part) => (part.type === 'text' ? part.text : ''))
            .join('')}
        </p>
      ))}
      <button disabled={busy} onClick={() => sendMessage({ text: 'Hello' })}>
        Send a test message
      </button>
      {error && (
        <p role="alert">Could not send your message. Please try again.</p>
      )}
    </section>
  );
}
```

**app/chat/page.jsx**

```jsx filename="app/chat/page.jsx"
'use client';

import { useChat } from '@chat-adapter/web/react';

export default function ChatPage() {
  const { messages, sendMessage, status, error } = useChat({
    api: '/api/chat',
    threadId: 'support',
  });
  const busy = status === 'submitted' || status === 'streaming';

  return (
    <section aria-label="Chat">
      {messages.map((message) => (
        <p key={message.id}>
          {message.parts
            .map((part) => (part.type === 'text' ? part.text : ''))
            .join('')}
        </p>
      ))}
      <button disabled={busy} onClick={() => sendMessage({ text: 'Hello' })}>
        Send a test message
      </button>
      {error && (
        <p role="alert">Could not send your message. Please try again.</p>
      )}
    </section>
  );
}
```

Use `messages` to render the conversation and `sendMessage({ text })` to submit text from your own input. The helper also exposes `stop()` to cancel a response.

After configuring authentication, sign in and open `/chat`. Select **Send a test message** to send `Hello`; the bot should respond with `You said: Hello`. The `support` conversation ID is scoped to the authenticated user by the adapter. Generate a different conversation ID when you want to start a new conversation.

For a fuller chat interface, see the [official Next.js example](https://github.com/vercel/chat/tree/main/examples/nextjs-chat).

# Chat SDK with Nitro

Use a Nitro route to receive Slack events and process them with Chat SDK. This guide uses Nitro 3 and its `nitro` package. For a Nuxt 4 app using Nitro 2, follow the [Nuxt guide](/docs/chat-sdk/frameworks/nuxt).

## Prerequisites

Start with an existing Nitro project configured for [deployment on Vercel](/docs/frameworks/backend/nitro), the latest [Vercel CLI](/docs/cli), and permission to install an app in your Slack workspace.

## Install Chat SDK

From your project directory, install the packages with pnpm:

```bash filename="Terminal"
pnpm add chat @chat-adapter/slack @chat-adapter/state-redis @vercel/connect
```

## Create your bot

## Add the webhook route

Enable filesystem routing in `nitro.config.ts`. Merge these options into your existing configuration:

**nitro.config.ts**

```typescript filename="nitro.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from 'nitro';

export default defineConfig({
  serverDir: './',
  preset: 'vercel',
});
```

**nitro.config.js**

```javascript filename="nitro.config.js"
import { defineConfig } from 'nitro';

export default defineConfig({
  serverDir: './',
  preset: 'vercel',
});
```

Create `routes/api/webhooks/slack.post.ts`. With `serverDir: './'`, this maps to `/api/webhooks/slack`. Use `routes/api/` rather than a top-level `api/` directory for [Nitro on Vercel](https://nitro.build/deploy/providers/vercel#api-routes).

**routes/api/webhooks/slack.post.ts**

```typescript filename="routes/api/webhooks/slack.post.ts"
import { defineHandler } from 'nitro';
import { bot } from '../../../lib/bot';

export default defineHandler((event) => {
  return bot.webhooks.slack(event.req, {
    waitUntil: (task) => event.waitUntil(task),
  });
});
```

**routes/api/webhooks/slack.post.js**

```javascript filename="routes/api/webhooks/slack.post.js"
import { defineHandler } from 'nitro';
import { bot } from '../../../lib/bot';

export default defineHandler((event) => {
  return bot.webhooks.slack(event.req, {
    waitUntil: (task) => event.waitUntil(task),
  });
});
```

Nitro 3 exposes the Web `Request` as `event.req`. Return the adapter's response directly and use `event.waitUntil` to track background work. Leave the request body unread until the adapter handles it.

# Chat SDK with Nuxt

Use a Nuxt server API route to receive Slack events and pass them to Chat SDK. This guide targets Nuxt 4 with Nitro 2 and H3 1. For a standalone Nitro 3 app, use the [Nitro guide](/docs/chat-sdk/frameworks/nitro).

## Prerequisites

Start with an existing Nuxt project configured for [deployment on Vercel](/docs/frameworks/full-stack/nuxt), the latest [Vercel CLI](/docs/cli), and permission to install an app in your Slack workspace.

## Install Chat SDK

From your project directory, install the packages with pnpm:

```bash filename="Terminal"
pnpm add chat @chat-adapter/slack @chat-adapter/state-redis @vercel/connect @vercel/functions
```

## Create your bot

Create `lib/bot.ts` at the project root. This bot uses Vercel Connect for Slack authentication, stores subscriptions in Redis, and responds to mentions and thread replies. Keep this module on the server.

**lib/bot.ts**

```typescript filename="lib/bot.ts"
import { Chat } from 'chat';
import { createSlackAdapter } from '@chat-adapter/slack';
import { createRedisState } from '@chat-adapter/state-redis';

  await thread.subscribe();
  await thread.post('Hello! Reply here to chat.');

bot.onSubscribedMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(message.text);
});
```

**lib/bot.js**

```javascript filename="lib/bot.js"
import { Chat } from 'chat';

  await thread.subscribe();
  await thread.post('Hello! Reply here to chat.');
});

bot.onSubscribedMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(message.text);
});
```

## Add the webhook route

Create `server/api/webhooks/slack.post.ts`. Nuxt auto-imports `defineEventHandler` and `toWebRequest` for server routes. The `.post` suffix limits the route to POST requests.

**server/api/webhooks/slack.post.ts**

```typescript filename="server/api/webhooks/slack.post.ts"
import { waitUntil } from '@vercel/functions';
import { bot } from '../../../lib/bot';

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  return bot.webhooks.slack(toWebRequest(event), {
    waitUntil,
  });
});
```

**server/api/webhooks/slack.post.js**

```javascript filename="server/api/webhooks/slack.post.js"
import { waitUntil } from '@vercel/functions';
import { bot } from '../../../lib/bot';

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  return bot.webhooks.slack(toWebRequest(event), {
    waitUntil,
  });
});
```

H3's [`toWebRequest`](https://v1.h3.dev/utils/request#towebrequestevent) converts the incoming event to the Web `Request` expected by Chat SDK. Pass it through without first calling `readBody` or `readRawBody`.

`waitUntil` from `@vercel/functions` registers background work with the Vercel invocation so the bot can finish after the adapter responds. Use this helper for Nitro 2's Node.js Vercel preset; `event.waitUntil` does not connect those tasks to the invocation.

Deploy with Nuxt's server output, rather than a static-only build, so the webhook route runs on Vercel.

## Connect Slack and deploy

From the project directory, link your app to Vercel and connect a Redis database:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel link
vercel integration add upstash/upstash-kv
```

Ensure the integration supplies `REDIS_URL` in the project's **Production** environment. If you already have Redis, add its connection URL as `REDIS_URL` in your project's [environment variables](/docs/environment-variables). Use separate databases for development and production.

Create a Slack connector and allow token requests from the project's Production and Development environments. Attach its trigger to your production webhook route:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel connect create slack --name my-bot --triggers
vercel connect attach slack/my-bot --environment production --environment development --triggers --trigger-path /api/webhooks/slack
```

Follow the prompts to authorize and install the Slack app. If you choose a different connector name, update `slack/my-bot` in your bot configuration and attach command.   await thread.post(`You said: ${message.text}`);
```javascript filename="lib/bot.js"
});

bot.onNewMention(async (thread) => {
  await thread.subscribe();
  await thread.post('Hello! Reply here to chat.');
});

bot.onSubscribedMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(message.text);
});
```

The `ai-sdk` protocol matches the Vue client below. Keep the Redis state adapter so message history is shared across function instances.

### Add the browser endpoint

Create `server/api/chat.post.ts`. For Nuxt 4 with Nitro 2, convert the H3 event with `toWebRequest` and use Vercel's `waitUntil` to register background work:

**server/api/chat.post.ts**

```typescript filename="server/api/chat.post.ts"
import { waitUntil } from '@vercel/functions';
import { bot } from '../../lib/bot';

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  return bot.webhooks.web(toWebRequest(event), { waitUntil });
});
```

**server/api/chat.post.js**

```javascript filename="server/api/chat.post.js"
import { waitUntil } from '@vercel/functions';
import { bot } from '../../lib/bot';

export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  return bot.webhooks.web(toWebRequest(event), { waitUntil });
});
```

### Connect the browser client

Create `app/pages/chat.vue`. Keep the object returned by `useChat` intact; destructuring its properties loses Vue reactivity:

```html filename="app/pages/chat.vue"
<script setup>
import { useChat } from '@chat-adapter/web/vue';

const chat = useChat({ api: '/api/chat', threadId: 'support' });
</script>

<template>
  <section aria-label="Chat">
    <div v-for="message in chat.messages" :key="message.id">
      <template v-for="(part, index) in message.parts" :key="index">
        <p v-if="part.type === 'text'">{{ part.text }}</p>
      </template>
    </div>
    <button
      :disabled="chat.status === 'submitted' || chat.status === 'streaming'"
      @click="chat.sendMessage({ text: 'Hello' })"
    >
      Send a test message
    </button>
    <p v-if="chat.error" role="alert">
      Could not send your message. Please try again.
    </p>
  </section>
</template>
```

The client sends directly to `/api/chat`; no Connect trigger is needed for browser traffic. `chat.sendMessage({ text })` submits a message, and `chat.stop()` cancels a response.

After configuring authentication, sign in and open `/chat`. Select **Send a test message** to send `Hello`; the bot should respond with `You said: Hello`. The `support` conversation ID is scoped to the authenticated user by the adapter. Generate a different conversation ID when you want to start a new conversation.

For a fuller chat interface, see the [official Nuxt example](https://github.com/vercel/chat/tree/main/examples/nuxt-chat).

- [Add more platform adapters](/docs/chat-sdk/adapters)

description: "Use Chat SDK with Next.js, Nuxt, Hono, Nitro, or TanStack Start on Vercel."

source: "https://vercel.com/docs/chat-sdk/frameworks"

# Chat SDK Frameworks

Chat SDK works with frameworks that handle standard Web `Request` and `Response` objects. Your framework receives the webhook, passes it to a Chat SDK adapter, and keeps the function running while your bot processes the event.

## Choose your framework

Each guide uses a Slack bot with Redis state and [Vercel Connect](/docs/connect/frameworks/chat-sdk) for credentials and webhook delivery.

| Framework | Webhook route | Background processing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Next.js](/docs/chat-sdk/frameworks/nextjs) | App Router Route Handler | `after` from `next/server` |
| [Nuxt](/docs/chat-sdk/frameworks/nuxt) | Nuxt 4 server API route | `waitUntil` from `@vercel/functions` |
| [Hono](/docs/chat-sdk/frameworks/hono) | Hono POST handler | `waitUntil` from `@vercel/functions` |
| [Nitro](/docs/chat-sdk/frameworks/nitro) | Nitro 3 filesystem route | `event.waitUntil` |
| [TanStack Start](/docs/chat-sdk/frameworks/tanstack-start) | React server route | `waitUntil` from `@vercel/functions` |

For a new Next.js bot, follow the [quickstart](/docs/chat-sdk/quickstart) to scaffold it with `create-chat-sdk`. The other guides show how to add Chat SDK to an existing framework project.

## Share bot behavior across frameworks

Define your `Chat` instance and event handlers in a server-only module. The framework route passes incoming requests to `bot.webhooks.slack`; Chat SDK handles verification, event parsing, and dispatching to your handlers. Keep the request body unread until it reaches the adapter.

Use a [persistent state adapter](/docs/chat-sdk/adapters#state-adapters) to share subscriptions and locks across function instances. Keep bot credentials and database connections on the server.

## Process events after responding

Pass your framework's background-task function as the webhook handler's `waitUntil` option. This lets the adapter acknowledge the webhook while your event handlers continue running.

Background work is still subject to the function's [maximum duration](/docs/functions/configuring-functions/duration). Use [Workflows](/docs/workflows) for tasks that need durable execution or must wait for an external event.

## Next steps

- [Choose platform and state adapters](/docs/chat-sdk/adapters)
- [Connect an eve agent](/docs/chat-sdk/eve)
- [Read the Chat SDK webhook API](https://chat-sdk.dev/docs/usage#webhook-routing)

# Chat SDK with TanStack Start

Use a TanStack Start React server route to receive Slack events and pass them to Chat SDK. The route runs on the server alongside your application's UI.

## Prerequisites

Start with an existing TanStack Start project configured for [deployment on Vercel](/docs/frameworks/full-stack/tanstack-start), the latest [Vercel CLI](/docs/cli), and permission to install an app in your Slack workspace.

## Install Chat SDK

From your project directory, install the packages with pnpm:

```bash filename="Terminal"
pnpm add chat @chat-adapter/slack @chat-adapter/state-redis @vercel/connect @vercel/functions
```

## Create your bot

Create `lib/bot.ts` at the project root. This bot uses Vercel Connect for Slack authentication, stores subscriptions in Redis, and responds to mentions and thread replies. Keep this module on the server.

**lib/bot.ts**

```typescript filename="lib/bot.ts"
import { Chat } from 'chat';
import { createSlackAdapter } from '@chat-adapter/slack';
import { createRedisState } from '@chat-adapter/state-redis';
import { connectSlackAdapter } from '@vercel/connect/chat';

export const bot = new Chat({
  userName: 'my-bot',
  adapters: {
    slack: createSlackAdapter({
      ...connectSlackAdapter('slack/my-bot'),
    }),
  },
  state: createRedisState(),
});

bot.onNewMention(async (thread) => {
  await thread.subscribe();
  await thread.post('Hello! Reply here to chat.');
});

bot.onSubscribedMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(message.text);
});
```

**lib/bot.js**

```javascript filename="lib/bot.js"
import { Chat } from 'chat';
import { createSlackAdapter } from '@chat-adapter/slack';
import { createRedisState } from '@chat-adapter/state-redis';
import { connectSlackAdapter } from '@vercel/connect/chat';

export const bot = new Chat({
  userName: 'my-bot',
  adapters: {
    slack: createSlackAdapter({
      ...connectSlackAdapter('slack/my-bot'),
    }),
  },
  state: createRedisState(),
});

bot.onNewMention(async (thread) => {
  await thread.subscribe();
  await thread.post('Hello! Reply here to chat.');
});

bot.onSubscribedMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(message.text);
});
```

## Add the webhook route

Create `src/routes/api/webhooks/slack.ts` with a POST handler:

**src/routes/api/webhooks/slack.ts**

```typescript filename="src/routes/api/webhooks/slack.ts"
import { createFileRoute } from '@tanstack/react-router';
import { waitUntil } from '@vercel/functions';
import { bot } from '../../../../lib/bot';

export const Route = createFileRoute('/api/webhooks/slack')({
  server: {
    handlers: {
      POST: ({ request }) => bot.webhooks.slack(request, { waitUntil }),
    },
  },
});
```

**src/routes/api/webhooks/slack.js**

```javascript filename="src/routes/api/webhooks/slack.js"
import { createFileRoute } from '@tanstack/react-router';
import { waitUntil } from '@vercel/functions';
import { bot } from '../../../../lib/bot';

export const Route = createFileRoute('/api/webhooks/slack')({
  server: {
    handlers: {
      POST: ({ request }) => bot.webhooks.slack(request, { waitUntil }),
    },
  },
});
```

The handler receives a Web `Request` and returns the adapter's `Response`. Pass `waitUntil` from `@vercel/functions` so the bot can finish processing after acknowledging the event. Import the bot only from server code.

Run your framework's development or build command to update the generated route tree. Keep the [Nitro Vite plugin configured for Vercel](/docs/frameworks/full-stack/tanstack-start#nitro-configuration) so the server route is deployed as a function.

## Connect Slack and deploy

From the project directory, link your app to Vercel and connect a Redis database:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel link
vercel integration add upstash/upstash-kv
```

Ensure the integration supplies `REDIS_URL` in the project's **Production** environment. If you already have Redis, add its connection URL as `REDIS_URL` in your project's [environment variables](/docs/environment-variables). Use separate databases for development and production.

Create a Slack connector and allow token requests from the project's Production and Development environments. Attach its trigger to your production webhook route:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel connect create slack --name my-bot --triggers
vercel connect attach slack/my-bot --environment production --environment development --triggers --trigger-path /api/webhooks/slack
```

Follow the prompts to authorize and install the Slack app. If you choose a different connector name, update `slack/my-bot` in your bot configuration and attach command. Connect manages the Slack credentials and verifies provider events before forwarding them. The adapter verifies the forwarded request with Vercel OIDC.

Deploy your app:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel --prod
```

Invite the bot to a Slack channel and mention it. It should reply with a greeting and echo subsequent replies in that thread. Check [runtime logs](/docs/observability/runtime-logs) if it does not respond.

Vercel deployments receive `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN` automatically. For local outbound API calls, configure a development `REDIS_URL` and run `vercel env pull .env.local`. This supplies a Development OIDC token, which can access the connector because the attachment above enables Development.

Connect forwards inbound events to deployed URLs, not `localhost`. To test inbound events before production, [attach the trigger to a Preview branch](/docs/cli/connect#vercel-connect-attach).

## Add browser chat with the Web Adapter

The [Web Adapter](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/web) lets a browser chat UI use the same bot as Slack. Browser messages go to `onDirectMessage`, and the adapter streams the bot's replies back to the client. Your app authenticates these requests; Vercel Connect continues to handle the Slack integration.

### Configure the adapter

Install the Web Adapter and its client dependencies:

```bash filename="Terminal"
pnpm add @chat-adapter/web @tanstack/ai-react
```

Implement `getUserFromSession(request)` in `lib/auth.ts` using your application's authentication provider. This is an application-defined helper, not a Chat SDK export. It must validate the session and return a stable `{ id: string, name?: string }` for a signed-in user, or `null` to reject the request with HTTP 401. User IDs must not contain `:`. See [Web Adapter authentication](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/web#authentication).

Update `lib/bot.ts` with the Web Adapter and a direct-message handler, keeping the Slack adapter, Redis state, and existing handlers:

**lib/bot.ts**

```typescript filename="lib/bot.ts"
import { Chat } from 'chat';
import { createWebAdapter } from '@chat-adapter/web';
import { getUserFromSession } from './auth';
import { createSlackAdapter } from '@chat-adapter/slack';
import { createRedisState } from '@chat-adapter/state-redis';
import { connectSlackAdapter } from '@vercel/connect/chat';

export const bot = new Chat({
  userName: 'my-bot',
  adapters: {
    web: createWebAdapter({
      userName: 'my-bot',
      protocol: 'ag-ui',
      getUser: getUserFromSession,
    }),
    slack: createSlackAdapter({
      ...connectSlackAdapter('slack/my-bot'),
    }),
  },
  state: createRedisState(),
});

bot.onDirectMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(`You said: ${message.text}`);
});

bot.onNewMention(async (thread) => {
  await thread.subscribe();
  await thread.post('Hello! Reply here to chat.');
});

bot.onSubscribedMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(message.text);
});
```

**lib/bot.js**

```javascript filename="lib/bot.js"
import { Chat } from 'chat';

  userName: 'my-bot',

    }),
  },

});

  await thread.post(`You said: ${message.text}`);
});

bot.onNewMention(async (thread) => {
  await thread.subscribe();
  await thread.post('Hello! Reply here to chat.');
});

bot.onSubscribedMessage(async (thread, message) => {
  await thread.post(message.text);
});
```

This example uses TanStack AI in the browser, so the Web Adapter must use `protocol: 'ag-ui'`. If you instead use the AI SDK React helper, select `ai-sdk` and install its client dependencies. See [Web Adapter client options](https://chat-sdk.dev/adapters/official/web#framework-integrations).

### Add the browser endpoint

Create `src/routes/api/chat.ts` to receive browser requests and return the adapter's stream:

**src/routes/api/chat.ts**

```typescript filename="src/routes/api/chat.ts"
import { createFileRoute } from '@tanstack/react-router';
import { waitUntil } from '@vercel/functions';
import { bot } from '../../../lib/bot';

export const Route = createFileRoute('/api/chat')({
  server: {
    handlers: {
      POST: ({ request }) => bot.webhooks.web(request, { waitUntil }),
    },
  },
});
```

**src/routes/api/chat.js**

```javascript filename="src/routes/api/chat.js"

import { bot } from '../../../lib/bot';

export const Route = createFileRoute('/api/chat')({
  server: {
    handlers: {
      POST: ({ request }) => bot.webhooks.web(request, { waitUntil }),
    },
  },
});
```

### Connect the browser client

Create `src/routes/chat.tsx`. Connect TanStack AI to the server route with `fetchServerSentEvents`:

**src/routes/chat.tsx**

```tsx filename="src/routes/chat.tsx"
import { fetchServerSentEvents, useChat } from '@tanstack/ai-react';
import { createFileRoute } from '@tanstack/react-router';

export const Route = createFileRoute('/chat')({ component: ChatPage });

function ChatPage() {
  const { messages, sendMessage, status, error } = useChat({
    connection: fetchServerSentEvents('/api/chat'),
    threadId: 'support',
  });
  const busy = status === 'submitted' || status === 'streaming';

  return (
    <section aria-label="Chat">
      {messages.map((message) => (
        <p key={message.id}>
          {message.parts
            .map((part) => (part.type === 'text' ? part.content : ''))
            .join('')}
        </p>
      ))}
      <button disabled={busy} onClick={() => sendMessage('Hello')}>
        Send a test message
      </button>
      {error && (
        <p role="alert">Could not send your message. Please try again.</p>
      )}
    </section>
  );
}
```

**src/routes/chat.jsx**

```jsx filename="src/routes/chat.jsx"
import { fetchServerSentEvents, useChat } from '@tanstack/ai-react';
import { createFileRoute } from '@tanstack/react-router';

export const Route = createFileRoute('/chat')({ component: ChatPage });

function ChatPage() {
  const { messages, sendMessage, status, error } = useChat({
    connection: fetchServerSentEvents('/api/chat'),
    threadId: 'support',
  });
  const busy = status === 'submitted' || status === 'streaming';

  return (
    <section aria-label="Chat">
      {messages.map((message) => (
        <p key={message.id}>
          {message.parts
            .map((part) => (part.type === 'text' ? part.content : ''))
            .join('')}
        </p>
      ))}
      <button disabled={busy} onClick={() => sendMessage('Hello')}>
        Send a test message
      </button>
      {error && (
        <p role="alert">Could not send your message. Please try again.</p>
      )}
    </section>
  );
}
```

TanStack AI sends a string with `sendMessage(text)` and exposes text parts as `part.content`. Keep the bot imported only in the server endpoint, and let the framework regenerate the route tree after adding both routes.

After configuring authentication, sign in and open `/chat`. Select **Send a test message** to send `Hello`; the bot should respond with `You said: Hello`. The `support` conversation ID is scoped to the authenticated user by the adapter. Generate a different conversation ID when you want to start a new conversation.

For a fuller chat interface, see the [official TanStack Start example](https://github.com/vercel/chat/tree/main/examples/tanstack-start-chat).

title: "Chat SDK with AI Gateway"
