# Anatomy of the Checks API

Checks API extends the build and deploy process once your deployment is ready. Each check behaves like a webhook that triggers specific events, such as `deployment.created`, `deployment.ready`, and `deployment.succeeded`. The tests are verified before domains are assigned.

To learn more, see the [Supported Webhooks Events docs](/docs/webhooks/webhooks-api#supported-event-types).

The workflow for registering and running a check is as follows:

1. A check is created after the `deployment.created` event
2. When the `deployment.ready` event triggers, the check updates its `status` to `running`
3. When the check is finished, the `status` updates to `completed`

If a check is "rerequestable", your integration users get an option to [rerequest and rerun the failing checks](#rerunning-checks).

### Types of Checks

Depending on the type, checks can block the domain assignment stage of deployments.

- **Blocking Checks**: Prevents a successful deployment and returns a `conclusion` with a `state` value of `canceled` or `failed`. For example, a [Core Check](/docs/checks#types-of-flows-enabled-by-checks-api) returning a `404` error results in a `failed` `conclusion` for a deployment
- **Non-blocking Checks**: Return test results with a successful deployment regardless of the `conclusion`

A blocking check with a `failed` state is configured by the developer (and not the integration).

### Associations

Checks are always associated with a specific deployment that is tested and validated.

### Body attributes

| Attributes      | Format             | Purpose                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| --------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `blocking`      | Boolean            | Tells Vercel if this check needs to block the deployment                                                                                                                                             |
| `name`          | String             | Name of the check                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `detailsUrl`    | String (optional)  | URL to display in the Vercel dashboard                                                                                                                                                               |
| `externalId`    | String (optional)  | ID used for external use                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `path`          | String (optional)  | Path of the page that is being checked                                                                                                                                                               |
| `rerequestable` | Boolean (optional) | Tells Vercel if the check can rerun. Users can trigger a `deployment.check-rerequested` [webhook](/docs/webhooks/webhooks-api#deployment.check-rerequested), through a button on the deployment page |
| `conclusion`    | String (optional)  | The result of a running check. For [blocking checks](#types-of-checks) the values can be `canceled`, `failed`, `neutral`, `succeeded`, `skipped`. `canceled` and `failed`                            |
| `status`        | String (optional)  | Tells Vercel the status of the check with values: `running` and `completed`                                                                                                                          |
| `output`        | Object (optional)  | Details about the result of the check. Vercel uses this data to display actionable information for developers. This helps them debug failed checks                                                   |

The check gets a `stale` status if there is no status update for more than one hour (`status = registered`). The same applies if the check is running (`status = running`) for more than five minutes.

### Response

| Response      | Format | Purpose                                                                           |
| ------------- | ------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `status`      | String | The status of the check. It expects specific values like `running` or `completed` |
| `state`       | String | Tells the current state of the connection                                         |
| `connectedAt` | Number | Timestamp (in milliseconds) of when the configuration was connected               |
| `type`        | String | Name of the integrator performing the check                                       |

### Response codes

| Status | Outcome                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `200`  | Success                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `400`  | One of the provided values in the request body is invalid, **OR** one of the provided values in the request query is invalid                                                  |
| `403`  | The provided token is not from an OAuth2 client **OR** you do not have permission to access this resource **OR** the API token doesn't have permission to perform the request |
| `404`  | The check was not found **OR** the deployment was not found                                                                                                                   |
| `413`  | The output provided is too large                                                                                                                                              |

## Rich results

### Output

The `output` property can store any data like [Web Vitals](/docs/speed-insights) and [Virtual Experience Score](/docs/speed-insights/metrics#predictive-performance-metrics-with-virtual-experience-score). It is defined under a `metrics` field:

| Key                      | [Type](/docs/rest-api#types) | Description                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `TBT`                    | [Map](/docs/rest-api#types)          | The [Total Blocking Time](/docs/speed-insights/metrics#total-blocking-time-tbt), measured by the check                                                  |
| `LCP`                    | [Map](/docs/rest-api#types)          | The [Largest Contentful Paint](/docs/speed-insights/metrics#largest-contentful-paint-lcp), measured by the check                                        |
| `FCP`                    | [Map](/docs/rest-api#types)          | The [First Contentful Paint](/docs/speed-insights/metrics#first-contentful-paint-fcp), measured by the check                                            |
| `CLS`                    | [Map](/docs/rest-api#types)          | The [Cumulative Layout Shift](/docs/speed-insights/metrics#cumulative-layout-shift-cls), measured by the check                                          |
| `virtualExperienceScore` | [Map](/docs/rest-api#types)          | The overall [Virtual Experience Score](/docs/speed-insights/metrics#predictive-performance-metrics-with-virtual-experience-score) measured by the check |

Each of these keys has the following properties:

| Key             | [Type](/docs/rest-api#types)  | Description                                                                                                                            |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `value`         | [Float](/docs/rest-api#types) | The value measured for a particular metric, in milliseconds. For `virtualExperienceScore` this value is the percentage between 0 and 1 |
| `previousValue` | [Float](/docs/rest-api#types) | A previous value for comparison purposes                                                                                               |
| `source`        | [Enum](/docs/rest-api#types)  | `web-vitals`                                                                                                                           |

### Metrics

`metrics` makes [Web Vitals](/docs/speed-insights) visible on checks. It is defined inside `output` as follows:

```json filename="checks-metrics.json"
{
  "path": "/",
  "output": {
    "metrics": {
      "FCP": {
        "value": 1200,
        "previousValue": 1400,
        "source": "web-vitals"
      },
      "LCP": {
        "value": 1200,
        "previousValue": 1400,
        "source": "web-vitals"
      },
      "CLS": {
        "value": 1200,
        "previousValue": 1400,
        "source": "web-vitals"
      },
      "TBT": {
        "value": 1200,
        "previousValue": 1400,
        "source": "web-vitals"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

> **💡 Note:** All fields are required except `previousValue`. If
> `previousValue` is present, the delta will be shown.

### Rerunning checks

A check can be "rerequested" using the `deployment.check-rerequested` webhook. Add the `rerequestable` attribute, and you can rerequest failed checks.

A rerequested check triggers the `deployment.check-rerequested` webhook. It updates the check `status` to `running` and resets the `conclusion`, `detailsUrl`, `externalId`, and `output` fields.

### Skipping Checks

You can "Skip" to stop and ignore check results without affecting the alias assignment. You cannot skip active checks. They continue running until built successfully, and assign domains as the last step.

### Availability of URLs

For "Running Checks", only the [Automatic Deployment URL](/docs/deployments/generated-urls) is available. [Automatic Branch URL](/docs/deployments/generated-urls#generated-from-git) and [Custom Domains](/docs/domains/working-with-domains/add-a-domain) will apply once the checks finish.

### Order of execution

Checks may take different times to run. Each integrator determines the running order of the checks. While [Vercel REST API](/docs/integrations/create-integration/vercel-api-integrations) determines the order of check results.

### Status and conclusion

When Checks API begins running on your deployment, the `status` is set to `running`. Once it gets a `conclusion`, the `status` updates to `completed`. This results in a successful deployment.

However, your deployment will fail if the `conclusion` updates to one of the following values:

| Conclusion  | `blocking=true` |
| ----------- | --------------- |
| `canceled`  | Yes             |
| `failed`    | Yes             |
| `neutral`   | No              |
| `succeeded` | No              |
| `skipped`   | No              |

title: "Working with Checks"
description: "Vercel automatically keeps an eye on various aspects of your web application using the Checks API. Learn how to use Checks in your Vercel workflow here."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.886Z"

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Working with Checks

Checks are tests and assertions created and run after every successful deployment. **Checks API** defines your application's quality metrics, runs end-to-end tests, investigates APIs' reliability, and checks your deployment.

Most testing and CI/CD flows occur in synthetic environments. This leads to false results, overlooked performance degradation, and missed broken connections.

## Types of flows enabled by Checks API

| Flow Type        | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Core**         | Checks `200` responses on specific pages or APIs. Determine the deployment's health and identify issues with code, errors, or broken connections                                                                  |
| **Performance**  | Collects [core web vital](/docs/speed-insights) information for specific pages and compares it with the new deployment. It helps you decide whether to build the deployment or block it for further investigation |
| **End-to-end**   | Validates that your deployment has all the required components to build successfully. And identifies any broken pages, missing images, or other assets                                                            |
| **Optimization** | Optimizes information about the bundle size. Ensures that your website manages large assets like package and image size                                                                                           |

## Checks lifecycle

![The depiction of how the Checks lifecycle works.](https://7nyt0uhk7sse4zvn.public.blob.vercel-storage.com/docs-assets/static/docs/integrations/checks/checks-overview-light.png)

The diagram shows the complete lifecycle of how a check works:

1. When a [deployment](/docs/deployments) is created, Vercel triggers the `deployment.created` webhook. This tells integrators that checks can now be registered
2. Next, an integrator uses the Checks API to create checks defined in the integration configuration
3. When the deployment is built, Vercel triggers the `deployment.ready` webhook. This notifies integrators to begin checks on the deployment
4. Vercel waits until all the created checks receive an update
5. Once all checks receive a `conclusion`, aliases will apply, and the deployment will go live

Learn more about this process in the [Anatomy of Checks API](/docs/checks/creating-checks)

## Checks integrations

You can create a [native](/docs/integrations#native-integrations) or [connectable account](/docs/integrations#connectable-accounts) integration that works with the checks API to facilitate testing of deployments for Vercel users. The [Checks API reference](/docs/checks/checks-api) lists the endpoints your integration calls to create and update checks.

### Install integrations

Vercel users can find and install your integration from the [Marketplace](/marketplace) under [testing](/marketplace/category/testing), [monitoring](/marketplace/category/monitoring) or [observability](/marketplace/category/observability).

### Build your Checks integration

Once you have [created your integration](/docs/integrations/create-integration/marketplace-product), [publish](/docs/integrations/create-integration/submit-integration) it to the marketplace by following these guidelines:

- Provide low or no configuration solutions for developers to run checks
- A guided onboarding process for developers from the installation to the end result
- Provide relevant information about the outcome of the test on the Vercel dashboard
- Document how to go beyond the default behavior to build custom tests for advanced users

title: "Vercel CI Configuration Reference"
description: "Reference for the turbo.json tags and vercel.json keys that configure Vercel CI."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.886Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/ci/configuration"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Vercel CI Configuration Reference

## Creating task dependencies

Tasks that are tagged to run in CI will have their dependencies run in CI, too.

```json filename="turbo.json" {8}
{
  "tasks": {
    "build": {
      "dependsOn": ["^build"]
    },
    "test": {
      "dependsOn": ["^build"],
      "tags": ["ci"]
    }
  }
}
```

Using [Turborepo's task composition rules](https://turborepo.dev/docs/crafting-your-repository/configuring-tasks#depending-on-tasks-in-dependencies-with-), Vercel CI will run the `build` tasks that a `test` task depends on before executing the `test` task.

You can also set the `ci` tag in a [Package Configuration](https://turborepo.dev/docs/reference/package-configurations).

```json filename="packages/web/turbo.json" {5}
{
  "extends": ["//"],
  "tasks": {
    "test": {
      "tags": ["ci"]
    }
  }
}
```

This runs that task for the package even when the root `turbo.json` does not enable it, giving you the power to compose your CI declarations.

## Excluding tasks

Add the `!ci` tag to keep a task from being selected to run in Vercel CI. The `!ci` tag takes precedence over the `ci` tag, so a task with both tags doesn't run.

Use `!ci` in a [Package Configuration](https://turborepo.dev/docs/reference/package-configurations) to opt one package out of a task that the root `turbo.json` runs in CI. In the example below, the root `turbo.json` runs `test` for every package:

```json filename="turbo.json" {4}
{
  "tasks": {
    "test": {
      "tags": ["ci"]
    }
  }
}
```

The package's `turbo.json` excludes its own `test` task:

```json filename="packages/legacy/turbo.json" {5}
{
  "extends": ["//"],
  "tasks": {
    "test": {
      "tags": ["!ci"]
    }
  }
}
```

Vercel CI runs `test` for every package except `packages/legacy`.

`!ci` doesn't remove a task from the dependencies of other tasks. If a task that runs in Vercel CI depends on a task tagged `!ci`, Vercel CI still runs the dependency first.

## Resource sizing

Vercel CI assigns 2 CPUs and 4 GB of memory to each task by default.

Add a `ci:cpus:<count>` tag to assign up to 32 CPUs to a task:

```json filename="turbo.json" {4}
{
  "tasks": {
    "test": {
      "tags": ["ci", "ci:cpus:8"]
    }
  }
}
```

Memory resources are assigned at 2 GB per CPU:

| CPUs | Memory |
| ---- | ------ |
| 1    | 2 GB   |
| 2    | 4 GB   |
| 4    | 8 GB   |
| 8    | 16 GB  |
| 16   | 32 GB  |
| 32   | 64 GB  |

To change the CPU allocation for one package, add the tag in that package's [Package Configuration](https://turborepo.dev/docs/reference/package-configurations). Start the `tags` array with `$TURBO_EXTENDS$` so the task keeps the `ci` tag from the root `turbo.json`:

```json filename="packages/web/turbo.json" {5}
{
  "extends": ["//"],
  "tasks": {
    "test": {
      "tags": ["$TURBO_EXTENDS$", "ci:cpus:16"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Bootstrapping resources

Before your tasks run, Vercel CI bootstraps each run by cloning your repository and installing its dependencies. The install step uses 4 CPUs and 8 GB of memory by default.

If dependency installation is slow or runs out of memory, set `ci.bootstrapping.resources.vcpus` in the `vercel.json` file at the root of your repository:

```json filename="vercel.json" {5-7}
{
  "ci": {
    "bootstrapping": {
      "installEnv": {},
      "resources": {
        "vcpus": 16
      }
    }
  }
}
```

- `vcpus` must be a whole number from 1 to 32.
- Memory is assigned at 2 GB per CPU, so this example requests 16 CPUs and 32 GB of memory.
- This setting only applies to dependency installation. It doesn't change the resources assigned to your tasks.
- An invalid `resources` value makes your `ci` configuration invalid. Vercel CI will ignore your configuration.

## Installing additional tools

To install a tool that your package manager doesn't provide, set `ci.bootstrapping.installCommand` in `vercel.json`. Before you install a tool, check whether the image already includes it. See [Pre-installed software](/docs/ci/image#pre-installed-software) for the full list.

Your install command doesn't run on the same instance as your tasks. Vercel CI handles each run in these steps:

1. During bootstrapping, Vercel CI clones your repository and runs the install command on a separate instance that always uses the Amazon Linux image.
2. Vercel CI saves a copy of your repository directory, including everything the install command added to it.
3. Each task runs on its own instance, starting from that copy.

A tool reaches your tasks only if the install command puts it inside your repository directory. The tool must also work on the image your task uses, so if your task uses the Ubuntu image, install a build that runs on both images.

The install command replaces the default dependency install, so it must also install your dependencies. In this example, the install command installs dependencies with pnpm, then runs a script that downloads [ShellCheck](https://www.shellcheck.net/):

```json filename="vercel.json" {4}
{
  "ci": {
    "bootstrapping": {
      "installCommand": "pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && sh scripts/install-ci-tools.sh",
      "installEnv": {}
    }
  }
}
```

The script downloads ShellCheck into a `.bin` directory in your repository:

```bash filename="scripts/install-ci-tools.sh"
set -eu
mkdir -p .bin
curl -fsSL https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/releases/download/v0.11.0/shellcheck-v0.11.0.linux.x86_64.tar.xz \
  | tar -xJ --strip-components=1 -C .bin shellcheck-v0.11.0/shellcheck
```

Your tasks can then run the tool from that directory:

```json filename="package.json"
{
  "scripts": {
    "lint:shell": "./.bin/shellcheck scripts/*.sh"
  }
}
```

- The install command runs from the root of your repository, or from your project's root directory if you've set one.
- Your tasks only receive files inside your repository. Files the install command writes anywhere else, like your home directory, aren't available to your tasks. This includes system packages that you install with `dnf` or `apt-get`.
- When you set `ci.bootstrapping`, you must also set `ci.bootstrapping.installEnv`, even if it's empty.
- Add `.bin` to your `.gitignore` file so you don't commit the downloaded tool.

## Testing against your deployments

A task can wait for the Vercel deployment of your commit, then send requests to it, for example to run end-to-end tests. Vercel CI authenticates those requests with an OpenID Connect (OIDC) token, so they work even when the deployment uses [Deployment Protection](/docs/deployment-protection).

For a complete Playwright example, see [Running end-to-end tests](/docs/ci/guides/end-to-end-tests).

### Depend on a deployment

Add `<package>#deployment` to the task's `dependsOn`, and add the `ci:oidc:deployments` tag. In the example below, the `test:e2e` task in `apps/web` waits for the `web` package's deployment:

```json filename="apps/web/turbo.json" {5-7}
{
  "extends": ["//"],
  "tasks": {
    "test:e2e": {
      "dependsOn": ["web#deployment"],
      "tags": ["ci", "ci:oidc:deployments"],
      "passThroughEnv": ["VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URLS"]
    }
  }
}
```

- Vercel CI resolves `web#deployment` to the Vercel project connected to your repository whose root directory is the `web` package's directory. Exactly one project must match.
- The task starts after that deployment succeeds. You don't need to define a `deployment` task in `turbo.json`.
- A task with `ci:oidc:deployments` must depend on its own package's deployment.

> **💡 Note:** Vercel CI only treats `<package>#deployment` as a Vercel deployment when the
> package has no `deployment` script in its `package.json`. If the package has
> one, Vercel CI runs that script like any other task instead of waiting for
> the Vercel deployment. Tasks that depend on it don't receive
> `VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URLS`, and tasks with `ci:oidc:deployments` fail. To use
> deployment dependencies, rename the script.

### Send requests to the deployment

Vercel CI gives the task these environment variables:

| Variable                    | Value                                                                                 |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URLS`    | A JSON object that maps each package name to its deployment's hostname                |
| `VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_TARGETS` | A JSON object that maps each package name to `production` or `preview`               |

Turborepo filters environment variables, so add the variables your task reads to its `passThroughEnv`, as shown in the example above.

When the task sends a request to its own package's deployment hostname, Vercel CI adds the OIDC token in the `x-vercel-trusted-oidc-idp-token` header. You don't need to handle the token yourself. The token isn't available in an environment variable, and Vercel CI doesn't send it to other hosts, including the deployment's aliases and custom domains.

The task also receives the environment variables of its deployment's project, limited to the variables its `env` and `passThroughEnv` allow.

Deployments built from the same repository and Vercel team trust Vercel CI automatically. For deployments from another repository, add a [Trusted Sources](/docs/deployment-protection/methods-to-bypass-deployment-protection/trusted-sources) rule for Vercel CI.

### Call other projects

To send the token to production deployments of other projects on your team, add up to five `ci:oidc:project:<project-id>` tags alongside `ci:oidc:deployments`:

```json filename="apps/web/turbo.json" {9}
{
  "extends": ["//"],
  "tasks": {
    "test:e2e": {
      "dependsOn": ["web#deployment"],
      "tags": [
        "ci",
        "ci:oidc:deployments",
        "ci:oidc:project:prj_123456789"
      ],
      "passThroughEnv": ["VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URLS", "VERCEL_OIDC_PROJECT_URLS"]
    }
  }
}
```

- `VERCEL_OIDC_PROJECT_URLS` maps each project ID to the hostname of its current production deployment. Vercel CI only sends the token to that hostname.
- Each project's production deployment must be ready. If it isn't, the task fails with a configuration error.
- A project built from another repository needs a Trusted Sources rule that trusts Vercel CI for production.

### Turn OIDC off

Add `ci:oidc:none` to a task to turn OIDC off for that task. A task's `ci:oidc` tags take precedence over the `ci:oidc` tags in its package's top-level `tags`.

title: "Vercel CI Environment Variables"
description: "Manage environment variables and secrets for Vercel CI runs."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.886Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/ci/environment-variables"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Vercel CI Environment Variables

Use repository CI environment variables for secrets and values scoped to one repository. Use Shared Environment Variables to reuse a value across repositories. Use constants in `vercel.json` for non-secret values that you want to commit with your code.

If you're moving from GitHub Actions, follow the [migration guide](/kb/guide/github-actions-to-vercel-ci) to map repository secrets, organization secrets, and workflow `env` values to Vercel CI.

## Make variables available to your tasks

Vercel CI runs each task with Turborepo. By default, Turborepo uses [Strict Mode](https://turborepo.dev/docs/crafting-your-repository/using-environment-variables#strict-mode), which removes every environment variable that your `turbo.json` doesn't list. A variable you add to Vercel CI doesn't reach your task until you list it.

Add each variable your task reads to the task's `env` key:

```json filename="turbo.json" {5}
{
  "tasks": {
    "test": {
      "tags": ["ci"],
      "env": ["API_TOKEN"]
    }
  }
}
```

- Variables in `env` are part of the task's hash, so changing their value causes a cache miss. To pass a variable without changing the hash, use `passThroughEnv` instead.
- Use `globalEnv` or `globalPassThroughEnv` for variables that every task needs.
- This doesn't apply to dependency installation. `ci.bootstrapping.installEnv` values reach your install command directly.

## Add a repository CI environment variable

1. Open [**CI environment variables**](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%7E%2Fsettings%2Fenvironment-variables%3Fview%3Dci) in the Vercel dashboard.
2. Select the repository that should receive the variable.
3. Select **Add Variable**.
4. Enter the key and value. Select **Secret** for sensitive values that should be write-only.
5. Select **Add Variable**.

Vercel CI makes the variable available to later runs for that repository.

## Install private npm packages

Add a repository CI environment variable named `NPM_RC`. Select **Secret**, then enter your complete npm configuration as its value:

```ini
//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=your_access_token_here
```

Vercel CI writes `NPM_RC` to `$HOME/.npmrc` while installing dependencies, then removes the file. For a custom registry, update the registry hostname and add any required scope configuration.

## Reuse a Shared Environment Variable

To use the same value across repositories, create or edit a Shared Environment Variable from the **Shared** tab. Include the **Preview** environment, then select each repository under **Link to CI (Optional)**.

## Add constants in `vercel.json`

Add a `ci` key to the `vercel.json` file at the root of your repository. Use `ci.bootstrapping.installEnv` for values needed while installing dependencies. Use `ci.tasks` to assign values to a task name or a specific `package#task` selector:

```json filename="vercel.json" {6-8}
{
  "ci": {
    "bootstrapping": {
      "installEnv": {
        "NODE_OPTIONS": {
          "constant": {
            "value": "--max-old-space-size=4096"
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Constants in `vercel.json` override linked Shared Environment Variables with the same key. Do not commit secrets to `vercel.json`.

title: "Running End-to-End Tests in Vercel CI"
description: "Run Playwright tests against the Vercel deployment of every commit with Vercel CI."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.886Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/ci/guides/end-to-end-tests"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Running End-to-End Tests in Vercel CI

In this tutorial, you'll set up Vercel CI to run [Playwright](https://playwright.dev/) tests against the Vercel deployment of each commit. The tests run in Chromium and work with deployments that use [Deployment Protection](/docs/deployment-protection).

You'll configure a task that:

1. Waits for your app's Vercel deployment to finish.
2. Starts the official Playwright container image with Docker.
3. Runs your tests against the deployment's URL.

## Prerequisites

- Vercel CI [enabled for your repository](/docs/ci#getting-started).
- A web app in your monorepo at `apps/web`, with the package name `web` in its `package.json`.
- A Vercel project connected to your repository with its root directory set to `apps/web`.
- `@playwright/test` in the app's `devDependencies`.

## Set up the tests

- ### Add the Vercel CI task
  Add an `e2e:ci` task to your app's `turbo.json`:
  ```json filename="apps/web/turbo.json"
  {
    "extends": ["//"],
    "tasks": {
      "e2e:ci": {
        "dependsOn": ["web#deployment"],
        "tags": ["ci", "ci:cpus:8", "ci:oidc:deployments"],
        "passThroughEnv": ["VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URLS"]
      }
    }
  }
  ```
  - `web#deployment` makes the task wait for the `web` deployment of the same commit.
  - `ci:oidc:deployments` authenticates requests to that deployment, so the tests can reach it even when Deployment Protection is on.
  - `ci:cpus:8` gives the browser more CPUs than the default of 2.
  - `passThroughEnv` lets the task read the deployment's URL from `VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URLS`.
  To learn more about each setting, see [Testing against your deployments](/docs/ci/configuration#testing-against-your-deployments).

- ### Point Playwright at the deployment
  Vercel CI gives your task the deployment's address in `VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URLS`. This variable holds a JSON object that maps each package name to its deployment's hostname. The hostname has no protocol:
  ```json
  { "web": "web-a1b2c3d4e-acme.vercel.app" }
  ```
  Playwright needs a full URL, so the container script in the next steps reads the `web` hostname, adds `https://`, and passes the result to Playwright as `BASE_URL`. The value moves through each stage like this:

  | Stage                                       | Value                                       |
  | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
  | `VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URLS` in the task        | `{"web":"web-a1b2c3d4e-acme.vercel.app"}`   |
  | `host` in `scripts/e2e-ci.sh`               | `web-a1b2c3d4e-acme.vercel.app`             |
  | `BASE_URL` in the Playwright container      | `https://web-a1b2c3d4e-acme.vercel.app`     |
  | `page.goto('/')` in a test                  | `https://web-a1b2c3d4e-acme.vercel.app/`    |

  If your app's package name isn't `web`, use that name as the key instead.

  Read the base URL from `BASE_URL` in your Playwright configuration. The fallback to `localhost` lets you run the same tests against your local dev server:
  ```ts filename="apps/web/playwright.config.ts"
  import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';

  export default defineConfig({
    testDir: './e2e',
    use: {
      baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
    },
  });
  ```
  Then add a test:
  ```ts filename="apps/web/e2e/home.spec.ts"
  import { expect, test } from '@playwright/test';

  test('home page loads', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/');
    await expect(page.locator('body')).toBeVisible();
  });
  ```

- ### Trust the Vercel CI certificate authority
  Vercel CI uses its own certificate authority (CA) for network traffic. Chromium doesn't read the `SSL_CERT_FILE` variable that other tools use, so it rejects HTTPS connections until you import the CA into its certificate database.

  Create a script that imports the CA bundle, then runs the command you pass to it:
  ```bash filename="apps/web/scripts/trust-ci-ca.sh"
  #!/bin/sh
  set -eu

  bundle=${SSL_CERT_FILE:?SSL_CERT_FILE must point to the Vercel CI CA bundle}

  apt-get update -qq
  apt-get install -y -qq libnss3-tools >/dev/null

  mkdir -p /tmp/ci-ca /root/.pki/nssdb
  awk '/-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----/ { n += 1; out = sprintf("/tmp/ci-ca/%03d.crt", n) }
    out { print > out }
    /-----END CERTIFICATE-----/ { close(out); out = "" }' "$bundle"

  certutil -N -d sql:/root/.pki/nssdb --empty-password
  for cert in /tmp/ci-ca/*.crt; do
    certutil -A -d sql:/root/.pki/nssdb -n "$(basename "$cert")" -t C,, -i "$cert"
  done

  exec "$@"
  ```
  This script only configures Chromium. Firefox and WebKit store trusted certificates differently and need additional setup.

- ### Run Playwright in a container
  Create a script that starts the Playwright image that matches your installed version, then runs your tests inside it:
  ```bash filename="apps/web/scripts/e2e-ci.sh"
  #!/bin/sh
  set -eu

  host=$(node -p 'JSON.parse(process.env.VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URLS).web')
  version=$(node -p 'require("@playwright/test/package.json").version')
  repo=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)

  exec vercel-ci-docker-run --rm --init --ipc=host --user root \
    --volume "$repo:$repo" \
    --workdir "$PWD" \
    --env CI \
    --env "BASE_URL=https://$host" \
    "mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v$version" \
    sh scripts/trust-ci-ca.sh ./node_modules/.bin/playwright test
  ```
  - `host` reads the `web` deployment's hostname from `VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URLS`. The `.web` key is your app's package name.
  - `--env "BASE_URL=https://$host"` turns the hostname into the URL that `playwright.config.ts` reads. The container doesn't inherit the task's environment variables, so the script passes `BASE_URL` and `CI` explicitly.
  - `vercel-ci-docker-run` works like `docker run` and adds the Vercel CI CA bundle to the container. The trust script reads it from `SSL_CERT_FILE`. To learn more, see [Running containers in your tasks](/docs/ci/image#running-containers-in-your-tasks).
  - The container mounts your repository, so it uses the dependencies Vercel CI already installed.
  - `--ipc=host` gives Chromium enough shared memory.
  Add the script to your app's `package.json`:
  ```json filename="apps/web/package.json"
  {
    "scripts": {
      "e2e:ci": "sh scripts/e2e-ci.sh"
    }
  }
  ```

- ### Push your changes
  Commit the files and push them to GitHub. On the next push, Vercel CI waits for the `web` deployment, then runs `web#e2e:ci` against it.

  To find the run and its logs, open [the CI tab](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%7E%2Fci\&title=) in the dashboard, or run [`vercel ci`](/docs/cli/ci) from your repository.

## Next steps

- [Make other environment variables available to your tests](/docs/ci/environment-variables#make-variables-available-to-your-tasks)
- [Call other projects from your tests](/docs/ci/configuration#call-other-projects)
- [Understand what your test runs cost](/docs/ci/pricing)

title: "Commenting on Pull Requests from Vercel CI"
description: "Post the deployment URL to the pull request for each commit from a Vercel CI task."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.886Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/ci/guides/github-comments"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Commenting on Pull Requests from Vercel CI

In this tutorial, you'll add a Vercel CI task that comments on your pull request with the URL of the commit's Vercel deployment. On each new push, the task updates the same comment instead of adding a new one.

You'll configure a task that:

1. Waits for your app's Vercel deployment.
2. Finds the open pull request for the commit with the GitHub API.
3. Creates or updates a comment with the deployment's URL.

## Prerequisites

- Vercel CI [enabled for your repository](/docs/ci#getting-started).
- An app in your monorepo at `apps/web`, with the package name `web`, and a Vercel project connected to your repository with its root directory set to `apps/web`.
- Permission to create a GitHub fine-grained personal access token for the repository.

## Set up the comment

- ### Create a GitHub token
  Vercel CI doesn't give your tasks a GitHub token, so you need to create one:
  1. In GitHub, create a [fine-grained personal access token](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new).
  2. Under **Repository access**, select only your repository.
  3. Under **Permissions**, set **Pull requests** to **Read and write**.
  4. Copy the token.

- ### Store the token in Vercel CI
  Add the token as a [repository CI environment variable](/docs/ci/environment-variables#add-a-repository-ci-environment-variable) named `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and select **Secret**.

- ### Add the task
  Add a `comment` task to your app's `turbo.json`:
  ```json filename="apps/web/turbo.json"
  {
    "extends": ["//"],
    "tasks": {
      "comment": {
        "dependsOn": ["web#deployment"],
        "tags": ["ci", "ci:oidc:deployments"],
        "passThroughEnv": ["GITHUB_TOKEN", "VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URLS"],
        "cache": false
      }
    }
  }
  ```
  - `web#deployment` makes the task wait for the `web` deployment of the commit. Vercel CI only provides `VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URLS` to tasks with `ci:oidc:deployments` that depend on their package's deployment. To learn more, see [Testing against your deployments](/docs/ci/configuration#testing-against-your-deployments).
  - `passThroughEnv` lets the task read the token and the deployment URL.
  - `cache: false` makes the task run for every commit, so the comment always shows the latest deployment.
  To comment only after your tests pass, add your test task to `dependsOn`, for example `"web#e2e:ci"` from [Running end-to-end tests](/docs/ci/guides/end-to-end-tests).

- ### Write the comment script
  Create a script that finds the pull request and posts the comment. Replace `your-org/your-repo` with your repository:
  ```js filename="apps/web/scripts/comment.mjs"
  import { execFileSync } from 'node:child_process';

  const repository = 'your-org/your-repo';
  const marker = '<!-- vercel-ci-deployment -->';

  const token = process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN;
  const host = JSON.parse(process.env.VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_URLS).web;
  const sha = execFileSync('git', ['rev-parse', 'HEAD'], {
    encoding: 'utf8',
  }).trim();

  async function github(path, init = {}) {
    const response = await fetch(`https://api.github.com${path}`, {
      ...init,
      headers: {
        Accept: 'application/vnd.github+json',
        Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
        'X-GitHub-Api-Version': '2026-03-10',
        ...init.headers,
      },
    });
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`GitHub returned ${response.status} for ${path}`);
    }
    return response.json();
  }

  const pulls = await github(`/repos/${repository}/commits/${sha}/pulls`);
  const pull = pulls.find((candidate) => candidate.state === 'open');
  if (!pull) {
    console.log(`No open pull request for ${sha}.`);
    process.exit(0);
  }

  const body = `${marker}\nDeployment for ${sha.slice(0, 7)}: https://${host}`;
  const comments = await github(
    `/repos/${repository}/issues/${pull.number}/comments?per_page=100`,
  );
  const existing = comments.find((comment) => comment.body?.startsWith(marker));

  if (existing) {
    await github(`/repos/${repository}/issues/comments/${existing.id}`, {
      method: 'PATCH',
      body: JSON.stringify({ body }),
    });
  } else {
    await github(`/repos/${repository}/issues/${pull.number}/comments`, {
      method: 'POST',
      body: JSON.stringify({ body }),
    });
  }
  console.log(`Commented on #${pull.number}.`);
  ```
  - Vercel CI checks out your commit without Git remotes or branch information, so the script gets the commit with `git rev-parse HEAD` and sets the repository itself.
  - The hidden `marker` identifies the comment, so later runs update it instead of adding a new one.
  Add the script to your app's `package.json`:
  ```json filename="apps/web/package.json"
  {
    "scripts": {
      "comment": "node scripts/comment.mjs"
    }
  }
  ```

- ### Push your changes
  Commit the files, push them to a branch, and open a pull request. After the `web` deployment finishes, Vercel CI runs `web#comment`, and the comment appears on the pull request.

## Next steps

- [Run end-to-end tests against your deployment](/docs/ci/guides/end-to-end-tests)
- [Learn more about CI environment variables](/docs/ci/environment-variables)

title: "Running Integration Tests with a Database in Vercel CI"
description: "Start a Postgres container next to your tests in Vercel CI with Turborepo\"
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.886Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/ci/guides/integration-tests"

# Running Integration Tests with a Database in Vercel CI

In this tutorial, you'll run integration tests against a real Postgres database in Vercel CI. You'll use Turborepo's [`with` key](https://turborepo.dev/docs/reference/configuration#with) to start the database next to your tests, so both run in the same compute instance and Turborepo stops the database when your tests finish.

You'll configure:

1. A task that runs Postgres in a Docker container.
2. A test task that starts the database with `with`, waits until it's ready, and runs your tests.

## Prerequisites

- Vercel CI [enabled for your repository](/docs/ci#getting-started).
- An app in your monorepo at `apps/api` that you want to test, with the package name `api`.
- An empty package for the database at `packages/db`, with the package name `db`.

## Set up the tests

- ### Add a task that runs Postgres
  Add a script that runs the official Postgres image to `packages/db/package.json`:
  ```json filename="packages/db/package.json"
  {
    "name": "db",
    "private": true,
    "scripts": {
      "postgres": "docker run --rm --name ci-postgres -p 5432:5432 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres postgres:17"
    }
  }
  ```
  Then mark the task as persistent, because it runs until something stops it:
  ```json filename="packages/db/turbo.json"
  {
    "extends": ["//"],
    "tasks": {
      "postgres": {
        "persistent": true,
        "cache": false
      }
    }
  }
  ```
  Vercel CI starts Docker before your task runs, so the task can use `docker run` without any setup. To learn more, see [Running containers in your tasks](/docs/ci/image#running-containers-in-your-tasks).

- ### Start the database with your tests
  Add a `test:integration` task to your app's `turbo.json`, and list the database task in `with`:
  ```json filename="apps/api/turbo.json"
  {
    "extends": ["//"],
    "tasks": {
      "test:integration": {
        "with": ["db#postgres"],
        "tags": ["ci", "ci:cpus:4"]
      }
    }
  }
  ```
  - `with` starts `db#postgres` at the same time as `test:integration`, in the same compute instance. When the tests finish, Turborepo stops the database, and the container removes itself.
  - `db#postgres` doesn't need a `ci` tag. Vercel CI only runs it as part of `test:integration`.
  - `ci:cpus:4` gives the database and your tests more CPUs than the default of 2, because they share the instance.

- ### Wait for the database
  Postgres takes a few seconds to start, and Docker might need to download the image first. Add a script that waits until Postgres accepts connections:
  ```bash filename="apps/api/scripts/wait-for-postgres.sh"
  #!/bin/sh
  set -eu

  for _ in $(seq 1 120); do
    if docker exec ci-postgres pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      exit 0
    fi
    sleep 1
  done

  echo "Postgres didn't start within 120 seconds." >&2
  exit 1
  ```
  The `-h 127.0.0.1` flag checks the TCP port that your tests connect to. Without it, `pg_isready` can report that Postgres is ready while the image is still initializing the database.

- ### Write a test
  Install a Postgres client in your app:
  ```bash package-manager
  npm i -D pg
  ```
  Then add a test that connects to the database:
  ```js filename="apps/api/test/database.test.js"
  import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
  import { test } from 'node:test';
  import pg from 'pg';

  test('runs a query against Postgres', async () => {
    const client = new pg.Client({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });
    await client.connect();
    try {
      const { rows } = await client.query('SELECT 1 + 1 AS sum');
      assert.equal(rows[0].sum, 2);
    } finally {
      await client.end();
    }
  });
  ```
  Add the `test:integration` script to your app's `package.json`. It waits for the database, then runs the tests with the database's connection string:
  ```json filename="apps/api/package.json"
  {
    "name": "api",
    "type": "module",
    "scripts": {
      "test:integration": "sh scripts/wait-for-postgres.sh && DATABASE_URL=postgres://postgres:postgres@localhost:5432/postgres node --test"
    }
  }
  ```
  The example sets `DATABASE_URL` inside the script because the database only exists for this task. To use a value from Vercel CI instead, see [Make variables available to your tasks](/docs/ci/environment-variables#make-variables-available-to-your-tasks).

- ### Push your changes
  Commit the files and push them to GitHub. When your changes affect `api`, Vercel CI runs `api#test:integration`, which starts Postgres, runs your tests, and stops the database.

  You can run the same task locally with Docker installed:
  ```bash filename="terminal"
  turbo run api#test:integration
  ```

## Next steps

- [Run end-to-end tests against your deployment](/docs/ci/guides/end-to-end-tests)
- [Post results to your pull requests](/docs/ci/guides/github-comments)
- [Learn how Vercel CI bills for CPU time](/docs/ci/pricing)

title: "Images"
description: "Learn about the container images Vercel CI uses to run your tasks, and how to choose one."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.886Z"

# Images

Vercel CI runs each task in a Linux container. You can choose between two images:

| Image        | Base image                                                                | Tag                 |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| Amazon Linux | [Amazon Linux 2023](https://aws.amazon.com/linux/amazon-linux-2023/) | `ci:os:amazonlinux` |
| Ubuntu       | [Ubuntu 24.04](https://releases.ubuntu.com/24.04/)                        | `ci:os:ubuntu`      |

Tasks without a `ci:os` tag use the Amazon Linux image. Both images run on the `x86_64` architecture.

## Pre-installed software

Both images include the same Node.js release and a standard set of CI tools:

| Software                                    | Amazon Linux                                     | Ubuntu                                              |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------- |
| Node.js                                     | `24.18.0`, with `npm` and `npx`                  | `24.18.0`, with `npm`, `npx`, and `corepack`        |
| Git                                         | `git`                                            | `git`, `openssh-client`                             |
| Build tools for native Node.js addons       | `gcc-c++`, `make`                                | `g++`, `make`, `python3`                            |
| Docker                                      | `docker`                                         | `docker.io`                                         |
| Archive tools                               | `tar`, `gzip`, `xz`, `zstd`                      | `tar`, `gzip`, `xz-utils`, `zstd`                   |
| Other utilities                             | `jq`, `diffutils`, `curl`                        | `jq`, `diffutils`, `curl`, `ca-certificates`        |
| Package manager                             | `dnf`                                            | `apt-get`                                           |

To use a tool that isn't in this list, install it during bootstrapping. See [Installing additional tools](/docs/ci/configuration#installing-additional-tools).

## Running containers in your tasks

Your tasks can build and run Docker containers. Both images include Docker, and Vercel CI starts the Docker daemon before your task's command runs, so you don't need to start it yourself.

For example, a task can build your app's image and run its tests inside the container:

```json filename="package.json"
{
  "scripts": {
    "test:container": "docker build -t my-app . && docker run --rm my-app npm test"
  }
}
```

### HTTPS requests from inside a container

Vercel CI uses its own certificate authority (CA) for your tasks' network traffic. Containers you start with `docker run` don't trust that CA by default, so HTTPS requests from inside them can fail with certificate errors.

To fix this, use `vercel-ci-docker-run` instead of `docker run`. It's included in both images and accepts the same arguments:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel-ci-docker-run --rm node:24 npm view next version
```

`vercel-ci-docker-run` mounts the Vercel CI CA bundle into the container at `/run/vercel/ca-certificates.crt` and points these environment variables at it:

- `AWS_CA_BUNDLE`
- `CARGO_HTTP_CAINFO`
- `CURL_CA_BUNDLE`
- `GIT_SSL_CAINFO`
- `GRPC_DEFAULT_SSL_ROOTS_FILE_PATH`
- `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`, with `NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=1`
- `NPM_CONFIG_CAFILE`
- `PIP_CERT`
- `REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE`
- `SSL_CERT_FILE`

`vercel-ci-docker-run` only replaces `docker run`. It doesn't configure Docker Compose or `docker build`. Applications with their own trust store might need extra setup in their image.

## Choosing an image for a task

Add a `ci:os` tag next to the `ci` tag on a task in your root `turbo.json`:

```json filename="turbo.json" {4}
{
  "tasks": {
    "test": {
      "tags": ["ci", "ci:os:ubuntu"]
    }
  }
}
```

A task can have only one `ci:os` tag. Tagging a task with both `ci:os:amazonlinux` and `ci:os:ubuntu` makes your Vercel CI configuration invalid.

## Choosing an image for a package

To set the default image for every task in a package, add a `ci:os` tag to the top-level `tags` field of the package's [Package Configuration](https://turborepo.dev/docs/reference/package-configurations):

```json filename="apps/web/turbo.json" {3}
{
  "extends": ["//"],
  "tags": ["ci:os:ubuntu"]
}
```

A `ci:os` tag on a task takes precedence over the package's top-level `ci:os` tag.

To change the image for one task in one package, add the tag to that task in the Package Configuration. Start the `tags` array with `$TURBO_EXTENDS$` so the task keeps the `ci` tag from the root `turbo.json`:

```json filename="apps/web/turbo.json" {5}
{
  "extends": ["//"],
  "tasks": {
    "test": {
      "tags": ["$TURBO_EXTENDS$", "ci:os:ubuntu"]
    }
  }
}
```

## Dependency installation

Vercel CI installs your repository's dependencies with the Amazon Linux image, whatever `ci:os` tags your tasks use. To change the resources for this step, see [Bootstrapping resources](/docs/ci/configuration#bootstrapping-resources).

# Vercel CI

Vercel CI intelligently schedules your tasks so that you do as little work as possible every time you or your agent pushes code.

- Your [Turborepo Task Graph](https://turborepo.dev/docs/core-concepts/package-and-task-graph#task-graph) is used to find the minimal set of tasks to run. If a task isn't affected by your code changes or has already been cached, it will be restored from cache or skipped.
- Vercel CI runs every independent task in the Task Graph in parallel. You don't configure concurrency, so it stays correct as your codebase changes.
- Dependencies are cached across runs and installed once per run. Every task then starts from a snapshot of that setup instead of reinstalling.
- [Vercel Remote Cache](https://vercel.com/docs/monorepos/remote-caching#vercel-remote-cache) is enabled with zero-configuration.
- Each task is executed in its own isolated compute and given the right amount of compute for its needs. This substantially improves resource provisioning and makes task execution faster.

> **💡 Note:** Vercel CI is in Beta. Features and configuration may change.

## How it works

Vercel CI watches your repository for new code changes. On each `git push`:

1. Turborepo determines the set of tasks that are tagged with `"tags": ["ci"]` in `turbo.json`.
2. For those tasks, [Vercel Remote Cache](https://vercel.com/docs/monorepos/remote-caching#vercel-remote-cache) is checked to see which tasks have already been cached.
3. The remaining set of uncached, tagged tasks are marked for execution.
4. Each task is executed in dependency order, and in its own compute instance.
5. The status of your tasks are posted back to your source code forge. If one or more tasks fail, Vercel CI is marked as failed.

## Getting started

If your Turborepo checks run in GitHub Actions, follow [Migrate from GitHub Actions to Vercel CI](/kb/guide/github-actions-to-vercel-ci) to move your tasks and secrets, compare both pipelines, and switch your required status checks.

### Prerequisites

- Vercel CI requires Turborepo 2.11.7 or later.
- Vercel CLI 64.3.1 or later

### Set up with an agent

Use the Vercel CI setup Skill to have your coding agent select initial tasks, configure Vercel CI, and open a pull request. Open your repository in your agent, then copy and send this prompt:

**Agent prompt**

```text
Set up Vercel CI for this repository. Run `npx skills use vercel/ci@setup` and follow the skill's instructions to select initial tasks, configure Vercel CI, and open a pull request.
```

### Manual set up

#### Enable Vercel CI

You must explicitly enable Vercel CI for your repository before it can run tasks.

Connect your GitHub repository to a Vercel project on your team. Then, from a local clone of your repository, run:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel ci enable
```

#### Run a task

Add the `ci` tag to each task that Vercel CI should run. Vercel CI uses the Turborepo task graph to run each affected `package#task` selector and its dependencies.

In the example below, the `test` task will run in Vercel CI.

```json filename="turbo.json" {4}
{
  "tasks": {
    "test": {
      "tags": ["ci"]
    }
  }
}
```

## Finding tasks and logs

In the dashboard, all of the CI runs for your team can be found in [the CI tab](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%7E%2Fci\&title=).

For programmatic and agentic access, Vercel CI is available in:

- [Vercel CLI](/docs/cli/ci) (version 64.3.1 or later)
- [Vercel MCP](/docs/agent-resources/vercel-mcp)
- [Our OpenAPI specification](/docs/rest-api)

Additionally, PRs have a link to your CI run available in the GitHub merge box, alongside all your other PR's checks.

## Communicating with your source forge

You can use [branch protection rules](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/managing-a-branch-protection-rule) to prevent Pull Requests from merging when failures in Vercel CI are present. This prevents you from merging unwanted code, and works the same way as blocking on a GitHub Action failure.

## Limitations

- Vercel CI currently only offers Linux for its base image.
- GitHub is currently the only supported source code forge.
- Public repositories are not currently supported.
- Pushing code to GitHub with `git push` is currently the only supported trigger.
- A repository must not have projects connected to multiple Vercel teams.

## Learn more

- [Configuration](/docs/ci/configuration): Set task dependencies and configure resource sizes.
- [Environment variables](/docs/ci/environment-variables): Add secrets and constants for your CI runs.
- [Images](/docs/ci/image): Choose the operating system your tasks run on, and run Docker containers in your tasks.
- [Guides](/docs/ci/guides): Follow complete examples, like running end-to-end tests and commenting on pull requests.
- [Pricing](/docs/ci/pricing): Understand how Vercel CI usage is billed.

title: "Vercel CI Pricing"

# Vercel CI Pricing

Vercel CI bills for the compute your runs use, measured in CPU minutes. A CPU minute is one CPU running for one minute, matching [Builds pricing](https://vercel.com/docs/builds#pricing).

## Pricing

| Plan | Price |
| --- | --- |
| Hobby | 200 CPU minutes per month included |
| Pro | $0.0035 per CPU minute |
| Enterprise | Custom |


## How Vercel CI calculates CPU minutes

Vercel CI runs each step of a run in its own compute instance. For each instance, Vercel CI multiplies the number of CPUs by the time the instance runs:

- **CPUs**: The number of requested CPUs.
- **Time**: From when the task starts until it stops, including shutdown. Vercel CI rounds up to the next second, with a minimum of 1 second.

For example, a task with 8 CPUs that runs for 2 minutes and 30 seconds uses 8 × 2.5 = 20 CPU minutes.

## What uses CPU minutes

Each run uses CPU minutes for these steps:

| Step                                    | CPUs                                                                                                                |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Bootstrapping                           | 4 by default. Change it with [`ci.bootstrapping.resources.vcpus`](/docs/ci/configuration#bootstrapping-resources). |
| Each task that runs                     | 2 by default. Change it with a [`ci:cpus` tag](/docs/ci/configuration#resource-sizing).                             |

Tasks that Vercel CI restores from cache or skips because your changes don't affect them don't run, so they don't use CPU minutes.

title: "Telemetry"
description: "Vercel CLI collects telemetry data about general usage."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.886Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/cli/about-telemetry"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Telemetry

> **💡 Note:** Participation in this program is optional, and you may
> [opt-out](#how-do-i-opt-out-of-vercel-cli-telemetry) if you would prefer not
> to share any telemetry information.

## Why is telemetry collected?

Vercel CLI Telemetry collects telemetry to improve Vercel's products and services, including the developer experience, platform performance, and AI features. For full details on how Vercel uses the data it collects, see our [Privacy Notice](https://vercel.com/legal/privacy-policy).

## What is being collected?

Vercel takes privacy and security seriously. Vercel CLI Telemetry tracks general usage information, such as commands and arguments used. This includes:

- Command invoked (`vercel build`, `vercel deploy`, `vercel login`, etc.)
- Version of the Vercel CLI
- General machine information (e.g. number of CPUs, macOS/Windows/Linux, whether or not the command was run within CI)
- Identifiers associated with your account

You can view exactly what is being collected by setting the following environment variable: `VERCEL_TELEMETRY_DEBUG=1`.

When this environment variable is set, data will **not be sent to Vercel**.
The data will only be printed out to the [*stderr* stream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_streams), prefixed with `[telemetry]`.

An example telemetry event looks like this:

```json
{
  "id": "cf9022fd-e4b3-4f67-bda2-f02dba5b2e40",
  "eventTime": 1728421688109,
  "key": "subcommand:ls",
  "value": "ls",
  "teamId": "team_9Cdf9AE0j9ef09FaSdEU0f0s",
  "sessionId": "e29b9b32-3edd-4599-92d2-f6886af005f6"
}
```

## What about sensitive data?

Vercel CLI Telemetry **does not** collect any metrics which may contain sensitive data, including, but not limited to: environment variables, file paths, contents of files, logs, or serialized JavaScript errors.

## How do I opt-out of Vercel CLI telemetry?

You may use the [vercel telemetry](/docs/cli/telemetry) command to manage the telemetry collection status. This sets a global configuration value on your computer.

You may opt-out of telemetry data collection by running `vercel telemetry disable`:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel telemetry disable
```

You may check the status of telemetry collection at any time by running `vercel telemetry status`:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel telemetry status
```

You may re-enable telemetry if you'd like to re-join the program by running the following:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel telemetry enable
```

Alternatively, you may opt-out by setting an environment variable: `VERCEL_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1`. This will only apply for runs where the environment variable is set and will not change your configured telemetry status.

title: "vercel activity"
description: "View activity events for your Vercel project or team, filtered by type, date range, and project."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.886Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/cli/activity"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# vercel activity

The `vercel activity` command displays [activity events](/docs/activity-log) for your linked project. You can filter events by type, date range, and project, or view all events across your team.

By default, running `vercel activity` shows events scoped to the linked project. Use `--all` to see all events across your team, or `--project` to target a specific project.

## Usage

```bash filename="terminal"
# List events for the linked project
vercel activity
vercel activity ls

# List all team events from the last 30 days
vercel activity ls --all --since 30d

# Filter by event type
vercel activity ls --type deployment --since 7d
```

*Using the \`vercel activity\` command to view activity events.*

## Unique options

These options only apply to the `vercel activity` command.

### Type

The `--type` option filters events by event type. You can repeat the flag or use comma-separated values. Run `vercel activity types` to see all available event types.

```bash filename="terminal"
# Single type
vercel activity --type deployment

# Multiple types with repeated flags
vercel activity --type deployment --type project-created

# Comma-separated types
vercel activity --type deployment,project-created
```

### Since

The `--since` option, shorthand `-s`, shows events after a specific date. You can use ISO 8601 format or relative values like `1d`, `7d`, or `30d`.

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel activity --since 7d
vercel activity --since 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z
```

### Until

The `--until` option, shorthand `-u`, shows events before a specific date. Accepts the same formats as `--since`.

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel activity --since 30d --until 7d
```

### Project

The `--project` option, shorthand `-p`, filters events by a specific project name or ID. This overrides the auto-detected linked project.

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel activity --project my-app
```

### All

The `--all` option, shorthand `-a`, shows all events across your team instead of scoping to the linked project.

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel activity --all --since 30d
```

You can't use `--all` and `--project` together.

### Limit

The `--limit` option specifies the maximum number of events to return. The default is 20, and the maximum is 100.

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel activity --limit 50
```

### Next

The `--next` option paginates through results. After each page, the command prints the value to pass to `--next` for the following page.

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel activity --next 1706140800000
```

### Format

The `--format` option controls the output format. Set it to `json` to output structured JSON, which makes it easier to pipe to other tools like [jq](https://jqlang.github.io/jq/).

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel activity --format json | jq '.events[]'
```

## Subcommands

### `vercel activity ls`

Lists activity events. This is the default subcommand when running `vercel activity` without arguments.

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel activity ls
vercel activity ls --all
vercel activity ls --project my-app
```

The output includes a scope header showing whether you're viewing team-wide events (via `--all`) or project-specific events (via `--project`).

When using `--format json`, the response includes a `scope` object with `teamSlug` and `projectIds` to indicate the scope of the results:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel activity ls --format json | jq '.scope'
```

### `vercel activity types`

Lists all available event types with descriptions. Use this to find valid values for the `--type` filter.

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel activity types
vercel activity types --format json
```

## Examples

List deployment events from the last week:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel activity --type deployment --since 7d
```

List all team events and output as JSON:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel activity --all --format json | jq '.events[] | {type, text: .text}'
```

Paginate through results:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel activity --limit 10
# Use the --next value from the output to get the next page
vercel activity --limit 10 --next 1706140800000
```

## Global Options

- [`--debug`](/docs/cli/global-options#debug)
- [`--global-config`](/docs/cli/global-options#global-config)

# vercel agent

The `vercel agent` command writes a section related to Vercel deployment best practices in your project's agent guidance file so coding agents and assistants have context for how the project should build, deploy, and integrate with Vercel features. The section is wrapped in `<!-- VERCEL BEST PRACTICES START -->` and `<!-- VERCEL BEST PRACTICES END -->` markers so it can be re-applied non-destructively.

The target file is `AGENTS.md` by default; when run from Claude Code, the target is `CLAUDE.md`.

## Usage

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel agent init
```

*Using the \`vercel agent init\` command to include a section about Vercel best practices in
the agent guidance file of the current directory.*

The command checks whether the target file already exists and whether it already contains the section on Vercel best practices:

- If the file doesn't exist, the command creates it with just the marked section.
- If the file exists without the markers, the command appends a marked section to the end. Your existing content is preserved.
- If the file exists and already contains the markers, the command updates only the content between the markers, leaving the rest of the file untouched.

You're prompted to confirm the change before any write. The command never replaces an entire existing file.

## Examples

### Add Vercel best practices to the current project

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel agent init
```

*Run interactively to add or update the marked section in the target file.*

### Skip the confirmation prompt

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel agent init --yes
```

*Use \`--yes\` (shorthand \`-y\`) in CI or other non-interactive environments to
skip the confirmation prompt. Required in non-interactive shells.*

## Unique options

These are options that only apply to the `vercel agent` command.

### Yes

The `--yes` option, shorthand `-y`, skips the confirmation prompt. Required when running in a non-interactive shell.

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel agent init --yes
```

*Skip the confirmation prompt that asks before writing to the target file.*

## Global Options

The following [global options](/docs/cli/global-options) can be passed when using the `vercel agent` command:

- [`--cwd`](/docs/cli/global-options#current-working-directory)
- [`--debug`](/docs/cli/global-options#debug)
- [`--global-config`](/docs/cli/global-options#global-config)
- [`--help`](/docs/cli/global-options#help)
- [`--local-config`](/docs/cli/global-options#local-config)
- [`--no-color`](/docs/cli/global-options#no-color)
- [`--non-interactive`](/docs/cli/global-options#non-interactive)
- [`--scope`](/docs/cli/global-options#scope)
- [`--team`](/docs/cli/global-options#team)
- [`--token`](/docs/cli/global-options#token)
- [`--version`](/docs/cli/global-options#version)

For more information on global options and their usage, refer to the [options section](/docs/cli/global-options).

title: "vercel agent-runs"
description: "Find projects with Agent Runs, list recent runs, and inspect run metadata and conversation traces from the command line."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.886Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/cli/agent-runs"

# vercel agent-runs

The `vercel agent-runs` command reads [Agent Runs](/docs/agent-runs) data from your terminal. Use it to investigate an eve agent's lifecycle events, subagents, messages, reasoning, tool calls, and token usage.

## Usage

Find projects with Agent Runs activity, then list and inspect runs for a project:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel agent-runs projects --scope my-team
vercel agent-runs list --scope my-team --project my-app
vercel agent-runs inspect run_1234567890 --scope my-team --project my-app
vercel agent-runs trace run_1234567890 --scope my-team --project my-app
```

Replace `run_1234567890` with a run ID from the list response. The `list`, `inspect`, and `trace` commands use your [linked project](/docs/cli/link) unless you pass `--project`. The `projects` command works at the team level. From an unlinked directory, pass [`--scope`](/docs/cli/global-options#scope) for `projects`, and both `--scope` and `--project` for the other commands. When selecting a different team from a linked directory, pass both flags to select a project in that team.

All four commands query the `production` environment by default. Use `--environment preview` for preview deployments. When inspecting a run from a filtered list, keep the same team, project, environment, and time window.

## Subcommands

### List projects

`vercel agent-runs projects` finds projects in the selected team with Agent Runs activity:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel agent-runs projects --scope my-team --since 7d
vercel agent-runs projects --environment preview --json
```

### List runs

`vercel agent-runs list` (alias `ls`) lists runs for a project. Filter by time or title, and limit the number of results per page:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel agent-runs list --environment preview --since 1d
vercel agent-runs list --query "checkout" --limit 20
vercel agent-runs list --project my-app --json
```

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--query <TEXT>`, `-q` | Search runs by title. `--search` is a deprecated alias. |
| `--limit <N>`, `-n` | Number of runs per page, up to 100. |
| `--next <CURSOR>` | Continue a list using the cursor from the previous response. |

To continue a list, use the next-page command printed by the CLI. Cursor-based JSON responses expose the next cursor in `pagination.next`. Keep the same team, project, environment, and query. The cursor preserves the time window, so omit `--since` and `--until` when continuing:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel agent-runs list --project my-app --next "$NEXT_CURSOR" --json
```

Set `NEXT_CURSOR` to the cursor from the previous response. A page can contain no runs and still provide a next cursor. Continue while a cursor is available, and start without `--next` if it is invalid or expired. If the CLI prints a numeric next-page value instead, use its complete suggested command, including the time filters.

### Inspect a run

`vercel agent-runs inspect <runId>` retrieves a run's metadata, lifecycle events, usage, and subagent data:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel agent-runs inspect run_1234567890
vercel agent-runs inspect run_1234567890 --environment preview --json
```

### Read a trace

`vercel agent-runs trace <runId>` retrieves the conversation trace, including turns, messages, reasoning, tool calls, token usage, and tool inputs and outputs:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel agent-runs trace run_1234567890
vercel agent-runs trace run_1234567890 --json --max-field-length 0
```

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--max-field-length <N>` | Limit individual string fields before formatting. Defaults to 8000; positive values are capped at 50,000. Use `--json --max-field-length 0` to output fields without CLI truncation. |
| `--next <CURSOR>` | Fetch newer trace activity using a cursor from a previous response. |
| `--previous <CURSOR>` | Fetch older trace activity using a cursor from a previous response. |

Markdown output separately shortens displayed messages, reasoning, and tool inputs and outputs to 2,000 characters, even with `--max-field-length 0`. Use `--json` to retain fields omitted from the Markdown view, such as per-turn token usage, and combine it with `--max-field-length 0` for untruncated field values. This doesn't combine trace pages or restore content the service didn't return.

You can't combine `--next` and `--previous`. Use the continuation commands printed by the CLI, or the `pagination.next` and `pagination.previous` cursors in JSON output. Keep the same run, team, project, environment, and time window:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel agent-runs trace run_1234567890 --next "$NEXT_CURSOR" --json
vercel agent-runs trace run_1234567890 --previous "$PREVIOUS_CURSOR" --json
```

Set each variable to the corresponding cursor from the previous response. A trace page may contain only part of a conversation. Follow available cursors before treating the response as the complete run.

## Shared options

These options apply to all four subcommands unless noted:

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--environment <ENVIRONMENT>`, `-e` | Query `production` or `preview`. Defaults to `production`. |
| `--since <TIME>`, `-s` | Start of the time window, as an ISO 8601 timestamp or a relative value such as `1h` or `7d`. |
| `--until <TIME>`, `-u` | End of the time window. Requires `--since` and defaults to now. Accepts the same formats as `--since`. |
| `--project <NAME\|ID>`, `-p` | Override the linked project. Applies to `list`, `inspect`, and `trace`. |
| `--json` | Print the API response as JSON to standard output. Trace strings still respect `--max-field-length`. |

For example, list runs from a specific time window:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel agent-runs list --since 7d --until 1d
```

## Use output in scripts and coding agents

Every subcommand supports `--json`. Without `--json`, the CLI renders recognized conversation turns as Markdown, including when you pipe or redirect output. If it can't find turns to render, it prints the response as JSON instead. This lets a coding agent inspect traces through shell commands without an MCP connection:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel agent-runs list --json
vercel agent-runs trace run_1234567890 > agent-run.md
vercel agent-runs trace run_1234567890 --json --max-field-length 0 > agent-run.json
```

The trace contains only the content Agent Runs collected. Review [trace sampling](/docs/agent-runs#configure-tracing-for-existing-deployments) and [trace content settings](/docs/agent-runs#configure-agent-runs-trace-content) if expected activity or fields are missing.

## Global Options

The following [global options](/docs/cli/global-options) can be passed when using the `vercel agent-runs` command:

- [`--cwd`](/docs/cli/global-options#current-working-directory)
- [`--debug`](/docs/cli/global-options#debug)
- [`--global-config`](/docs/cli/global-options#global-config)
- [`--help`](/docs/cli/global-options#help)
- [`--local-config`](/docs/cli/global-options#local-config)
- [`--no-color`](/docs/cli/global-options#no-color)
- [`--non-interactive`](/docs/cli/global-options#non-interactive)
- [`--scope`](/docs/cli/global-options#scope)
- [`--team`](/docs/cli/global-options#team)
- [`--token`](/docs/cli/global-options#token)
- [`--version`](/docs/cli/global-options#version)

For more information on global options and their usage, refer to the [options section](/docs/cli/global-options).

## Related

- [Agent Runs](/docs/agent-runs)
- [Agent Runs tools in Vercel MCP](/docs/agent-resources/vercel-mcp/tools/agent-runs)
- [vercel traces](/docs/cli/traces)

title: "vercel ai-gateway"
description: "Manage AI Gateway resources from the Vercel CLI: API keys, budgets, routing rules, virtual models, models, leaderboards, and coding agent setup."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.886Z"
