## Cron job duration

The duration limits for Cron jobs are identical to those of [Vercel Functions](/docs/functions/limitations#max-duration). See the [`maxDuration`](/docs/functions/limitations#max-duration) documentation for more information.

In most cases, these limits are sufficient. However, if you need more processing time, it's recommended to split your cron jobs into different units or distribute your workload by combining cron jobs with regular HTTP requests with your API.

## Cron job error handling

Vercel will not retry an invocation if a cron job fails. You can check for error [logs](/docs/logs/runtime) through the **View Log** button in the **Cron Jobs** section in the sidebar.

## Cron jobs with dynamic routes

Cron jobs can be created for [dynamic routes](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/dynamic-routes):

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "crons": [
    {
      "path": "/api/sync-slack-team/T0CAQ10TZ",
      "schedule": "0 5 * * *"
    },
    {
      "path": "/api/sync-slack-team/T4BOE34OP",
      "schedule": "0 5 * * *"
    }
  ]
}
```

## Handling nonexistent paths

If you create a cron job for a path that doesn't exist, it generates a [404 error](/docs/errors/NOT_FOUND). However, **Vercel still executes your cron job**. You can analyze your logs to check if there are any issues.

## Cron jobs and deployments

Creating a new deployment will not interrupt your running cron jobs; they will continue until they finish.

## Controlling cron job concurrency

If your cron job runs longer than the interval between invocations, Vercel can trigger a second instance while the first is still running. This can lead to race conditions, duplicate processing, or data corruption.

To prevent concurrent runs, use a lock mechanism like [Redis distributed locks](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/clients/patterns/distributed-locks/) in your cron job. A lock ensures only one instance runs at a time by checking if another instance is already active before starting.

You can also prevent overlapping runs by:

- **Reducing execution time**: Optimize your job to finish before the next invocation
- **Setting timeouts**: Use [`maxDuration`](/docs/functions/limitations#max-duration) to force long-running jobs to stop
- **Increasing the interval**: Run your cron job less frequently

### Cron job delivery and idempotency

Cron job delivery is best effort. Most invocations run as scheduled, but occasional transient network errors can prevent a request from reaching your function. In those cases, your function does not execute, and no runtime log is created for that scheduled run.

Cron delivery can also occasionally invoke the same scheduled run more than once. Because of this, cron jobs should be resilient to both missed runs and duplicate runs.

Design your operations to be **idempotent** and reconciliation-based so each run can safely reprocess outstanding work since the last successful run. For example:

- **Good**: "Set user status to active" (running twice has the same effect)
- **Bad**: "Increment user credit by 10" (running twice doubles the credit)

To make operations resilient:

- Use unique IDs to track which events you've already processed
- Check state before making changes (e.g., "if not already active, then activate")
- Store results with timestamps or version numbers
- Query and process all work since the last successful run to catch up after a missed invocation

Use both locks (to prevent concurrent runs) and idempotent reconciliation (to handle duplicate or missed runs safely) for the most reliable cron jobs.

## Running cron jobs locally

Cron jobs are API routes. You can run them locally by making a request to their endpoint. For example, if your cron job is in `/api/cron`, you could visit the following endpoint in your browser: `http://localhost:3000/api/cron`. You should be aware that while your browser may follow redirects, [cron job invocations in production will not](#cron-jobs-and-redirects) follow redirects.

There is currently no support for `vercel dev`, `next dev`, or other framework-native local development servers.

## Cron jobs and redirects

Cron jobs do not follow redirects. When a cron-triggered endpoint returns a 3xx redirect status code, the job completes without further requests. Redirect responses are treated as final for each invocation.

A common source of redirects is the Next.js [`trailingSlash`](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/trailingSlash) option. When it's enabled, a request to `/api/cron` redirects to `/api/cron/`, so the cron job never reaches your function. Add the trailing slash to the `path` in your cron job configuration, such as `"path": "/api/cron/"`.

The view logs button on the cron job overview can be used to verify the response of the invocations and gain further insights.

## Cron jobs logs

Cron jobs are logged as function invocations from the **Logs** section in your project dashboard sidebar(/dashboard). You can view the logs for a cron job from the list on the [Cron jobs settings page](/docs/cron-jobs/manage-cron-jobs#viewing-cron-jobs) of the project:

1. From the list of cron jobs, select **View Logs**.
2. This will take you to the [runtime logs](/docs/logs/runtime#request-path) view with a `requestPath` filter to your cron job such as `requestPath:/api/my-cron-job`.

See [how to view runtime logs](/docs/logs/runtime#view-runtime-logs) for more information.

Note that when cron jobs respond with a redirect or a cached response, they will not be shown in the logs.

## Cron jobs accuracy

Hobby users have two cron job restrictions. First, cron jobs can only run [once per day](/docs/cron-jobs/usage-and-pricing#hobby-scheduling-limits). Expressions that run more frequently will fail deployment. Second, Vercel may invoke these cron jobs at any point within the specified hour to help distribute load across all accounts. For example, an expression like `0 8 * * *` could trigger an invocation anytime between `08:00:00` and `08:59:59`.

For all other teams, cron jobs will be invoked within the minute specified. For instance, the expression `5 8 * * *` would trigger an invocation between `08:05:00` and `08:05:59`.

## Rollbacks and promotions with cron jobs

When you [Instant Rollback](/docs/instant-rollback) to a previous deployment, Vercel restores the cron job definitions associated with that deployment. If cron jobs are enabled for the project, Vercel invokes those jobs from the next scheduled invocation onward.

Instant Rollback preserves the project's **Disable Cron Jobs** setting.

### Which `CRON_SECRET` value a rollback restores

Rolling back restores the target deployment's copy of `CRON_SECRET` along with its cron job definitions. If you rotated the secret after that deployment was built, the rollback puts the older secret back in use, and the handler on that deployment already expects it. You don't need the plaintext to recover a secret this way.

You can only roll back to a deployment that [previously served production traffic](/docs/instant-rollback#eligible-deployments), and your plan decides how far back you can reach for an older secret. On Pro and Enterprise, you can roll back to any eligible deployment. On Hobby, you can only roll back to the immediately previous deployment. Your [deployment retention policy](/docs/deployment-retention) decides how long those deployments stay available.

Redeploying an older deployment won't bring its secret back. A redeploy builds a new deployment, which captures whatever your project settings hold now. See [Rotating environment variables](/docs/environment-variables/rotating-secrets).

### Which `CRON_SECRET` value a promotion uses

A promotion that rebuilds captures your current project settings. A promotion that only moves domains keeps the deployment's existing copy:

| Action                                                                                                                                | Rebuilds | Secret sent with cron invocations   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------- |
| [Promote a preview deployment to production](/docs/deployments/promoting-a-deployment#promote-a-deployment-from-preview-to-production) | Yes      | Your current project settings value |
| [Promote a staged production build](/docs/deployments/promoting-a-deployment#staging-and-promoting-a-production-deployment)            | No       | The promoted deployment's own copy  |
| [Instant Rollback](/docs/instant-rollback)                                                                                             | No       | The target deployment's own copy    |

### Scheduled runs during a promotion or rollback

Your production domains move first, and Vercel repoints the cron schedules at the new deployment shortly after. A run scheduled inside that gap can still reach the deployment you just moved away from, or it can be skipped.

The secret stays correct either way, because each invocation carries the secret of the deployment it reaches. Plan for a missed or repeated run instead, following [Cron job delivery and idempotency](#cron-job-delivery-and-idempotency).

## Troubleshooting cron jobs

If a cron job doesn't run or doesn't appear in the logs, check these causes:

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The job doesn't run on a preview deployment | Cron jobs run only on production deployments. | Test the endpoint by requesting it directly, and check scheduled runs on the production deployment. |
| The job doesn't run at the expected time | The expression doesn't match the intended schedule, or your plan restricts how often jobs run. | Check the expression and the [usage and pricing](/docs/cron-jobs/usage-and-pricing) limits for your plan. Hobby jobs can run [anywhere within the scheduled hour](#cron-jobs-accuracy). |
| Every invocation returns `401` | The `Authorization` header doesn't match `CRON_SECRET`. | Check the value for characters that aren't valid in a header. See [Securing cron jobs](#securing-cron-jobs). |
| The job runs but doesn't appear in the logs | The endpoint returned a redirect or a cached response. | Remove the redirect, such as one caused by `trailingSlash`. See [Cron jobs and redirects](#cron-jobs-and-redirects). In a Next.js route handler, add `export const dynamic = 'force-dynamic';` so the function runs on every invocation. |
| The job is blocked before it reaches your function | A [WAF custom rule](/docs/vercel-firewall/vercel-waf/custom-rules) matches the cron request. | Review your firewall rules and exclude the cron job's path from rules that deny or challenge traffic. |
| The job targets the wrong path | The function was renamed or moved after you configured the job. | Update the `path` in your cron job configuration to match a route in the deployment. |
| The job isn't listed in the project settings | The build didn't register the job. | Run [`vercel build --prod`](/docs/cli/build) locally and confirm that `.vercel/output/config.json` contains a `crons` array with your job. |

A valid build registers each job in `.vercel/output/config.json`:

```json filename=".vercel/output/config.json"
{
  "crons": [{ "path": "/api/example-cron", "schedule": "0 5 * * *" }]
}
```

# Cron Jobs

> Cron Jobs are available on all plans

Cron jobs are time-based scheduling tools used to automate repetitive tasks. By using a specific syntax called a [cron expression](#cron-expressions), you can define the frequency and timing of each task. This helps improve efficiency and ensures that important processes are performed consistently.

Some common use cases of cron jobs are:

- Automating backups and archiving them
- Sending email and Slack notifications
- Updating Stripe subscription quantities

Vercel supports cron jobs for [Vercel Functions](/docs/functions). Cron jobs can be added through [`vercel.json`](/docs/project-configuration) or the [Build Output API](/docs/build-output-api/configuration#crons).

See [Managing Cron Jobs](/docs/cron-jobs/manage-cron-jobs) for information on duration, error handling, deployments, concurrency control, and local execution. To learn about usage limits and pricing information, see the [Usage and Pricing](/docs/cron-jobs/usage-and-pricing) page.

A scheduled endpoint can enqueue a job or start a workflow when the work needs retries or durable execution. Compare [background worker options](/docs/background-workers) to choose how your scheduled work runs.

## Getting started with cron jobs

Learn how to set up and configure cron jobs for your project using our [Quickstart](/docs/cron-jobs/quickstart) guide.

## How cron jobs work

To trigger a cron job, Vercel makes an HTTP GET request to your project's production deployment URL, using the `path` provided in your project's `vercel.json` file. For example, Vercel might request the following endpoint to trigger a cron job: `https://*.vercel.app/api/cron`.

Vercel Functions triggered by a cron job on Vercel will always contain `vercel-cron/1.0` as the user agent. Each request also includes an `x-vercel-cron-schedule` header containing the cron expression that triggered the invocation (e.g., `0 5 * * *`). You can use this header to determine which schedule triggered your function when multiple cron jobs share the same path.

## Cron expressions

Vercel supports the following cron expressions format:

| Field        | Value Range     | Example Expression | Description                                          |
| ------------ | --------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Minute       | 0 - 59          | `5 * * * *`        | Triggers at 5 minutes past the hour                  |
| Hour         | 0 - 23          | `* 5 * * *`        | Triggers every minute, between 05:00 AM and 05:59 AM |
| Day of Month | 1 - 31          | `* * 5 * *`        | Triggers every minute, on day 5 of the month         |
| Month        | 1 - 12          | `* * * 5 *`        | Triggers every minute, only in May                   |
| Day of Week  | 0 - 6 (Sun-Sat) | `* * * * 5`        | Triggers every minute, only on Friday                |

### Validate cron expressions

To validate your cron expressions, you can use the following tool to quickly verify the syntax and timing of your scheduled tasks to ensure they run as intended.

You can also use [crontab guru](https://crontab.guru/) to validate your cron expressions.

### Cron expression limitations

- Cron jobs on Vercel do not support alternative expressions like `MON`, `SUN`, `JAN`, or `DEC`
- You cannot configure both day of the month and day of the week at the same time. When one has a value, the other must be `*`
- The timezone is always UTC

## More resources

- [Managing Cron Jobs](/docs/cron-jobs/manage-cron-jobs)
- [Usage and Pricing](/docs/cron-jobs/usage-and-pricing)

# Getting started with cron jobs

This guide will help you get started with using cron jobs on Vercel. Cron jobs are scheduled tasks that run at specific times or intervals. They are useful for automating tasks. You will learn how to create a cron job that runs every day at 5 am UTC by creating a Vercel Function and configuring it in your `vercel.json` file.

**Agent prompt**

```text
Help me set up a Cron Job in this project. First, make sure the Vercel CLI is installed (`npm i -g vercel`). If I'm using Claude Code or Cursor, install the Vercel Plugin (`npx plugins add vercel/vercel-plugin`). For other agents, install Vercel Skills (`npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills`). Then: 1. Create a Vercel Function at app/api/hello/route.ts that runs a scheduled task. 2. Add a cron schedule to vercel.json that triggers this function on a recurring schedule. 3. Run `vercel env pull` to sync environment variables locally. 4. Deploy with `vercel --prod` and use `vercel inspect` to verify the cron job is configured.
```

## Prerequisites

- [A Vercel account](/signup)
- [A project](/docs/projects/managing-projects#creating-a-project) with a [Vercel Function](/docs/functions)

- ### Create a function
  This function contains the code that will be executed by the cron job. This example function returns a greeting.
  > For \['nextjs']:
  > **💡 Note:** To stream responses you must use Route Handlers in the App Router, even if the
  > rest of your app uses the Pages Router.
  ```ts v0="build" filename="app/api/hello/route.ts" framework=nextjs
  export function GET(request: Request) {
    return new Response('Hello from Vercel!');
  }
  ```
  ```js v0="build" filename="app/api/hello/route.js" framework=nextjs
  export function GET(request) {
    return new Response('Hello from Vercel!');
  }
  ```
  ```ts filename="api/hello.ts" framework=other
  export function GET(request: Request) {
    return new Response('Hello from Vercel!');
  }
  ```
  ```js filename="api/hello.js" framework=other
  export function GET(request) {
    return new Response('Hello from Vercel!');
  }
  ```
  ```ts v0="build" filename="app/api/hello/route.ts" framework=nextjs-app
  export function GET(request: Request) {
    return new Response('Hello from Vercel!');
  }
  ```
  ```js v0="build" filename="app/api/hello/route.js" framework=nextjs-app
  export function GET(request) {
    return new Response('Hello from Vercel!');
  }
  ```

- ### Create or update your `vercel.json` file
  Create or go to your [`vercel.json`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#functions) file and add the following code:
  ```json filename="vercel.json"
  {
    "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
    "crons": [
      {
        "path": "/api/hello",
        "schedule": "0 5 * * *"
      }
    ]
  }
  ```
  The `crons` property is an array of cron jobs. Each cron job has two properties:
  - The `path`, which must start with `/`
  - The `schedule` property, which must be a string that represents a [cron expression](/docs/cron-jobs#cron-expressions). In this example, the job is scheduled to execute every day at 5:00 am UTC

- ### Deploy your project.
  When you deploy your project, Vercel's build process creates the cron job. Vercel invokes cron jobs only for [production](/docs/deployments/environments#production-environment) deployments and not for [preview](/docs/deployments/environments#preview-environment-pre-production) deployments

  You can also deploy to your production domain using the CLI:
  ```bash filename="terminal"
  vercel deploy --prod
  ```

Your cron job is now active and will call the `/api/hello` path every day at 5:00 am UTC.

## Next steps

Now that you have created a cron job, you can learn more about how to manage and configure them:

- [Learn about managing cron jobs](/docs/cron-jobs/manage-cron-jobs)
- [Explore usage and pricing](/docs/cron-jobs/usage-and-pricing)

# Usage & Pricing for Cron Jobs

> Cron Jobs are available on all plans

Cron jobs invoke [Vercel Functions](/docs/functions). This means the same [usage](/docs/limits) and [pricing](/pricing) limits will apply.

|                | **Number of cron jobs per project** | **Minimum interval** | **Scheduling precision** |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------ |
| **Hobby**      | 100 cron jobs                       | Once per day         | Per-hour (±59 min)       |
| **Pro**        | 100 cron jobs                       | Once per minute      | Per-minute               |
| **Enterprise** | 100 cron jobs                       | Once per minute      | Per-minute               |

### Hobby scheduling limits

> **💡 Note:** Hobby accounts are limited to cron jobs that run **once per day**. Cron
> expressions that would run more frequently will fail during deployment.

Hobby plans have two restrictions on cron jobs:

1. **Daily execution limit**: Cron jobs can only run once per day. Expressions like `0 * * * *` (per-hour) or `*/30 * * * *` (every 30 minutes) will fail deployment with the error:
   *Hobby accounts are limited to daily cron jobs. This cron expression would run more than once per day.*

2. **Timing precision**: Vercel cannot assure a timely cron job invocation. For example, a cron job configured as `0 1 * * *` (every day at 1 am) will trigger anywhere between 1:00 am and 1:59 am.

For cron jobs that run more frequently or with precise timing, **upgrade to our [Pro](/docs/plans/pro-plan) plan**.

## Pricing

Cron jobs are included in **all plans**.

You use a function to invoke a cron job, and therefore [usage](/docs/limits) and [pricing](/pricing) limits for these functions apply to all cron job executions:

- [Functions limits and pricing](/docs/functions/usage-and-pricing)

description: "Learn how to configure custom error pages for 5xx server errors on Vercel."

# Custom error pages

> Custom error pages are available on Enterprise plans

Custom error pages let you replace Vercel's platform error pages with your own branded experience. These include errors like [function invocation timeouts](/docs/errors/function_invocation_timeout) or [when your functions are throttled](/docs/errors/function_throttled).

Custom error pages help you:

- **Maintain brand consistency**: Keep your visual identity intact even during platform outages
- **Improve user experience**: Provide helpful messaging, support links, or status page references
- **Reduce user confusion**: Guide users on what to do next instead of showing a technical error

## How it works

When you deploy your project, Vercel automatically scans your build output for error pages and configures routes to cover all platform errors. For most cases, you only need to create a single `500` error page. Vercel automatically uses it as the fallback for all platform errors, so you don't need to design a separate page for each error type.

If a custom error page exists for a specific status code, Vercel uses it; otherwise, it falls back to your `500` error page if one exists.

## Error page tokens

You can include request IDs and error codes in your error pages using metadata tokens. When Vercel serves a custom error page, it replaces these tokens with actual values.

| Token                   | Description                                                                         |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `::vercel:REQUEST_ID::` | Matches the [`x-vercel-id`](/docs/headers/request-headers#x-vercel-id) header value |
| `::vercel:ERROR_CODE::` | The [error code](/docs/errors) (e.g., `FUNCTION_INVOCATION_TIMEOUT`)                |

> **💡 Note:** Vercel strongly recommends embedding these tokens to help users reference a specific request when contacting support.

## Getting started

Custom error pages must be static files in your build output. Common approaches include:

- Static HTML files (e.g., `500.html`, `504.html`)
- Framework error pages (Next.js App Router: `app/500/page.tsx`, Pages Router: `pages/500.tsx`)
- Files in your public directory

For example, you can create a custom error page by adding a static `500.html` file to your project's `public` directory:

```html filename="public/500.html"
<!doctype html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>Something went wrong</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Something went wrong</h1>
    <p>We're working on it. Please try again later.</p>
    <p>Request ID: ::vercel:REQUEST_ID::</p>
    <p>Error: ::vercel:ERROR_CODE::</p>
  </body>
</html>
```

Deploy your project, and Vercel will serve this page for all platform errors.

For example, if you add only two custom error pages (`500.html` and `504.html`), the routing behavior will be as follows:

| Error     | Destination            |
| --------- | ---------------------- |
| 500       | `/500.html`            |
| 501...503 | `/500.html` (fallback) |
| 504       | `/504.html`            |
| 505...511 | `/500.html` (fallback) |

### Examples

- [Custom error pages with App Router](https://github.com/vercel/examples/tree/main/cdn/custom-error-pages-app-dir/)
- [Custom error pages with public directory](https://github.com/vercel/examples/tree/main/cdn/custom-error-pages-public-dir/)

## Limits

- Custom error pages must be static. Since these pages handle platform errors, they can't rely on server-side rendering or dynamic content that might also fail.

title: "Daemon Configuration Reference"
description: "Every field you can set on a daemon in the daemons key of vercel.json."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.902Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/daemons/config-reference"

# Daemon Configuration Reference

You declare daemons with the top-level `daemons` key in `vercel.json`. The key is an object that maps each daemon name to its configuration:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "daemons": {
    "worker": {
      "root": "worker/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "command": ["node", "worker.js"],
      "instances": { "iad1": 2 },
      "resources": { "requests": { "memory": "2Gi" } }
    }
  }
}
```

A daemon configuration object supports the following fields:

| Field                                                             | Type                     | Required |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | -------- |
| [`root`](#root)                                                   | `string`                 | Yes      |
| [`entrypoint`](#entrypoint)                                       | `string`                 | Yes      |
| [`instances`](#instances)                                         | `Record<string, number>` | Yes      |
| [`command`](#command)                                             | `string[]`               | No       |
| [`resources`](#resources)                                         | `object`                 | No       |
| [`livenessProbe`](#livenessprobe)                                 | `LivenessProbe`          | No       |
| [`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`](#terminationgraceperiodseconds) | `number`                 | No       |
| [`bindings`](#bindings)                                           | `ServiceBinding[]`       | No       |

Vercel rejects any other field, including service fields such as `framework`, `runtime`, and `buildCommand`.

## Daemon names

The keys of the `daemons` object are daemon names. A daemon name:

- Contains only lowercase letters, separated by a single `_`, a double `__`, or one or more `-`. For example, `worker`, `email_sender`, and `celery-beat` are valid, and `Worker`, `worker1`, and `_worker` aren't.
- Is 64 characters or fewer.

Vercel pushes each daemon's image to a repository named `daemon.<name>`, with repeated hyphens collapsed into one. Two names that collapse to the same repository, such as `a-b` and `a--b`, fail the build.

Daemon names and [service](/docs/services) names don't conflict. A project can have a service and a daemon with the same name.

## root

**Type:** `string`

Required. The path to the daemon's source directory, relative to `vercel.json`. The path must stay inside the project.

Vercel doesn't publish files under a daemon's `root` as static assets of your deployment. If the project's output directory is the same directory as a daemon's `root`, the build fails. Choose a separate output directory.

## entrypoint

**Type:** `string`

Required. The path to the `Dockerfile` or `Containerfile` to build, relative to `root`. Name the file `Dockerfile` or `Containerfile`, optionally with a suffix, such as `Dockerfile.worker`. The name is case-insensitive. The directory that contains the file is the build context.

Vercel passes your deployment's environment variables to the build as build arguments, and builds the image for the Linux `amd64` architecture.

## instances

**Type:** `Record<string, number>`

Required. The number of instances to run in each region, keyed by [region ID](/docs/regions). Each count is an integer from `0` to `100`.

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "daemons": {
    "worker": {
      "root": "worker/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "instances": { "iad1": 2, "cdg1": 1 }
    }
  }
}
```

Vercel runs instances only in the regions listed. Set every count to `0` to stop the daemon without removing it. See [Scaling a daemon](/docs/daemons/managing-daemons#scaling-a-daemon).

## command

**Type:** `string[]`

The command and arguments to run in the container, as an array of strings. `command` replaces the image's `ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD`. When you don't set `command`, Vercel runs the image's `ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD`. The build fails if the image defines neither and `command` isn't set.

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "daemons": {
    "celery": {
      "root": "backend/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "command": ["celery", "-A", "app", "worker", "--loglevel=info"],
      "instances": { "iad1": 1 }
    }
  }
}
```

The array can contain up to 128 items, and each item can be up to 4,096 characters. Vercel doesn't run `command` through a shell. To use shell features such as environment variable expansion, run a shell explicitly, for example `["sh", "-c", "exec node worker.js --id $WORKER_ID"]`.

## resources

**Type:** `object`

The compute resources for each instance. `resources.requests.memory` sets the memory, and Vercel allocates CPU based on the memory you choose:

| `resources.requests.memory` | Memory | vCPUs |
| --------------------------- | ------ | ----- |
| `"1Gi"`                     | 1 GiB  | 1     |
| `"2Gi"` (default)           | 2 GiB  | 1     |
| `"4Gi"`                     | 4 GiB  | 2     |
| `"8Gi"`                     | 8 GiB  | 4     |

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "daemons": {
    "worker": {
      "root": "worker/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "instances": { "iad1": 1 },
      "resources": { "requests": { "memory": "4Gi" } }
    }
  }
}
```

When you set `resources`, `requests` and `memory` are required.

## livenessProbe

**Type:** `LivenessProbe`

An HTTP `GET` health check that Vercel requests periodically to check that the instance is still healthy. A response with an HTTP status from `200` to `399` counts as a success. Read more in [Health checks and restarts](/docs/daemons#health-checks-and-restarts).

A changed `livenessProbe` applies to instances started after it deploys; already-running instances keep the probe they started with.

A `LivenessProbe` object has the following fields:

| Field                 | Type              | Default | Description                                                                                                                                                     |
| --------------------- | ----------------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `httpGet`             | `LivenessHttpGet` | None    | Required. The HTTP request Vercel sends.                                                                                                                        |
| `initialDelaySeconds` | `number`          | `0`     | Seconds to wait after the container starts before the first probe. An integer from `0` to `86400`.                                                              |
| `periodSeconds`       | `number`          | `10`    | Seconds between probes, measured start to start. An integer from `1` to `86400`.                                                                                |
| `timeoutSeconds`      | `number`          | `1`     | Seconds to wait for a response before the probe counts as a failure. An integer from `1` to `86400`.                                                            |
| `failureThreshold`    | `number`          | `3`     | Consecutive failures before Vercel restarts the container. An integer from `1` to `10`.                                                                         |
| `successThreshold`    | `number`          | `1`     | Accepted by the schema, but the current controller behaves as if the value is 1, so one successful check resets the failure count. An integer from `1` to `10`. |

A `LivenessHttpGet` object has the following fields:

| Field         | Type                   | Default   | Description                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------- | ---------------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `port`        | `number`               | None      | Required. The port Vercel connects to. An integer from `1` to `65535`. The process must listen on this port inside the container.                       |
| `path`        | `string`               | `"/"`     | The request path. Must start with `/`.                                                                                                                  |
| `host`        | `string`               | localhost | The host to connect to. The probe runs from inside the instance, so it defaults to localhost.                                                           |
| `scheme`      | `"HTTP"` \| `"HTTPS"`  | `"HTTP"`  | The scheme Vercel uses for the request.                                                                                                                 |
| `httpHeaders` | `LivenessHttpHeader[]` | None      | Headers to add to the request. Each `LivenessHttpHeader` is an object with string `name` and `value` fields. A `Host` header sets the request's `Host`. |

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "daemons": {
    "worker": {
      "root": "worker/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "instances": { "iad1": 1 },
      "livenessProbe": {
        "httpGet": { "port": 1234, "path": "/health" },
        "initialDelaySeconds": 5
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## terminationGracePeriodSeconds

**Type:** `number`

The number of seconds Vercel waits after sending `SIGTERM` before it terminates the instance. The value is an integer from `0` to `3600`. The default is `30`. A changed value applies to instances started after it deploys; already-running instances keep the grace period they started with.

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "daemons": {
    "worker": {
      "root": "worker/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "instances": { "iad1": 1 },
      "terminationGracePeriodSeconds": 50
    }
  }
}
```

Raise the value when your process needs more time to finish work after `SIGTERM`. See [Graceful shutdown](/docs/daemons#graceful-shutdown).

## bindings

**Type:** [`ServiceBinding[]`](/docs/services/bindings#binding-fields)

[Service bindings](/docs/services/bindings) that let the daemon call [services](/docs/services) in the same deployment. Each binding has the same fields as a service binding: `type` is `"service"`, `service` names a service in `services`, `format` is `"url"`, and `env` is the environment variable that receives the service's URL.

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "services": {
    "api": { "root": "api/", "entrypoint": "main:app" }
  },
  "daemons": {
    "worker": {
      "root": "worker/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "instances": { "iad1": 1 },
      "bindings": [
        { "type": "service", "service": "api", "format": "url", "env": "API_URL" }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

A binding can only target a service. Daemons don't receive traffic, so services can't bind to daemons, and a daemon can't bind to another daemon. Each binding in a daemon must use a different `env`.

# Daemons Limits

The following limits apply to Vercel Daemons during the beta. Vercel may raise limits as the beta progresses.

## Configuration limits

| Limit                          | Value                                  |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| Daemon name length             | 64 characters                          |
| `root` and `entrypoint` length | 512 characters each                    |
| `command` items                | 128 items, up to 4,096 characters each |
| Instances per region           | 100 per daemon                         |
| Daemons per project            | 100                                    |

See the [Daemon configuration reference](/docs/daemons/config-reference) for the naming rules and allowed values of each field.

## Instance limits

| Limit                 | Value                                             |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Memory per instance   | 1 GiB, 2 GiB, 4 GiB, or 8 GiB (default 2 GiB)     |
| vCPUs per instance    | 1, 1, 2, or 4, based on memory                    |
| Shutdown grace period | 30 seconds after `SIGTERM` by default, configurable up to 3,600 seconds with [`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`](/docs/daemons/config-reference#terminationgraceperiodseconds) |
| CPU architecture      | Linux `amd64`                                     |
| Image source          | A `Dockerfile` or `Containerfile` in your project |

## Default quotas

Each team has default quotas for daemons during the beta. The quotas apply across all of the team's projects. To raise a quota, contact [Vercel Support](/help) or your account team.

| Plan                                 | Instance sizes          | Quota per team                                                      |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Hobby](/docs/plans/hobby)           | 1 GiB or 2 GiB (1 vCPU) | 5 Active CPU-hours and 420 GB-hours of Provisioned Memory per month |
| [Pro](/docs/plans/pro-plan)          | All sizes               | 16 vCPUs and 32 GiB of memory running at once                       |
| [Enterprise](/docs/plans/enterprise) | All sizes               | Custom. Contact your account team                                   |

Each project environment also runs at most 50 daemon instances across all of its daemons and regions. When a deployment or scaling change requests more, Vercel starts instances for older daemons first and logs an error on each daemon that doesn't get its full count. To raise this limit, contact [Vercel Support](/help) or your account team.

Hobby has two monthly quotas:

- **Active CPU** counts the CPU time your code spends executing. Time spent waiting for work doesn't count.
- **Provisioned Memory** counts the memory of each instance for every hour it runs, including time spent waiting for work. For example, one 2 GiB instance that runs without stopping reaches 420 GB-hours in about 9 days.

When a Hobby team reaches either quota, Vercel stops the team's daemons until the first of the next month (UTC) or until the team upgrades to Pro.

## Pricing

On Pro and Enterprise, daemons are billed for Active CPU and Provisioned Memory. See [Pricing](/pricing) for the rates. Hobby teams aren't billed for daemons, and the Hobby quotas apply instead.

## Unsupported features

Daemons don't support the following features during the beta:

| Feature                         | Alternative                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Preview deployments             | Daemons run only in the production environment. Test changes by running the daemon's image locally. See [Local development](/docs/daemons#local-development). |
| Inbound HTTP or TCP traffic     | Use [Services](/docs/services) or [Vercel Functions](/docs/functions) for workloads that respond to requests.                                              |
| Autoscaling                     | Set instance counts in your configuration, or override them from the dashboard, the Vercel CLI, or the [REST API](/docs/rest-api/daemons/override-a-project-daemon-s-instance-counts). See [Scaling a daemon](/docs/daemons/managing-daemons#scaling-a-daemon). |
| Persistent local storage        | Store state in [Vercel Blob](/docs/vercel-blob) or a database from the [Marketplace](/docs/marketplace-storage).                                           |
| Running in `vercel dev`         | Run the daemon's image locally with Docker. See [Local development](/docs/daemons#local-development).                                                      |
| Service bindings and rewrites   | Daemons can't be the target of a [service binding](/docs/services/bindings) or a rewrite.                                                                  |
| Builds without a Dockerfile     | Add a `Dockerfile` or `Containerfile` to the daemon's `root`.                                                                                              |
| Root directory set to a subfolder | Projects with a [root directory](/docs/builds/configure-a-build#root-directory) such as `apps/web` can't add daemons yet.                                |

title: "Managing Daemons"
description: "Deploy, scale, stop, and monitor Vercel Daemons with vercel.json and the dashboard."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.902Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/daemons/managing-daemons"

# Managing Daemons

You declare daemons with the `daemons` key in `vercel.json`. Changes to daemon configuration in `vercel.json` take effect when the deployment that contains them becomes your production deployment, including when you roll back to it. You can override a daemon's instance counts in each region without deploying a new configuration. To declare a daemon for the first time, see the [Daemons quick start](/docs/daemons#quick-start).

## Deploying changes to a daemon

Vercel updates daemons when a deployment becomes your production deployment. This happens when you deploy to production, [promote a deployment](/docs/deployments/promoting-a-deployment), use [Instant Rollback](/docs/instant-rollback), or complete a [rolling release](/docs/rolling-releases):

- **New instances**: Vercel starts new instances of every daemon in the new production deployment right away.
- **Out-of-date instances**: Vercel sends `SIGTERM` to the instances from the previous production deployment, then stops them after the shutdown grace period.
- **Removed daemons**: When the new production deployment doesn't declare a daemon, Vercel stops all of that daemon's instances.
- **Scaling overrides**: When a daemon has a [scaling override](#scaling-from-the-dashboard), Vercel keeps the override's counts instead of the `instances` from the new production deployment.

For a short time during a rollout, both versions of a daemon run at once: the old instances finish their current work during the grace period while the new ones start. When an old instance receives `SIGTERM`, it should stop taking new work immediately and only finish the work in progress. Make sure both versions can run side by side, for example by processing messages from the same queue and by keeping database migrations compatible with the previous version. See [Graceful shutdown](/docs/daemons#graceful-shutdown) for how to handle `SIGTERM`.

## Scaling a daemon

Each daemon runs a fixed number of instances in each region. Vercel doesn't currently autoscale daemons. You can set the counts in `vercel.json`, or override them from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI.

### Scaling with `vercel.json`

To change the number of instances, set [`instances`](/docs/daemons/config-reference#instances) to a map of region IDs to instance counts, then deploy to production:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "daemons": {
    "worker": {
      "root": "worker/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "instances": { "iad1": 3, "cdg1": 2 }
    }
  }
}
```

The map replaces the previous one. Regions that you remove from the map stop their instances.

### Scaling from the dashboard

To override a daemon's instance counts without a new deployment:

1. In your project's dashboard, open **Daemons** and select the daemon.
2. Select **Scale**.
3. Set the number of instances in each region, then select **Scale Daemon**.

The counts you set are a scaling override. Vercel uses them instead of the `instances` from your production deployment, and they stay in place when you deploy again, so changes to `instances` in `vercel.json` don't take effect while an override is set. To go back to the counts from your production deployment, select **Scale**, then **Clear scaling overrides**.

You need permission to update the project to set scaling overrides.

### Scaling from the CLI

To set a scaling override from [Vercel CLI](/docs/cli) 64.3.0 or later, pass `<region>=<count>` pairs to `vercel daemons scale`:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel daemons scale worker iad1=3 fra1=0
```

The CLI enables fine-grained scaling, so regions you don't name keep their current counts. The counts you set are a scaling override and stay in place across deployments. To clear the override and go back to the counts from your production deployment, run:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel daemons scale worker --reset
```

## Stopping a daemon

To stop all instances of a daemon without a new deployment, [set a scaling override](#scaling-from-the-dashboard) with `0` instances in every region.

To stop all instances of a daemon and keep its configuration in your deployment, set `instances` to an empty map, or set every region to `0`, then deploy to production:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "daemons": {
    "worker": {
      "root": "worker/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "instances": {}
    }
  }
}
```

To delete a daemon, remove it from `daemons` in `vercel.json` and deploy to production.

When a project is [paused](/docs/projects/managing-projects#pausing-a-project), for example by [spend management](/docs/spend-management#pausing-projects), Vercel stops all of its daemon instances. They start again when you resume the project.

## Inspecting daemons from the CLI

[Vercel CLI](/docs/cli) 64.3.0 or later can list, inspect, scale, and restart daemons and their instances. Every `vercel daemons` command targets the production environment, and accepts `--project` to choose a project and `--json` for machine-readable output:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel daemons ls
vercel daemons inspect worker
vercel daemons instances ls worker
vercel daemons instances inspect <instance-id> --since 1h
vercel daemons instances restart <instance-id>
```

`vercel daemons instances ls` lists every daemon's instances when you don't name a daemon. To view daemon logs from the CLI, filter `vercel logs` on the daemon source:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel logs --query 'source:daemon'
```

## Viewing daemon logs

Vercel collects each instance's `stdout` and `stderr` output. Daemon logs appear in your project's [Logs](/docs/logs/runtime) with the source `daemon`, the daemon's name in the `daemonName` field, and the instance's ID in the `daemonInstanceId` field. To see one daemon's logs, filter with `daemon:<name>`; to follow a single instance, filter with `daemonInstanceId:<id>`.

To see a daemon's instances and their logs, open **Daemons** in your project's dashboard and select the daemon.

## Monitoring a daemon's usage

The daemon's page in the dashboard charts CPU usage, memory usage, running instances, and data transfer for the time range you select. The charts are available on every plan; [Observability Plus](/docs/observability/observability-plus) extends how far back you can look.

title: "Daemons"
description: "Run long-running background workers, such as queue consumers and workflow workers, next to your app with Vercel Daemons."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.902Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/daemons"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Daemons

> Daemons are available in Public Beta on all plans

Vercel Daemons run long-running background processes from container images, such as queue consumers, workflow workers, and job runners. Each daemon pulls work from a queue, workflow engine, or external API and processes it continuously.

Vercel keeps your configured number of instances running in each region and restarts instances that exit or crash. Daemons run on [Fluid compute](/docs/fluid-compute), the same compute platform as Vercel Functions.

Daemons are available on all plans, including Hobby, within each plan's quotas. Hobby has monthly quotas for Active CPU and Provisioned Memory. A daemon that is mostly waiting for work uses less Active CPU, but it uses Provisioned Memory for every hour it runs. See [Default quotas](/docs/daemons/limits#default-quotas).

## When to use daemons

Use a daemon when your process owns a continuous loop to retrieve work. Common examples include:

- **Queue consumers** that poll [Vercel Queues](/docs/queues/poll-mode), Amazon SQS, Kafka, or Redis, including workers for Celery, Sidekiq, and BullMQ.
- **Workflow workers** that retrieve tasks from a workflow engine.
- **Job runners**, such as self-hosted CI runners that wait for jobs.

Daemons complement other primitives, such as [Vercel Functions](/docs/functions) to serve HTTP traffic, [Vercel Workflows](/docs/workflows) for durable execution, and [Vercel Queues](/docs/queues) for serverless message processing with preview deployment support. Use [Cron Jobs](/docs/cron-jobs) to run code on a schedule, [Vercel Sandbox](/docs/sandbox) to run untrusted code in isolation, and [Services](/docs/services) to define multiple apps in a single project.

Compare [background worker options](/docs/background-workers) to choose between continuous processes, queued jobs, and durable workflows. For detailed examples and migrations, see [Running background workers on Vercel](/kb/guide/background-workers-on-vercel).

## How daemons work

A daemon is a named resource in your project that runs one or more instances of the same workload. Each instance is an identical, interchangeable copy of the process:

1. **Build**: During the build, Vercel builds each daemon's `Dockerfile` or `Containerfile` and pushes the image to [Vercel Container Registry](/docs/container-registry) as a repository named `daemon.<name>`.
2. **Deploy**: When a deployment becomes your production deployment, including after a [promotion](/docs/deployments/promoting-a-deployment) or [rollback](/docs/instant-rollback), Vercel rolls out its configured daemons in each region while gracefully terminating instances from the previous deployment.
3. **Run**: Your daemon runs continuously. Vercel forwards each instance's `stdout` and `stderr` output to your project's [Logs](/docs/logs/runtime) in the dashboard.
4. **Retry**: Vercel maintains the requested instance counts and restarts instances that exit, crash, or fail their [health checks](#health-checks-and-restarts).
5. **Scale**: You can override a daemon's instance counts without a new deployment. Overrides stay in place across deployments until you clear them. See [Scaling a daemon](/docs/daemons/managing-daemons#scaling-a-daemon).
6. **Stop**: When it's time to stop your process, such as during a rollout or a manual restart, Vercel sends a `SIGTERM` signal. Your process has time to clean up resources before Vercel terminates it. See [Graceful shutdown](#graceful-shutdown).

> **💡 Note:** During the beta phase, daemons only run in production environments. Daemons
> in preview deployments are not supported.

## Quick start

Package a long-running Node.js process as a daemon and deploy two instances to `iad1` (Washington, D.C., USA).

Daemons use Dockerfile syntax to package code. In your worker's source directory, add a `Dockerfile` that builds a runnable version of your application:

```docker filename="worker/Dockerfile"
FROM node:24-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "worker.js"]
```

Then, declare a daemon using the `daemons` key in your project configuration:

#### vercel.json

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "daemons": {
    "worker": {
      "root": "worker/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "instances": { "iad1": 2 }
    }
  }
}
```

#### vercel.toml

```toml filename="vercel.toml"
#:schema https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json
[daemons.worker]
root = "worker/"
entrypoint = "Dockerfile"
instances = { iad1 = 2 }
```

Deploy your project to production. Vercel will roll out two instances of `worker` to `iad1`, and their output will appear in your project's [Logs](/docs/logs/runtime).

## Attach daemons to an existing app

Daemons run alongside your existing app without changing how Vercel builds it. For example, you can use [Services](/docs/services) to run a Next.js frontend alongside a FastAPI Python backend, then add BullMQ and Celery workers to consume work from each app.

Define a `Dockerfile` for each worker in `workers/bullmq-worker/` and `workers/celery-worker/`, then add both daemons under the top-level `daemons` key in your project configuration:

#### vercel.json

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "services": {
    "web": { "root": "web/" },
    "api": { "root": "api/", "entrypoint": "main:app" }
  },
  "rewrites": [
    { "source": "/api/(.*)", "destination": { "service": "api" } },
    { "source": "/(.*)", "destination": { "service": "web" } }
  ],
  "daemons": {
    "bullmq-worker": {
      "root": "workers/bullmq-worker/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "instances": { "iad1": 1 }
    },
    "celery-worker": {
      "root": "workers/celery-worker/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "instances": { "iad1": 1 }
    }
  }
}
```

#### vercel.toml

```toml filename="vercel.toml"
#:schema https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json
[services.web]
root = "web/"

[services.api]
root = "api/"
entrypoint = "main:app"

[[rewrites]]
source = "/api/(.*)"
destination = { service = "api" }

[[rewrites]]
source = "/(.*)"
destination = { service = "web" }

[daemons.bullmq-worker]
root = "workers/bullmq-worker/"
entrypoint = "Dockerfile"
instances = { iad1 = 1 }

[daemons.celery-worker]
root = "workers/celery-worker/"
entrypoint = "Dockerfile"
instances = { iad1 = 1 }
```

See the [Daemon configuration reference](/docs/daemons/config-reference) for every field.

## Health checks and restarts

By default, Vercel restarts an instance when its process exits or crashes. To also catch a process that is running but stuck, add a `livenessProbe` to the daemon. Vercel sends an HTTP `GET` request to the instance on a schedule and restarts it when enough consecutive checks fail.

First, serve a health endpoint from the same process as the work loop. The worker examples above don't start an HTTP server, so adding a probe to them unchanged would fail every check and restart the instance repeatedly:

```ts filename="worker/worker.ts"
import { createServer } from 'node:http';

createServer((req, res) => {
  res.statusCode = req.url === '/health' ? 200 : 404;
  res.end();
}).listen(1234);

// Start the work loop next to the server.
```

Then, point the `livenessProbe` at the endpoint's port and path:

#### vercel.json

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "daemons": {
    "worker": {
      "root": "worker/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "instances": { "iad1": 1 },
      "livenessProbe": {
        "httpGet": { "port": 1234, "path": "/health" },
        "initialDelaySeconds": 5
      }
    }
  }
}
```

#### vercel.toml

```toml filename="vercel.toml"
#:schema https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json
[daemons.worker]
root = "worker/"
entrypoint = "Dockerfile"
instances = { iad1 = 1 }
livenessProbe.httpGet = { port = 1234, path = "/health" }
livenessProbe.initialDelaySeconds = 5
```

A check succeeds on an HTTP status from `200` to `399`. Redirects are not followed, so a `3xx` response counts as a success. A check fails on a connection error, no response within `timeoutSeconds`, or any other status.

Checks run from inside the instance, starting `initialDelaySeconds` after the container starts and repeating every `periodSeconds`. Each instance is probed separately, and the schedule restarts from scratch after every restart. A changed `livenessProbe` applies only to instances started after it deploys.

Keep `timeoutSeconds` below `periodSeconds`, and make the endpoint cheap and based on whether the process can make progress rather than on downstream dependencies. See [`livenessProbe`](/docs/daemons/config-reference#livenessprobe) in the configuration reference for every field and default.

### Health states

Each instance is **pending** until its first check completes, **passing** while checks succeed, and **failing** after a failed check. A success resets the failure count, and `failureThreshold` consecutive failures trigger a restart.

### Restart policy

The same policy covers failed health checks, exits, and crashes:

- Liveness-triggered restarts send `SIGKILL` immediately and do not honor [`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`](#graceful-shutdown).
- Restarts use exponential backoff, waiting 1 second and doubling up to a cap of 5 minutes. A run of at least 5 minutes resets the backoff.
- After 10 minutes of runs each shorter than 5 minutes, Vercel stops restarting the instance and replaces it with a new one.

### Example timeline

With the configuration above and the remaining defaults (`periodSeconds` 10, `timeoutSeconds` 1, `failureThreshold` 3):

- **0s**: the container starts.
- **5s**: the first check returns `200`. Checks continue every 10 seconds.
- **~605s**: the app has hung, and the check times out after 1 second (1 of 3). The checks at 615s and 625s also fail.
- **~625s**: Vercel kills the container. The run lasted over 5 minutes, so it restarts 1 second later, and the first check runs 5 seconds after that.
- If every run keeps failing, restarts wait 2, 4, 8, 16 seconds, and so on. After 10 minutes of short runs, Vercel replaces the instance.

## Graceful shutdown

As a new version of your daemon rolls out, Vercel stops instances from the previous version. To let your process finish current tasks and clean up resources, Vercel sends a `SIGTERM` signal. Stop accepting new work immediately and start draining resources. By default, Vercel waits 30 seconds after sending `SIGTERM`, then terminates the process if it's still running. The same shutdown sequence applies when you reduce instance counts or remove a daemon.

To change how long Vercel waits, set [`terminationGracePeriodSeconds`](/docs/daemons/config-reference#terminationgraceperiodseconds) on the daemon. The value is an integer number of seconds from `0` to `3600`:

#### vercel.json

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "daemons": {
    "worker": {
      "root": "worker/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "instances": { "iad1": 1 },
      "terminationGracePeriodSeconds": 50
    }
  }
}
```

#### vercel.toml

```toml filename="vercel.toml"
#:schema https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json
[daemons.worker]
root = "worker/"
entrypoint = "Dockerfile"
instances = { iad1 = 1 }
terminationGracePeriodSeconds = 50
```

An instance can stop at any time, so make jobs idempotent and interrupted jobs safe to retry. An idempotent job produces the same result if it runs more than once. For example, acknowledge a queue message only after you finish processing it.

Handle `SIGTERM` to stop taking new work and finish the work in progress:

### Node.js (TypeScript)

```ts filename="worker/worker.ts"
const shutdown = new AbortController();

process.on('SIGTERM', () => shutdown.abort());

async function processNextJob(signal: AbortSignal): Promise<void> {
  // Wait for one unit of work, for example with a long-polling queue
  // receive that stops when `signal` aborts, then process it. Back off
  // when there's no work so the loop doesn't spin.
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  while (!shutdown.signal.aborted) {
    await processNextJob(shutdown.signal);
  }
  process.exit(0);
}

void main();
```

### Python

```python filename="worker/worker.py"
import signal
from threading import Event

shutdown = Event()

signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, lambda signum, frame: shutdown.set())


def process_next_job(shutdown: Event) -> None:
    # Replace this wait with a bounded queue poll, then process the job.
    # Finish processing before returning, even if shutdown is requested.
    shutdown.wait(timeout=1)


while not shutdown.is_set():
    process_next_job(shutdown)

# Close queue connections and other resources before exiting.
```

## Service bindings

A daemon can call the [services](/docs/services) in its project through [service bindings](/docs/services/bindings), without exposing those services to public traffic. Bindings always point to the deployment that started the instance. After a promotion or rollback, instances from the previous deployment keep calling that deployment's services until they stop.

Declare the bindings on the daemon:

#### vercel.json

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "services": {
    "api": { "root": "api/", "entrypoint": "main:app" }
  },
  "daemons": {
    "worker": {
      "root": "worker/",
      "entrypoint": "Dockerfile",
      "instances": { "iad1": 1 },
      "bindings": [
        { "type": "service", "service": "api", "format": "url", "env": "API_URL" }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

#### vercel.toml

```toml filename="vercel.toml"
#:schema https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json

[services.api]
root = "api/"
entrypoint = "main:app"

[daemons.worker]
root = "worker/"
entrypoint = "Dockerfile"
instances = { iad1 = 1 }

[[daemons.worker.bindings]]
type = "service"
service = "api"
format = "url"
env = "API_URL"
```

Each instance receives the service's URL in the binding's environment variable and calls it like any other HTTP endpoint:

```ts filename="worker/worker.ts"
await fetch(new URL('jobs/next', process.env.API_URL));
```

## Environment variables and OIDC

Each instance receives your deployment's [environment variables](/docs/environment-variables). Vercel passes the same variables to the image build as build arguments.

Vercel also sets the following environment variables on each instance:

| Variable | Description | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `VERCEL_REGION` | The region the instance runs in. Vercel ignores a `VERCEL_REGION` that you define. | `iad1` |
| `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN_FILE` | The path of the file that holds the instance's [OIDC token](/docs/oidc). | `/var/run/secrets/vercel.com/token` |

Use the OIDC token to authenticate with other services. The token is valid for 30 minutes, and Vercel refreshes the file about every 5 minutes, so read the file each time you need a token. To read the token, use [`@vercel/oidc`](/docs/oidc/reference) 4.0.0 or later for Node.js, or `vercel-oidc` 0.10.0 or later for Python.

## Local development

`vercel dev` currently doesn't run daemons. When your configuration contains `daemons`, `vercel dev` prints a warning and starts the rest of your project. Run your daemon locally with Docker:

```bash filename="Terminal"
docker build -t worker worker/
docker run --env-file .env.local worker
```

Use `vercel env pull` to download your project's development environment variables into `.env.local`.

## FAQ

### What does the Daemons beta support?

During the beta, daemons run in production deployments with manually configured instance counts and ephemeral storage. You can scale daemons from the Vercel dashboard or the Vercel CLI.

Preview deployments, autoscaling, and persistent storage aren't supported. See [Daemons limits](/docs/daemons/limits) for all limits and available alternatives.

### How do I update a daemon's image, command, or environment variables?

The container image, command, and environment variables are part of the deployment. To change them, create a new production deployment. The `command` field replaces the image's `ENTRYPOINT` and `CMD`. See [Managing daemons](/docs/daemons/managing-daemons).

### How do I change the number of instances?

Deploy new `instances` counts or set a scaling override without a new deployment. Overrides stay in place across deployments until you clear them. See [Scaling a daemon](/docs/daemons/managing-daemons#scaling-a-daemon).

### Does a daemon use my Hobby quota while it waits for work?

It uses the Provisioned Memory quota, and it uses the Active CPU quota only while your code executes. The Active CPU quota counts the CPU time your code spends executing, not uptime. Time spent waiting, such as long polling an empty queue, doesn't count, so a daemon that is mostly waiting for work will use less of your monthly Active CPU quota. Some work that looks like waiting still uses CPU: for example, HTTPS requests require cipher operations such as encryption, decryption, and signing, which consume Active CPU. The Provisioned Memory quota counts the memory of each instance for every hour it runs. See [Default quotas](/docs/daemons/limits#default-quotas) for each plan's quota and what happens when you reach it.

### Can I build daemons with `vercel build` on my machine?

Yes. During the beta, set `VERCEL_ENABLE_DAEMONS_BOA=1` when you run `vercel build` locally.

# Build Settings

## Build Command

| Parameter       | Type     | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| --------------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `build-command` | `string` | Setting this value is equivalent to enabling the **Override** toggle for that field in the dashboard. (The value of the Build Command defined in the Build & Development section of the General Project Settings.) |

This allows you to define a custom Build command that is normally automatically configured based on your Project's framework.

The example below shows a source URL using the `build-command` parameter to set the Build command to `npm run build`:

```bash filename="source url"
https://vercel.com/new/clone?repository-url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fvercel%2Fnext.js%2Ftree%2Fcanary%2Fexamples%2Fhello-world&build-command=npm%20run%20build
```

## Install Command

| Parameter         | Type     | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ----------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `install-command` | `string` | Setting this value is equivalent to enabling the **Override** toggle for that field in the dashboard. (The value of the Install Command defined in the Build & Development section of the General Project Settings.) |

This allows you to define a custom Install command that is normally automatically configured based on the following:

| Lock File           | Install Command | Package Manager Version                                                                                                          |
| ------------------- | --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pnpm-lock.yaml`    | `pnpm install`  | `pnpm 6/7/8/9/10` See [supported package managers](/docs/package-managers#supported-package-managers) for pnpm detection details |
| `package-lock.json` | `npm install`   | `npm`                                                                                                                            |
| `bun.lockb`         | `bun install`   | `bun 1`                                                                                                                          |
| `bun.lock`          | `bun install`   | `bun 1`                                                                                                                          |
| None                | `npm install`   | N/A                                                                                                                              |

The example below shows a source URL using the `install-command` parameter to set the Install command to `npm install`:

```bash filename="source url"
https://vercel.com/new/clone?repository-url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fvercel%2Fnext.js%2Ftree%2Fcanary%2Fexamples%2Fhello-world&install-command=npm%20install
```

## Development Command

| Parameter     | Type     | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `dev-command` | `string` | Setting this value is equivalent to enabling the **Override** toggle for that field in the dashboard. (The value of the Development Command defined in the Build & Development section of the General Project Settings.) |

This allows you to define a custom development command if you are using `vercel dev` to test your project locally. Each framework has its own development command and this will be set automatically based on your selected framework.

The example below shows a source URL using the `dev-command` parameter to set the Development command to `next dev --port $PORT`:

```bash filename="source url"
https://vercel.com/new/clone?repository-url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fvercel%2Fnext.js%2Ftree%2Fcanary%2Fexamples%2Fhello-world&dev-command=next%20dev%20--port%20%24PORT
```

## Ignored Build Command

| Parameter        | Type     | Description                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ---------------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ignore-command` | `string` | Setting this value is equivalent to enabling the **Override** toggle for that field in the dashboard. (The value of the Ignored Build Step section of the General Project Settings.) |

This allows you to define an Ignored Build Step to determine when your project should build and deploy.

The example below shows a source URL using the `ignore-command` parameter to set the Ignored Build Step command to `npx turbo-ignore`:

```bash filename="source url"
https://vercel.com/new/clone?repository-url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fvercel%2Fnext.js%2Ftree%2Fcanary%2Fexamples%2Fhello-world&ignore-command=npx%20turbo-ignore
```

## Root Directory

| Parameter        | Type     | Description                                                                                           |
| ---------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `root-directory` | `string` | Setting this value is equivalent to enabling the **Override** toggle for that field in the dashboard. |

This allows you to define the path of the directory relative to the root of the Project folder where your source code is located. By default it is empty and equivalent to the root of the repository.

The example below shows a source URL using the `root-directory` parameter to set the Root Directory to `apps/frontend`:

```bash filename="source url"
https://vercel.com/new/clone?repository-url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fvercel-support%2Fyarn-ws-monorepo&root-directory=apps%2Ffrontend
```

## Output Directory

| Parameter          | Type     | Description                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------ | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `output-directory` | `string` | Setting this value is equivalent to enabling the **Override** toggle for that field in the dashboard. (The value of the Output Directory defined in the General Project Settings.) |

This allows you to define the output directory's path relative to the Project folder's root. Usually, this is automatically configured based on your Project's framework.

The example below shows a source URL using the `output-directory` parameter for a monorepo where the application output is generated to `dist/apps/app/.next`:

```bash filename="source url"
https://vercel.com/new/clone?repository-url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fvercel%2Fnext.js%2Ftree%2Fcanary%2Fexamples%2Fhello-world&output-directory=dist%2Fapps%2Fapp%2F.next
```
