# Connecting an AWS Account for BYOC

> Bring Your Own Cloud is available on Enterprise plans and is set up through your Vercel account team. Contact your account team to request access.

Connect an AWS account to your Vercel team so [Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC)](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud) can invoke the Lambda functions you provision there. You connect each AWS account once per team, and every BYOC project on the team can reuse the connection.

The Vercel dashboard lists BYOC account connections in the **Vercel Private Cloud** section of your team's **Networking** settings.

## Prerequisites

- An Enterprise team with BYOC enabled. Your Vercel account team enables BYOC for you.
- Permission to manage your team's **Networking** settings. If you see the message "You need additional permissions to view Private Cloud accounts", ask a team Owner for access.
- Permission in your AWS account to create IAM roles and attach policies to them.
- The [AWS CLI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html) v2, if you follow the command examples. You can also use the AWS Console or an infrastructure-as-code tool such as Terraform.

## The two IAM roles BYOC uses

BYOC uses two separate IAM roles in your AWS account:

| Role                 | Assumed by              | Purpose                                                                            |
| -------------------- | ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Invocation role      | Vercel                  | Lets Vercel call `lambda:InvokeFunction` on your BYOC functions                    |
| Lambda execution role | AWS Lambda (`lambda.amazonaws.com`) | Grants your functions logging access and any AWS permissions your application needs |

You register the invocation role with Vercel on this page. You pass the execution role to your provisioning tool when you [deploy](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/deploy-with-cli).

## Connect your AWS account

- ### Open the Add AWS Account dialog
  1. Go to your team's **Settings** → [**Networking**](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%7E%2Fsettings%2Fnetworking\&title=Networking).
  2. In the **Vercel Private Cloud** section, click **Add Account**.
  The **Add AWS Account** dialog shows the **External ID** for your team, the **IAM Trust Policy**, and the **IAM Permissions Policy** for the invocation role. The external ID is your Vercel team ID. Keep the dialog open while you create the role.

- ### Create the invocation role with its trust policy
  The trust policy lets Vercel assume the invocation role. Copy the **IAM Trust Policy** from the dialog, without changes, into a file named `trust-policy.json`. The policy uses your Vercel team ID as its external ID.

  Create the role with the two settings Vercel requires:
  - The tag `VercelFunction` with the value `true`
  - A maximum session duration of 12 hours (43,200 seconds)
  ```bash filename="Terminal"
  aws iam create-role \
    --role-name VercelPrivateCloudRole \
    --assume-role-policy-document file://trust-policy.json \
    --max-session-duration 43200 \
    --tags Key=VercelFunction,Value=true
  ```
  The role can have any valid name. This example uses `VercelPrivateCloudRole`, the name the dashboard suggests.
  > **💡 Note:** Registration fails if the role is missing the `VercelFunction` tag or has a
  > maximum session duration shorter than 12 hours.

- ### Grant permission to invoke your functions
  The permissions policy lets the invocation role call your Lambda functions. Copy the **IAM Permissions Policy** from the dialog into a file named `invoke-policy.json`, replacing `<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>` with your 12-digit AWS account ID:
  ```json filename="invoke-policy.json"
  {
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
      {
        "Sid": "InvokeFunctionsInAccount",
        "Effect": "Allow",
        "Action": "lambda:InvokeFunction",
        "Resource": "arn:aws:lambda:*:<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>:function:*"
      }
    ]
  }
  ```
  Attach it to the invocation role as an inline policy:
  ```bash filename="Terminal"
  aws iam put-role-policy \
    --role-name VercelPrivateCloudRole \
    --policy-name VercelInvokeFunctions \
    --policy-document file://invoke-policy.json
  ```
  This policy allows Vercel to invoke current and future functions, versions, and aliases in your account across all AWS regions. It doesn't grant permission to create, change, or delete functions. The `VercelFunction` tag belongs on the IAM role only. Your Lambda functions don't need it.

  If you narrow the `Resource` pattern to specific function ARNs, update the policy before each deployment so it covers every function in that deployment's descriptor. See the [AWS Lambda permissions reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-api-permissions-ref.html) for resource formats.

- ### Register the account in Vercel
  In the **Add AWS Account** dialog:
  1. Enter your 12-digit **AWS Account ID**.
  2. Enter the **IAM Role Name** of the invocation role, such as `VercelPrivateCloudRole`.
  3. Click **Add Account**.
  Vercel checks that it can assume the role with the required session duration and shows **Account Registered** when the check passes. Registration doesn't check the Lambda invocation permissions or whether any functions exist.

- ### Refresh credentials and wait for Active
  A newly registered account shows the **No Credentials** status. Click **Refresh Credentials** on the account row to request the first set of credentials, then wait until the status changes to **Active**.

  After the first refresh, Vercel refreshes the credentials automatically. Keep the role's trust policy, permissions policy, tag, and session duration in place so automatic refreshes keep working.

  **Active** means Vercel has valid credentials for the role. It doesn't confirm that your functions can be invoked. Missing invocation permissions or **Expired** credentials cause BYOC requests and deployments to fail.

## Create the Lambda execution role

Your BYOC functions run as a Lambda execution role, which is separate from the invocation role. One execution role can serve all functions in an application. Create it with a trust policy for the Lambda service and the AWS managed policy for CloudWatch logging:

```bash filename="Terminal"
aws iam create-role \
  --role-name byoc-lambda-execution \
  --assume-role-policy-document '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"lambda.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}'

aws iam attach-role-policy \
  --role-name byoc-lambda-execution \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole
```

Add any other permissions your application needs, such as access to Amazon S3 or Amazon DynamoDB, to this role. Save the role ARN, for example `arn:aws:iam::<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>:role/byoc-lambda-execution`, for your provisioning tool.

The identity that runs your provisioning tool needs `iam:PassRole` on the execution role. For the full list of permissions, see [Provisioning identity permissions](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/provisioning-reference#provisioning-identity-permissions).

## Account statuses

| Status             | Meaning                                                                                       | Action                                                                                         |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **No Credentials** | The account is registered, but Vercel hasn't obtained credentials yet                        | Click **Refresh Credentials**                                                                  |
| **Active**         | Vercel has valid credentials for the invocation role and refreshes them automatically        | None                                                                                           |
| **Expired**        | Vercel's credentials have expired and automatic refresh hasn't succeeded                     | Check the role's trust policy, tag, and session duration, then select **Refresh Credentials** from the account's menu |

## Disconnect an AWS account

Before you disconnect an account, replace or remove any deployments that depend on it. Deployments that use a disconnected account can't invoke their functions.

1. Go to your team's **Settings** → [**Networking**](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%7E%2Fsettings%2Fnetworking\&title=Networking).
2. In the **Vercel Private Cloud** section, open the menu on the account row.
3. Select **Disconnect** and confirm.

Disconnecting removes the registration and stored credentials from Vercel and stops automatic credential refresh. It doesn't delete the IAM roles, Lambda functions, or any other resources in your AWS account.

Credentials that Vercel obtained before you disconnected stay valid until they expire, for up to 12 hours. To revoke them immediately, [revoke the role's active sessions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_revoke-sessions.html) in AWS.

## Next steps

- [Deploy with BYOC using the Vercel CLI](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/deploy-with-cli)
- [Review the BYOC provisioning reference](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/provisioning-reference)

description: "Build a project, provision its functions in your AWS account, and complete a Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) deployment with the Vercel CLI."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.997Z"

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Deploying with BYOC Using the Vercel CLI

> Bring Your Own Cloud is available on Enterprise plans and is set up through your Vercel account team. Contact your account team to request access.

Create a [Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC)](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud) deployment from your machine or CI with the Vercel CLI. You initialize a deployment, build it, generate its AWS resource descriptor, provision the functions in your AWS account, and then tell Vercel to complete the deployment.

## Prerequisites

- An AWS account [connected to your Vercel team](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/connect-aws-account) with the **Active** status.
- The ARN of a [Lambda execution role](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/connect-aws-account#create-the-lambda-execution-role) in that account.
- macOS or Linux with Node.js 20 or later. `vercel deploy describe` doesn't run on Windows.
- Vercel CLI 63.1.2 or later. Install the latest version with `npm i -g vercel@latest`.
- The [AWS CLI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html) v2 and [`jq`](https://jqlang.org/download/).
- AWS credentials for an identity with the [provisioning permissions](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/provisioning-reference#provisioning-identity-permissions).
- A Vercel project with its build settings and environment variables configured for the target environment.

## Set up a provisioning tool

The Vercel CLI generates the AWS resources to create, but doesn't create them. You need a provisioning tool that reads `descriptor.json` and creates the Lambda layers and functions in your account. Choose one of these options:

- **Generate a script with the BYOC agent skill**: Install the [BYOC skill](https://github.com/vercel-labs/vercel-byoc) in your application repository, then ask your coding agent to create a provisioning script.
- **Use your own tooling**: Build provisioning into your existing infrastructure tooling, such as Terraform or the AWS SDK, following the [BYOC provisioning reference](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/provisioning-reference).

To use the BYOC skill, install it from your application's directory:

```bash filename="Terminal"
npx skills add vercel-labs/vercel-byoc
```

Then ask your coding agent to create a project script, replacing the execution role ARN with your own:

```text filename="Prompt"
Using the BYOC skill, create `pnpm byoc:provision <deployment-id>` using the execution role arn:aws:iam::<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>:role/byoc-lambda-execution.
```

The rest of this guide runs that script as `pnpm byoc:provision`. If you use your own tooling, run your tool at the provisioning step instead.

## Deploy with BYOC

Run every command from your application's directory, and use the same deployment ID from initialization through completion.

> **💡 Note:** You have 15 minutes from `vercel deploy init` to `vercel deploy continue`.
> Finish linking the project, authenticating, and setting up your provisioning
> tool before you initialize the deployment.

- ### Set the deployment variables
  Set the values for your team, project, target environment, and AWS account. Use `preview` or `production` for the target, and keep the same value throughout:
  ```bash filename="Terminal"
  team_id="<TEAM_ID>"
  project_name="my-app"
  target="preview"
  aws_account_id="<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>"
  ```
  Authenticate the Vercel CLI with `vercel login`, and make sure your AWS credentials point to the intended account:
  ```bash filename="Terminal"
  aws sts get-caller-identity
  ```
  **Check**: The `Account` value in the output matches `aws_account_id`.

- ### Link the project and pull its settings
  Link your application to the Vercel project, then pull the project settings for the target environment:
  ```bash filename="Terminal"
  vercel link --yes --team "$team_id" --project "$project_name"
  vercel pull --yes --environment "$target" --scope "$team_id"
  ```
  **Check**: `.vercel/project.json` contains the intended team and project.

- ### Initialize the deployment
  Create a deployment on Vercel and save its ID. `vercel deploy init` uploads no files. The deployment waits for you to provision its functions:
  ```bash filename="Terminal"
  mkdir -p .vercel/byoc
  vercel deploy init --yes --target "$target" --scope "$team_id" --json > .vercel/byoc/init.json
  deployment_id=$(jq -er '.deployment.id // .id' .vercel/byoc/init.json)
  jq -r '.deployment.target // .target' .vercel/byoc/init.json
  ```
  The deployment ID is at `.id` when you run the command in a terminal, and at `.deployment.id` when the CLI runs non-interactively, such as in CI or from a coding agent. The `jq` expression above handles both.

  **Check**: The printed target is `production` for a production deployment, or `null` for a preview deployment. A new project's first deployment is assigned to production even when you request `preview`. If the target is wrong, [mark the deployment as failed](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/operations#abandon-a-pending-deployment) and initialize another.

- ### Build the application
  Build the application with the environment variables of the deployment you initialized:
  ```bash filename="Terminal"
  vercel build --id "$deployment_id" --target "$target" --yes
  ```
  **Result**: The build output is written to `.vercel/output`.

- ### Describe the AWS resources
  Package the functions and generate the descriptor for your AWS account:
  ```bash filename="Terminal"
  vercel deploy describe --id "$deployment_id" --aws-account-id "$aws_account_id"
  ```
  `vercel deploy describe` uses the team in `.vercel/project.json`, and fails if `--scope` or `VERCEL_ORG_ID` names a different team. It doesn't create any AWS resources.

  **Result**: The command writes these files under `.vercel/<deployment-id>/`:

  | Path              | Contents                                                       |
  | ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | `descriptor.json` | The Lambda functions and layers to create in your AWS account |
  | `zips/`           | One ZIP file per function                                      |
  | `layers/`         | One ZIP file per runtime layer                                 |
  | `build/`          | The original build output, moved from `.vercel/output`         |

  It also replaces `.vercel/output` with a version that contains no function code, plus a `provision.json` file that maps routes to Lambda functions. `vercel deploy continue` uploads this version.

  The function ZIP files contain your application code and environment variable values. Keep the `.vercel` directory private and keep the workspace until the deployment completes. For field-level details, see the [BYOC provisioning reference](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/provisioning-reference).

- ### Provision the functions in AWS
  Run your provisioning tool with the credentials of your provisioning identity. This example selects a local AWS CLI profile with `AWS_PROFILE`:
  ```bash filename="Terminal"
  AWS_PROFILE="byoc-provisioner" pnpm byoc:provision "$deployment_id"
  ```
  Your provisioning tool must create every layer and function in the descriptor, in each function's AWS region, and wait until each function reaches the `Active` state. The invocation role must allow `lambda:InvokeFunction` on every function you create.

  **Check**: Every function in `descriptor.json` exists in AWS with the `Active` state. To list the functions and regions the descriptor expects, run:
  ```bash filename="Terminal"
  jq -r '.functions[] | "\(.region) \(.configuration.FunctionName)"' ".vercel/$deployment_id/descriptor.json"
  ```

- ### Complete the deployment
  Tell Vercel the functions are ready. `vercel deploy continue` uploads the code-free output and `provision.json`, then waits for the deployment to finish:
  ```bash filename="Terminal"
  vercel deploy continue --id "$deployment_id" --scope "$team_id"
  vercel inspect "$deployment_id" --scope "$team_id" --wait
  ```
  **Check**: `vercel inspect` reports the `READY` status.

- ### Verify a function runs in your account
  Request a dynamic route through the exact deployment. Replace `/api/hello` with a route in your application that runs a function:
  ```bash filename="Terminal"
  vercel curl "/api/hello" --deployment "$deployment_id" --scope "$team_id" -- --fail-with-body --silent --show-error
  ```
  A static or cached response doesn't prove that BYOC is working. Confirm that the function ran in your account by checking its Amazon CloudWatch logs, using a function name and region from the descriptor:
  ```bash filename="Terminal"
  aws logs tail "/aws/lambda/your_function_name" --region us-east-1 --since 10m
  ```
  **Check**: The route returns the expected response, and the function's CloudWatch log group shows the invocation. If your functions run in multiple regions, confirm each region's functions exist and record which region handled your test requests.

## Customize provisioning

You can change how your provisioning tool creates functions, for example to attach functions to a VPC or add Lambda layers. Keep the generated function names, handlers, runtimes, memory, timeouts, environment variables, and tags exactly as they appear in the descriptor. Vercel invokes each function by its generated name, so renaming a function causes requests to it to fail. For the full list of values to preserve, see [Values to keep as generated](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/provisioning-reference#values-to-keep-as-generated).

If you attach functions to a VPC, route the subnets through a NAT gateway or equivalent egress so functions keep outbound internet access, and check your security group rules and DNS resolution.

For function packages larger than 50 MB, upload the ZIP files to a private Amazon S3 bucket in the same region as the function, and create the function from the bucket. See [Function package size](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/provisioning-reference#function-package-size).

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom                                                                                              | Cause                                                                                        | Fix                                                                                                                                                       |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Deployment dpl_... was not found, or manual provisioning is not enabled for this team.`              | BYOC isn't enabled for the team, or the deployment ID belongs to a different team            | Confirm the deployment ID and linked team. Ask your Vercel account team to confirm BYOC is enabled.                                                        |
| `vercel deploy describe` reports a scope or project mismatch                                          | `--scope`, `VERCEL_ORG_ID`, or `VERCEL_PROJECT_ID` doesn't match `.vercel/project.json`      | Remove the conflicting value or relink the project.                                                                                                       |
| `vercel deploy describe` rejects the build as unsupported                                             | The build includes functions using the Edge runtime or the container runtime, or Services    | Move those functions to the Node.js or Python runtime, and remove Services from the project. See [BYOC limitations](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud#byoc-limitations). |
| `No prebuilt output found in ".vercel/output"`                                                       | `vercel deploy continue` ran from a different directory, or before `vercel deploy describe` | Run every command from the application's directory, in order.                                                                                             |
| `Provisioning exceeded the maximum allowed time.`                                                    | More than 15 minutes passed between `vercel deploy init` and `vercel deploy continue`       | Start a new deployment. See [Failures and retries](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/operations#failures-and-retries).                                |
| The deployment is `READY`, but dynamic routes fail                                                   | The invocation role can't invoke the functions, or the account credentials are **Expired**  | Check the invocation role's permissions policy and the account status in [Connect AWS Account](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/connect-aws-account). |

## Next steps

- [Operate BYOC deployments](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/operations), including retries and cleanup
- [Review the BYOC provisioning reference](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/provisioning-reference)

# Deploying with BYOC from GitHub Actions

> Bring Your Own Cloud is available on Enterprise plans and is set up through your Vercel account team. Contact your account team to request access.

Keep the [Vercel Git integration](/docs/git) for a [Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC)](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud) project, so every push creates a preview or production deployment that GitHub Actions builds, provisions in your AWS account, and completes.

This setup is optional. You can also run BYOC deployments from any CI system with the [Vercel CLI flow](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/deploy-with-cli).

## How the GitHub Actions flow works

With the BYOC Git flow turned on, Vercel doesn't build your pushes itself. Instead:

1. You push a commit, and the Vercel Git integration creates a BYOC deployment that waits for provisioning.
2. Vercel sends the `deployment.build-requested` webhook to a webhook relay that you host. The relay can run on any service that can receive the webhook. The setup on this page deploys it as an AWS Lambda function in your AWS account.
3. The relay verifies the webhook signature and starts your GitHub Actions workflow through a GitHub App.
4. The workflow checks out the deployment's exact commit and runs the [CLI flow](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/deploy-with-cli) with the existing deployment ID: `vercel build --id`, `vercel deploy describe`, provisioning, and `vercel deploy continue`.

The workflow authenticates to Vercel and AWS with OpenID Connect (OIDC), which gives each run short-lived credentials without storing long-lived access keys for either service. Builds run separately from the AWS provisioning credentials.

The 15-minute provisioning window starts when Vercel creates the deployment, so time spent waiting in the GitHub Actions queue counts toward it.

## Prerequisites

- A working [CLI deployment](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/deploy-with-cli) for the project, including the AWS account connection and the Lambda execution role.
- Administrator access to the GitHub repository.
- AWS permissions to create the relay's supporting resources: a Lambda function, an AWS Secrets Manager secret, and IAM roles.
- A Vercel team Owner to configure OIDC authentication for the Vercel CLI. If OIDC authentication for the CLI isn't available on your team, ask your Vercel account team to enable it.
- The [BYOC agent skill](https://github.com/vercel-labs/vercel-byoc) installed in your application repository with `npx skills add vercel-labs/vercel-byoc`.

## Set up GitHub Actions for BYOC

- ### Generate the integration
  From your application repository, ask your coding agent to generate the integration, using your AWS CLI profile and execution role ARN:
  ```text filename="Prompt"
  Set up GitHub Actions for this project's BYOC deployments using AWS profile byoc-admin and Lambda execution role arn:aws:iam::<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>:role/byoc-lambda-execution.
  ```
  The agent identifies your Vercel project, confirms the AWS account and region, and generates four pieces:

  | Piece                   | Purpose                                                                                  |
  | ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | GitHub Actions workflow | Builds, describes, provisions, and continues each requested deployment                   |
  | Provisioning scripts    | Create the Lambda layers and functions from `descriptor.json`                            |
  | Webhook relay           | Receives `deployment.build-requested` and starts the workflow                            |
  | Infrastructure template | Creates the relay, its secret, and the AWS roles the workflow assumes through OIDC       |

  The local AWS profile is used only for setup. The workflow itself uses OIDC.

- ### Create and install the GitHub App
  The relay starts workflows through a GitHub App. Create it with these settings:
  1. Create a private GitHub App under the account or organization that owns the repository.
  2. Grant **Repository permissions** → **Actions**: **Read and write**, and leave incoming webhooks turned off.
  3. Install the App on the BYOC repository only.
  4. Generate and download a private key for the App.
  Give the agent the App ID, the installation ID, and the local path to the private key file. Don't paste the key into a chat or commit it to the repository.

- ### Deploy and verify the integration
  Have the agent deploy the infrastructure template and upload the relay code. The agent stores the GitHub App private key and the webhook signing secret in AWS Secrets Manager in your selected account and region, and grants the relay access to the secret.

  The agent then publishes the workflow on the repository's default branch and registers a project-specific Vercel webhook for `deployment.build-requested` with signature verification.

  **Check**: Before you turn on the flow, have the agent report these results:
  - **Relay**: The relay's URL and log location, plus the secret's name and region in AWS Secrets Manager.
  - **Vercel authentication**: A GitHub Actions job can obtain temporary Vercel credentials and read the intended project.
  - **AWS authentication**: A GitHub Actions job can assume the provisioning role in the intended AWS account.

- ### Turn on the BYOC Git flow
  Connect the project to the Vercel Git integration, or reuse an existing connection. Then turn on the BYOC Git flow by adding the `manualProvisioning` property to your project's `vercel.json`, keeping your other settings:
  ```json filename="vercel.json"
  {
    "manualProvisioning": true
  }
  ```
  Alternatively, set the project environment variable `VERCEL_MANUAL_PROVISIONING` to `1` for each environment that should use the BYOC Git flow.

  You don't need either setting for the [CLI flow](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/deploy-with-cli).

- ### Test preview and production deployments
  Push a new commit to a preview branch.

  **Check**:
  - The GitHub Actions workflow runs for the commit.
  - The Vercel deployment reaches `READY`.
  - An existing dynamic route returns the expected response.
  If the deployment uses [Deployment Protection](/docs/deployment-protection), have the agent configure [Protection Bypass for Automation](/docs/deployment-protection/methods-to-bypass-deployment-protection/protection-bypass-automation) so the workflow's check can reach the deployment.

  Repeat the test on your production branch to verify production deployments.

> **💡 Note:** Run only one workflow per deployment ID at a time. If a run fails while the
> deployment is still waiting for provisioning, rerun it with the same
> deployment ID. See [Failures and
> retries](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/operations#failures-and-retries).

## Next steps

- [Operate BYOC deployments](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/operations), including retries, cleanup, and credential rotation
- [Review the BYOC provisioning reference](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/provisioning-reference)

description: "Retry failed Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) deployments, clean up AWS resources, monitor logs, and rotate credentials."

# Operating BYOC Deployments

> Bring Your Own Cloud is available on Enterprise plans and is set up through your Vercel account team. Contact your account team to request access.

With [Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC)](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud), your team operates the AWS side of every deployment. Retry or abandon failed deployments, clean up AWS resources you no longer need, and monitor the functions and credentials your deployments depend on.

## Failures and retries

When a BYOC deployment fails, check the deployment status in Vercel with `vercel inspect <deployment-id>`, and the output of the failed CLI command or CI job. The right next step depends on the deployment's state:

| Deployment state                                                     | What to do                                                                                                                                                         |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Still waiting for provisioning, within 15 minutes of initialization | Fix the cause, then retry with the same deployment ID, generated files, and resource inventory. Reuse the functions and layers you already created when they match. |
| Failed, canceled, or timed out                                       | Start a new deployment with `vercel deploy init`, or redeploy through Vercel. The new deployment gets a new ID. Keep the old inventory for cleanup.                |
| `READY`                                                              | Don't provision it again. Test the deployment, or create a new deployment for any changes.                                                                         |

To change code in a deployment that's still waiting for provisioning, rebuild and run `vercel deploy describe` again with the same deployment ID, then provision from the new descriptor. After `vercel deploy continue` succeeds, create a new deployment for further changes.

A deployment that waits longer than 15 minutes fails with the error `Provisioning exceeded the maximum allowed time.` and its `manualProvisioning.state` becomes `TIMEOUT`.

### Abandon a pending deployment

To stop a deployment that's still waiting for provisioning, mark it as failed with a reason:

```bash filename="Terminal"
vercel deploy continue --id "<DEPLOYMENT_ID>" --error "Initialized with the wrong target"
```

**Result**: The CLI prints `Marked deployment <DEPLOYMENT_ID> as errored`, and the deployment shows as failed in Vercel.

Failed and abandoned deployments can leave functions and layers in your AWS account. Add them to your cleanup process.

### Keep one worker per deployment

Run only one build and provisioning worker per deployment ID at a time. Two workers provisioning the same deployment can conflict on function creation. Persist the deployment ID, generated files, and resource inventory so a retry can pick up where the failed attempt stopped.

## Cleanup and retention

Deleting a deployment in Vercel doesn't delete its Lambda functions or layers in your AWS account. Your team decides when to remove them.

### Keep an inventory of AWS resources

Record the ARNs of the functions and layer versions created for each deployment, and store the inventory somewhere durable. The script generated by the [BYOC agent skill](https://github.com/vercel-labs/vercel-byoc) writes this inventory to `.vercel/<deployment-id>/provisioned.json`, marking which resources it created and which it reused.

Keep the resources for every deployment you still serve, including deployments you may [roll back](/docs/instant-rollback) to.

### Remove resources you no longer need

Use the inventory to delete only the resources created for deployments you no longer need:

1. Delete the functions that the inventory marks as created for that deployment.
2. Delete a layer version only after confirming that no remaining function uses it. Layers can be shared between deployments.
3. Keep the AWS account registration and the invocation role. Other deployments depend on them.

### Automate cleanup with the `deployment.cleanup` webhook

Vercel sends the [`deployment.cleanup`](/docs/webhooks/webhooks-api) webhook when it permanently deletes a deployment, after the 30-day recovery period ends. The webhook doesn't fire when a deployment is first marked for deletion.

To automate cleanup, build a handler that receives the webhook, looks up the deployment ID in your inventory, and deletes that deployment's resources. Treat cleanup as manual until you've configured and tested the handler.

## Logs and monitoring

BYOC spreads operational signals across Vercel, your CI system, and AWS:

| Signal                               | Where to find it                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Deployment status and build errors   | Vercel dashboard, `vercel inspect`, or the REST API                                                            |
| Build and provisioning job failures  | Your CI system, such as GitHub Actions                                                                        |
| Function logs and errors             | Vercel, as for any other deployment. Your functions also write to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, in the log group `/aws/lambda/<function-name>` in each function's region |
| Account credential status            | The **Vercel Private Cloud** section of your team's **Networking** settings                                   |

Assign an owner to monitor failed deployments, account credential status, and application health. Confirm with your Vercel account team which credential alerts are available for your team, and add your own monitoring for anything else you need, such as Amazon CloudWatch alarms on function errors and throttles.

## Rotating credentials

Rotate each credential type in the place it's stored:

- **Invocation role**: Vercel refreshes its credentials for the invocation role automatically. Keep the role's trust policy, permissions policy, `VercelFunction` tag, and 12-hour maximum session duration in place. If the account shows **Expired**, fix the role and select **Refresh Credentials**. See [Connecting an AWS account for BYOC](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/connect-aws-account#account-statuses).
- **GitHub App keys and webhook secrets**: If you [deploy from GitHub Actions](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/deploy-with-github-actions), update the key or secret in GitHub or Vercel and in the relay's stored secret together. Reload the relay and verify a deployment end to end before you retire the old credential.
- **OIDC credentials**: GitHub Actions obtains short-lived credentials for Vercel and AWS through OIDC on each run, so there are no long-lived keys to rotate.

## Related

- [BYOC provisioning reference](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/provisioning-reference)
- [Webhooks API reference](/docs/webhooks/webhooks-api)

# Bring Your Own Cloud

> Bring Your Own Cloud is available on Enterprise plans and is set up through your Vercel account team. Contact your account team to request access.

Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) lets you run the [Vercel Functions](/docs/functions) behind your project as AWS Lambda functions in your own AWS account. Vercel still routes requests, serves static assets, and manages the deployment, while your team owns the functions, their IAM permissions, and their network access.

BYOC is for teams with security, compliance, or data-residency requirements that say application code must run in a cloud account they control.

## How BYOC works

A BYOC deployment splits the work between Vercel and your AWS account. You build the application and create its functions in AWS, and Vercel wires up the deployment and invokes those functions when requests arrive.

### How a BYOC deployment is created

A BYOC deployment follows five stages, run from your machine or your CI environment:

1. **Initialize**: `vercel deploy init` creates a deployment on Vercel that waits for you to provision its functions. No files are uploaded at this stage.
2. **Build**: `vercel build --id` builds your application with the environment variables of that deployment.
3. **Describe**: `vercel deploy describe --id` packages each function as a ZIP file and writes a `descriptor.json` file that lists the AWS Lambda functions and layers to create. It doesn't create any AWS resources.
4. **Provision**: Your provisioning tool creates the Lambda functions and layers in your AWS account from the descriptor.
5. **Continue**: `vercel deploy continue --id` uploads your static assets and deployment metadata, without function code, and Vercel completes the deployment.

You have 15 minutes from initializing the deployment to running `vercel deploy continue`. After 15 minutes, the deployment fails with the error `Provisioning exceeded the maximum allowed time.`

For the full sequence, see [Deploying with BYOC using the Vercel CLI](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/deploy-with-cli). To start deployments from Git pushes instead, see [Deploying with BYOC from GitHub Actions](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/deploy-with-github-actions).

### How requests reach your functions

When a request arrives for a BYOC deployment:

1. The Vercel [CDN](/docs/cdn) receives the request and terminates TLS.
2. Vercel serves static assets and cached responses directly, without contacting your AWS account.
3. For a dynamic route, Vercel assumes an IAM role in your AWS account and invokes the matching Lambda function.
4. Your function's response returns through Vercel to the client.

Vercel invokes your functions with an IAM role that you create, called the invocation role. Vercel refreshes the credentials for that role automatically after you [connect your AWS account](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/connect-aws-account).

## What you own and what Vercel owns

With BYOC, your team takes on the parts of the platform that run in your AWS account:

| Area                       | Vercel                                                | Your team                                                                   |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Request routing and TLS    | Routes requests and terminates TLS at the Vercel CDN  | None                                                                        |
| Static assets              | Stores and serves static assets                       | None                                                                        |
| Builds                     | Provides the build and packaging commands in the CLI  | Runs builds on your own machines or CI                                      |
| Function code and runtime  | None                                                  | Creates, stores, and runs Lambda functions and layers in your AWS account   |
| IAM                        | Assumes the invocation role you grant                 | Creates and maintains the invocation role and the Lambda execution role     |
| Networking                 | None                                                  | Provides outbound internet access, VPC attachment, and security rules       |
| Quotas and scaling         | None                                                  | Maintains AWS service quotas, concurrency limits, and scaling headroom      |
| Logs                       | Shows deployment status and function logs, as for any other deployment | None                                                       |
| Cleanup                    | Sends the `deployment.cleanup` webhook                | Deletes AWS resources for deployments you no longer need                    |

Plan for someone on your team to own the AWS account continuously. Vercel can't raise your AWS quotas, recreate deleted functions, or fix IAM or network changes made in your account.

## When to use BYOC

Use BYOC when a security, compliance, or data-residency requirement means your application code must run in an AWS account you own.

If you need private connectivity to your backends but Vercel can run your compute, another networking option is usually a better fit:

| Requirement                                                                  | Option                                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| A known set of source IPs to add to a backend allowlist                      | [Static IPs](/docs/networking/static-ips)                   |
| A dedicated, single-tenant VPC with VPC peering or site-to-site VPN          | [Secure Compute](/docs/networking/secure-compute)           |
| Function code must run in your own AWS account                               | Bring Your Own Cloud                                        |

For a full comparison, see [Choosing a networking option](/docs/networking#choosing-a-networking-option).

## When not to use BYOC

BYOC isn't the right fit when:

- **All traffic must stay in your account**: TLS terminates at the Vercel CDN, and requests and responses pass through Vercel.
- **You need a government certification**: BYOC doesn't currently satisfy FedRAMP or other government certification requirements.
- **You rely on features BYOC doesn't support**: See [BYOC limitations](#byoc-limitations).
- **Your team can't own AWS operations**: BYOC moves function provisioning, quotas, and cleanup into your account.

## Security and data handling

BYOC keeps function code and function execution in your AWS account. Vercel receives only what it needs to serve the deployment and invoke your functions:

| Data                                              | Sent to Vercel                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Function code and runtime layers                  | No. Function packages stay on your build machine and in AWS.        |
| Static assets                                     | Yes                                                                 |
| Routing and function configuration metadata      | Yes                                                                 |
| Function-to-Lambda mappings (`provision.json`)    | Yes                                                                 |
| Your application's `package.json` files          | Yes                                                                 |
| Request and response data                         | Yes. Requests and responses pass through Vercel.                    |

Function packages that `vercel deploy describe` generates contain your application code and environment variable values. Keep the `.vercel` directory private on your build machine and in CI artifacts.

Review your data handling and compliance requirements with your Vercel account team.

## BYOC limitations

| Limitation                | Details                                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Cloud provider            | AWS only. Functions run on AWS Lambda.                                                                                                                       |
| Runtimes                  | Node.js and Python                                                                                                                                           |
| Unsupported function types | Functions using the [Edge runtime](/docs/functions/runtimes/edge) or the [container runtime](/docs/functions/runtimes/container), and [Services](/docs/services)                                        |
| Build environment         | macOS or Linux. `vercel deploy describe` doesn't run on Windows.                                                                                             |
| Provisioning window       | 15 minutes from `vercel deploy init` to `vercel deploy continue`                                                                                             |
| Network access            | The AWS account and subnets that host your functions need outbound internet access                                                                           |
| Government certifications | Doesn't currently satisfy FedRAMP or other government certification requirements                                                                            |

### Beta enhancements

Most features of [Vercel Functions](/docs/functions/limitations) work with BYOC, except for the following beta enhancements that aren't yet available:

- [**Extended max duration beta**](/docs/functions/configuring-functions/duration#extended-max-duration-beta): The standard maximum of 800 seconds applies on Pro and Enterprise plans.
- [**Large Functions beta**](/docs/functions/limitations#large-functions-beta): The standard bundle size limit of 250 MB applies, with a 500 MB limit for Python.

## Pricing

BYOC is an Enterprise feature with custom pricing. [Contact the Vercel sales team](/contact/sales) for BYOC pricing.

Your team also pays AWS directly for the resources BYOC creates in your account, including Lambda invocations and duration, Lambda layer storage, Amazon CloudWatch logs, and data transfer.

## Get started with BYOC

Set up BYOC in this order:

1. [Connect your AWS account](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/connect-aws-account) to your Vercel team.
2. [Deploy with the Vercel CLI](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/deploy-with-cli) to create your first BYOC deployment.
3. Optionally, [deploy from GitHub Actions](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/deploy-with-github-actions) or any other provider so Git pushes create BYOC deployments.
4. Review [operating BYOC deployments](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/operations) for retries, cleanup, and monitoring.

To build your own provisioning tool, see the [BYOC provisioning reference](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/provisioning-reference).

## Related

- [Networking overview](/docs/networking)
- [Secure Compute](/docs/networking/secure-compute)
- [Vercel Functions](/docs/functions)
- [Enterprise plan](/docs/plans/enterprise)

# BYOC Provisioning Reference

> Bring Your Own Cloud is available on Enterprise plans and is set up through your Vercel account team. Contact your account team to request access.

A [Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC)](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud) provisioning tool reads the files that `vercel deploy describe` generates and creates matching AWS Lambda layers and functions in your account. Use this reference to build or audit a provisioning tool, whether you use Terraform, the AWS SDK, the AWS CLI, or a script generated by the [BYOC agent skill](https://github.com/vercel-labs/vercel-byoc).

## Generated files

`vercel deploy describe --id <deployment-id> --aws-account-id <aws-account-id>` writes these files:

| Path                                    | Contents                                                                                       | Uploaded to Vercel |
| --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| `.vercel/<deployment-id>/descriptor.json` | The functions and layers to create, in the [descriptor format](#descriptor-file-format)       | No                 |
| `.vercel/<deployment-id>/zips/<sha256>.zip` | One function package per file. The file name is the SHA-256 hash of the ZIP contents.     | No                 |
| `.vercel/<deployment-id>/layers/<sha256>.zip` | One runtime layer package per file                                                        | No                 |
| `.vercel/<deployment-id>/build/`        | The original build output, moved from `.vercel/output`                                        | No                 |
| `.vercel/output/`                       | The build output with function code removed                                                   | Yes, by `vercel deploy continue` |
| `.vercel/output/provision.json`         | The mapping from routes to Lambda functions, in the [`provision.json` format](#route-mapping-file-format) | Yes, by `vercel deploy continue` |

`vercel deploy describe` creates the `.vercel/<deployment-id>/` directory with owner-only permissions (`0700`) and writes `descriptor.json` and the function ZIP files with mode `0600`. Function ZIP files include your application code and the deployment's environment variables, so keep them private in CI artifacts and caches.

If you run `vercel deploy describe` again for the same deployment, it reads the original build from `.vercel/<deployment-id>/build/` instead of the code-free `.vercel/output`.

## Descriptor file format

The descriptor file, `descriptor.json`, describes every Lambda layer and function to create for one deployment.

### Top-level fields

| Field          | Type     | Description                                                                                                  |
| -------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `version`      | `number` | Descriptor format version. Always `1`.                                                                       |
| `deploymentId` | `string` | The Vercel deployment ID, in the form `dpl_...`                                                              |
| `awsAccountId` | `string` | The 12-digit AWS account ID passed to `--aws-account-id`                                                     |
| `layers`       | `object` | A map from layer key to the layer ZIP file path, relative to the descriptor, such as `layers/<sha256>.zip`   |
| `functions`    | `array`  | One entry per Lambda function to create. See [Function fields](#function-fields).                            |

### Function fields

| Field           | Type       | Description                                                                                                  |
| --------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `code`          | `string`   | The function ZIP file path, relative to the descriptor, such as `zips/<sha256>.zip`                          |
| `region`        | `string`   | The AWS region to create the function in, such as `us-east-1`                                                |
| `layers`        | `string[]` | Keys into the top-level `layers` map, in the order the function needs them                                   |
| `configuration` | `object`   | Lambda function settings, using AWS `CreateFunction` parameter names. See [Configuration fields](#configuration-fields). |

A deployment that runs in several regions has one `functions` entry per function per region.

### Configuration fields

`configuration` uses the parameter names of the AWS Lambda [`CreateFunction`](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/api/API_CreateFunction.html) API, so you can pass it to the API with only the role, code, and layers added.

| Field                   | Type                     | Required | Description                                       |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------ | -------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `FunctionName`          | `string`                 | Yes      | The function name Vercel invokes                  |
| `Handler`               | `string`                 | Yes      | The entry point inside the function package      |
| `Runtime`               | `string`                 | Yes      | The Lambda runtime identifier                     |
| `MemorySize`            | `number`                 | Yes      | Memory in MB                                      |
| `Environment.Variables` | `Record<string, string>` | Yes      | Environment variables for the function            |
| `Tags`                  | `Record<string, string>` | Yes      | Tags to apply to the function                     |
| `Timeout`               | `number`                 | No       | Maximum execution time in seconds                 |
| `Architectures`         | `string[]`               | No       | The instruction set architecture, such as `x86_64` or `arm64` |
| `EphemeralStorage.Size` | `number`                 | No       | Size of the `/tmp` directory in MB                |

`configuration` never contains `Role`, `Code`, or `Layers`. Your provisioning tool supplies them:

| Parameter | Value to supply                                                                                       |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Role`    | The ARN of your Lambda execution role                                                                 |
| `Code`    | The function ZIP file at `code`, uploaded directly or from Amazon S3                                  |
| `Layers`  | The ARNs of the layer versions you published in the function's region, in the order of `layers`      |

### Example descriptor

This example shows the structure of a descriptor for one function in one region. Generated values differ for every deployment:

```json filename=".vercel/dpl_1234567890abcdefghij/descriptor.json"
{
  "version": 1,
  "deploymentId": "dpl_1234567890abcdefghij",
  "awsAccountId": "<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>",
  "layers": {
    "example_layer_key": "layers/example_layer_sha256.zip"
  },
  "functions": [
    {
      "code": "zips/example_function_sha256.zip",
      "region": "us-east-1",
      "layers": ["example_layer_key"],
      "configuration": {
        "FunctionName": "example_function_name",
        "Handler": "example_handler",
        "Runtime": "nodejs22.x",
        "MemorySize": 1024,
        "Timeout": 300,
        "Architectures": ["x86_64"],
        "Environment": {
          "Variables": {
            "EXAMPLE_VARIABLE": "example_value"
          }
        },
        "Tags": {
          "example_tag_key": "example_tag_value"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

## Provisioning requirements

A provisioning tool must do the following for every deployment:

1. **Publish layers per region**: For each region that a function uses, publish every layer it references. Use the layer key as the layer name, and reuse an existing layer version when its code hash matches the ZIP file.
2. **Create functions**: Create each function in its `region` with its `configuration`, plus `Role`, `Code`, and `Layers`.
3. **Wait for Active**: Wait until every function reaches the Lambda `Active` state before running `vercel deploy continue`.
4. **Grant invocation**: Make sure the invocation role allows `lambda:InvokeFunction` on every created function.
5. **Record an inventory**: Save the ARNs of the functions and layer versions you created, so you can [retry and clean up](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/operations) later.

Finish steps 1 to 4 and run `vercel deploy continue` within 15 minutes of `vercel deploy init`.

### Values to keep as generated

Vercel invokes functions by their generated names, and your build depends on the generated runtime settings. Keep these values exactly as they appear in the descriptor:

- `FunctionName`
- `Handler`
- `Runtime`, `Architectures`, `MemorySize`, `Timeout`, and `EphemeralStorage`
- `Environment.Variables`
- `Tags`
- The layer order in `layers`

You can add settings that the descriptor doesn't define, such as a VPC configuration, additional layers, or extra tags, through your provisioning tool. If you attach functions to a VPC, give the execution role the permissions Lambda needs to manage network interfaces, such as the AWS managed policy `AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole`, and route the subnets through a NAT gateway or equivalent egress.

### Existing functions

A function with the same name can already exist, for example from an earlier attempt at the same deployment. Reuse an existing function only when its code hash and full configuration match the descriptor. Don't update or overwrite a function that differs, because it may serve another deployment that's still receiving traffic. Stop and investigate the conflict instead.

### Function package size

AWS Lambda accepts function ZIP files up to 50 MB when you upload them directly. For larger packages, upload the ZIP file to a private Amazon S3 bucket in the same region as the function and create the function from the bucket. The standard Vercel Functions bundle size limits still apply. See [BYOC limitations](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud#byoc-limitations).

## Provisioning identity permissions

The identity that runs your provisioning tool needs permission to publish layers, create and read functions, tag them, and pass the execution role to Lambda. This example policy covers those actions. Replace `<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>` with your AWS account ID and `byoc-lambda-execution` with your execution role name:

```json filename="provisioner-policy.json"
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "ManageByocLayers",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "lambda:ListLayerVersions",
        "lambda:GetLayerVersion",
        "lambda:PublishLayerVersion"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ManageByocFunctions",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "lambda:CreateFunction",
        "lambda:GetFunction",
        "lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration",
        "lambda:TagResource"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:lambda:*:<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>:function:*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "PassExecutionRole",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "iam:PassRole",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>:role/byoc-lambda-execution",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "iam:PassedToService": "lambda.amazonaws.com"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Add `s3:PutObject` and `s3:GetObject` on your staging bucket if you upload large packages through Amazon S3, and `lambda:DeleteFunction` and `lambda:DeleteLayerVersion` if the same identity runs cleanup. Don't grant `AdministratorAccess` to the provisioning identity.

## Route mapping file format

The route mapping file, `provision.json`, maps each function route in your build to the Lambda function that serves it. Vercel reads it to decide which function to invoke for a request. Don't edit it.

| Field          | Type       | Description                                       |
| -------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Key            | `string`   | The function's route path in the build output     |
| `awsAccountId` | `string`   | The AWS account that hosts the function           |
| `functionName` | `string`   | The Lambda function name Vercel invokes           |
| `regions`      | `string[]` | The AWS regions the function runs in              |
| `digest`       | `string`   | The hash of the function package                  |
| `size`         | `number`   | The size of the function package in bytes         |

## Deployment provisioning states

A BYOC deployment includes a `manualProvisioning` object in the [Vercel REST API](/docs/rest-api) deployment response, for example from `GET /v13/deployments/{idOrUrl}`. The deployment stays in the `INITIALIZING` state until you run `vercel deploy continue`.

| `manualProvisioning.state` | Meaning                                                                                                   |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `PENDING`                  | The deployment is waiting for you to provision its functions and run `vercel deploy continue`             |
| `COMPLETE`                 | Vercel received the continuation. `manualProvisioning.completedAt` holds the completion timestamp.        |
| `TIMEOUT`                  | 15 minutes passed without a continuation, and the deployment failed                                       |

## CLI commands

| Command                                                                  | Purpose                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `vercel deploy init --target <environment> --json`                       | Create a deployment that waits for provisioning. Uploads no files.                              |
| `vercel build --id <deployment-id> --target <environment>`               | Build with the deployment's environment variables                                               |
| `vercel deploy describe --id <deployment-id> --aws-account-id <aws-account-id>` | Generate `descriptor.json`, function packages, and the code-free output. Add `--json` for machine-readable output. |
| `vercel deploy continue --id <deployment-id>`                            | Upload the code-free output and `provision.json`, then wait for the deployment to finish       |
| `vercel deploy continue --id <deployment-id> --error "<reason>"`         | Mark a pending deployment as failed                                                             |
| `vercel inspect <deployment-id> --wait`                                  | Wait for the deployment to finish and show its status                                           |
| `vercel curl <path> --deployment <deployment-id>`                        | Send a request to a specific deployment                                                         |

`vercel deploy describe` requires Vercel CLI 62.7.0 or later. Use Vercel CLI 63.1.2 or later for BYOC deployments.

## Webhook events

| Event                        | When it fires                                                                                                           | Used for                                                                                                    |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `deployment.build-requested` | Vercel created a BYOC deployment from a Git push and is waiting for your environment to build it                       | Starting builds from Git. See [Deploying with BYOC from GitHub Actions](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/deploy-with-github-actions). |
| `deployment.cleanup`         | A deployment is permanently deleted, after its 30-day recovery period                                                   | Triggering AWS resource cleanup. See [Cleanup and retention](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/operations#cleanup-and-retention). |

For webhook payloads, see the [webhooks API reference](/docs/webhooks/webhooks-api).

## Related

- [Operating BYOC deployments](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud/operations)
- [AWS Lambda `CreateFunction` API](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/api/API_CreateFunction.html)

# Networking

Connect your projects to backend services that require IP allowlisting, AWS PrivateLink, or dedicated private networking.

## Choosing a networking option

Vercel has four networking options: [Static IPs](/docs/networking/static-ips), [AWS PrivateLink](/docs/networking/privatelink), [Secure Compute](/docs/networking/secure-compute), and [Bring Your Own Cloud](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud). This section details the requirements and costs of each option.

| Option | Best for | What it adds | Network model | Plan |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Static IPs](/docs/networking/static-ips) | Teams that need IP allowlisting without infrastructure changes | A stable, dedicated egress surface you can allowlist | Multi-tenant compute, shared VPC with subnet-level isolation | Pro and Enterprise |
| [AWS PrivateLink](/docs/networking/privatelink) | Reaching an AWS-hosted service behind a PrivateLink endpoint service | Private connectivity to AWS services with no public internet exposure | Shared VPC, dedicated endpoint per connection | Requires Advanced Networking |
| [Secure Compute](/docs/networking/secure-compute) | Teams that need a private VPC, dedicated networks, or regulatory isolation | A network perimeter isolated from every other customer, with VPC peering | Single-tenant, dedicated VPC | Enterprise add-on |
| [Bring Your Own Cloud](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud) | Compliance or data-residency mandates that require workloads in your cloud | A network and compute boundary you own end to end | Compute runs in your own AWS account | Enterprise |

Review the requirement for each option and choose the first one that matches your situation:

- Your backend, database, or API needs a set of known source IPs to add to an allowlist, and public connectivity is acceptable. Use [Static IPs](/docs/networking/static-ips).
- Your target service is hosted on AWS behind a PrivateLink endpoint service, and traffic must stay off the public internet. Use [AWS PrivateLink](/docs/networking/privatelink).
- You need VPC peering into your own AWS environment, a dedicated single-tenant VPC, or network isolation to satisfy a regulatory requirement. Use [Secure Compute](/docs/networking/secure-compute).
- A compliance or data-residency mandate requires your compute to run inside your own AWS account. Use [Bring Your Own Cloud](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud).

## Static IPs (shared pool)

When your database or API needs to see traffic from known IP addresses, Static IPs give you shared static egress IPs that won't change. Perfect for Pro and Enterprise teams who need IP allowlisting without the complexity.

- **Use case**: IP allowlisting for databases, APIs, and legacy systems
- **Network**: Shared VPC with subnet-level isolation
- [**Pricing**](/docs/networking/static-ips#pricing): $100/month per project + [Private Data Transfer](/docs/pricing/regional-pricing) at regional rates

[Learn more about Static IPs](/docs/networking/static-ips)

## AWS PrivateLink

When an AWS-hosted service exposes an AWS PrivateLink endpoint, PrivateLink keeps traffic on the AWS private network instead of the public internet. It extends the same shared-network model as Static IPs with endpoint-specific routing and Vercel-managed DNS names.

- **Use case**: Private connectivity to RDS, SaaS with PrivateLink endpoints, S3 or DynamoDB gateway endpoints, and compliance-focused deployments
- **Network**: Shared VPC with dedicated endpoint interfaces per connection

[Learn more about AWS PrivateLink](/docs/networking/privatelink)

## Secure Compute

For when you need your own private Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). Secure Compute gives you dedicated networks with VPC peering, so your infrastructure stays completely isolated from other customers.

- **Use case**: Full network isolation and VPC peering
- **Network**: Dedicated VPC per customer

[Learn more about Secure Compute](/docs/networking/secure-compute)

## Bring Your Own Cloud

Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) runs your functions as AWS Lambda functions inside your own AWS account, so your function code and execution stay inside your cloud boundary. Vercel routes requests, serves static assets, and invokes your functions.

It exists to satisfy strict security, compliance, or data-residency mandates that require workloads to run in your own cloud. Because it moves infrastructure out of Vercel's managed boundary, plan for a substantial setup project and ongoing ownership of your AWS account's service quotas, scaling headroom, and account health.

- **Use case**: Compliance or data-residency mandates that require workloads in your cloud
- **Network**: Compute runs in your own AWS account

Bring Your Own Cloud is available on the Enterprise plan. To scope it, [contact the Vercel sales team](https://vercel.com/contact/sales) or your Vercel account team.

[Learn more about Bring Your Own Cloud](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud)

## Pricing

Static IPs and Secure Compute usage includes **Private Data Transfer** priced regionally based on the [regional pricing documentation](/docs/pricing/regional-pricing).

PrivateLink usage is tracked separately on your team's Usage tab. See [AWS PrivateLink](/docs/networking/privatelink) for setup and behavior.

[Bring Your Own Cloud](/docs/networking/bring-your-own-cloud) is an Enterprise feature with custom pricing. [Contact the Vercel sales team](https://vercel.com/contact/sales) to scope it.

| Resource | Pro Price |
| --- | --- |
| Static IPs | $100.00 |


### Understanding data transfer costs

Data transfer costs kick in for all traffic to or from your Vercel Functions, including those to external services and to the Vercel CDN:

- Database queries and responses
- API calls to third-party services
- File uploads and downloads
- Any other inbound or outbound network traffic

Keep tabs on your usage in the **Team Settings** **Usage** tab under the **Private Data Transfer** section.

title: "AWS PrivateLink"
description: "Connect Vercel deployments to AWS-hosted backends through AWS PrivateLink endpoint services without using the public internet."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:45.998Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/networking/privatelink"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# AWS PrivateLink

With PrivateLink, you can connect your Vercel deployments to AWS-hosted backend services over a private connection, without exposing traffic to the public internet. [Get started](#getting-started) by creating a PrivateLink connection.

## When to use PrivateLink

- Connect privately to AWS-hosted databases such as Amazon RDS, Aurora, Neon, or Redshift
- Connect to SaaS services that expose a PrivateLink endpoint (e.g. Snowflake, MongoDB Atlas, Confluent)
- Access internal services exposed through an AWS Network Load Balancer
- Connect to S3 or DynamoDB without traversing the public internet
- Meet security and compliance requirements (SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR) that prohibit public network exposure

## When not to use PrivateLink

PrivateLink only connects to services that have published an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service. If your backend is on-premises, in another cloud, or hasn't been exposed via PrivateLink, use [Static IPs](/docs/networking/static-ips) with allowlisting or Secure Compute with [VPC peering](/docs/networking/secure-compute#vpc-peering) / [VPN](/docs/networking/secure-compute#vpn-support) instead.

## How it works

When you create a PrivateLink connection, Vercel:

- **Provisions a dedicated VPC endpoint** in the shared network for your team, in 2 Availability Zones supported by the target service
- **Routes all outbound traffic** to that service through the endpoint, keeping it on the AWS private network
- **Assigns a dedicated AWS IAM role** to your team that the service provider can allowlist as a connection principal
- **Tracks data transfer per connection** so you can see usage broken down by service

Both deployed function traffic and build traffic can route through PrivateLink connections, with the same configuration model as Static IPs.

### Supported endpoint types

- **Interface Endpoints**: Used for services exposed behind an AWS Network Load Balancer, as well as AWS services like S3 and DynamoDB that publish interface endpoint services

Gateway Endpoints, Gateway Load Balancer Endpoints, and Resource Endpoints are not currently supported.

## Getting started

Follow these steps to create your first PrivateLink connection.

### Prerequisites

Before you start, confirm you have:

- A [Vercel project](/docs/projects) on a team with **Advanced Networking** enabled
- An AWS PrivateLink endpoint service you can connect to, either one that accepts all principals or one where an IAM role ARN can be added to the allowlist
- The **service name** (for example `com.amazonaws.vpce.<region>.vpce-svc-…`) and **AWS Region** from the provider

- ### Create the connection in Vercel
  1. From your project, navigate to **Settings** → **Networking** → **Advanced Networking** → [**AWS PrivateLink**](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%5Bproject%5D%2Fsettings%2Fnetworking%2Fadvanced%2Fprivate-link\&title=AWS+PrivateLink)
  2. Click **Add Connection**
  3. Enter a **Name** for the connection, select the **Region**, and enter the **Service Name** from the provider
  4. Optionally, enable **Private DNS** to resolve the service's own private DNS names (for example, a provider-specific hostname) from your deployments
  5. Click **Add Connection**

- ### Wait for the provider to accept the connection
  Vercel provisions the VPC endpoint and requests a connection to the endpoint service. If the service doesn't automatically accept connections, the endpoint stays in a **pending acceptance** state until the provider approves it. Share your team's **principal role ARN** (shown in the setup dialog) with the provider so they can allowlist it.

- ### Verify traffic
  Once the endpoint is available, redeploy your project and confirm requests to the backend succeed over the PrivateLink connection.

## Managing PrivateLink

### Routing Middleware support

PrivateLink connections are region-specific and do not apply to [Routing Middleware](/docs/routing-middleware), which runs at the edge.

### DNS

Each endpoint's DNS names are shown in the dashboard once the connection is available. You can connect in two ways:

- **AWS endpoint DNS names**: Use the AWS-generated `vpce-….vpce.amazonaws.com` hostnames listed on the endpoint. These resolve to the endpoint from your deployments without additional configuration.
- **Private DNS**: If you enable Private DNS on the connection, your deployments can also resolve the service's own private DNS names (for example, a provider-specific hostname) to the endpoint. Vercel resolves these names inside its network for your project's deployments.

### PrivateLink with deployment environments

Assigning a PrivateLink connection to a project applies to all environments in that project. Per-environment scoping is not supported.

### Regional considerations

- Each PrivateLink connection exists in a single AWS region. Create one connection per region when you need multi-region access.
- For multi-region private connectivity, each region needs its own VPC endpoint to the service, which means the service must either be available in every matching region or support cross-region PrivateLink connections.
- The endpoint service must be available in at least two Availability Zones that overlap with Vercel's network in that region. If there isn't enough overlap, provisioning fails. Ask your provider to expose the service in additional zones.
- Pick regions close to your provider to reduce latency.

## Limitations

- **Isolation**: Each connection is dedicated to your team, but the underlying VPC is shared with other customers. For full isolation, use Secure Compute.
- **Services** must publish an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service and either accept all principals or allowlist your team's IAM role.
- **Project-level configuration**: You cannot limit a connection to a single deployment environment inside a project.
- **Endpoint types**: Only interface endpoints are supported.

description: "Secure Compute provides dedicated private networks with VPC peering for Enterprise teams."
