# Getting Started with Routing Middleware

Routing Middleware lets you to run code before your pages load, giving you control over incoming requests. It runs close to your users for fast response times and are perfect for redirects, authentication, and request modification.

**Agent prompt**

```text
Help me set up Routing Middleware in this project. First, make sure the Vercel CLI is installed (`npm i -g vercel`). If I'm using Claude Code or Cursor, install the Vercel Plugin (`npx plugins add vercel/vercel-plugin`). For other agents, install Vercel Skills (`npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills`). Then, in the language this project uses: 1. Create the entrypoint at the project root: proxy.ts or proxy.js for TypeScript or JavaScript, or proxy.py with a top-level ASGI or WSGI app, such as `proxy = Proxy()` from the vercel-proxy package, for Python. 2. Set `proxy.entrypoint` in vercel.json to the file path for TypeScript or JavaScript, such as `proxy.ts`, or to `proxy:proxy` for Python. For Python, list the entrypoint's packages under `'vercel.proxy'` in `[dependency-groups]` in pyproject.toml. If using Next.js, skip vercel.json and add proxy.ts at the project root for Next.js 16+, or middleware.ts for earlier versions. 3. Add a redirect from /old-blog to /blog. 4. Set `proxy.matcher` to run on all paths except static files and images. 5. Test locally with `vercel dev`, then deploy with `vercel --prod`.
```

Routing Middleware is available on the [Node.js](/docs/functions/runtimes/node-js), [Bun](/docs/functions/runtimes/bun), and [Python](/docs/functions/runtimes/python) runtimes. Node.js is the default runtime for TypeScript and JavaScript Routing Middleware, and Python Routing Middleware runs on Python. To use Bun, set [`bunVersion`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#bunversion) in your `vercel.json` file.

## What you will learn

- Create your first Routing Middleware
- Redirect users based on URLs
- Add conditional logic to handle different scenarios
- Configure which paths your Routing Middleware runs on

## Prerequisites

- A Vercel project
- Basic knowledge of TypeScript, JavaScript, or Python

## Creating Routing Middleware

The following steps will guide you through creating your first Routing Middleware.

- ### Create a new file for your Routing Middleware
  Create a file called `proxy.ts`, `proxy.js`, or `proxy.py` in your project root and add the following code:
  #### TypeScript
  ```ts v0="build" filename="proxy.ts"
  export default function proxy(request: Request) {
    console.log('Request to:', request.url);
    return new Response('Logging request URL from Middleware');
  }
  ```
  #### Python
  ```python filename="proxy.py"
  from vercel.proxy import PlainTextResponse, Proxy, Request, Response

  proxy = Proxy()


  @proxy.route("/{path:path}")
  def log_request(request: Request) -> Response:
      print("Request to:", request.url)
      return PlainTextResponse("Logging request URL from Middleware")
  ```
  - Every request to your site will trigger this function
  - You log the request URL to see what's being accessed
  - You return a response to prove the middleware is running
  In Python, `Proxy` from the `vercel-proxy` helper package sends each request to the first route that matches its path, and `{path:path}` matches every path.

- ### Point Vercel at your Routing Middleware
  You can tell Vercel where your Routing Middleware is with the `proxy` property or with the file convention. Next.js apps must use the file convention instead, with `proxy.ts` in Next.js 16 and later, or `middleware.ts` in earlier versions.

  **Using the `proxy` property:** Set [`proxy.entrypoint`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#proxy) in `vercel.json`. Use the file path for TypeScript and JavaScript, or `module:attribute` for Python:
  #### TypeScript
  ```json filename="vercel.json"
  {
    "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
    "proxy": {
      "entrypoint": "proxy.ts"
    }
  }
  ```
  #### Python
  ```json filename="vercel.json"
  {
    "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
    "proxy": {
      "entrypoint": "proxy:proxy"
    }
  }
  ```
  Your Routing Middleware runs with only the packages in the `vercel.proxy` dependency group. Add the group, with the packages your Routing Middleware imports, to `pyproject.toml`:
  ```toml filename="pyproject.toml"
  [dependency-groups]
  "vercel.proxy" = ["vercel-proxy"]
  ```
  **Using the file convention (TypeScript and JavaScript):** Rename your file to `middleware.ts` or `middleware.js` and keep it in your project root, at the same level as your `package.json`. You don't need `vercel.json`. The `runtime` config is optional and defaults to `nodejs`:
  #### TypeScript
  ```ts filename="middleware.ts"
  export const config = {
    runtime: 'nodejs',
  };

  export default function middleware(request: Request) {
    console.log('Request to:', request.url);
    return new Response('Logging request URL from Middleware');
  }
  ```
  #### JavaScript
  ```js filename="middleware.js"
  export const config = {
    runtime: 'nodejs',
  };

  export default function middleware(request) {
    console.log('Request to:', request.url);
    return new Response('Logging request URL from Middleware');
  }
  ```
  Deploy your project and visit any page. You should see "Logging request URL from Middleware" instead of your normal page content.

- ### Redirecting users
  To redirect users based on their URL, add a new route to your project called `/blog`, and update your Routing Middleware to include a redirect condition:
  #### TypeScript
  ```ts v0="build" filename="proxy.ts"
  import { next } from '@vercel/functions';

  export default function proxy(request: Request) {
    const url = new URL(request.url);

    // Redirect old blog path to new one
    if (url.pathname === '/old-blog') {
      return new Response(null, {
        status: 302,
        headers: { Location: '/blog' },
      });
    }

    // Let other requests continue normally
    return next();
  }
  ```
  #### Python
  ```python filename="proxy.py"
  from vercel.proxy import Proxy, RedirectResponse, Request, Response

  proxy = Proxy()


  # Redirect old blog path to new one
  @proxy.route("/old-blog")
  def old_blog(request: Request) -> Response:
      return RedirectResponse("/blog", status_code=302)


  # Requests that match no route continue to your app unchanged
  ```
  - You use `new URL(request.url)` to parse the incoming URL
  - You check if the path matches `/old-blog`
  - If it does, you return a redirect response (status 302)
  - The `Location` header tells the browser where to go
  - For every other path, `next()` from the [`@vercel/functions`](/docs/functions/functions-api-reference/vercel-functions-package) package lets the request continue to your page. In Python, requests that match no route continue to your app unchanged
  Try visiting `/old-blog` - you should be redirected to `/blog`.

- ### Configure which paths trigger the middleware
  By default, Routing Middleware runs on every request. To limit it to specific paths, set `proxy.matcher` in `vercel.json`:
  #### TypeScript
  ```json filename="vercel.json"
  {
    "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
    "proxy": {
      "entrypoint": "proxy.ts",
      "matcher": [
        "/((?!static|favicon.ico).*)"
      ]
    }
  }
  ```
  #### Python
  ```json filename="vercel.json"
  {
    "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
    "proxy": {
      "entrypoint": "proxy:proxy",
      "matcher": [
        "/((?!static|favicon.ico).*)"
      ]
    }
  }
  ```
  - The `matcher` array defines which paths trigger your Routing Middleware
  - The regex excludes paths under `/static` and `/favicon.ico`, so requests for static files skip your Routing Middleware
  - You can also use simple patterns like `/blog/:path*` for specific sections
  If you use the file convention, export a [`config`](/docs/routing-middleware/js-reference#config-object) object with a `matcher` property instead:
  #### TypeScript
  ```ts filename="middleware.ts"
  export const config = {
    matcher: ['/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)'],
  };
  ```
  #### JavaScript
  ```js filename="middleware.js"
  export const config = {
    matcher: ['/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)'],
  };
  ```
  See [path matching](/docs/routing-middleware#path-matching) for the full matcher syntax.

- ### Debugging Routing Middleware
  When things don't work as expected:
  1. **Check the logs**: Log liberally and check your [Vercel dashboard](/dashboard) **Logs** section in the sidebar
  2. **Test the matcher**: Make sure your paths are actually triggering the Routing Middleware
  3. **Verify headers**: Log the request headers to see what's available
  4. **Test locally**: Routing Middleware works in development too so you can debug before deploying
  #### TypeScript
  ```ts filename="proxy.ts"
  export default function proxy(request: Request) {
    // Debug logging
    console.log('URL:', request.url);
    console.log('Method:', request.method);
    console.log('Headers:', Object.fromEntries(request.headers.entries()));

    // Your middleware logic here...
  }
  ```
  #### Python
  ```python filename="proxy.py"
  from vercel.proxy import ContinueResponse, Proxy, Request, Response

  proxy = Proxy()


  @proxy.route("/{path:path}")
  def debug(request: Request) -> Response:
      # Debug logging
      print("URL:", request.url)
      print("Method:", request.method)
      print("Headers:", dict(request.headers))

      # Your middleware logic here...
      return ContinueResponse()
  ```

## Middleware reference

#### TypeScript

| Detail                                                                   | Value                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Entrypoint**                                                           | Any path set with [`proxy.entrypoint`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#proxy), or `middleware.ts` in project root (`proxy.ts` for Next.js 16+) |
| **Export**                                                               | `export default function middleware(request: Request)` (or `export function proxy` for Next.js 16+)                                                    |
| **[Config export](/docs/routing-middleware/js-reference#config-object)** | `export const config = { matcher: [...] }`                                                                                                             |
| **Default runtime**                                                      | [`nodejs`](/docs/functions/runtimes/node-js)                                                                                                           |
| **Bun runtime**                                                          | Set [`bunVersion`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#bunversion) in `vercel.json` and `runtime: 'nodejs'` in config                              |
| **Request object**                                                       | Standard `Request` API                                                                                                                                 |
| **[Path matching](/docs/routing-middleware#path-matching)**              | Supports regex, named params, and wildcards in the `matcher` config                                                                                    |

#### Python

| Detail                                                      | Value                                                                                                   |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Entrypoint**                                              | A `module:attribute` value set with [`proxy.entrypoint`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#proxy) |
| **Export**                                                  | A top-level ASGI or WSGI app, such as `proxy = Proxy()`                                                 |
| **Default runtime**                                         | [Python](/docs/functions/runtimes/python)                                                               |
| **Dependencies**                                            | The `vercel.proxy` dependency group in `pyproject.toml`                                                 |
| **Request object**                                          | Starlette `Request`                                                                                     |
| **[Path matching](/docs/routing-middleware#path-matching)** | Supports regex, named params, and wildcards in `proxy.matcher`                                          |

Vercel adds [geolocation headers](/docs/routing-middleware#geolocation-headers), such as `x-vercel-ip-country`, to every request.

# Routing Middleware: JS Reference

Use this reference to write [Routing Middleware](/docs/routing-middleware) in TypeScript or JavaScript. For path matching and limits, see the [Routing Middleware overview](/docs/routing-middleware).

## Routing Middleware file location and name

You can tell Vercel where your Routing Middleware is in two ways.

### Using the `proxy` property

Set [`proxy.entrypoint`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#proxy) in `vercel.json` to a `.ts` or `.js` file, such as `proxy.ts` or `src/proxy.ts`:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "proxy": {
    "entrypoint": "proxy.ts"
  }
}
```

### Using the file convention

Name the file `middleware.ts` and place it at the root of your project, at the same level as your `package.json` file. The default runtime is [Node.js](/docs/functions/runtimes/node-js). See [Specify runtime](#specify-runtime).

> For \['nextjs', 'nextjs-app']:

In Next.js, place the `proxy.ts` file at the same level as your `app` or `pages` directory, even if you use a `src` directory.

### Default export

The Routing Middleware must be a default export, with the function being named anything you like. For example, you can name it `router`, `middleware`, or any other name that makes sense for your application.

```ts filename="proxy.ts"
export default function proxy(request: Request) {
  return new Response('Hello from your Middleware!');
}
```

```js filename="proxy.js"
export default function proxy(request) {
  return new Response('Hello from your Middleware!');
}
```

## `config` object

Routing Middleware will be invoked for **every route in your project**. If you only want it to be run on specific paths, you can define those either with a [custom matcher config](#match-paths-based-on-custom-matcher-config) or with [conditional statements](#match-paths-based-on-conditional-statements).

You can also use the [`runtime` option](#config-properties) to [specify which runtime](#specify-runtime) you would like to use. The default is `nodejs`.

While the `config` option is the preferred method, **as it does not get invoked on every request**, you can also use conditional statements to only run the Routing Middleware when it matches specific paths.

### Match paths based on custom matcher config

Export a `config` object with a `matcher` property to choose which paths run your Routing Middleware. The matcher accepts a single path or an array of paths:

```ts filename="middleware.ts"
export const config = {
  matcher: ['/about/:path*', '/dashboard/:path*'],
};
```

If you configure your entrypoint with [`proxy`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#proxy), set the matcher here or in `proxy.matcher`. See [path matching](/docs/routing-middleware#path-matching) for the matcher syntax, including regex support.

> For \['nextjs']:

> **💡 Note:** Routing Middleware run on **all** `/_next/data/` requests for
> `getServerSideProps` and `getStaticProps` pages for the sake of consistency.
> For more information see the [Next.js matcher
> docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/advanced-features/middleware#matcher).

### Match paths based on conditional statements

```ts filename="middleware.ts"
import { rewrite } from '@vercel/functions';

export default function middleware(request: Request) {
  const url = new URL(request.url);

  if (url.pathname.startsWith('/about')) {
    return rewrite(new URL('/about-2', request.url));
  }

  if (url.pathname.startsWith('/dashboard')) {
    return rewrite(new URL('/dashboard/user', request.url));
  }
}
```

See the [helper methods](#routing-middleware-helper-methods) below for more information on using the `@vercel/functions` package.

### Specify runtime

To set the runtime explicitly, update the `runtime` option as follows:

```ts filename="middleware.ts"
export const config = {
  runtime: 'nodejs',
};
```

To use the Bun runtime with Routing Middleware, set the [`bunVersion`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#bunversion) property in your `vercel.json` file as well as using the `runtime` config shown above to `nodejs`:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "bunVersion": "1.4.x"
}
```

### `config` properties

| Property  | Type                          | Description                                                                        |
| --------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `matcher` | `string / string[]`           | A string or array of strings that define the paths the Middleware should be run on |
| `runtime` | `string` (`nodejs`)           | A string that defines the Middleware runtime and defaults to `nodejs`              |

## Routing Middleware signature

The Routing Middleware signature is made up of two parameters: `request` and `context`. The `request` parameter is an instance of the [Request](/docs/functions/functions-api-reference#function-signature) object, and the `context` parameter is an object containing the [`waitUntil`](/docs/functions/functions-api-reference/vercel-functions-package#waituntil) method. **Both parameters are optional**.

| Parameter | Description                                                                                         | Next.js (/app) or (/pages)                                                                                                                        | Other Frameworks                                                                     |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `request` | An instance of the [Request](/docs/functions/functions-api-reference#function-signature) object      | [`Request`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Request) or [`NextRequest`](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy#nextrequest) | [`Request`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Request)                      |
| `context` | An extension to the standard [`Request`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Request) object | [`NextFetchEvent`](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy#nextfetchevent)                                                              | [`RequestContext`](/docs/routing-middleware/js-reference#requestcontext) |

Routing Middleware comes with built in helpers that are based on the native [`FetchEvent`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/FetchEvent), [`Response`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Response), and [`Request`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Request) objects.

[See the section on Routing Middleware helpers for more information](#routing-middleware-helper-methods).

```ts filename="middleware.ts" framework=nextjs-app
// config with custom matcher
export const config = {
  matcher: '/about/:path*',
};

export default function middleware(request: Request) {
  return Response.redirect(new URL('/about-2', request.url));
}
```

```js filename="middleware.js" framework=nextjs-app
// config with custom matcher
export const config = {
  matcher: '/about/:path*',
};

export default function middleware(request) {
  return Response.redirect(new URL('/about-2', request.url));
}
```

```ts filename="middleware.ts" framework=nextjs
// config with custom matcher
export const config = {
  matcher: '/about/:path*',
};

export default function middleware(request: Request) {
  return Response.redirect(new URL('/about-2', request.url));
}
```

```js filename="middleware.js" framework=nextjs
// config with custom matcher
export const config = {
  matcher: '/about/:path*',
};

export default function middleware(request) {
  return Response.redirect(new URL('/about-2', request.url));
}
```

```ts filename="middleware.ts" framework=other
// config with custom matcher
export const config = {
  matcher: '/about/:path*',
};

export default function middleware(request: Request) {
  return Response.redirect(new URL('/about-2', request.url));
}
```

```js filename="middleware.js" framework=other
// config with custom matcher
export const config = {
  matcher: '/about/:path*',
};

export default function middleware(request) {
  return Response.redirect(new URL('/about-2', request.url));
}
```

> **💡 Note:** If you're not using a framework, you must either add
> `"type": "module"` to your
> `package.json` or change your JavaScript Functions'
> file extensions from `.js` to
> `.mjs`

### Request

The `Request` object represents an HTTP request. It is a wrapper around the [Fetch API](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API) `Request` object. **When using TypeScript, you do not need to import the `Request` object, as it is already available in the global scope**.

#### Request properties

| Property         | Type                                                                          | Description                                         |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `url`            | `string`                                                                      | The URL of the request                              |
| `method`         | `string`                                                                      | The HTTP method of the request                      |
| `headers`        | `Headers`                                                                     | The headers of the request                          |
| `body`           | [`ReadableStream`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/ReadableStream) | The body of the request                             |
| `bodyUsed`       | `boolean`                                                                     | Whether the body has been read                      |
| `cache`          | `string`                                                                      | The cache mode of the request                       |
| `credentials`    | `string`                                                                      | The credentials mode of the request                 |
| `destination`    | `string`                                                                      | The destination of the request                      |
| `integrity`      | `string`                                                                      | The integrity of the request                        |
| `redirect`       | `string`                                                                      | The redirect mode of the request                    |
| `referrer`       | `string`                                                                      | The referrer of the request                         |
| `referrerPolicy` | `string`                                                                      | The referrer policy of the request                  |
| `mode`           | `string`                                                                      | The mode of the request                             |
| `signal`         | [`AbortSignal`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/AbortSignal)       | The signal of the request                           |
| `arrayBuffer`    | `function`                                                                    | Returns a promise that resolves with an ArrayBuffer |
| `blob`           | `function`                                                                    | Returns a promise that resolves with a Blob         |
| `formData`       | `function`                                                                    | Returns a promise that resolves with a FormData     |
| `json`           | `function`                                                                    | Returns a promise that resolves with a JSON object  |
| `text`           | `function`                                                                    | Returns a promise that resolves with a string       |
| `clone`          | `function`                                                                    | Returns a clone of the request                      |

> For \["nextjs", "nextjs-app"]:

To learn more about the [`NextRequest`](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy#nextrequest) object and its properties, visit the [Next.js documentation](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy#nextrequest).

### `waitUntil()`

The `waitUntil()` method is from the [`ExtendableEvent`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/ExtendableEvent/waitUntil) interface. It accepts a [`Promise`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise) as an argument, which will keep the function running until the `Promise` resolves.

It can be used to keep the function running after a response has been sent. This is useful when you have an async task that you want to keep running after returning a response.

The example below will:

- Send a response immediately
- Keep the function running for ten seconds
- Fetch a product and log it to the console

> For \["other"]:

> **💡 Note:** `Response.json()` is a new addition to the `Response` object and has not yet
> been added by the TypeScript team. This means that you will likely see a red
> error line under `Response.json()` in your editor. You can ignore this error,
> as it is a false positive.

```ts filename="middleware.ts" framework=nextjs
import type { NextFetchEvent } from 'next/server';

export const config = {
  matcher: '/',
};

const wait = (ms: number) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function getProduct() {
  const res = await fetch('https://api.vercel.app/products/1');
  await wait(10000);
  return res.json();
}

export default function middleware(request: Request, context: NextFetchEvent) {
  context.waitUntil(getProduct().then((json) => console.log({ json })));

  return new Response(JSON.stringify({ hello: 'world' }), {
    status: 200,
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },
  });
}
```

## Routing Middleware helper methods

You can use Vercel-specific helper methods to access a request's [geolocation](/docs/routing-middleware#geolocation-headers), [IP address](/docs/functions/functions-api-reference/vercel-functions-package#ipaddress), and more when deploying Middleware on Vercel.

> For \['nextjs', 'nextjs-app']:

You can access these helper methods with the `request` and `response` objects in your middleware handler method.

> **💡 Note:** These helpers are exclusive to Vercel, and will not work on other providers,
> even if your app is built with Next.js.

> For \['other']:

Add the `@vercel/functions` package to your project with:

**pnpm**

```bash
pnpm i @vercel/functions
```

**yarn**

```bash
yarn add @vercel/functions
```

**npm**

```bash
npm i @vercel/functions
```

**bun**

```bash
bun add @vercel/functions
```

To read a request's location, see [geolocation headers](/docs/routing-middleware#geolocation-headers).

### IP address

> For \['nextjs', 'nextjs-app']:

The `ip` object returns the IP address of the request from the headers, or `undefined`.

> For \['other']:

The `ipAddress()` helper returns the IP address of the request from the headers, or `undefined`.

```ts filename="middleware.ts" framework=all
import { ipAddress } from '@vercel/functions';
import { next } from '@vercel/functions';

export default function middleware(request: Request) {
  const ip = ipAddress(request);
  return next({
    headers: { 'x-your-ip-address': ip || 'unknown' },
  });
}
```

```js filename="middleware.js" framework=all
import { ipAddress } from '@vercel/functions';
import { next } from '@vercel/functions';

export default function middleware(request) {
  const ip = ipAddress(request);
  return next({
    headers: { 'x-your-ip-address': ip || 'unknown' },
  });
}
```

### `RequestContext`

The `RequestContext` is an extension of the standard `Request` object, which contains the [`waitUntil`](#waituntil) function. The following example works in middleware for all frameworks:

```ts filename="middleware.ts" framework=all
import type { RequestContext } from '@vercel/functions';

export default function handler(request: Request, context: RequestContext) {
  context.waitUntil(getAlbum().then((json) => console.log({ json })));

  return new Response(
    `Hello there, from ${request.url} I'm a Vercel Function!`,
  );
}

export const config = {
  matcher: '/',
};

async function getAlbum() {

  await wait(10000);
  return res.json();
}
```

### Rewrites

> For \['nextjs', 'nextjs-app']:

The `NextResponse.rewrite()` helper returns a response that rewrites the request to a different URL.

> For \['other']:

The `rewrite()` helper returns a response that rewrites the request to a different URL.

```ts filename="middleware.ts" framework=nextjs-app
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';
import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server';
// Trigger this middleware to run on the `/about` route
export const config = {
  matcher: '/about',
};

export default function middleware(request: NextRequest) {
  // Rewrite to URL
  return NextResponse.rewrite('/about-2');
}
```

### Continuing the Routing Middleware chain

> For \['nextjs', 'nextjs-app']:

The `NextResponse.next()` helper returns a Response that instructs the function to continue the middleware chain. It takes the following optional parameters:

> For \['other']:

The `next()` helper returns a Response that instructs the function to continue the middleware chain. It takes the following optional parameters:

| Parameter    | type                     | Description                 |
| ------------ | ------------------------ | --------------------------- |
| `headers`    | `Headers[]` or `Headers` | The headers you want to set |
| `status`     | `number`                 | The status code             |
| `statusText` | `string`                 | The status text             |

The following example adds a custom header, then continues the Routing Middleware chain:

```ts filename="middleware.ts" framework=nextjs
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';
import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server';

export function middleware(request: NextRequest) {
  // Clone the request headers and set a new header `x-hello-from-middleware1`
  const requestHeaders = new Headers(request.headers);
  requestHeaders.set('x-hello-from-middleware1', 'hello');

  // You can also set request headers in NextResponse.next
  const response = NextResponse.next({
    request: {
      // New request headers
      headers: requestHeaders,
    },
  });

  // Set a new response header `x-hello-from-middleware2`
  response.headers.set('x-hello-from-middleware2', 'hello');
  return response;
}
```

```js filename="middleware.js" framework=nextjs
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'

export function middleware(request) {
  // Clone the request headers and set a new header `x-hello-from-middleware1`
  const requestHeaders = new Headers(request.headers)
  requestHeaders.set('x-hello-from-middleware1', 'hello')

  // You can also set request headers in NextResponse.next
  const response = NextResponse.next({
    request: {
      // New request headers
      headers: requestHeaders,
    },
  })

  // Set a new response header `x-hello-from-middleware2`
  response.headers.set('x-hello-from-middleware2', 'hello')
  return response
}
```

# Routing Middleware

> Routing Middleware is available on all plans

Routing Middleware **executes code *before* a request is processed on a site**, and are built on top of [fluid compute](/docs/fluid-compute). Based on the request, you can modify the response.

Because it runs globally before the cache, Routing Middleware is an effective way of providing personalization to statically generated content. Depending on the incoming request, you can execute custom logic, rewrite, redirect, add headers and more, before returning a response.

You can write Routing Middleware in TypeScript or JavaScript, which run on [Node.js](/docs/functions/runtimes/node-js) or [Bun](/docs/functions/runtimes/bun), or in Python, which runs on [Python](/docs/functions/runtimes/python). See [runtime options](#runtime-options) for details.

## Static configuration or Routing Middleware

If your routing logic doesn't need custom code, use static configuration instead of Routing Middleware. Static rules run directly on the CDN without invoking your code on every request, so they're faster and use fewer resources.

You can express these common tasks with static configuration in [`vercel.json`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json) or [project routing rules](/docs/routing/project-routing-rules):

| Task                                                      | Static configuration                                                                                                                  |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Redirect paths                                            | [Redirects](/docs/routing/redirects)                                                                                                  |
| Rewrite to another path or an external origin             | [Rewrites](/docs/routing/rewrites)                                                                                                    |
| Add response headers                                      | [`headers`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#headers)                                                                          |
| Add, change, or remove request headers sent to your app   | [Route transforms](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#transform-object-definition)                                                         |
| Route based on a header, cookie, query parameter, or host | [`has` and `missing` conditions](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#conditional-matching-with-has-and-missing)            |

Use Routing Middleware when the decision depends on logic that static rules can't express, such as verifying a session token, calling an API, or assigning visitors to an A/B test.

## Creating Routing Middleware

To add Routing Middleware to your app, point the [`proxy`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#proxy) property in `vercel.json` at your entrypoint:

#### TypeScript

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "proxy": {
    "entrypoint": "proxy.ts"
  }
}
```

```ts v0="build" filename="proxy.ts"
import { next } from '@vercel/functions';

export default function proxy(request: Request) {
  const url = new URL(request.url);

  // Redirect old paths
  if (url.pathname === '/old-page') {
    return new Response(null, {
      status: 302,
      headers: { Location: '/new-page' },
    });
  }

  // Continue to the next handler
  return next();
}
```

#### Python

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "proxy": {
    "entrypoint": "proxy:proxy"
  }
}
```

```python filename="proxy.py"
from vercel.proxy import Proxy, RedirectResponse, Request, Response

proxy = Proxy()


# Redirect old paths
@proxy.route("/old-page")
def old_page(request: Request) -> Response:
    return RedirectResponse("/new-page", status_code=302)


# Requests that match no route continue to your app unchanged
```

```toml filename="pyproject.toml"
[dependency-groups]
"vercel.proxy" = ["vercel-proxy"]
```

The entrypoint can live in a subdirectory, such as `src/proxy.ts` or `app.proxy:proxy`. See the [JS reference](/docs/routing-middleware/js-reference) and the [Python reference](/docs/routing-middleware/python-reference) for each language's API.

In TypeScript and JavaScript, you can also skip `vercel.json` and use the `middleware.ts` file convention. See the [JS reference](/docs/routing-middleware/js-reference#using-the-file-convention).

Your Routing Middleware must use the same runtime as your app. If the runtimes don't match, the build fails with `proxy_runtime_mismatch`.

> **💡 Note:** You can't use `proxy` with frameworks that build their own routing
> middleware, such as Next.js and Astro. In Next.js 16 and later, add a
> `proxy.ts` file at your project root instead, or a `middleware.ts` file in
> earlier versions. See the [Next.js proxy
> documentation](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy)
> for details.

## Path matching

Without a matcher, your Routing Middleware runs on **every** request, including requests for static files. This adds latency and cost to each request. Set `proxy.matcher` to one path or a list of paths:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "proxy": {
    "entrypoint": "proxy.ts",
    "matcher": ["/about/:path*", "/dashboard/:path*"]
  }
}
```

Each matcher must start with `/`. In TypeScript and JavaScript, you can also export a [`config`](/docs/routing-middleware/js-reference#match-paths-based-on-custom-matcher-config) object with a `matcher` property instead.

The following examples show `matcher` values.

### Match a single path

```json
"/about/:path*"
```

### Match using regex

The matcher has full [regex](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Regular_Expressions) support for cases such as negative lookaheads or character matching.

#### Match based on a negative lookahead

To match all request paths except for the ones starting with:

- `api` (API routes)
- `_next/static` (static files)
- `favicon.ico` (favicon file)

```json
["/((?!api|_next/static|favicon.ico).*)"]
```

#### Match based on character matching

To match `/blog/123` but not `/blog/abc`:

```json
["/blog/:slug(\\d{1,})"]
```

For help on writing your own regex path matcher, see [Path to regexp](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp#path-to-regexp-1).

## Geolocation headers

Vercel adds geolocation headers, such as `x-vercel-ip-country` and `x-vercel-ip-city`, to every request your Routing Middleware receives. See [request headers](/docs/headers/request-headers) for the full list.

The following example redirects visitors from one country away from a page:

#### TypeScript

```ts filename="proxy.ts"
import { geolocation, next } from '@vercel/functions';

export default function proxy(request: Request) {
  const url = new URL(request.url);
  const { country } = geolocation(request);

  if (url.pathname === '/secret-page' && country === 'SE') {
    return Response.redirect(new URL('/login', request.url));
  }

  return next();
}
```

#### Python

```python filename="proxy.py"
from vercel.proxy import ContinueResponse, Proxy, RedirectResponse, Request, Response

proxy = Proxy()


@proxy.route("/secret-page")
def secret_page(request: Request) -> Response:
    if request.headers.get("x-vercel-ip-country") == "SE":
        return RedirectResponse("/login")
    return ContinueResponse()
```

In TypeScript and JavaScript, read them with the [`geolocation()`](/docs/functions/functions-api-reference/vercel-functions-package#geolocation) helper from `@vercel/functions`. In Python, read them from `request.headers`.

## Logging

Routing Middleware has full support for the [`console`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/Console) API, including `time`, `debug`, `timeEnd`. Logs will appear inside your Vercel project by clicking **View Functions Logs** next to the deployment.

## Using a database with Routing Middleware

If your Routing Middleware depends on a database far away from one of [our supported regions](/docs/regions), the overall latency of API requests could be slower than expected, due to network latency while connecting to the database from a distant region. To avoid this issue, use a global database. Vercel has multiple global storage products, including [Global Config](/docs/global-config) and [Vercel Blob](/docs/vercel-blob). You can also explore the storage category of the [Vercel Marketplace](/marketplace?category=storage) to learn which option is best for you.

## Limits on requests

The following limits apply to requests processed by Routing Middleware:

| Name                              | Limit |
| --------------------------------- | ----- |
| Maximum URL length                | 14 KB |
| Maximum request body length       | 4 MB  |
| Maximum number of request headers | 64    |
| Maximum request headers length    | 16 KB |

## Runtime options

TypeScript and JavaScript Routing Middleware runs on the [Node.js](/docs/functions/runtimes/node-js) runtime by default. To use [Bun](/docs/functions/runtimes/bun), set [`bunVersion`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#bunversion) in your `vercel.json` file. With the `middleware.ts` file convention, also set the [`runtime` config](/docs/routing-middleware/js-reference#specify-runtime) to `nodejs`.

Python Routing Middleware runs on the [Python](/docs/functions/runtimes/python) runtime.

## Pricing

Routing Middleware is priced using the [fluid compute](/docs/fluid-compute) model, which means you are charged by the amount of compute resources used by your Routing Middleware. See the [fluid compute pricing documentation](/docs/functions/usage-and-pricing) for more information.

## Observability

The [Vercel Observability dashboard](/docs/observability) provides visibility into your routing middleware usage, including invocation counts and performance metrics. You can get more [insights](/docs/observability/insights) with [Observability Plus](/docs/observability/observability-plus):

- Analyze invocations by request path
- Break down actions by type, such as redirects or rewrites
- View rewrite targets and frequency
- Use the query builder for custom insights

# Routing Middleware: Python Reference

Use the [`vercel-proxy`](https://pypi.org/project/vercel-proxy/) package to write [Routing Middleware](/docs/routing-middleware) in Python. It routes requests by path and provides responses that continue, rewrite, or answer a request. For path matching and limits, see the [Routing Middleware overview](/docs/routing-middleware).

Python Routing Middleware works with apps on the Python runtime, such as [FastAPI](/docs/frameworks/backend/fastapi), [Flask](/docs/frameworks/backend/flask), and [Django](/docs/frameworks/full-stack/django).

## Setup

### Install `vercel-proxy`

Your Routing Middleware runs separately from your app, with only the packages in the `vercel.proxy` dependency group of your `pyproject.toml`. Add `vercel-proxy` to that group:

```bash
uv add --group vercel.proxy vercel-proxy
```

Or add the group to `pyproject.toml` yourself:

```toml filename="pyproject.toml"
[dependency-groups]
"vercel.proxy" = ["vercel-proxy"]
```

Add any other packages your Routing Middleware imports to the same group. Requests to your Routing Middleware fail if one is missing. Projects that only use `requirements.txt` should switch to `pyproject.toml`.

### Set the entrypoint

Set [`proxy.entrypoint`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#proxy) in `vercel.json` to the module that defines your `Proxy` and the name of the `Proxy`, separated by a colon:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "proxy": {
    "entrypoint": "proxy:proxy"
  }
}
```

| `entrypoint`         | Loads                          |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `proxy:proxy`        | `proxy` from `proxy.py`        |
| `app.proxy:proxy`    | `proxy` from `app/proxy.py`    |
| `middleware:handler` | `handler` from `middleware.py` |

- The name must be defined at the module's top level, by assignment, `def`, or `from ... import`.
- A plain file path such as `proxy.py` isn't accepted. Use `module:attribute`.
- The entrypoint can also name any other ASGI or WSGI app instead of a `Proxy`.

## `Proxy`

`Proxy` routes each request to a handler. Create one at the top level of your entrypoint module:

```python filename="proxy.py"
from urllib.parse import quote

from vercel.proxy import ContinueResponse, Proxy, RedirectResponse, Request, Response

proxy = Proxy()


@proxy.route("/old-blog/{slug}")
def old_blog(request: Request) -> Response:
    slug = quote(request.path_params["slug"])
    return RedirectResponse(f"/blog/{slug}", status_code=308)


@proxy.route("/api/{path:path}")
def api(request: Request) -> Response:
    return ContinueResponse(request_headers={"x-api-version": "2"})
```

| Argument   | Type                  | Description                                                                                       |
| ---------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fallback` | `Response` or handler | What to do with requests that match no route. See [Fallback](#fallback)                           |
| `strict`   | `bool`                | Require exact path matches, including trailing slashes. See [Trailing slashes](#trailing-slashes) |

`Proxy` only receives requests that match `proxy.matcher`. See [path matching](/docs/routing-middleware#path-matching).

## Routes

`@proxy.route(path)` registers a handler for requests whose path matches. Each request goes to the first matching route, in the order you registered the routes. Handlers can be sync or async.

A path can capture parts of the URL with placeholders. Your handler reads the captured values from `request.path_params`:

```python filename="proxy.py"
from vercel.proxy import Proxy, Request, Response, RewriteResponse

proxy = Proxy()


@proxy.route("/users/{user_id:int}")
def user(request: Request) -> Response:
    return RewriteResponse(f"/profiles/{request.path_params['user_id']}")
```

The following placeholders are available:

| Placeholder   | Matches                                                         |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `{name}`      | One path segment, as a string                                   |
| `{name:type}` | One path segment, converted to `str`, `int`, `float`, or `uuid` |
| `{name:path}` | Any part of the path, including `/`                             |

> **💡 Note:** Captured values are URL-decoded. Quote them with `urllib.parse.quote` before
> you build a URL from them. Check any value that chooses a destination, such
> as a host or a path that contains `..`.

### Match methods and hosts

You can limit a route to certain HTTP methods or hosts:

```python filename="proxy.py"
@proxy.route("/admin", methods=["GET", "POST"], host="admin.example.com")
def admin(request: Request) -> Response:
    return RewriteResponse("/internal/admin")
```

| Argument  | Type        | Description                                                                                                                     |
| --------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `methods` | `list[str]` | HTTP methods the route accepts. Omit it to accept every method                                                                  |
| `host`    | `str`       | Hostname the route accepts. It can capture values like the path, such as `"{tenant}.example.com"`. Omit it to accept every host |

### Trailing slashes

Trailing slashes are optional by default. `Proxy` first matches each request against every route as sent, then with the trailing slash added or removed. A route that matches the path exactly wins.

To require exact matches, pass `strict=True`:

```python filename="proxy.py"
proxy = Proxy(strict=True)
```

## Fallback

Requests that match no route go to the fallback. By default, they continue to your app unchanged.

To change this, pass a response or a handler as `fallback`:

```python filename="proxy.py"
from vercel.proxy import JSONResponse, Proxy

proxy = Proxy(fallback=JSONResponse({"error": "not found"}, status_code=404))
```

You can also set the fallback with the `@proxy.fallback` decorator. It replaces any fallback you passed to `Proxy()`:

```python filename="proxy.py"
@proxy.fallback
def fallback(request: Request) -> Response:
    return RewriteResponse("/404")
```

## Request

`Request` is a Starlette [`Request`](https://starlette.dev/requests/). Use `method`, `url`, `headers`, `query_params`, `cookies`, `path_params`, and `client` to decide how to route it.

To read a request's location, see [geolocation headers](/docs/routing-middleware#geolocation-headers).

## Responses

Every handler returns a response. The response type decides what happens to the request. Responses are based on Starlette's [responses](https://starlette.dev/responses/).

### Continue or rewrite the request

| Response               | What happens                                                                 |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ContinueResponse()`   | The request continues to the original URL                                    |
| `RewriteResponse(url)` | Vercel serves the request from `url`. The URL the client sees doesn't change |

A continue or rewrite always has status `200` and no body. To change the status code, [answer the request](#answer-the-request) instead.

### Change headers on the forwarded request

`ContinueResponse` and `RewriteResponse` take `request_headers`, a dictionary of headers to set on the request your app receives. A `None` value removes the header:

```python filename="proxy.py"
@proxy.route("/{path:path}")
def add_region(request: Request) -> Response:
    return ContinueResponse(request_headers={"x-region": "eu", "cookie": None})
```

### Answer the request

`Response`, `JSONResponse`, `PlainTextResponse`, `HTMLResponse`, and `RedirectResponse` answer the request directly. The request doesn't reach your app. They take the same arguments as the Starlette classes of the same name:

```python filename="proxy.py"
from vercel.proxy import JSONResponse, Proxy, Request, Response

proxy = Proxy()


@proxy.route("/api/health")
def health(request: Request) -> Response:
    return JSONResponse({"status": "ok"})
```

`RedirectResponse` defaults to status `307`. Pass `status_code` to use a different status.

### Set response headers and cookies

`headers`, `set_cookie`, and `delete_cookie` work on every response, as in Starlette:

```python filename="proxy.py"
@proxy.route("/")
def home(request: Request) -> Response:
    response = ContinueResponse()
    response.set_cookie("bucket", "b", max_age=86400)
    return response
```

Header names starting with `x-middleware-` are reserved for Vercel. Starlette background tasks aren't supported.

## Function options

Set duration, memory, and other options with the [`functions`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#functions) property. Use the module's file path as the key, not the `module:attribute` value:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "proxy": {
    "entrypoint": "app.proxy:proxy"
  },
  "functions": {
    "app/proxy.py": {
      "maxDuration": 10
    }
  }
}
```

## Troubleshooting

| Error                        | Cause                                                                                                                      | Fix                                                                                  |
| ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `invalid_proxy_entrypoint`   | `entrypoint` is a plain `.py` path                                                                                         | Use `module:attribute`, such as `proxy:proxy`                                        |
| `proxy_entrypoint_not_found` | The module file doesn't exist                                                                                              | Check the module path. `app.proxy` loads `app/proxy.py`                              |
| `PYTHON_HANDLER_NOT_FOUND`   | The attribute isn't defined at the module's top level                                                                      | Define it at the top level, such as `proxy = Proxy()`                                |
| `proxy_runtime_mismatch`     | Your app doesn't use the Python runtime                                                                                    | Write your Routing Middleware in the same language as your app                       |
| Every matched request fails  | The `vercel.proxy` dependency group is missing, or lacks `vercel-proxy` or another package your Routing Middleware imports | Add the packages to `"vercel.proxy"` under `[dependency-groups]` in `pyproject.toml` |

# SAML Single Sign-On

> SAML is available on Enterprise and Pro plans
>
> Those with the owner role can access this feature

To manage the [members](/docs/rbac/managing-team-members) of your team through a third-party identity provider like [Okta](https://www.okta.com/) or [Auth0](https://auth0.com/), you can set up the Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) [feature](#configuring-saml-sso) from your team's settings.

Once enabled, all team members will be able to log in or access [Preview](/docs/deployments/environments#preview-environment-pre-production) and Production Deployments using your [selected identity provider](/docs/saml#saml-providers). Any new users signing up with SAML will automatically be added to your team.

For Enterprise customers, you can also automatically manage team member roles and provisioning by setting up [Directory Sync](/docs/directory-sync).

![The SAML SSO settings for a Team.](https://7nyt0uhk7sse4zvn.public.blob.vercel-storage.com/docs-assets/static/docs/concepts/teams/saml-settings.png)

## Configuring SAML SSO

1. To configure SAML SSO for your team, you must be an [owner](/docs/rbac/access-roles/team-level-roles) of the team
2. From your [dashboard](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2Fdashboard\&title=Open+Dashboard), ensure your team is selected in the team switcher
3. Open **Settings** in the sidebar and select [**Security & Privacy**](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%7E%2Fsettings%2Fsecurity\&title=Go+to+Security+settings)
4. Navigate to the **Authentication and User Provisioning** section. In the **SAML** row, select **Configure** and follow the walkthrough to configure SAML SSO for your team with your identity provider of choice
5. As a further step, you may want to [enforce SAML SSO](#enforcing-saml) for your team

> **💡 Note:** Pro teams will first need to purchase the SAML SSO add-on from their [Billing settings](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%7E%2Fsettings%2Fbilling%23paid-add-ons) before it can be configured.

## Custom Attributes

### Session lifetime

Use the optional `session_lifetime` attribute in your identity provider's SAML configuration to customize how long SAML SSO sessions last. Its value is an integer number of seconds between 86,400 (1 day) and 2,592,000 (30 days), inclusive, applied when the team member logs in. When `session_lifetime` is not used, sessions last 24 hours by default, after which team members must re-authenticate with the third-party SAML provider.

## Enforcing SAML

For additional security, SAML SSO can be enforced for a team so that all [team members](/docs/rbac/managing-team-members) **cannot access any team information** unless their current session was authenticated with SAML SSO.

1. To enforce SAML SSO for your team, you must be an [owner](/docs/rbac/access-roles/team-level-roles) and currently be authenticated with SAML SSO. This ensures that your configuration is working properly before tightening access to your team information
2. From your [dashboard](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2Fdashboard\&title=Open+Dashboard), open **Settings** in the sidebar and select [**Security & Privacy**](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%7E%2Fsettings%2Fsecurity\&title=Go+to+Security+settings). Then go to the **Authentication and User Provisioning** section
3. Toggle the **Require Team Members to login with SAML** switch to **Enabled**

![SAML SSO configured and enforced.](https://7nyt0uhk7sse4zvn.public.blob.vercel-storage.com/docs-assets/static/docs/concepts/teams/saml-enforced.png)

> **💡 Note:** When modifying your SAML configuration, the option for enforcing will
> automatically be turned off. Please verify your new configuration is working
> correctly by re-authenticating with SAML SSO before re-enabling the option.

## Authenticating with SAML SSO

Once you have configured SAML, your [team members](/docs/rbac/managing-team-members) can use SAML SSO to log in or sign up to Vercel. To login:

1. Select the **Continue with SAML SSO** button on the authentication page, then enter your team's URL.
   Your team slug is the identifier in the URLs for your team. For example, the identifier for vercel.com/acme is `acme`.
2. Select **Continue with SAML SSO** again to be redirected to the third-party authentication provider to finish authenticating. Once completed, you will be logged into Vercel.

### Customizing the login page

You can choose to share a Vercel login page that only shows the option to log in with SAML SSO. This prevents your team members from logging in with an account that's not managed by your identity provider.

To use this page, you can set the `saml` query param to your team URL. For example:

```text
https://vercel.com/login?saml=team_id
```

![Vercel's login page showing only the SAML SSO login button.](https://7nyt0uhk7sse4zvn.public.blob.vercel-storage.com/docs-assets/static/docs/concepts/teams/saml-login-custom-light.png)

## Managing team members

When using SAML SSO, team members authenticate through your identity provider, and new users who sign up with SAML are added to your team. After that, you manage team member roles and removals manually through the Vercel dashboard.

For automatic provisioning and de-provisioning of team members based on your identity provider, consider upgrading to [Directory Sync](/docs/directory-sync), which is available on Enterprise plans.

## SAML providers

Vercel supports the following third-party SAML providers:

- [Okta](https://www.okta.com/)
- [Auth0](https://auth0.com/)
- [Google](https://accounts.google.com/)
- [Microsoft Entra (formerly Azure Active Directory)](https://www.microsoft.com/en-in/security/business/identity-access/microsoft-entra-single-sign-on)
- [Microsoft ADFS](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/active-directory-federation-services)
- [OneLogin](https://onelogin.com/)
- [Duo](https://duo.com/product/single-sign-on-sso/)
- [JumpCloud](https://jumpcloud.com/)
- [PingFederate](https://www.pingidentity.com/en/platform/capabilities/single-sign-on.html)
- [ADP](https://apps.adp.com/en-US/home)
- [Keycloak](https://www.keycloak.org/)
- [Cyberark](https://www.cyberark.com/products/single-sign-on/)
- [OpenID](https://openid.net/)
- [VMware](https://techdocs.broadcom.com/us/en/vmware-cis/other/vmware-identity-manager/3-3.html)
- [LastPass](https://www.lastpass.com/)
- [miniOrange](https://www.miniorange.com/products/single-sign-on-sso)
- [NetIQ](https://www.microfocus.com/en-us/cyberres/identity-access-management/secure-login)
- [Oracle Cloud](https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/paas/content-cloud/administer/enable-single-sign-sso.html)
- [Salesforce](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.sso_about.htm\&type=5)
- [CAS](https://www.apereo.org/projects/cas)
- [ClassLink](https://www.classlink.com/)
- [Cloudflare](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/applications/configure-apps/dash-sso-apps/)
- [SimpleSAMLphp](https://simplesamlphp.org/)
