title: "Schedules Concepts"
description: "Learn how Vercel Schedules handles environments, deployments, jitter, one-time schedules, late runs, and duplicate deliveries."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.063Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/schedules/concepts"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Schedules Concepts

This page explains what happens between declaring a schedule and your code running. Read it before you rely on a schedule for work where timing or duplicates matter.

## How a schedule runs

Each time a schedule's expression matches, Vercel creates a run for that occurrence:

1. Vercel picks a start time within the schedule's [jitter window](#jitter).
2. Vercel delivers the run to the schedule's target on the **current deployment** of the schedule's environment or branch. This isn't necessarily the deployment that first declared the schedule.
3. Your function, route, or queue consumer does the work.

Every run has an **execution ID**. It stays the same for every delivery of that occurrence, so you can use it to [detect duplicates](#duplicate-runs). Every run also has a **scheduled time**, the time the expression matched. The scheduled time doesn't include jitter.

Runs are independent. A slow run doesn't delay the next one, so two runs of the same schedule can overlap.

## Environments

Vercel keeps a separate set of schedules for production, each [custom environment](/docs/deployments/environments#custom-environments), each Preview branch, and CLI deployments by each user. A CLI user environment can also include the Git branch reported by the deployment. Changing a schedule in one environment doesn't affect the others.

### Static schedules and deployments

Vercel applies a deployment's static schedules when that deployment becomes the current deployment of its environment or branch. This includes promotions and [rollbacks](/docs/instant-rollback): rolling back production restores the schedules from the deployment you roll back to.

Static schedules start in different states depending on the environment:

| Environment | Initial state of a new static schedule |
| --- | --- |
| Production | Active |
| Preview branches | Inactive |
| Custom environments | Inactive by default. You can [change this per environment](/docs/schedules/manage#run-static-schedules-in-a-custom-environment). |

Inactive schedules don't run until you [enable them](/docs/schedules/manage#manage-schedules-across-environments), so a Preview branch can't run a production job by accident. Once you enable or disable a static schedule, it keeps that state across later deployments. Changing a custom environment's default doesn't change the state of schedules that already exist.

### Dynamic schedules and environments

When your code calls `@vercel/schedules`, the SDK uses the environment or branch of the deployment that runs the code. A Preview deployment on the `feature-x` branch creates, lists, and changes schedules for `feature-x` only.

The `vercel schedules` CLI manages production schedules by default. Pass `--environment` for a custom environment, `--git-branch` for a Preview branch, `--user` for CLI deployments by a Vercel user ID, or `--local` for a `vercel dev` session. You can combine `--user` and `--git-branch`. See [Choose an environment](/docs/cli/schedules#choose-an-environment).

## Jitter

Jitter spreads runs across a short window instead of starting every schedule at the same second. A schedule set for 09:00 with a 5-minute jitter window starts at some point between 09:00 and 09:05.

| Plan | Jitter window |
| --- | --- |
| Hobby | Always 15 minutes |
| Pro and Enterprise | 1 to 15 minutes. Defaults to 1 minute. |

The shortest interval between a cron schedule's runs must be at least as long as its jitter window. For example, a schedule that runs every 5 minutes can use a jitter window of up to 5 minutes. Because Hobby always uses a 15-minute window, Hobby cron schedules can run at most once every 15 minutes.

To set the window, use `jitter` in [`vercel.json`](/docs/schedules/configuration#schedule-properties), the [SDK](/docs/schedules/sdk#create-a-schedule), or the [CLI](/docs/cli/schedules#create-a-schedule).

## Timezones

Each schedule evaluates its expression in an [IANA timezone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones), such as `America/New_York`. The default is UTC.

Named timezones follow daylight saving time. A schedule set for `0 9 * * *` in `America/New_York` runs at 09:00 New York time all year, which is 13:00 UTC in summer and 14:00 UTC in winter.

## One-time schedules

A one-time schedule runs once at a local date and time, such as `2026-10-01T09:00`, in the schedule's timezone. You can only create one-time schedules as dynamic schedules, with the [SDK](/docs/schedules/sdk#create-a-one-time-schedule) or the [CLI](/docs/cli/schedules#create-a-schedule).

After a one-time schedule's scheduled time passes:

- Its state stays `active`. There's no separate completed state.
- You can't enable, disable, or update it.
- You can [delete it](/docs/schedules/manage#delete-a-schedule) once its run has been dispatched. While the run is still being dispatched, for up to five jitter windows after the scheduled time, deleting it fails with `schedule_single_at_passed`.
- Vercel removes it about 30 days after its scheduled time, and it stops counting toward your [team's schedule limit](/docs/schedules/limits#schedules-per-team) as soon as its run is dispatched.

You can still [run it manually](/docs/schedules/manage#run-a-schedule-now) before its scheduled time.

## Schedule states

A schedule is either `active` or `inactive`. Only active schedules run on their cadence. You can [run any schedule manually](/docs/schedules/manage#run-a-schedule-now), whatever its state.

You can also enable a schedule until a set time. While that window is open, the schedule is `active` and has an `activeUntil` timestamp. When the time passes, the schedule becomes `inactive` and `activeUntil` is cleared. Vercel keeps the schedule, so you can enable it again later. Use this to run a Preview schedule for a few hours while you test it, without leaving it on.

## Late and missed runs

If Vercel can't deliver a run on time, it delivers the run late. Each occurrence has an expiry. If Vercel still can't deliver the run when the occurrence expires, Vercel skips it.

An occurrence expires after its jitter window plus the shortest interval between the schedule's runs. Vercel counts that interval as at least 10 minutes, so a short delay doesn't make a frequent schedule skip runs.

These runs never expire:

- One-time schedules
- Runs you start manually from the dashboard, SDK, or CLI
- Cron schedules that set a day of the month or a month, such as monthly or yearly schedules

Vercel uses the shortest interval between runs, not the time until the next run. For `0 9 * * 1-5` (weekdays at 09:00), the shortest interval is one day. Friday's occurrence expires on Saturday at 09:01, even though the next run is on Monday.

### Catching up after a delay

When delivery resumes, Vercel delivers every occurrence that hasn't expired. A frequent schedule can run several times in quick succession. For example, an every-minute schedule delayed for 2 hours runs up to 12 times when delivery resumes, once for each occurrence from the last 11 minutes.

If your task should only run close to its scheduled time, compare the scheduled time to the current time and return early.

## Duplicate runs

Vercel delivers each run once in normal operation, but it can't rule out a duplicate delivery. Make your handler safe to run more than once. Use the execution ID to detect a run you've already processed. See [Make your handler safe to run more than once](/docs/schedules/handle-runs#make-your-handler-safe-to-run-more-than-once).

## Retries

How Vercel handles a failed run depends on the target:

| Target | Retries |
| --- | --- |
| Function | No. Vercel doesn't retry a run if your function throws, returns an error, or times out. |
| Path | No. Vercel doesn't retry a run if your route returns an error or times out. |
| Queue topic | Yes. The queue retries delivery to your consumer until it succeeds or the message expires. See [Queues retries](/docs/queues/concepts#retries). |

If a failed run must be retried, target a queue topic.

## Related

- [Handling scheduled runs](/docs/schedules/handle-runs)
- [Managing schedules](/docs/schedules/manage)
- [Limits](/docs/schedules/limits)

last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.063Z"

# Schedules Configuration Reference

Static schedules live in the `schedules` property of `vercel.json`. Vercel applies them when you deploy. To create schedules at runtime instead, use the [SDK](/docs/schedules/sdk) or the [CLI](/docs/cli/schedules).

## The `schedules` property

`schedules` is an object. Each key is a schedule name, and each value defines when the schedule runs and what it targets:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "functions": {
    "api/cleanup.ts": {
      "experimentalTriggers": [{ "type": "schedule/v1beta" }]
    }
  },
  "schedules": {
    "cleanup": {
      "schedule": "0 * * * *",
      "timezone": "America/New_York",
      "jitter": 5,
      "function": "api/cleanup"
    },
    "daily-report": {
      "schedule": "0 9 * * *",
      "path": "/api/daily-report",
      "requestMethod": "GET"
    },
    "nightly-export": {
      "schedule": "0 2 * * *",
      "topic": "exports"
    }
  }
}
```

## Schedule properties

| Property | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `schedule` | `string` | Yes | Five-field [cron expression](#cron-expressions), evaluated in `timezone` |
| `timezone` | `string` | No | IANA timezone, such as `America/New_York`. Defaults to `UTC`. |
| `jitter` | `integer` | No | [Jitter window](/docs/schedules/concepts#jitter) in minutes, from 1 to 15. Defaults to 1 on Pro and Enterprise. Hobby always uses 15. |
| `function` | `string` | One target | [Function identifier](#function-identifiers) of a private function with a `schedule/v1beta` trigger |
| `service` | `string` | No | Name of the [service](/docs/services) that owns `function`. Only valid with `function`. See [Target a function in a service](#target-a-function-in-a-service). |
| `path` | `string` | One target | Path on your deployment to send an HTTP request to. Must start with `/`. Up to 512 characters. |
| `requestMethod` | `"GET"` or `"POST"` | No | HTTP method for `path`. Defaults to `POST`. Only valid with `path`. |
| `topic` | `string` | One target | [Vercel Queues](/docs/queues) topic to publish to. Letters, digits, `_`, and `-` only. |

Set exactly one target: `function`, `path`, or `topic`. Static schedules don't accept a payload or a namespace. They always use the `default` namespace.

To learn how to write the code for each target, see [Handling scheduled runs](/docs/schedules/handle-runs).

## Schedule names

The key of each entry is the schedule's name. Names identify a schedule across deployments, so keep them stable. Renaming a schedule deletes the old schedule and creates a new one, with its own state and execution history.

Names and namespaces follow the same rules:

- 1 to 256 characters
- Start with an ASCII letter or digit
- Contain only ASCII letters, digits, `.`, `_`, and `-`

Static schedule names must be unique within the project. Dynamic schedule names must be unique within their namespace. On Hobby, a deployment can declare up to 100 static schedules. See [Limits](/docs/schedules/limits#hobby-limits).

### Static and dynamic schedules with the same name

Static schedules share the `default` namespace with dynamic schedules in the same environment, so the two can collide:

- If you create a dynamic schedule with the name of an existing static schedule in `default`, the request fails with `schedule_already_exists`.
- If a deployment declares a static schedule whose name a dynamic schedule in `default` already uses, Vercel skips that static schedule. The deployment still succeeds, and the dynamic schedule keeps its expression, target, payload, and state. The deployment's other static schedules apply as usual.

To use the static schedule, rename it or [delete the dynamic schedule](/docs/schedules/manage#delete-a-schedule). Vercel creates the static schedule the next time a deployment that declares it becomes the current deployment of the environment or branch. To avoid collisions, create dynamic schedules in a namespace other than `default`.

## Function identifiers

The `function` property takes the function's path in the build output, not its source filename. The identifier is the path relative to `.vercel/output/functions`, without the `.func` suffix.

To find it:

1. Run `vercel build`.
2. Look in `.vercel/output/functions` for the function's `.func` directory.
3. Use its relative path without `.func`. Keep any nested directories.

For example:

| Source file | Build output | `function` value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `api/cleanup.ts` | `.vercel/output/functions/api/cleanup.func` | `api/cleanup` |
| `api/jobs/report.ts` | `.vercel/output/functions/api/jobs/report.func` | `api/jobs/report` |

The function must declare a `schedule/v1beta` trigger, and that must be its only trigger:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "functions": {
    "api/cleanup.ts": {
      "experimentalTriggers": [{ "type": "schedule/v1beta" }]
    }
  }
}
```

The trigger makes the function private. It has no public URL, and only Vercel's scheduler can invoke it. Don't add routes or rewrites that point to it.

If no function in the build output matches `function`, or the function doesn't have the `schedule/v1beta` trigger, the deployment fails.

## Target a function in a service

A [service](/docs/services) has its own build output. To target a function in a service, set `service` to the service name and `function` to the function's path within that service's output:

1. Run `vercel build`.
2. Look in `.vercel/output/services/<service-name>/functions`.
3. Use the function's relative path without `.func`.

The following schedule targets `.vercel/output/services/worker/functions/index.func`:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "schedules": {
    "cleanup": {
      "schedule": "0 * * * *",
      "service": "worker",
      "function": "index"
    }
  }
}
```

`vercel dev` doesn't run schedules that target a function in a service yet. It fails with `DEV_SCHEDULE_SERVICE_FUNCTION_UNSUPPORTED`. Deploy to test these schedules.

## Cron expressions

Schedules use the same five-field cron syntax as [Cron Jobs](/docs/cron-jobs#cron-expressions):

| Field | Values | Example | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Minute | 0 to 59 | `5 * * * *` | 5 minutes past every hour |
| Hour | 0 to 23 | `0 5 * * *` | Every day at 05:00 |
| Day of month | 1 to 31 | `0 0 5 * *` | Midnight on the 5th of each month |
| Month | 1 to 12 | `0 0 1 5 *` | Midnight on May 1 |
| Day of week | 0 to 6 (Sunday to Saturday) | `0 9 * * 1-5` | 09:00 on weekdays |

Expressions can use digits, `*`, `,`, `-`, and `/`, with a single space between fields. They can't use:

- Named days or months, such as `MON` or `JAN`
- Both a day of the month and a day of the week in the same expression

The shortest interval between runs must be at least as long as the jitter window. On Hobby, that means a cron schedule can run at most once every 15 minutes. See [Limits](/docs/schedules/limits).

## One-time expressions

One-time schedules are only available as dynamic schedules. Pass a local date and time in `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm` format, such as `2026-10-01T09:00`, to the SDK's `at` field or the CLI's `--at` option. Vercel evaluates it in the schedule's `timezone`.

- You can add `:00` seconds. Vercel stores the value with `:00` either way.
- Don't include `Z`, a UTC offset, fractional seconds, or non-zero seconds.

## Build Output API

Frameworks can declare static schedules in their [Build Output API](/docs/build-output-api) output. Add a `schedules` object to `.vercel/output/config.json` with the same properties as `vercel.json`:

```json filename=".vercel/output/config.json"
{
  "version": 3,
  "schedules": {
    "cleanup": {
      "schedule": "0 3 * * *",
      "function": "_vercel/schedule"
    }
  }
}
```

Declare the trigger in the target function's `.vc-config.json`:

```json filename=".vercel/output/functions/_vercel/schedule.func/.vc-config.json"
{
  "runtime": "nodejs22.x",
  "handler": "index.mjs",
  "launcherType": "Nodejs",
  "experimentalTriggers": [{ "type": "schedule/v1beta" }]
}
```

[`vercel build`](/docs/cli/build#schedule-configuration) combines a framework's schedules with the schedules in `vercel.json`. If the same name appears in both, the build fails with `SCHEDULE_NAME_CONFLICT`.

## Related

- [Handling scheduled runs](/docs/schedules/handle-runs)
- [Limits](/docs/schedules/limits)
- [`vercel build` reference](/docs/cli/build#schedule-configuration)

title: "Handling Scheduled Runs"
description: "Write the private function, route, or queue consumer that a schedule runs, and make it safe to run more than once."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.063Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/schedules/handle-runs"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Handling Scheduled Runs

When a schedule fires, Vercel delivers a run to the schedule's target. This page shows how to write the code that receives the run for each target type.

## Choosing a target

| Target | Use it when | Retries | Available for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Function](#function-targets) | You want a private function that nobody else can call. | No | Static schedules |
| [Path](#path-targets) | You're migrating a Cron Job, or the route must stay public. | No | Static schedules |
| [Queue topic](#queue-targets) | Failed runs must be retried, or you need a payload or dynamic schedules. | Yes | Static and dynamic schedules |

## Function targets

A function target runs a Vercel Function that has no public URL. Only Vercel's scheduler can invoke it, so you don't need to check a secret.

1. Install the SDK:

   ```bash package-manager
   npm i @vercel/schedules
   ```

2. Create the function and wrap your task in `handleSchedule`:

   ```ts filename="api/cleanup.ts"
   import { handleSchedule } from '@vercel/schedules';

   export const POST = handleSchedule(async (metadata, request) => {
     console.log(`${metadata.name} run ${metadata.executionId}`);
     await deleteExpiredRecords();
   });
   ```

3. Add a `schedule/v1beta` trigger to the function and point a schedule at it in `vercel.json`:

   ```json filename="vercel.json"
   {
     "functions": {
       "api/cleanup.ts": {
         "experimentalTriggers": [{ "type": "schedule/v1beta" }]
       }
     },
     "schedules": {
       "cleanup": {
         "schedule": "0 * * * *",
         "function": "api/cleanup"
       }
     }
   }
   ```

   The `function` value is the function's build output path, not its source filename. See [Function identifiers](/docs/schedules/configuration#function-identifiers). For a function in a [service](/docs/services), also set [`service`](/docs/schedules/configuration#target-a-function-in-a-service).

A function with the `schedule/v1beta` trigger can't also have a queue trigger.

### What `handleSchedule` does

`handleSchedule` reads the run's details from the request headers and passes them to your callback with the original `Request`:

- If the request isn't a valid schedule run, it returns a `400` response and doesn't call your callback.
- If your callback finishes, it returns a `200` response.
- If your callback throws, the error propagates to your framework or runtime, which typically returns a `500` response.

The response status shows up in your function logs and the schedule's execution history. It doesn't affect the schedule, and Vercel doesn't retry the run.

The callback's first argument is [`ScheduleMetadata`](/docs/schedules/sdk#schedule-metadata):

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `scheduleId` | `string` | ID of the schedule |
| `executionId` | `string` | ID of this run. Stays the same if the run is delivered more than once. |
| `name` | `string` | Schedule name |
| `namespace` | `string` | Schedule namespace. Static schedules use `default`. |
| `scheduledAt` | `Date` | Time the expression matched. Doesn't include jitter, so the run can arrive later. |
| `source` | `string` | `static` or `dynamic` |
| `expression` | `string` | The cron expression, or the local datetime of a one-time schedule |

To read the details without wrapping your handler, call `parseScheduleEvent(request)`. It returns the same `ScheduleMetadata`, or throws a `ScheduleEventParseError` if the request isn't a schedule run.

### Handle several schedules in one function

Several schedules can target the same function. Use `metadata.name` to decide what to run:

```ts filename="api/maintenance.ts"
import { handleSchedule } from '@vercel/schedules';

export const POST = handleSchedule(async (metadata) => {
  switch (metadata.name) {
    case 'hourly-cleanup':
      await deleteExpiredRecords();
      break;
    case 'nightly-report':
      await sendReport();
      break;
  }
});
```

## Path targets

A path target sends an HTTP request to a route on your deployment, like a [Cron Job](/docs/cron-jobs). The route is public, so anyone can call it. Protect it with a secret.

1. Add a schedule with a `path` in `vercel.json`. Path schedules send a `POST` request by default. Set `requestMethod` to `GET` if your route handles `GET`:

   ```json filename="vercel.json"
   {
     "schedules": {
       "daily-report": {
         "schedule": "0 9 * * *",
         "path": "/api/daily-report",
         "requestMethod": "GET"
       }
     }
   }
   ```

2. Add a `CRON_SECRET` [environment variable](/docs/environment-variables) to your project. Use a random string of at least 16 characters. Vercel sends it in the `Authorization` header of every path request.

3. Check the header in your route before doing any work:

   ```ts filename="api/daily-report.ts"
   export async function GET(request: Request) {
     const authHeader = request.headers.get('authorization');
     const cronSecret = process.env.CRON_SECRET;

     if (!cronSecret || authHeader !== `Bearer ${cronSecret}`) {
       return new Response('Unauthorized', { status: 401 });
     }

     await sendReport();
     return new Response(null, { status: 200 });
   }
   ```

Path requests include the same headers as Cron Job requests, plus the schedule headers that function targets receive. That means:

- A route that already handles a Cron Job keeps working.
- You can wrap a path route in `handleSchedule` to read `ScheduleMetadata`. `handleSchedule` accepts both `GET` and `POST`. It doesn't check `CRON_SECRET`, so keep the check.

See [Request headers](#request-headers) for the full list.

## Queue targets

A queue target publishes a message to a [Vercel Queues](/docs/queues) topic each time the schedule fires. A consumer on that topic processes the message. If the consumer fails, the queue retries it.

Queue topics are the only target for dynamic schedules, and the only target that supports a payload.

1. Install the Queues and Schedules SDKs:

   ```bash package-manager
   npm i @vercel/queue @vercel/schedules
   ```

2. Create a consumer with `handleCallback`:

   ```ts filename="api/daily-reports.ts"
   import { handleCallback } from '@vercel/queue';
   import type { ScheduleQueueMessage } from '@vercel/schedules';

   type ReportPayload = { reportType: string };

   export const POST = handleCallback<ScheduleQueueMessage<ReportPayload>>(
     async (message) => {
       console.log(`Running ${message.name}, scheduled for ${message.scheduledAt}`);
       await generateReport(message.payload?.reportType ?? 'summary');
     },
   );
   ```

   [`ScheduleQueueMessage`](/docs/schedules/sdk#queue-messages) types the message. Its parameter types the payload.

3. Subscribe the consumer to a topic and point a schedule at the same topic:

   ```json filename="vercel.json"
   {
     "functions": {
       "api/daily-reports.ts": {
         "experimentalTriggers": [
           { "type": "queue/v2beta", "topic": "daily-reports" }
         ]
       }
     },
     "schedules": {
       "daily-report": {
         "schedule": "0 9 * * *",
         "topic": "daily-reports"
       }
     }
   }
   ```

To create a queue schedule at runtime instead, use [`Schedules.create`](/docs/schedules/sdk#create-a-schedule) with `target: { topic: 'daily-reports' }`.

### Queue message format

The message body is a JSON object with the schedule's details at the top level:

```json
{
  "scheduleId": "sch_abc123",
  "executionId": "schx_def456",
  "name": "daily-report",
  "namespace": "default",
  "scheduledAt": "2026-09-15T09:00:00.000Z",
  "source": "dynamic",
  "payload": {
    "reportType": "summary"
  }
}
```

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `scheduleId` | `string` | ID of the schedule |
| `executionId` | `string` | ID of this run. Stays the same if the run is delivered more than once. |
| `name` | `string` | Schedule name |
| `namespace` | `string` | Schedule namespace |
| `scheduledAt` | `string` | ISO 8601 time the expression matched. Doesn't include jitter. |
| `source` | `"static"` or `"dynamic"` | How the schedule was defined |
| `payload` | `unknown` | The payload you set on a dynamic schedule. Omitted when the schedule has no payload. Static schedules never include it. |

## Make your handler safe to run more than once

A run can arrive more than once, and a delayed schedule can [catch up](/docs/schedules/concepts#catching-up-after-a-delay) with several runs in a row. Queue targets also retry failed deliveries. Write your handler so a repeated run doesn't repeat its side effects.

The execution ID is the same for every delivery of a run, so you can use it to detect a run you've already processed. Function targets get it as `metadata.executionId`, and queue targets get it as `message.executionId`.

## Request headers

Function and path targets receive a request with an empty body. The run's details are in the headers. `handleSchedule` and `parseScheduleEvent` read these for you.

| Header | Sent to | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ce-specversion` | Function and path | `1.0` |
| `ce-type` | Function and path | `com.vercel.schedule.v1beta` |
| `ce-source` | Function and path | `/schedule/{namespace}/{name}` |
| `ce-id` | Function and path | Execution ID of this run |
| `ce-vssscheduleid` | Function and path | Schedule ID |
| `ce-vssschedulename` | Function and path | Schedule name |
| `ce-vssnamespace` | Function and path | Schedule namespace |
| `ce-vssscheduledat` | Function and path | ISO 8601 time the expression matched, without jitter |
| `ce-vssschedulesource` | Function and path | `static` or `dynamic` |
| `ce-vssexpression` | Function and path | The cron expression, or the local datetime of a one-time schedule |
| `user-agent` | Path only | `vercel-cron/1.0` |
| `x-vercel-cron-schedule` | Path only | The cron expression |
| `authorization` | Path only | `Bearer <CRON_SECRET>`, when you set `CRON_SECRET` |

> **💡 Note:** Function targets don't receive `authorization` or the Cron Job headers.
> Don't require them in a function handler.

## Related

- [Concepts](/docs/schedules/concepts): Learn about retries, duplicates, and late runs.
- [Configuration reference](/docs/schedules/configuration): Look up every schedule property.
- [Testing schedules locally](/docs/schedules/local-development): Run your handler with `vercel dev`.

title: "Vercel Schedules: API Reference"
description: "Reference for the Vercel Schedules HTTP API: authenticate, choose an environment, and create, list, update, enable, disable, invoke, and delete schedules."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.063Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/schedules/http-api"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Vercel Schedules: API Reference

The Schedules HTTP API is a REST API for managing static and dynamic schedules. The [`@vercel/schedules`](/docs/schedules/sdk) JS SDK and the [`vercel schedules`](/docs/cli/schedules) CLI both use it. Call it directly when you can't use the SDK, such as from another language or an external system.

All endpoints use this base URL:

```bash
https://vercel-schedules.com
```

Requests and responses use JSON. Send `Content-Type: application/json` with every request that has a body.

## Authentication

Send a token in the `Authorization` header:

```bash
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

The API accepts two kinds of tokens:

| Token | Use it from | Team and project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [OIDC token](/docs/oidc) | Code running in a Vercel deployment, in `VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN` | Taken from the token. Don't pass `teamId` or `projectId`. |
| [Vercel access token](/docs/rest-api#creating-an-access-token) | Scripts, CI, and external systems | Pass `projectId` in the query string. Pass `teamId` unless the project belongs to your default team. |

For example, with an access token:

```bash filename="terminal"
curl "https://vercel-schedules.com/v1/schedules?teamId=team_a1b2c3&projectId=prj_d4e5f6" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VERCEL_TOKEN"
```

From a deployment, with its OIDC token:

```bash filename="terminal"
curl "https://vercel-schedules.com/v1/schedules" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN"
```

A request with a missing or invalid token fails with `403` and code `forbidden`. An access token can only manage schedules that its user's role allows. See [Permissions](/docs/schedules/manage#permissions).

## Choose an environment

Vercel keeps a [separate set of schedules](/docs/schedules/concepts#environments) for each environment. With an access token, choose one with a query parameter. Without one, requests use production.

| Query parameter | Selects |
| --- | --- |
| `env` | `production`, or a custom environment by name or ID |
| `branch` | A Preview branch of the project's connected Git repository |
| `user` | CLI deployments by a Vercel user ID. Combine with `branch` for CLI deployments associated with a branch. |

Pass at most one of these, except `user` with `branch`. If the custom environment, branch, or user doesn't have a deployment yet, the request fails with `400`.

OIDC tokens always use the environment of the deployment that issued them. Requests with an OIDC token can't pass `env`, `branch`, or `user`.

## Namespaces

Every endpoint that reads or changes one schedule, and the list endpoint, accepts a `namespace` query parameter. It defaults to `default`. When you create a schedule, pass `namespace` in the request body instead. See [Multi-tenant schedules](/docs/schedules/multi-tenant).

## The schedule object

Endpoints that return a schedule use this shape:

```json
{
  "scheduleId": "sch_01JC4Z8Q3W5V7X9Y2A4B6C8D0E",
  "ownerId": "team_a1b2c3",
  "projectId": "prj_d4e5f6",
  "name": "nightly-report",
  "namespace": "reports",
  "timezone": "America/New_York",
  "expression": { "type": "cron", "cron": "0 3 * * *" },
  "jitter": 5,
  "target": { "type": "queue", "topic": "nightly-report" },
  "state": "active",
  "source": "dynamic",
  "createdAt": 1793750400000,
  "updatedAt": 1793750400000
}
```

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `scheduleId` | `string` | Schedule ID |
| `ownerId` | `string` | ID of the team that owns the schedule |
| `projectId` | `string` | ID of the project |
| `name` | `string` | Schedule name |
| `namespace` | `string` | Schedule namespace |
| `timezone` | `string` | IANA timezone. Defaults to `UTC`. |
| `expression` | `object` | `{ "type": "cron", "cron": string }`, or `{ "type": "single", "at": string }` for a [one-time schedule](/docs/schedules/concepts#one-time-schedules) |
| `jitter` | `integer` | [Jitter window](/docs/schedules/concepts#jitter) in minutes. Omitted when the schedule uses the plan default. |
| `target` | `object` | `{ "type": "queue", "topic": string }`. Static schedules can also have `{ "type": "function", "function": string, "service"?: string }` or `{ "type": "path", "path": string, "requestMethod"?: "GET" \| "POST" }`. |
| `state` | `string` | `active` or `inactive` |
| `activeUntil` | `integer` | Unix timestamp in milliseconds when a [temporarily enabled](/docs/schedules/manage#enable-a-schedule-temporarily) schedule becomes inactive. Only present while that window is open. |
| `source` | `string` | `static` for schedules from your configuration, `dynamic` for schedules created with the API |
| `createdAt` | `integer` | Unix timestamp in milliseconds |
| `updatedAt` | `integer` | Unix timestamp in milliseconds |

Responses don't include a schedule's payload.

## Endpoints

| Method | Path | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | [`/v1/schedules`](#list-schedules) | List schedules |
| `POST` | [`/v1/schedules`](#create-a-schedule) | Create a dynamic schedule |
| `GET` | [`/v1/schedules/{name}`](#get-a-schedule) | Get a schedule |
| `PATCH` | [`/v1/schedules/{name}`](#update-a-schedule) | Update a dynamic schedule |
| `DELETE` | [`/v1/schedules/{name}`](#delete-a-schedule) | Delete a dynamic schedule |
| `POST` | [`/v1/schedules/{name}/enable`](#enable-a-schedule) | Enable a schedule |
| `POST` | [`/v1/schedules/{name}/disable`](#disable-a-schedule) | Disable a schedule |
| `POST` | [`/v1/schedules/{name}/invoke`](#invoke-a-schedule) | Run a schedule now |

### List schedules

**`GET /v1/schedules`**

Lists static and dynamic schedules in one namespace, one page at a time.

| Query parameter | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `namespace` | `string` | No | Namespace to list. Defaults to `default`. |
| `limit` | `integer` | No | Page size, from 1 to 100. Defaults to 20. |
| `cursor` | `string` | No | `cursor` from the previous page |

Returns `200`:

```json
{
  "data": [
    {
      "scheduleId": "sch_01JC4Z8Q3W5V7X9Y2A4B6C8D0E",
      "ownerId": "team_a1b2c3",
      "projectId": "prj_d4e5f6",
      "name": "nightly-report",
      "namespace": "reports",
      "timezone": "America/New_York",
      "expression": { "type": "cron", "cron": "0 3 * * *" },
      "jitter": 5,
      "target": { "type": "queue", "topic": "nightly-report" },
      "state": "active",
      "source": "dynamic",
      "createdAt": 1793750400000,
      "updatedAt": 1793750400000
    }
  ],
  "cursor": "eyJQSyI6Ii4uLiIsIlNLIjoiLi4uIn0"
}
```

`data` holds [schedule objects](#the-schedule-object), ordered by name. When `cursor` is `null`, there are no more pages. A page can hold fewer than `limit` schedules, or none, and still have a `cursor`, so keep reading until `cursor` is `null`.

### Create a schedule

**`POST /v1/schedules`**

Creates a dynamic schedule that publishes to a [queue topic](/docs/schedules/handle-runs#queue-targets). It's active as soon as you create it.

```bash filename="terminal"
curl -X POST "https://vercel-schedules.com/v1/schedules?teamId=team_a1b2c3&projectId=prj_d4e5f6" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VERCEL_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "nightly-report",
    "namespace": "reports",
    "expression": { "type": "cron", "cron": "0 3 * * *" },
    "timezone": "America/New_York",
    "jitter": 5,
    "target": { "type": "queue", "topic": "nightly-report" },
    "payload": { "report": "daily-summary" }
  }'
```

| Body field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `string` | No | Unique within the namespace. See [naming rules](/docs/schedules/configuration#schedule-names). Vercel generates a name when you omit it. |
| `namespace` | `string` | No | Defaults to `default` |
| `expression` | `object` | Yes | `{ "type": "cron", "cron": string }` with a five-field [cron expression](/docs/schedules/configuration#cron-expressions), or `{ "type": "single", "at": string }` with a [local date and time](/docs/schedules/configuration#one-time-expressions) |
| `target` | `object` | Yes | `{ "type": "queue", "topic": string }`. Dynamic schedules only support queue topics. |
| `timezone` | `string` | No | IANA timezone for the expression. Defaults to `UTC`. |
| `jitter` | `integer` | No | Jitter window in minutes, from 1 to 15. On Hobby, omit it or pass `15`. |
| `payload` | any JSON value | No | Up to 16 KB. Vercel includes it in the `payload` field of each [queue message](/docs/schedules/handle-runs#queue-message-format). |

The body can't contain other fields. Returns `201` with the new [schedule object](#the-schedule-object). Returns `409` with `schedule_already_exists` if a schedule with the same name exists in the namespace.

### Get a schedule

**`GET /v1/schedules/{name}`**

Returns `200` with one static or dynamic [schedule object](#the-schedule-object). Pass `namespace` in the query string for a schedule outside the `default` namespace. Returns `404` with `not_found` if the schedule doesn't exist.

### Update a schedule

**`PATCH /v1/schedules/{name}`**

Changes a dynamic schedule. Fields you leave out keep their current values:

```bash filename="terminal"
curl -X PATCH "https://vercel-schedules.com/v1/schedules/nightly-report?namespace=reports&teamId=team_a1b2c3&projectId=prj_d4e5f6" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VERCEL_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "expression": { "type": "cron", "cron": "0 4 * * *" }, "jitter": null }'
```

| Body field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `expression` | `object` | New expression of the same type. You can't change a cron schedule to a one-time schedule, or the reverse. |
| `target` | `object` | New queue topic, as `{ "type": "queue", "topic": string }` |
| `timezone` | `string` | New IANA timezone |
| `jitter` | `integer` or `null` | New jitter window. Pass `null` to return to the plan default. |
| `payload` | any JSON value or `null` | New payload. Pass `null` to remove it. |

Returns `200` with the updated [schedule object](#the-schedule-object). Returns `409` with:

- `static_schedule` for a static schedule. Edit your configuration and redeploy instead.
- `schedule_type_change_not_allowed` if you change the expression type
- `schedule_single_at_passed` for a one-time schedule whose scheduled time has passed

### Delete a schedule

**`DELETE /v1/schedules/{name}`**

Deletes a dynamic schedule and stops its future runs. Returns `200`:

```json
{ "scheduleId": "sch_01JC4Z8Q3W5V7X9Y2A4B6C8D0E" }
```

Returns `409` with `static_schedule` for a static schedule, or with `schedule_single_at_passed` for a one-time schedule whose run is still being dispatched. See [Delete a schedule](/docs/schedules/manage#delete-a-schedule) for what happens to pending runs.

### Enable a schedule

**`POST /v1/schedules/{name}/enable`**

Makes a static or dynamic schedule run on its cadence. The body is optional. To enable the schedule until a set time, pass `until`:

```json
{ "until": 1793757600000 }
```

| Body field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `until` | `integer` | Unix timestamp in milliseconds when the schedule becomes inactive again. Must be in the future. |

Returns `200` with the updated [schedule object](#the-schedule-object). Enabling without `until` keeps the schedule active indefinitely and clears any `activeUntil`. Passing `until` replaces an existing end time, but fails with `409` and `schedule_already_active` if the schedule is already active indefinitely. Disable it first.

### Disable a schedule

**`POST /v1/schedules/{name}/disable`**

Stops a static or dynamic schedule from running on its cadence. Send no body. Returns `200` with the updated [schedule object](#the-schedule-object).

### Invoke a schedule

**`POST /v1/schedules/{name}/invoke`**

Runs a static or dynamic schedule now, without changing its state or cadence. Works on inactive schedules. Send no body.

Returns `204` with no body once Vercel accepts the run. Your target receives it shortly afterward. Each request starts a new run, so don't retry a request that succeeded.

## Errors

Failed requests return a JSON body with a machine-readable code and a message:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "schedule_already_exists",
    "message": "Schedule already exists"
  }
}
```

| Status | Codes |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | `bad_request`, `invalid_cron_expression`, `invalid_jitter`, `jitter_exceeds_cadence`, `single_at_in_past`, `payload_too_large`, `active_until_in_past`, `schedule_limit_exceeded` |
| `403` | `forbidden`, `not_enabled` |
| `404` | `not_found` |
| `409` | `schedule_already_exists`, `schedule_already_active`, `schedule_single_at_passed`, `schedule_type_change_not_allowed`, `static_schedule` |
| `429` | `rate_limited`, `feature_blocked` |
| `503` | `service_unavailable` |

The [JS SDK Reference](/docs/schedules/sdk#errors) describes what causes each code.

### Retries

- **`429` with `rate_limited`**: You exceeded an [API request limit](/docs/schedules/limits#api-requests). Wait for the number of seconds in the `Retry-After` header. The response also includes `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, and `X-RateLimit-Reset`.
- **`429` with `feature_blocked`**: Your Hobby team went over its [usage limits](/docs/schedules/limits#hobby-limits). Retrying doesn't help until the next billing period.
- **`503` with `service_unavailable`**: Wait for the number of seconds in the `Retry-After` header and retry. A write may have been applied before the error, so a retried create can return `409` with `schedule_already_exists`, and a retried delete can return `404`. Treat those as success.

## Related

- [JS SDK Reference](/docs/schedules/sdk)
- [`vercel schedules` reference](/docs/cli/schedules)
- [Limits](/docs/schedules/limits)

title: "Schedules Limits"
description: "Limits for Vercel Schedules, including schedules per team, run frequency, jitter, Hobby usage, and API requests."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.063Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/schedules/limits"

# Schedules Limits

Schedules are in beta, and these limits may change before general availability.

## Limits by plan

| Limit | Hobby | Pro | Enterprise |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Schedules per team | 1,000 | 10,000 | 100,000 |
| Jitter window | Always 15 minutes | 1 to 15 minutes. Defaults to 1 minute. | 1 to 15 minutes. Defaults to 1 minute. |
| Most frequent cron schedule | Every 15 minutes | Every minute, with a 1-minute jitter window | Every minute, with a 1-minute jitter window |
| Payload size | 16 KB | 16 KB | 16 KB |
| Execution history | 90 days | 90 days | 90 days |

### Schedules per team

The team limit counts static and dynamic schedules across all projects, environments, and branches. A one-time schedule stops counting after Vercel dispatches its scheduled run, even though the schedule remains visible for about 30 days. When your team reaches the limit, creating a dynamic schedule fails with `schedule_limit_exceeded`.

### Hobby limits

On Hobby:

- A deployment can declare up to 100 static schedules in `vercel.json` and its framework's build output. If a deployment declares more, it fails.
- Each billing period, a team can create up to 500 dynamic schedules and run its schedules up to 5,000 times. Scheduled and manual runs both count toward the run limit.

When a Hobby team goes over its creation or run limit, Vercel blocks the following until the next billing period starts:

- Creating and enabling schedules, which fail with `feature_blocked`
- Running schedules manually
- Scheduled runs, which Vercel skips

To remove the limits, [upgrade to Pro](/docs/plans/hobby#upgrading-to-pro).

### Frequency and jitter

A cron schedule's shortest interval between runs must be at least as long as its jitter window. Because Hobby always uses a 15-minute jitter window, Hobby cron schedules can run at most once every 15 minutes. On Hobby, the SDK and CLI reject any `jitter` value other than `15`.

### What happens to schedules when you move to Hobby

When a team downgrades to Hobby, or you transfer a project to a Hobby team, Vercel deletes the schedules that Hobby doesn't allow. Vercel deletes a schedule if either of the following is true:

- Its cron expression can run more often than every 15 minutes, such as `* * * * *` or `*/5 * * * *`
- Its `jitter` value is less than `15`

Vercel keeps all other schedules, and they run with the 15-minute Hobby jitter window. A deleted schedule doesn't come back when the team upgrades or when you transfer the project back to a Pro or Enterprise team.

To keep a schedule, update it before you downgrade or transfer the project. Change its cron expression to run at most once every 15 minutes, and remove its `jitter` value or set it to `15`.

Vercel applies [static schedules](/docs/schedules/configuration) from `vercel.json` when you deploy. On Hobby, deployments don't recreate a deleted static schedule until you update it in `vercel.json` to meet the Hobby limits. On Pro and Enterprise, your next deployment recreates it.

### What happens to schedules when you move from Hobby to Pro or Enterprise

When a team upgrades from Hobby, or you transfer a project from a Hobby team to a Pro or Enterprise team, Vercel keeps every schedule. Schedules with `jitter` set to `15` keep the 15-minute jitter window. Schedules without a `jitter` value use the default 1-minute jitter window.

## API requests

The Schedules API applies the following request limits per team. Operations in the same row share a limit across the SDK, CLI, and dashboard:

| Operations | Pro and Enterprise | Hobby |
| --- | --- | --- |
| List schedules, inspect a schedule, and list execution history | 100 per second | 100 per minute |
| Create, update, and enable schedules | 100 per second | 100 per minute |
| Delete and disable schedules | 50 per second | 50 per minute |
| Invoke schedules | 10 per second | 10 per minute |

When you exceed a limit, the API returns a `rate_limited` error. Wait for the number of seconds in `retryAfter` before retrying. Local commands that use `--local` don't send requests to the Schedules API.

## Usage

A schedule's runs use the resources of its target. Function and path targets create [Vercel Functions](/docs/functions/usage-and-pricing) invocations. Queue targets publish [Vercel Queues](/docs/queues/pricing) messages and invoke your consumer. To stop a schedule's usage, [disable](/docs/schedules/manage#enable-and-disable-a-schedule) or [delete](/docs/schedules/manage#delete-a-schedule) it.

## Related

- [Concepts](/docs/schedules/concepts)
- [Configuration reference](/docs/schedules/configuration)

title: "Testing Schedules Locally"
description: "Run static and dynamic schedules on your machine with vercel dev, trigger runs on demand, and learn what differs from production."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.063Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/schedules/local-development"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Testing Schedules Locally

`vercel dev` runs a local scheduler, so you can test schedules and your handlers without deploying. Local schedules never touch your production schedules.

## Start the local scheduler

Run the development server from your project directory:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel dev
```

`vercel dev` starts a local Schedules service and then:

- Loads the static schedules from `vercel.json` and your framework's build output, and reloads them when the configuration changes
- Configures `@vercel/schedules` in your app to use the local service, so SDK calls create and change local dynamic schedules
- Delivers runs to your local functions, routes, and queue consumers with the same headers and message format as production
- Applies the same validation rules, error codes, jitter, and [late-run expiry](/docs/schedules/concepts#late-and-missed-runs) as production

Local schedules run on their cadence while `vercel dev` is running. If your machine sleeps, occurrences that expired in the meantime are skipped when it wakes, as they would be in production.

Path targets receive the same headers as in production, including `user-agent: vercel-cron/1.0` and `x-vercel-cron-schedule`. They also receive `Authorization: Bearer <CRON_SECRET>` when `CRON_SECRET` is set in your development environment.

To choose the port for the local Schedules service, pass `--schedules-port`:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel dev --schedules-port 5784
```

## Run a schedule on demand

You don't need to wait for a schedule's next run. In a second terminal, invoke it with `--local`:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel schedules invoke cleanup --local
```

The run appears in the `vercel dev` output.

## Manage local schedules

Pass `--local` to `vercel schedules` to manage the schedules in the running `vercel dev` session instead of production:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel schedules list --local
vercel schedules create send-reminder --at 2026-11-01T09:00 --topic reminders --local
vercel schedules disable cleanup --local
vercel schedules enable cleanup --for 1h --local
```

`--local` connects to the session for the current project directory. Use `--cwd` to choose another directory. Local commands don't need a login or a linked project.

`vercel schedules` with `--local`:

- Works with `list`, `inspect`, `create`, `update`, `enable`, `disable`, `invoke`, and `delete`
- Fails if no `vercel dev` session is running, or if it can't tell which session to use. It never falls back to production.
- Can't be combined with `--environment`, `--git-branch`, `--user`, `--scope`, `--team`, or `--token`

## Differences from production

| Behavior | Local | Production |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Schedule state | Exists only for the current `vercel dev` session | Persists |
| Execution history | Read the `vercel dev` output. `vercel schedules executions list` doesn't support `--local`. | Dashboard and CLI |
| Function targets in a [service](/docs/services) | Not supported. `vercel dev` fails with `DEV_SCHEDULE_SERVICE_FUNCTION_UNSUPPORTED`. Deploy to test them. | Supported |
| Hobby jitter and team schedule limits | Not enforced | [Enforced](/docs/schedules/limits) |

Locally, you can't create a one-time schedule for a time that a daylight saving time change skips or repeats in the schedule's timezone. Choose a different time.

## Related

- [Handling scheduled runs](/docs/schedules/handle-runs)
- [`vercel schedules` reference](/docs/cli/schedules)
- [`vercel dev` reference](/docs/cli/dev)

title: "Managing Schedules"
description: "View, enable, disable, and run schedules across environments, and check their execution history from the dashboard, CLI, or SDK."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.064Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/schedules/manage"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Managing Schedules

You can manage static and dynamic schedules from the dashboard, the [`vercel schedules`](/docs/cli/schedules) CLI, or the [`@vercel/schedules`](/docs/schedules/sdk) SDK. None of these actions require a redeploy.

| Action | Static schedules | Dynamic schedules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| View, enable, disable, and run | Dashboard, CLI, or SDK | Dashboard, CLI, or SDK |
| Update | Edit your configuration and redeploy | CLI or SDK |
| Delete | Remove it from your configuration and redeploy | CLI or SDK |

## View your schedules

1. Open your project in the Vercel dashboard and select **Schedules**.
2. Use the **Environment** filter to choose production or a custom environment. For a Preview branch, select **Preview** and then the branch.
3. Optionally, filter by status, source (static or dynamic), or namespace.

To see schedules across every project on your team, open your team's **Schedules** page.

From the CLI, list schedules in production:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel schedules list
vercel schedules inspect cleanup
```

Every `vercel schedules` command uses production by default. To manage another environment, see [Manage schedules across environments](#manage-schedules-across-environments).

From your code, call `Schedules.list()` or `Schedules.get()`. See the [JS SDK Reference](/docs/schedules/sdk#list-schedules).

## Run a schedule now

Run a schedule immediately to test it. A manual run doesn't change the schedule's state or cadence, and it works on inactive schedules.

- **Dashboard**: Select the schedule and click **Run Schedule**.
- **CLI**: Run `vercel schedules invoke cleanup`.
- **SDK**: Call `Schedules.invoke({ name: 'cleanup' })`.

Your target receives the run the same way as a scheduled one.

## Enable and disable a schedule

Disable a schedule to stop it from running on its cadence without losing its configuration. Enable it to resume.

New static schedules in Preview branches start inactive. New static schedules in custom environments start inactive unless you [change the environment's default](#run-static-schedules-in-a-custom-environment). See [Manage schedules across environments](#manage-schedules-across-environments).

**Dashboard:**

1. Select the schedule.
2. Open the menu next to **Run Schedule**.
3. Select **Disable** or **Enable**.

**CLI:**

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel schedules disable cleanup
vercel schedules enable cleanup
```

**SDK:**

```ts
import { Schedules } from '@vercel/schedules';

await Schedules.disable({ name: 'cleanup' });
await Schedules.enable({ name: 'cleanup' });
```

A static schedule keeps the state you set across later deployments.

### Enable a schedule temporarily

You can enable a schedule until a set time. When the time passes, the schedule becomes inactive again. This is useful for testing a Preview schedule without leaving it on.

- **Dashboard**: Open the menu next to **Run Schedule** and select **Enable for 1 Hour**, **Enable for 6 Hours**, or **Enable for 24 Hours**.
- **CLI**: Run `vercel schedules enable cleanup --for 2h`, or pass `--until` with an ISO 8601 time.
- **SDK**: Pass `until` to `Schedules.enable()`:

  ```ts
  await Schedules.enable({
    name: 'cleanup',
    until: new Date(Date.now() + 2 * 60 * 60 * 1000),
  });
  ```

While the window is open, the schedule has an `activeUntil` timestamp. Enabling it again with a new end time replaces the old one. Enabling it without an end time keeps it active indefinitely.

You can't add an end time to a schedule that's already active indefinitely. Disable it first, then enable it with an end time.

## Manage schedules across environments

Vercel keeps a [separate set of schedules](/docs/schedules/concepts#environments) for production, each custom environment, each Preview branch, and CLI deployments by each user. Changing a schedule in one environment doesn't affect the others, so you can test a schedule on a branch without touching production.

### Choose an environment

Each tool picks the environment differently:

| Tool | How to choose |
| --- | --- |
| Dashboard | On the project's **Schedules** page, use the **Environment** filter. For a Preview branch, select **Preview** and then the branch. |
| CLI | Pass `--environment <name-or-id>` for a custom environment, `--git-branch <branch>` for a Preview branch, or `--user <user-id>` for CLI deployments by a user. Combine `--user` and `--git-branch` for CLI deployments associated with a branch. Without these options, commands use production. |
| SDK | Calls apply to the environment of the deployment that runs your code. You can't choose a different one. |

The CLI options work with every `vercel schedules` command, including `executions list`:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel schedules list --git-branch feature-x
vercel schedules executions list cleanup --environment staging
vercel schedules list --user user_123 --git-branch feature-x
```

You can't combine `--environment` with `--git-branch` or `--user`. You can't use any of these options with `--local`. See [Choose an environment](/docs/cli/schedules#choose-an-environment) in the CLI reference.

### Permissions

Team members with the [Developer](/docs/rbac/access-roles#developer-role) or [Project Developer](/docs/rbac/access-roles#project-developer) role can create, change, run, and delete schedules in Preview branches and custom environments. In production, they can only view schedules. Owners, Members, and Project Administrators can manage schedules in every environment.

### Test a static schedule on a Preview branch

New static schedules in Preview branches start inactive, so a branch can't run a production job by accident. To test a schedule on a branch:

1. Push the branch with the schedule in `vercel.json`. Vercel adds the schedule to the branch when the deployment is ready.
2. Open the **Schedules** page, select **Preview**, and select the branch.
3. Select the schedule and click **Run Schedule** to run it once. You don't need to enable it first.
4. To test it on its cadence, open the menu next to **Run Schedule** and select **Enable for 1 Hour**. It turns off again on its own.

From the CLI:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel schedules invoke cleanup --git-branch feature-x
vercel schedules enable cleanup --git-branch feature-x --for 1h
```

Runs go to the branch's current deployment, so later pushes to the branch pick up your handler changes.

### Run static schedules in a custom environment

In a custom environment such as `staging`, new static schedules start inactive by default. Enable each one once. It stays enabled across later deployments to that environment:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel schedules enable cleanup --environment staging
```

To make new static schedules in a custom environment start active instead:

1. In your project's **Settings**, open **Environments** and select the custom environment.
2. In the **Schedules** section, turn on **Create New Schedules as Active**.
3. Click **Save**.

The setting applies only to static schedules that Vercel creates after you save it. Schedules that already exist in the environment keep their current state, so turning the setting on doesn't enable a schedule you disabled, and turning it off doesn't disable any schedules.

### Dynamic schedules outside production

When code in a Preview or custom environment deployment calls `@vercel/schedules`, it creates and changes schedules for that branch or environment, not production. Dynamic schedules are active as soon as you create them, in every environment.

To inspect or clean up those schedules, pass the same `--git-branch` or `--environment` option to the CLI:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel schedules list --git-branch feature-x --namespace tenant_abc123
vercel schedules delete daily-digest --git-branch feature-x --namespace tenant_abc123
```

## Check execution history

Select a schedule in the dashboard to see its next run and its execution history. On the schedule page, you can:

- View the run count, error rate, and average duration
- Search for a run by execution ID
- Filter scheduled and manual runs
- Filter successful and failed runs

Vercel keeps execution history for 90 days. Outcomes, error rates, and durations come from recorded function requests. For queue targets, they reflect the consumer that processed the message. Runs without a recorded outcome aren't included in the metrics.

From the CLI, list a schedule's recent runs:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel schedules executions list cleanup --since 7d
```

See [`vercel schedules executions list`](/docs/cli/schedules#list-execution-history) for all options.

## Update a schedule

To change a **static** schedule, edit it in `vercel.json` and redeploy. Vercel applies the change when the deployment becomes current.

To change a **dynamic** schedule, call `Schedules.update()` or run `vercel schedules update`. Properties you leave out keep their current values:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel schedules update cleanup --cron "0 3 * * *"
```

See [Update a dynamic schedule](/docs/schedules/sdk#update-a-schedule) for the full set of options.

## Delete a schedule

To delete a **static** schedule, remove it from `vercel.json` and redeploy.

To delete a **dynamic** schedule, call `Schedules.delete()` or run `vercel schedules delete`:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel schedules delete cleanup
```

When you delete a schedule:

- Its future runs stop. If a run is already waiting to be delivered, Vercel skips it. A run that Vercel has already delivered keeps running.
- It no longer appears in the dashboard, CLI, or SDK, and it stops counting toward your [team's schedule limit](/docs/schedules/limits#schedules-per-team).
- You can create a new schedule with the same name right away. The new schedule gets a new ID and starts with no execution history.

You can delete a one-time schedule before it runs or after its run has been dispatched. While the run is still being dispatched, deleting it fails with `schedule_single_at_passed`. Try again a few minutes later. If you don't delete it, Vercel removes it about 30 days after its scheduled time.

### When Vercel deletes schedules

Vercel also deletes schedules in these cases:

| Event | What Vercel deletes |
| --- | --- |
| You remove a static schedule from your configuration | That schedule, when the new deployment becomes the current deployment of its environment or branch |
| A Preview branch no longer has a current deployment | Every static and dynamic schedule for that branch |
| Production or a custom environment no longer has a current deployment | Static schedules only. Dynamic schedules are kept. |
| You delete the project | Every schedule in the project |
| The team moves to Hobby, or you transfer the project to a Hobby team | Schedules that exceed the [Hobby limits](/docs/schedules/limits#what-happens-to-schedules-when-you-move-to-hobby) |

When a project is paused, Vercel skips its scheduled runs but doesn't delete any schedules.

## Related

- [`vercel schedules` reference](/docs/cli/schedules)
- [JS SDK Reference](/docs/schedules/sdk)
- [Concepts](/docs/schedules/concepts)

title: "Migrating from Cron Jobs to Schedules"
description: "Move Cron Jobs in vercel.json to Schedules without changing your route code, then optionally make the route private."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.064Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/schedules/migrate-from-cron-jobs"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Migrating from Cron Jobs to Schedules

[Cron Jobs](/docs/cron-jobs) are a legacy feature and will be migrated to Schedules in the future. You can migrate now with a configuration change. Your route code keeps working as it is.

After you migrate, you can:

- Set a timezone for each schedule instead of using UTC
- Enable, disable, or run each schedule without redeploying
- Run schedules in Preview branches and custom environments
- See the execution history of each schedule
- Switch to a private function or a queue topic later

## What stays the same

A schedule with a `path` target calls your route the same way a Cron Job does:

- The `user-agent` header is `vercel-cron/1.0`.
- The `x-vercel-cron-schedule` header contains the cron expression.
- If you set `CRON_SECRET`, the `Authorization` header contains `Bearer <CRON_SECRET>`, so your [`CRON_SECRET` check](/docs/cron-jobs/manage-cron-jobs#securing-cron-jobs) keeps working.

Path schedules send a `POST` request by default, but Cron Jobs send `GET`. Set `requestMethod` to `GET` when you migrate so your route handler doesn't need to change.

Schedule requests also include [schedule headers](/docs/schedules/handle-runs#request-headers), such as the execution ID and scheduled time.

## Migrate your Cron Jobs

- ### Find your Cron Jobs
  Cron Jobs live in the `crons` property of `vercel.json`:
  ```json filename="vercel.json"
  {
    "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
    "crons": [
      { "path": "/api/daily-report", "schedule": "0 9 * * *" },
      { "path": "/api/cleanup", "schedule": "0 * * * *" }
    ]
  }
  ```
  You can also see them on the **Cron Jobs** tab of your project's **Schedules** page in the dashboard.

- ### Replace `crons` with `schedules`
  For each Cron Job, add an entry to `schedules`. Use a [name](/docs/schedules/configuration#schedule-names) as the key, keep the same `path` and `schedule`, and add `"requestMethod": "GET"`:
  ```json filename="vercel.json"
  {
    "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
    "schedules": {
      "daily-report": {
        "schedule": "0 9 * * *",
        "path": "/api/daily-report",
        "requestMethod": "GET"
      },
      "cleanup": {
        "schedule": "0 * * * *",
        "path": "/api/cleanup",
        "requestMethod": "GET"
      }
    }
  }
  ```
  Remove the `crons` entries in the same change. If you keep both, your route runs twice for each occurrence.
  > **💡 Note:** Cron Jobs always run in UTC, and schedules default to UTC. Leave out
  > `timezone` to keep the same run times. If you add a `timezone`, update the
  > cron expression so the schedule still runs when you expect.

- ### Deploy to production
  Deploy your project:
  ```bash filename="terminal"
  vercel deploy --prod
  ```
  Vercel creates the schedules when the deployment becomes your production deployment, and stops running the Cron Jobs you removed.

- ### Verify the schedules
  1. Open your project in the Vercel dashboard and select **Schedules**.
  2. Check that your schedules appear in the list.
  3. Select a schedule and click **Run Schedule** to test it without waiting for its next run.
  You can also run a schedule from the CLI:
  ```bash filename="terminal"
  vercel schedules invoke daily-report
  ```

## Timing differences

Schedules start within a [jitter window](/docs/schedules/concepts#jitter) instead of at an exact time. The limits also differ by plan:

| Plan | Cron Jobs | Schedules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Hobby** | At most once per day, at any time within the scheduled hour | At most once every 15 minutes, within a 15-minute jitter window |
| **Pro and Enterprise** | At the scheduled minute | Within the jitter window, which defaults to 1 minute and can be set from 1 to 15 minutes |

On Pro and Enterprise, add `jitter` to change the window:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "schedules": {
    "cleanup": {
      "schedule": "0 * * * *",
      "path": "/api/cleanup",
      "requestMethod": "GET",
      "jitter": 5
    }
  }
}
```

## Pausing a schedule

**Disable Cron Jobs** on the **Cron Jobs** tab of the **Schedules** page only pauses Cron Jobs. It doesn't affect schedules. To pause a schedule, select it and choose **Disable** from the menu next to **Run Schedule**, or run:

```bash filename="terminal"
vercel schedules disable cleanup
```

Disabling a static schedule doesn't require a redeploy. See [Managing schedules](/docs/schedules/manage#enable-and-disable-a-schedule).

## Making the route private

A Cron Job path is a public URL, so anyone can call it unless you check `CRON_SECRET`. After you migrate, you can switch to a function target. Function targets have no public URL, and only Vercel's scheduler can invoke them.

1. Install `@vercel/schedules` and wrap your handler in `handleSchedule`.
2. Add a `schedule/v1beta` trigger to the function.
3. Replace `path` and `requestMethod` with `function`.

See [Function targets](/docs/schedules/handle-runs#function-targets) for the full steps. Keep the same schedule name so Vercel updates the existing schedule instead of creating a new one.

## Next steps

- [Concepts](/docs/schedules/concepts): Learn how environments, late runs, and retries work.
- [Handling scheduled runs](/docs/schedules/handle-runs): Make your handler safe to run more than once.
- [`vercel schedules`](/docs/cli/schedules): Manage schedules from the terminal.

title: "Creating Schedules for Each Customer"
description: "Use schedule namespaces to give each customer in a multi-tenant app their own recurring and one-time schedules."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.068Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/schedules/multi-tenant"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Creating Schedules for Each Customer

In a multi-tenant app, each customer (tenant) often needs their own schedules, like a daily digest at a time they choose. Use one **namespace** per tenant to keep their schedules separate.

Schedule names are unique within a namespace, so every tenant can have a schedule named `daily-digest`. Use the name for the kind of job and the namespace for the tenant. One queue consumer can then handle every tenant.

Namespaces are only available for [dynamic schedules](/docs/schedules#static-and-dynamic-schedules). Static schedules always use the `default` namespace.

## Choose a namespace for each tenant

Namespaces follow the same rules as [schedule names](/docs/schedules/configuration#schedule-names): 1 to 256 ASCII letters, digits, `.`, `_`, and `-`, starting with a letter or digit.

If your tenant IDs already match these rules, such as `tenant_abc123`, use them directly. Otherwise, map each ID to a valid string, for example by replacing other characters with `-`. Make sure the mapping can't give two tenants the same namespace.

## Create a schedule for a tenant

When a tenant turns on a recurring job, create a dynamic schedule in their namespace. Store any settings the job needs in the payload:

```ts filename="lib/digest.ts"
import { Schedules } from '@vercel/schedules';

export async function enableDigest(tenantId: string, timezone: string) {
  await Schedules.create({
    name: 'daily-digest',
    namespace: tenantId,
    target: { topic: 'tenant-jobs' },
    expression: { type: 'cron', cron: '0 9 * * *' },
    timezone,
    payload: { reportType: 'summary' },
  });
}
```

All tenants can share the `tenant-jobs` topic. Each message includes the namespace, so your consumer knows which tenant the run is for.

For a one-time job, such as a trial expiring, use a `single` expression:

```ts
await Schedules.create({
  name: 'trial-ending',
  namespace: tenantId,
  target: { topic: 'tenant-jobs' },
  expression: { type: 'single', at: '2026-11-15T09:00' },
  timezone: 'America/New_York',
});
```

## Handle tenant runs

Create one consumer on the shared topic. Read the tenant from `message.namespace` and the job from `message.name`:

```ts filename="api/tenant-jobs.ts"
import { handleCallback } from '@vercel/queue';
import type { ScheduleQueueMessage } from '@vercel/schedules';

type TenantJobMessage = ScheduleQueueMessage<{ reportType?: string }>;

export const POST = handleCallback<TenantJobMessage>(async (message) => {
  const tenantId = message.namespace;

  switch (message.name) {
    case 'daily-digest':
      await sendDigest(tenantId, message.payload?.reportType ?? 'summary');
      break;
    case 'trial-ending':
      await sendTrialReminder(tenantId);
      break;
  }
});
```

Subscribe the consumer to the topic in `vercel.json`:

```json filename="vercel.json"
{
  "functions": {
    "api/tenant-jobs.ts": {
      "experimentalTriggers": [{ "type": "queue/v2beta", "topic": "tenant-jobs" }]
    }
  }
}
```

## Manage a tenant's schedules

Pass the tenant's namespace to every SDK method:

```ts
import { Schedules } from '@vercel/schedules';

const { data } = await Schedules.list({ namespace: tenantId });

await Schedules.update({
  name: 'daily-digest',
  namespace: tenantId,
  timezone: 'America/Los_Angeles',
});

await Schedules.invoke({ name: 'daily-digest', namespace: tenantId });
```

## Delete a tenant's schedules

When you remove a tenant, delete all of their schedules so they stop running and no longer count toward your [team's schedule limit](/docs/schedules/limits#schedules-per-team):

```ts filename="lib/tenants.ts"
import { Schedules, SchedulesApiError } from '@vercel/schedules';

export async function deleteTenantSchedules(tenantId: string) {
  const names: string[] = [];
  let cursor: string | undefined;

  do {
    const page = await Schedules.list({ namespace: tenantId, cursor });
    names.push(...page.data.map((schedule) => schedule.name));
    cursor = page.cursor ?? undefined;
  } while (cursor);

  for (const name of names) {
    try {
      await Schedules.delete({ name, namespace: tenantId });
    } catch (error) {
      // A one-time schedule can't be deleted while its run is being dispatched.
      // Vercel removes it about 30 days after its scheduled time.
      if (
        error instanceof SchedulesApiError &&
        error.code === 'schedule_single_at_passed'
      ) {
        continue;
      }
      throw error;
    }
  }
}
```

A one-time schedule can't be deleted while its run is being dispatched, which can take a few minutes after its scheduled time.

- [Handling scheduled runs](/docs/schedules/handle-runs#queue-targets)
- [Limits](/docs/schedules/limits)

title: "Schedules"
description: "Run code on a recurring cron schedule or once at a specific time, and create schedules at runtime for each of your users."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.068Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/schedules"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Schedules

With Vercel Schedules, you can run code on a recurring [cron](/docs/schedules/configuration#cron-expressions) cadence or once at a specific time. A schedule can call a route, run a private function, or send a message to a [Vercel Queue](/docs/queues). You can also create schedules at runtime, so each of your users can get their own reminder, report, or cleanup job.

Schedules replace [Cron Jobs](/docs/cron-jobs). They add timezones, private targets, one-time runs, execution history, and a way to pause or run a schedule without redeploying.

## Use cases

Schedules are useful when you need to:

- **Run recurring maintenance**: Delete expired records, rotate data, or refresh caches every hour or every night.
- **Send reports and digests**: Email a daily summary at 09:00 in each customer's timezone.
- **Run a task once, later**: Send a reminder, expire a trial, or publish a post at a specific date and time.
- **Let users choose when work runs**: Create, update, and delete schedules from your app as users change their settings.

## Static and dynamic schedules

You can define a schedule in two ways:

- **Static schedules** live in your project configuration, such as `vercel.json`. Vercel applies them when you deploy, so they change with your code.
- **Dynamic schedules** are created at runtime with the [`@vercel/schedules`](/docs/schedules/sdk) SDK or the [`vercel schedules`](/docs/cli/schedules) CLI. They take effect immediately and don't require a deployment.

Use static schedules for jobs that belong to your app, like a nightly cleanup. Use dynamic schedules for jobs your app creates on behalf of users, like a reminder for each customer.

| | Static | Dynamic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Defined in** | `vercel.json` or Build Output API `config.json` | `@vercel/schedules` SDK or `vercel schedules` CLI |
| **Takes effect** | When you deploy | Immediately |
| **Targets** | Path, function, or queue topic | Queue topic only |
| **Recurring (cron)** | Supported | Supported |
| **One-time** | Not supported | Supported |
| **Payload** | Not supported | Optional JSON payload |
| **Namespace** | Always `default` | Any namespace you choose |
| **Update or delete** | Edit your configuration and redeploy | SDK or CLI |
| **Enable, disable, or run now** | Dashboard, SDK, or CLI | Dashboard, SDK, or CLI |

## Targets

Each schedule has one target. When the schedule fires, Vercel delivers the run to that target:

| Target | What happens | Available for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Function** | Vercel invokes a private Vercel Function that has no public URL. | Static schedules |
| **Path** | Vercel sends an HTTP request to a path on your deployment, like a Cron Job. | Static schedules |
| **Queue topic** | Vercel publishes a message to a [Vercel Queues](/docs/queues) topic. A consumer on that topic processes it, with retries. | Static and dynamic schedules |

To choose a target and write the code that runs, see [Handling scheduled runs](/docs/schedules/handle-runs).

## Schedules and Cron Jobs

If you use Cron Jobs today, you can [migrate to Schedules](/docs/schedules/migrate-from-cron-jobs) without changing your route code:

| | Cron Jobs | Schedules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Targets** | HTTP `GET` to a public path | HTTP `GET` or `POST` to a path, a private function, or a queue topic |
| **Timezone** | UTC only | Any IANA timezone, per schedule |
| **One-time runs** | Not supported | Supported with dynamic schedules |
| **Create at runtime** | Not supported | Supported with dynamic schedules |
| **Payload** | Not supported | Optional JSON payload with dynamic schedules |
| **Pause or run without redeploying** | Pause all Cron Jobs in the project | Enable, disable, or run each schedule |
| **Preview and custom environments** | Production only | Production, Preview branches, and custom environments |
| **Execution history** | Function logs only | Per schedule, in the dashboard and CLI |
| **Timing** | Pro and Enterprise: the scheduled minute. Hobby: once per day, any time within the scheduled hour. | Within a [jitter window](/docs/schedules/concepts#jitter) of 1 to 15 minutes. Hobby can run every 15 minutes. |

> **💡 Note:** Schedules are in beta. Behavior, APIs, and limits may change before general
> availability.

## Use Schedules with a coding agent

If you use a coding agent, install the `vercel-schedules` [agent skill](/docs/agent-resources/skills). It helps your agent choose between static and dynamic schedules, pick a target, write handlers, and migrate from Cron Jobs:

```bash filename="terminal"
npx skills add vercel/vercel-plugin --skill vercel-schedules
```

The skill is also included in the [Vercel Plugin](/docs/agent-resources/vercel-plugin).

## Resources

**Getting started**: Run a private function every hour with a static schedule. [Learn more →](/docs/schedules/quickstart)

**Concepts**: Learn how environments, jitter, late runs, and delivery work. [Learn more →](/docs/schedules/concepts)

**Handling scheduled runs**: Write the function, route, or queue consumer that a schedule runs. [Learn more →](/docs/schedules/handle-runs)

**Managing schedules**: Enable, disable, run, and monitor schedules. [Learn more →](/docs/schedules/manage)

**Multi-tenant schedules**: Give each customer their own schedules with namespaces. [Learn more →](/docs/schedules/multi-tenant)

**Configuration reference**: Look up every static schedule property and cron syntax. [Learn more →](/docs/schedules/configuration)

**JS SDK Reference**: Create and manage dynamic schedules with @vercel/schedules. [Learn more →](/docs/schedules/sdk)

**API Reference**: Call the Schedules API directly from any language. [Learn more →](/docs/schedules/http-api)

**CLI reference**: Manage schedules from the terminal with vercel schedules. [Learn more →](/docs/cli/schedules)

**Limits**: Check schedule counts, frequency, and jitter limits by plan. [Learn more →](/docs/schedules/limits)

title: "Getting Started with Schedules"
description: "Run a private Vercel Function every hour with a static schedule in vercel.json, test it locally, and deploy it."
last_updated: "2026-11-05T17:25:46.068Z"
source: "https://vercel.com/docs/schedules/quickstart"
